provisions.evidence: Which validators check aggregate state instead of structural input only? Look at each validator body.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST limit its checks to structural input, leaving aggregate state decisions to Domain.
provisions.rationale: Structural input and aggregate state fail for different reasons and at different times: malformed input is rejected before Domain runs, while a state refusal needs the loaded aggregate. A validator that checked state would need the aggregate, which pulls persistence into validation. A validator rejects an empty title, a malformed identifier, or an invalid page size, and Domain decides whether the expense above the threshold carries a receipt. Every validator for a message reports validity findings under `litespec/backend/application#report-input-problems-as-validity-findings`, so the caller learns the whole form in one answer.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` takes a command carrying an expense identifier and an employee identifier with the amount, currency, and receipt. The validator rejects an empty expense identifier or an empty employee identifier, and accepts every well-formed pair.

Whether the expense above the threshold carries a receipt is an aggregate state decision, so the validator leaves it to Domain. Domain rejects an expense above the threshold that carries no receipt with `result/submit-expense.receipt-missing`, which carries the stable code `spending.receipt-missing`.

provisions.heading: Shape Query Results from Declared Output
provisions.evidence: Which query result types miss a declared `include` group, field, freshness, or visibility? Look at each result type beside its record's `output`.
provisions.statement: A query result type MUST carry the `include` groups its record's `output` declares, with their fields, freshness, and visibility.
provisions.rationale: The record's `output` names each group with its fields, their classification, the aggregates it reads, and the freshness the caller can rely on: `immediate`, `snapshot`, `bounded`, or `advisory`. The result type carries one member per group, so the caller reads what the record promises and nothing more. A group with `visibleWhen` appears only when its condition holds, and a group wider than its `reads` names the approved requirement widening it in `cites`. A query with `builtAsynchronously` carries a `bounded` or `advisory` freshness with its lag scenario.
provisions.example: The expense-list result carries its `rows` group with the declared fields, freshness, and visibility.

provisions.heading: Take One Timestamp per Message
provisions.evidence: Which handlers read time outside the scoped clock stamped once per message? Look at the clock reads in each handler.
provisions.statement: Each handler MUST read the message timestamp from the scoped clock the pipeline stamps once per message.
provisions.rationale: A handler that reads the clock two or three times in one decision records different times for one act, sometimes around an outside call. One timestamp per message fixes the moment the message starts, and every decision in the handling answers to the same time. The shared clock stays for infrastructure only.
provisions.example: The approve handler stamps its approval with the handled clock, not with a fresh clock read.

provisions.heading: Take Repositories from Declared Changes and Reads
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` (level S) for a handler that takes a repository whose aggregate sits outside the aggregates its record names in `changes` and `reads`; one domain repository serves each named aggregate.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST write only the aggregates its record's `changes` names, through one domain repository per aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A write outside `changes` is behavior the record hides, so the stack reader fails `write-undeclared` on it. Under `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage` the handler normally takes one domain repository for the one aggregate it changes and stages only that aggregate. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates takes one repository per named aggregate and stages each one. A query handler likewise projects only over the aggregates its record's `reads` names, through the read session.
provisions.example: The `approve-expense` handler takes the expense repository and no other; staging a second aggregate fails the check unless the record declares `consistency: atomic` over both.

provisions.heading: Use This Use-Case Layout
provisions.evidence: Which use-case paths, event handler folders, or result part names break the layout? Look at each path under the modules.
provisions.statement: Place each use case in a folder named for it inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate, with the use case files flat inside and shared types in the node layer folders.
provisions.rationale: One folder per use case inside its `UseCases/` folder holds everything a reviewer needs to judge it in one place, and the module tree lets a reader move from a handler to its endpoint without a map. A use case file's layer comes from its role suffix, so Application files sit beside the endpoint and transport models in the one folder.
provisions.example:
The layout reads as follows:

```text
{Product}/
  Application/                            product layer folder: pipeline positions and pipeline stages, and nothing else
  Posts/                                  single aggregate whose name matches the module: use cases sit in the module UseCases folder
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/  Exceptions/  IntegrationEvents/  Commands/  Ports/
    Application/                          a port several Posts use cases name sits here
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/                        one folder per use case, flat: Command, Query, Result, Handler, Validator,
                                          Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel, mapping
      GetPost/
      ListPosts/
        ListPostsQueryResultItem          a result part named after its result
      OnPostPublished/                    one folder per fact, holding every handler of that fact
        NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler   one event handler class with its mark
    Jobs/
  Customers/                              two aggregates: use cases nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/  Exceptions/  IntegrationEvents/  Commands/  Ports/
    CustomerAccounts/
      Application/                        aggregate-owned types sit in the aggregate layer folder
      UseCases/
        RestrictAccount/
    Consents/
      UseCases/
        GrantConsent/
    UseCases/                             use cases no single aggregate owns, with one On{Fact} folder per reaction
    Jobs/
```

Module, aggregate, and use case order, including the single-aggregate flat form, follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

Only a use case or an event handler folder gets a folder below its `UseCases/` folder. Any other type sits in the node layer folder that owns it, chosen by `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`, so every folder name below a `UseCases/` folder names one use case or one fact. An event handler lives in the `On{Fact}` folder for the fact it handles inside the module `UseCases/` folder, named under `litespec/workspace/naming#group-event-handlers-by-the-fact-they-handle`, with its mark under `litespec/backend/application#keep-reaction-implementations-explicit`. A folder named for a service, a technical kind, or a caller breaks that reading; it is drift rather than a second convention.

provisions.heading: Validate Query Input
provisions.evidence: Which queries with paging, filters, or ranges lack a query validator? Look at each such query beside the pipeline validators.
provisions.statement: Each query carrying paging, filters, or ranges MUST declare a query validator run by the pipeline.
provisions.rationale: An unvalidated page size or range reaches the store unchecked, and each query handler clamps its own input or none does. A query validator runs in the same pipeline step as command validators, so reads and writes answer to the same input rule.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query validates its page size through its query validator.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Process Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Which host entry points build a second provider or skip the Infrastructure entry point? Look at each host entry point.
provisions.statement: A host MUST register its own transport services and call the Infrastructure entry point without building a second provider.
provisions.rationale: Each host registers its own services and calls the shared Infrastructure entry point, so the full composition of a process is visible in one place. A second provider built mid-registration would resolve a different object graph than the host runs. WebApi and Worker are the only composition roots: Domain contains no registration code, and Application exposes contracts without resolving services.

provisions.heading: Create a Worker Project When Background Work Needs Its Own Process
provisions.evidence: Which background work needing its own process runs outside a Worker project? Look at the execution-host decision beside the solution project list.
provisions.statement: An application MUST create a Worker project when background work needs independent scaling, independent deployment, or isolation from request-path resource limits.
provisions.rationale: A shared process couples scaling, deployment, and resource limits: a restart to deploy an endpoint change interrupts a dispatch loop, and request load and dispatch load compete for one thread pool where neither scales alone. When background work needs independent scaling, deployment, or isolation, it gets its own process. A product with one deployable unit and modest background load accepts that coupling deliberately, which is why the choice is declared rather than assumed.
provisions.example: An application with an outbox dispatching a few messages each minute can run it in WebApi. An application dispatching continuously, or one whose dispatch needs to survive an endpoint deployment, creates the Worker project.

provisions.heading: Declare the Execution Host for Work That Outlives a Request
provisions.evidence: Which execution host runs durable dispatch, queue consumption, or scheduled work without a naming decision? Look for the decision record under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`.
provisions.statement: An application MUST declare the execution host that runs its durable dispatch, queue consumption, and scheduled work.
provisions.rationale: The declared host is either the WebApi process or a Worker project. A rule that only restricts when a Worker exists leaves unsaid where the work runs without one, so a project can host background services inside WebApi while breaking no named rule and recording no decision. Naming the host makes the choice visible whichever way it goes. The declaration lives in a Decision record following `litespec/core/model#record-each-technical-choice-as-a-decision`. Durable dispatch and queue consumption follow the outbox extension, and scheduled work follows the jobs extension. The host is a composition decision, not a code-placement decision. The hosted operations live in Worker or Infrastructure, because they hold provider and scheduling concerns: in Worker when the project exists, otherwise in Infrastructure. The host registers them.
provisions.example: A Decision naming WebApi as the execution host states that durable dispatch shares the request process, and states what an unavailable process costs.

provisions.heading: Keep Business Invariants in Domain
provisions.evidence: Which state transitions or invariants run outside their aggregate or value object, or repeat in a handler? Look at the handlers beside the aggregates they call.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, command-handler, job, query-handler, reaction, value-object
provisions.statement: An aggregate or value object MUST be the only place that enforces a state transition or invariant.
provisions.rationale: The aggregate or value object that owns data is the only code that sees every change to it. A rule duplicated in a handler drifts from the aggregate that owns it, and then the same action is allowed through one path and refused through another.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementation Types Hidden
provisions.evidence: Which handlers, validators, definitions, persistence implementations, or endpoint implementations escape their own layer or stay open to extension? Look at the implementations in each layer.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, endpoint, query-handler, reaction, repository, validator
provisions.statement: An application MUST keep each handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, and endpoint implementation inside its own layer and closed to extension.
provisions.rationale: Hidden implementations keep each layer's surface to the contracts other layers actually use. A public handler invites direct construction that bypasses the pipeline, and an inheritable one invites overrides that split behavior across subclasses. Messages, results, and ports stay public only when another layer uses them, and automatic discovery is not a reason to widen visibility.

provisions.heading: Keep Service Registration in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Which service registration calls sit outside host entry points and host registration modules? Look at the registration calls in each layer.
provisions.statement: Keep service registration in host entry points and host registration modules.
provisions.rationale: Registration lives where the process is composed, so hosts and their registration modules hold every registration call. Domain and Application declare abstractions, so a registration call inside either inverts the dependency direction.
provisions.example:
One registration entry point per outer layer keeps the call order visible.

```text
infrastructure: register providers and options
webapi: register transport, authentication, and documentation
```

The Infrastructure entry point receives configuration and host environment values needed to bind and validate provider options. The WebApi entry point owns error details, authentication, authorization, endpoint discovery, and API documentation.

provisions.heading: Organize Code by Module, Aggregate and Use Case
provisions.evidence: Which module, aggregate, or use case folders resolve to no declared record, use a folder name their level forbids, or carry a technical-grouping name? Look at the folder paths in each module.
provisions.statement: Every module MUST organize its code as the module tree with one folder per declared aggregate, one `UseCases/` folder per aggregate and module, one folder per declared use case inside its `UseCases/` folder, and one `On{Fact}/` folder per reaction inside the module `UseCases/` folder, using only the folder names its level allows.
provisions.rationale: One folder per declared aggregate and one folder per declared use case inside its `UseCases/` folder let a reader move from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint without a map. The closed folder names at each level keep that reading exact: a folder outside the allowed set is refused, so no second organization grows beside the tree. A module publishes what other modules may name in its `Contracts/` folder sorted by kind, use cases no single aggregate owns sit in the module `UseCases/` folder, and each reaction sits in one `On{Fact}/` folder beside them. An aggregate stays flat only when its plural name equals the single module name. A folder named for a technical grouping rather than a module defeats the rule, because the next unrelated type fits it. `Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, and `Misc` inside a layer are the names that do this.
provisions.example:
```text
# single-aggregate module whose aggregate name matches the module: the aggregate stays flat
Organizations/
  Contracts/
    Identifiers/  Exceptions/  IntegrationEvents/  Commands/  Ports/
  Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
  UseCases/
    CreateOrganization/      use case, flat: Command, Result, Handler, Validator, Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel

# multi-aggregate module: module, then aggregate folder, then UseCases, then use case
Spending/
  Contracts/
    Identifiers/  Exceptions/  IntegrationEvents/  Commands/  Ports/
  Expenses/
    Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
    UseCases/
      SubmitExpense/
      ApproveExpense/
  Policies/
    Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
    UseCases/
      DefinePolicy/

# module-level work beside the aggregates
Spending/
  UseCases/
    ReadExpenseDirectory/     a use case no single aggregate owns
    OnExpenseReimbursed/      a reaction
  Jobs/
```

The placement check asserts the folder names directly, because a rule only a reviewer checks stops holding at the first missed file.

```text
fail when a type path contains Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc
```

provisions.heading: Own Each Layer's Contract Types
provisions.evidence: Which outward contracts reuse an inner layer's type outside shared-kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers? Look at the contracts in each layer's folders.
provisions.statement: A layer MUST define its own outward contracts rather than reuse an inner layer's type, except for shared-kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers.
provisions.rationale: When each layer defines its own outward contracts, a change to an inner shape stops at the boundary instead of rippling through every outer layer. Shared-kernel values cross because the kernel is shared by definition, and aggregate typed identifiers cross because messages need to name their targets.

provisions.heading: Place a Type at the Lowest Folder That Holds Its Consumers
provisions.evidence: Which types sit above the lowest folder holding every consumer that names them? Look at each type beside its consumers, watching for Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc folders.
provisions.statement: A type MUST live at the lowest folder containing every consumer that names it.
provisions.rationale: Counting consumers gives each type exactly one folder, so placement needs no judgment call. The lowest folder is the use case folder when one use case names the type, the aggregate layer folder when several use cases of one aggregate name it, the module layer folder when several aggregates of one module name it, and the product layer folder when several modules name it with no module between them. A type another module names is published by its owning module in `Contracts/`; across modules a type is never shared. A use case file's layer comes from its role suffix, and a type only Infrastructure names is an Infrastructure type. Two kinds of type travel with something else rather than by their own consumer count. A type that exists only to shape one contract's input or output stays with that contract, and a closed enumerated set stays whole. The rule is mechanical, so placement is counted rather than judged. The product layer folders hold what remains after the count rather than a destination anyone chooses. A folder named for the absence of a reason (`Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, `Misc`) can refuse nothing. Such a folder accumulates until a tenth of the layer sits outside the module tree, unreviewed, and named for no aggregate. Domain's shared kernel is the one product `Domain/` folder a solution keeps. Its membership is closed by `litespec/backend/architecture#own-each-layers-contract-types` rather than open to whatever needs a home. A service that coordinates several aggregates lives in the module that owns the aggregates it reads and writes, not with whichever module calls it first.

provisions.heading: Point Dependencies Inward
provisions.evidence: Which references point outward, away from Domain? Look at the reference graph in the code.
provisions.statement: A reference MUST point inward, so Domain references no outer layer and WebApi composes the process.
provisions.rationale: Inner code names no outer code, so business rules compile and test without adapters or hosting. An outward reference would drag technical concerns into Domain or coordination into Infrastructure. Application coordinates Domain, Infrastructure implements the boundaries both declare, and the reference matrix in [Dependencies](../workspace/dependencies.md) applies exactly.
provisions.example:
Every reference points from an outer layer to an inner one, and Domain references none of the others.

![The four layers and their references: WebApi references Application and WebApi, and from Domain only typed identifiers and shared-kernel values; Infrastructure references Domain, Application, and Infrastructure; Application references Domain and Application; Domain references only Domain.](../assets/diagrams/backend-dependencies.svg)

provisions.heading: Read Another Module Only Through Its Contracts
provisions.evidence: Which cross-module reads bypass the owner's `Contracts/Ports/` read port or load another module's aggregate or repository? Look at the cross-module reads beside the `Contracts/` folders.
provisions.statement: A module needing another module's data MUST read it only through a read port in the owner's `Contracts/Ports/` folder that returns contract results keyed by typed id, or through its own query.
provisions.rationale: A read port in the owner's `Contracts/Ports/` folder keeps the owning module in charge of its data: the port returns contract results keyed by typed id, so the caller names targets without loading them. A module that loaded another module's aggregate or repository would couple its reads to the owner's consistency boundary and storage. Where no shared read fits, the module answers with its own query over data it already holds.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the reporting module reads expense totals through the spending module's read port in `Contracts/Ports/`, which returns contract results keyed by expense id; it loads no spending aggregate and no spending repository.

provisions.heading: Restrict Commands to Their Own Module Aggregates
provisions.evidence: Which commands change an aggregate outside their own module instead of dispatching that module's use case? Look at each command handler beside its module.
provisions.statement: A command MUST change only the aggregates of its own module, so an act on another module's aggregate runs as that module's use case, dispatched or triggered by an integration event.
provisions.rationale: Each module guards its own consistency boundaries, so a command from another module that wrote its aggregates would bypass the owning module's rules. An act on another module's aggregate is that module's use case: the caller dispatches it or triggers it through a published integration event, and the owning module enforces its own invariants.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a command that needs a policy change dispatches the policy module's use case or raises the integration event that triggers it; it writes no policy aggregate itself.

provisions.heading: Separate Command and Query Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which commands mutate outside one aggregate or skip the domain repository, or which queries load an aggregate or write? Look at the command and query handlers in Application.
provisions.statement: A command MUST mutate one aggregate through its domain repository while a query projects read results without loading an aggregate or writing.
provisions.rationale: Reads that load aggregates pay for invariant enforcement no read needs, and writes that read from projections enforce rules against stale shapes. Commands mutate one aggregate through its domain repository, following `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`, with a use case declaring `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates as the declared exception. Queries project read results without loading an aggregate and write nothing, following `litespec/backend/application#keep-query-handlers-free-of-writes`. An enabled persistence extension may replace the read boundary for named aggregate paths, but a command still enforces no invariant from a read projection.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Across Modules Only to Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Which reactions subscribe to another module's domain event instead of its published integration event? Look at each reaction trigger beside the integration events.
provisions.statement: A reaction to another module's fact MUST subscribe only to the published integration event.
provisions.rationale: A domain event stays inside the module that raised it, while the published integration event carries the fact outside. A reaction that subscribed to another module's domain event would couple to the owner's internals and break when they change. The integration event is the stable cross-module fact, so cross-module reactions answer it.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a reaction in the reporting module answers the published expense reimbursed integration event, never the spending domain event behind it.

provisions.heading: Test Structural Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Which structural boundaries have no analyzer or `model check` finding and no architecture test, or which architecture tests repeat a boundary a check covers? Look at the architecture tests beside the analyzer and `model check` runs.
provisions.statement: A structural boundary that no LiteSpec analyzer or `model check` finding covers MUST have an architecture test.
provisions.rationale: Layer references, package boundaries, visibility, module folders, and aggregate inheritance are invisible at runtime: the application runs the same with or without them, so each one needs mechanical proof on every run. The analyzers and `model check` already give that proof for the boundaries that a stack page names as checked and for the rows in the table below. A check over method bodies, for one, reports an outer-layer call inside a method, which a test over compiled signatures misses. An architecture test that repeats a covered boundary holds a second copy of a rule the build or the check already enforces, and the copy drifts while the analyzer or the check keeps reporting the breach. Architecture tests hold the rest: a boundary the checks cover only in part, and a structural decision the project itself made that no LiteSpec tool names. | Structural boundary | Covered by | |:---|:---| | A folder sits outside the closed set its level allows, or a module folder names no declared module | `folder-invalid` and `module-undeclared` from `litespec model check` | | A marked code element, test, or folder sits outside the folder its record names, or a folder names no declared record | `mark-folder-drift` and `code-placement-drift` from `litespec model check` | | A folder or type carries a technical grouping name such as `Shared`, `Common`, or `Helpers` outside the declared shared kernel | `name-reason-missing` from `litespec model check` |
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, no architecture test repeats the checks that report an outer-layer type in Domain, an enum in Domain, a command handler that holds a write session, or a handler that authorizes itself; the stack's checks report each one. The architecture suite keeps a test that no module reaches another module outside its `dependsOn`, and a type in the other module's `Contracts/` folder stays allowed.

provisions.heading: Align ID Representations at Every Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which identifiers read as different values across Domain, persistence, transport, or generated clients? Look at one identifier in each boundary form.
provisions.statement: Represent an identifier the same way in Domain, persistence, transport, and generated clients.
provisions.rationale: One identifier takes a different form at each boundary, and each form is correct in its own place. Alignment means every form still reads as the same value, so a reader tracing one identifier follows it across boundaries without translation.
provisions.example: Domain and Application hold the typed identifier; the [HTTP API](api.md) states the route, query, JSON, and contract forms, and [Persistence](persistence.md) states the stored form. Alignment means a reader recognizes one identifier in every form.

provisions.heading: Call the Marked Act from Each Command Handler
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-act-missing` (level S) for a command handler changing an entity aggregate that calls no root method marked with its use case. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: the handler and the root method sit in different projects, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A command handler changing an entity aggregate MUST change it by calling a root method marked with the handler's use case.
provisions.rationale: The use case names an act, and the aggregate performs it: the mark on the root method says which act the method is. A handler that changes its aggregate only through methods marked for other use cases performs an act its record never named, and a reader cannot tell from the use case which method to open. The use-case verb, the method name, and the raised event's tense agree under `litespec/backend/domain#raise-the-past-tense-of-a-methods-own-verb`. This provision states the marked form of `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`. A command that changes only stores, or that only runs other commands and lists nothing in `changes`, performs no act on a root, so it needs no marked call.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense handler calls `Reimburse` on the expense root, and `Reimburse` carries the mark `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense`.

provisions.heading: Create Valid Aggregates Through Named Factories
provisions.evidence: Which aggregate roots create instances outside a factory named for their business action? Look at the creation paths of each root.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST create instances only through a factory named for its business action.
provisions.rationale: A constructor carries no business name, so construction through constructors spreads creation rules across call sites. The factory is named for its business action, accepts typed identifiers, rejects empty identity and violated creation rules, selects the initial state, records required events, and returns a complete aggregate. A root created with its children composes them inside the same factory call. The children are built from typed values the caller supplies: a caller holding an already constructed child could mutate it after the invariant was checked, so the factory builds the children itself from those values.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` creates its expense through a factory named for submitting: the factory takes the expense and employee identifiers, rejects an empty identity, selects the submitted state, and records the submitted event.

provisions.heading: Declare Cross-Record Keys on the Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Which aggregates with a cross-record uniqueness rule miss `UniquenessKeys`, or carry other uniqueness code in Domain? Look at each such aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate needing a cross-record uniqueness key MUST expose its current keys through `UniquenessKeys`.
provisions.rationale: That method is the only uniqueness code in Domain: the aggregate declares its current keys, and persistence claims and releases them in the commit that changes the aggregate, following `litespec/backend/persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`. The aggregate computes keys from its own state and validates nothing about other records, because the store arbitrates the race.
provisions.example: In the library product, a book holding a list of copy barcodes returns each barcode from `UniquenessKeys`, so adding a copy claims the new barcode at commit. In the Claimwick product, a payout carrying a reference that is unique across payouts and adjustments returns that reference, so a duplicate reference fails the commit on either record.

provisions.heading: Define Collection Value Semantics Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Which collection values lack content equality with a matching hash under their declared ordering rule? Look at each collection value beside the module terms.
provisions.statement: A value object containing a collection MUST implement content equality and a matching hash for its declared ordering rule.
provisions.rationale: Default structural equality compares collection references rather than contents, so two value objects holding equal lists compare as different. Content equality with a matching hash compares what the value means. Creation copies incoming mutable collections and members return read-only views, so later mutation by the caller leaves the value unchanged. The module terms state whether order is part of the value.
provisions.example: A post-tags value holding an ordered list compares element by element with a matching hash. If order is not part of the value, creation normalizes to the documented comparison order before storing values.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Public Domain Contract in Documentation
provisions.evidence: Which public Domain types or members lack documentation of their business constraint, result, or refusal? Look at the documentation on each public member.
provisions.statement: Every public Domain type and member MUST carry documentation stating the business constraint, result, or refusal it represents.
provisions.rationale: A reader meeting a public Domain member needs to know the business rule behind it, not just its signature. Documentation states the business constraint, result, or refusal the member represents: a mutation method names its source states, resulting state, protected invariant, and recorded event. A summary that restates the member name adds nothing.

provisions.heading: Expose Repositories for One Aggregate Only
provisions.evidence: Which domain repositories serve more than one aggregate, expose non-Domain types, or offer a composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface? Look at each repository interface.
provisions.statement: A domain repository MUST serve exactly one aggregate root, exposing only aggregate and Domain types, with no composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface.
provisions.rationale: One domain repository per aggregate keeps the write side shaped by the aggregates it loads: a required load looks the aggregate up by identity and reports a missing aggregate through the missing-resource refusal, so a handler repeats no absence check, while an optional lookup is reserved for cases where absence is normal. A flow that finds a record or creates it is two use cases that the boundary owning the flow chooses between, following `litespec/backend/application#implement-one-outcome-path-per-command`. A composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface would expose store mechanics to every handler. This boundary is the write side only. Reading for a query uses a read model owned by Application and shaped by Infrastructure, and that path declares no Domain contract. A repository that gained a projection method would put query shapes in Domain, which is the coupling this layer exists to prevent.
provisions.example:
A post repository loads a post by identity and reports a missing post through the missing-resource refusal, plus a staging call that stages the aggregate.

The Infrastructure implementation owns that refusal. The command pipeline owns the commit. The staging call stages the aggregate through the selected provider.

provisions.heading: Express Transitions Through Business Methods
provisions.evidence: Which public mutations skip the state check or the invariant, or which lifecycle moves skip replacement or the transition event? Look at the public mutation methods of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: A public aggregate mutation method MUST check current state and protect its invariants, replacing state and recording its transition event when it moves the lifecycle.
provisions.rationale: A business-named method lets the handler call the publish behavior without testing the state first: the method checks the current state and protects its invariants, then replaces state and records the transition event when it moves the lifecycle. A generic `Set`, `Update`, `Process`, or `Handle` name hides which business action ran. A mutation that changes no lifecycle state, such as `ChangeTitle` on a draft, checks state and assigns without recording a transition. Checks run before replacement, and replacement runs before recording. A method that replaces state before checking an invariant leaves a rejected aggregate holding the new state.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` ends with `result/reimburse-expense.reimbursed` when the expense is approved, and with `result/reimburse-expense.not-approved` when it is not. The handler calls one business method, and the method checks the state, replaces it, and records `event/expense.reimbursed`.

An unapproved expense keeps its state, and the refusal carries the stable code `spending.not-approved`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case Its Own Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-count-invalid` (level S) for a root method carrying more than one use-case mark, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark on a method that changes no state.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate root method that changes state MUST perform the act of exactly one use case.
provisions.rationale: Each use case is its own path: its own caller, setup, refusals, events and scenarios. A method two use cases share couples them, so a change made for one silently changes the other, and neither scenario set describes the method. One method per act keeps each path readable on its own; logic the acts share moves into a private method of the root that each act calls. A method that only reads or computes performs no act and carries no mark.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a manager approving an expense and a delegate approving it for an absent manager both record an approval. The expense root offers `Approve` marked `use-case/spending.approve-expense` and `ApproveOnBehalf` marked `use-case/spending.approve-expense-on-behalf`, each raising its own event, and both call a private `RecordApproval`.

provisions.heading: Identify Aggregates with Strongly Typed Version 7 Values
provisions.evidence: Which aggregate identities escape the dedicated version 7 type, or which conversions, aliases, or creation paths bypass its validation? Look at each identity type and its creation paths.
provisions.statement: An aggregate identity MUST be a dedicated type wrapping one version 7 UUID, with no conversion, alias, or creation path that bypasses its validation.
provisions.rationale: A dedicated identity type stops one aggregate's identifier from passing where another's is expected, and with no conversion, alias, or creation path around its validation, there is no quiet route back to a bare value. The type rejects the empty value, and each factory also rejects its default. New values arrive from the caller: a factory takes its identifier as an argument, and a method that needs several identifiers takes a generator. Domain reads no clock and calls no static source of time or randomness. Version 7 values come from the caller-supplied generator, so Domain observes no business time and decides nothing about clocks. Persistence rejects a duplicate key and the write fails, which is the same path as any other write conflict, with the violation mapped to the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`.
provisions.example: A post identifier wraps one version 7 UUID, rejects the empty value, and parses from text through a named method.

provisions.heading: Keep Binary Floating Point Out of Exact Quantities
provisions.evidence: Which Domain values hold a binary floating-point type for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality? Look at the field, parameter and return types in Domain.
provisions.statement: A Domain value MUST NOT use binary floating point for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality.
provisions.rationale: Binary floating point represents most decimal fractions only approximately, so two amounts a person reads as equal compare as different, and totals drift by fractions of a cent. Exact decimal types keep equality and arithmetic exact.
provisions.example: A tax rate multiplied into a `Money` amount uses an exact decimal type. A measured latency in a diagnostic log is not a Domain quantity and is outside this rule.

provisions.heading: Keep Child Entities Inside the Aggregate Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which child entities expose mutable state outside their root? Look at the child entities beside their root, including collection views.
provisions.statement: A child entity MUST expose no mutable state outside its aggregate root, surfacing its collection as a read-only view.
provisions.rationale: A child that exposed mutable state would let outside code change aggregate data without passing the root's checks. The root creates, finds, and changes children through business methods, and collections surface as read-only views. A child with lifecycle states uses the same state types and no enumeration.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Independent of Outer Layers
provisions.evidence: Which Domain references reach beyond the language standard library and project-owned Domain types? Look at the references in the Domain code.
provisions.statement: The Domain code MUST reference only the language standard library and project-owned Domain types.
provisions.rationale: Domain that references only the language standard library and its own types compiles and tests with no infrastructure at all. Each banned reference would drag one outer concern into the business model: persistence metadata couples a rule to a store format, and dispatch plumbing couples it to delivery. Infrastructure registers a persisted discriminator instead, so Domain carries no serialization metadata.

provisions.heading: Model Every Aggregate Lifecycle with State Types
provisions.evidence: Which aggregates expose their lifecycle outside one state property and one closed hierarchy of per-state types? Look at the lifecycle declarations in each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST expose its lifecycle only through one state property backed by one closed hierarchy of per-state types.
provisions.rationale: Each lifecycle state can carry different facts: a published post carries its publication time, a draft does not. An enumeration, string discriminator, boolean flag, parallel nullable field, or computed state carries no state-specific data. State types hold that data, and aggregate methods own the transitions between them. A switch over the state types names each case in its own arm where the language requires a fallback, and a case with no arm reaches that fallback at run time.
provisions.example:
A post defines one abstract post state with draft and published cases, where the published case carries its publication time. Even an aggregate with one current state defines its hierarchy.

In the Claimwick product, `aggregate/spending.expense` records the `Submitted`, `Approved`, `Refused`, and `Reimbursed` states with their transitions: Submit from `use-case/spending.submit-expense` creates Submitted, Approve from `use-case/spending.approve-expense` moves Submitted to Approved, Refuse from `use-case/spending.refuse-expense` moves Submitted to Refused, and Reimburse from `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` moves Approved to Reimbursed. The approved case carries the approver and the decided time, and the reimbursed case carries the reimbursed time.

![Submit from submit-expense creates a Submitted expense, Approve from approve-expense moves it to Approved carrying the approver and the decided time, Refuse from refuse-expense moves it to Refused carrying the reason, and Reimburse from reimburse-expense moves an Approved expense to Reimbursed carrying the reimbursed time.](../assets/diagrams/backend-aggregate-lifecycle.svg)

provisions.heading: Model Every Closed Set of Domain Values as a Closed Type Hierarchy
provisions.evidence: Which closed sets escape one type hierarchy with named label lookups? Look at each closed set and its boundary lookups.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST model a closed set as one type hierarchy whose cases the type system can enumerate.
provisions.rationale: A closed set with case data needs a type per case: an enumeration carries no case data, admits undefined values, and forces parallel nullable fields when one case gains data. A closed hierarchy gives each case a named type that a switch can name in its own arm, and a case with no arm reaches the switch fallback at run time. A boundary converts a label to its case through a named lookup rather than through a string conversion, and an unrecognized label is a validation failure rather than a default case.
provisions.example:
A refund outcome defines pending, succeeded, failed, and reversed cases, where each case carries its own data.

This provision owns the Domain form. The same set is mirrored in Application under `litespec/backend/application#mirror-a-domain-closed-set-in-the-result`, on the wire under `litespec/backend/api#mirror-a-domain-closed-set-as-a-transport-model-of-the-same-shape`, and in storage under `litespec/backend/persistence#keep-serialization-behavior-out-of-domain`. Label-only sets cross the boundary as plain enumerations under `litespec/backend/api#publish-label-only-sets-as-string-enums`. A transport label converts to its type case before it reaches a Domain method.

provisions.heading: Model Money with Exact Decimal Values
provisions.evidence: Which monetary amounts escape the shared `Money` value with its currency and JSON shape? Look at each monetary amount in Domain.
provisions.statement: A monetary amount MUST use an exact decimal type inside one shared `Money` value object carrying an ISO 4217 currency code and serializing as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`.
provisions.rationale: Money needs exact arithmetic and an explicit currency on every value, and one shared `Money` object gives both. The owning module record defines supported currencies, scale, rounding, sign rules, and cross-currency arithmetic, and Infrastructure maps that precision explicitly. A use case fixed to one currency accepts an amount alone and states that currency in its record.
provisions.example:
```json
{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }
```

The amount serializes as a string, so no reader parses it as binary floating point.

provisions.heading: Organize a Module by Aggregate and Concept
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a domain event outside its aggregate's `Events` folder.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate a `Domain/` folder named with its plural root name, holding its own states, events, refusals, and concepts.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate `Domain/` folder holds everything one aggregate owns: its states, events, refusals, and concepts. A reader finds the full aggregate in one place instead of hunting shared folders. A single aggregate stays flat only when its plural root name equals the module name, and separate aggregates keep separate lifecycle, event, and refusal folders.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}/
  Domain/                         the shared kernel: the root, event, identity, and refusal contracts
  Posts/                          one aggregate whose name matches the module: kept flat in the module folder
    Domain/
      Post
      PostId
      PostTitle
      PostRepository
      States/
        PostState
        PostDraftState
        PostPublishedState
        PostArchivedState
      Events/
        PostCreatedEvent
        PostPublishedEvent
      Refusals/
        PostIdentityRequired
        PostAlreadyPublished
  Shipping/                       one aggregate whose name differs from the module, with a domain union in a concept folder
    Shipments/
      Domain/
        Shipment
        ShipmentId
        ShipmentRepository
        Outcomes/
          ShipmentOutcome
          ShipmentDeliveredOutcome
          ShipmentReturnedOutcome
          ShipmentLostOutcome
        States/
          ShipmentState
          ShipmentPendingState
          ShipmentDispatchedState
          ShipmentDeliveredState
        Events/
          ShipmentOutcomeRecordedEvent
  Customers/                      more than one aggregate: one plural folder per aggregate
    CustomerAccounts/
      Domain/
        CustomerAccount
        CustomerAccountId
        CustomerAccountRepository
        States/
          CustomerAccountState
          CustomerAccountClaimedState
        Events/
          CustomerAccountRestrictedEvent
    Consents/
      Domain/
        Consent
        ConsentId
        ConsentRepository
        States/
          ConsentState
          ConsentGrantedState
        Events/
          ConsentGrantedEvent
```

Each aggregate's domain repository stays with the aggregate it loads. The module, aggregate, and use case order follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. Each stack page states the file names and extensions that carry this layout.

provisions.heading: Pass Nondeterministic Values into Domain
provisions.evidence: Which Domain methods read a clock, a random source or a new identifier instead of receiving it? Look at the calls Domain code makes.
provisions.statement: Domain behavior MUST receive time, randomness, and new identifiers as arguments rather than read them, and read no clock.
provisions.rationale: Domain behavior that read a clock or generated identifiers would return different results for the same call, which makes tests nondeterministic. Receiving time, randomness, and new identifiers as arguments keeps every Domain call a pure function of its inputs: a test supplies explicit values and stays deterministic. Application obtains each value through an owned port and passes it in. A method that needs more than one value receives a clock or a generator through its arguments, and version 7 identifiers come from the caller-supplied generator.

provisions.heading: Place Every Constituent Type in Its Aggregate's Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `constituent-parent-missing` (level A) for an unmarked Domain type whose folder holds no aggregate root and is not the product `Domain/` folder, and the model output lists each constituent under its aggregate.
provisions.statement: A Domain constituent type, meaning an identifier, a state type, a closed set, a child entity, a value object, or a repository interface, MUST sit in the `Domain/` folder of the aggregate it belongs to, or in the product `Domain/` folder.
provisions.rationale: A constituent serves no record of its own: it is part of its aggregate, whose record already states the states, transitions, and data the constituent holds. A mark on each would write that fact a second time, and the two copies would drift. The folder already says which aggregate a constituent belongs to, so the builder derives the link from it, and a type in a folder that holds no aggregate root and is not the product `Domain/` folder is the one place the derivation fails. A domain service that holds one rule calculation is not a constituent: it carries its `rule/` mark.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `ExpenseState` and `IExpenseRepository` sit beside the `Expense` root in `Spending/Expenses/Domain/` and carry no mark; the builder lists them as constituents of `aggregate/spending.expense`. `Money` sits in the product `Domain/` folder and belongs to no aggregate.

provisions.heading: Raise Immutable Facts as Domain Events
provisions.evidence: Which domain events mutate, misname their aggregate or fact, or carry more than business data? Look at each domain event.
provisions.statement: A domain event MUST be immutable and carry business data only.
provisions.rationale: A domain event records a completed fact for reactions to consume. Its name states the aggregate and the completed fact, following `litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root` and `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`, so a reader knows which aggregate raised the fact without opening the file. The event carries business data only: typed identifiers and the values its reactions need, with no aggregate, session, service, mutable collection, or thrown error, because any of those would couple reactions to the raising aggregate. Envelope identity, such as message identity and causation identity, lives on the published integration event that carries the fact outside the process. That integration event names the domain event in `translates`.

provisions.heading: Raise the Declared Events from the Marked Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `act-event-undeclared` (level S) for a marked method raising an event its use case does not list, and `act-event-unimplemented` (level S) for a listed event no marked method raises.
provisions.statement: The root methods marked with a use case MUST together raise exactly the events that use case lists in `raises`.
provisions.rationale: The use case record states the facts its act leaves behind, and reactions subscribe to those facts. A marked method that raises an event the record does not list starts a consequence nobody reviewed, and a listed event that no marked method raises is a promise the code does not keep.
provisions.example: `use-case/spending.submit-expense` raises `event/expense.submitted`, and the `Submit` method marked with it raises `ExpenseSubmittedEvent` and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Raise the Past Tense of a Method's Own Verb
provisions.evidence: Which state-changing aggregate methods raise an event named for another verb? Look at the events each changed aggregate method raises.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate method that changes state MUST raise an event named for the past tense of its verb.
provisions.rationale: The command raises nothing; the aggregate root raises its domain event inside its own method. An event named for another verb tells the reader the act finished under a name the code never spoke, and reactions subscribe to a vocabulary the aggregate does not own. The event name takes the past tense of the act's verb, as `litespec/core/domain-model#name-every-event-in-the-past-tense` requires for every event. An event name may place the past tense as a whole word followed by a complement that opens with a preposition or particle. A method that sets a state names that state in its event, and a method may raise further events for the consequences of its act, as long as one of its events names the act itself.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `Approve` on an expense raises `event/expense.approved` and passes. `Approve` raising `event/expense.signed-off` is reported, because that name belongs to another act.

provisions.heading: Reference Other Aggregates by ID
provisions.evidence: Which aggregates store another aggregate as an object reference instead of a typed identifier? Look at the fields of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST store another aggregate's typed identifier rather than an object reference.
provisions.rationale: An object reference between aggregates loads one aggregate's data through another, which couples their consistency boundaries and their storage. A typed identifier keeps each aggregate loadable on its own: Application loads each aggregate through its domain repository when a command coordinates several, with `consistency: atomic` citing the rule in `cites`.

provisions.heading: Reject Business Violations with Dedicated Refusals
provisions.evidence: Which rejected business rules end outside a dedicated refusal with its stable code, or leak transport status? Look at each rejection beside its refusal.
provisions.statement: A rejected business rule MUST end its use case in a dedicated refusal carrying its stable code.
provisions.rationale: One refusal per rejected rule lets each boundary map outcomes without parsing messages: the refusal names the failed rule and the stable code travels to the caller. The name leads with the aggregate root. Domain raises no standard library, validation, transport, or provider failure for a business rejection, and carries no transport status. Refusal names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`; this provision owns the one-refusal-per-rule shape and the code each refusal carries.
provisions.example:
A refund allocation rule ends its use case in its own refusal, rather than sharing one refusal with a code passed at the call site.

Two rules that share a caller-visible refusal code because a boundary maps them to one response still get two refusals. The shared code lives in the two refusals, not in a value passed by the aggregate. One refusal serves more than one input only when one rule fails from more than one input and the differing values travel as creation parameters.

Application validators handle malformed caller input through validity findings. Aggregate and value-object refusals remain the last defense when direct Domain use violates a rule. Command handlers do not catch expected Domain refusals. The host maps them to transport errors through the mapping the API page documents under `litespec/backend/api#defer-error-mapping-to-the-global-handler`.

provisions.heading: Reuse the Shared Domain Contracts Across Modules
provisions.evidence: Which shared Domain contracts repeat their declaration across modules? Look at the root, event, identity, and refusal contracts in each module.
provisions.statement: Declare the shared Domain contracts once in the product `Domain/` folder and reuse them across every module.
provisions.rationale: One declaration keeps the root, event, identity, and refusal mechanics identical in every module; a second declaration drifts from the first with the next fix.
provisions.example:
The shared contracts are the aggregate root, the domain event, the typed identity, and the refusal.

Event clearing is delivery mechanics, not a business mutation. Infrastructure calls it only after delivery accepts the pending events.

provisions.heading: Take Identity and Events from the Project Root Contract
provisions.evidence: Which aggregate roots take identity or event mechanics outside the project-owned root contract? Look at each aggregate root declaration.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST take its identity and event mechanics from the project-owned root contract.
provisions.rationale: One root contract gives every aggregate the same identity and event mechanics, so Infrastructure collects events from any aggregate the same way. The contract owns typed identity, pending events, recording, and clearing, and carries the aggregate version only as persistence metadata that Domain never reads or sets: no timestamp, audit, tenant, lifecycle, or other persistence behavior, because any of those would couple every aggregate to a concern only some need.

provisions.heading: Treat Aggregates as Consistency Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Which invariants admit a public mutation outside their aggregate root? Look at the public mutation entry points of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST be the only public mutation entry point for every invariant its transaction protects.
provisions.rationale: If outside code could set properties or call child mutations, it could change data without passing the root's checks. The root stands as the only public mutation entry point, so every change passes the invariant the transaction protects. A command with `consistency: atomic` changes every aggregate its `changes` names in one transaction, citing the rule in `cites` when it changes more than one.

provisions.heading: Use Immutable Value Objects for Domain Concepts
provisions.evidence: Which value objects mutate, compare by less than their complete value, or skip validation at creation? Look at each value object and its creation paths.
provisions.statement: A value object MUST be immutable, compare by its complete value, and validate every value at creation.
provisions.rationale: Immutability with comparison by complete value lets two instances with the same data stand in for each other. The value exposes no mutation and no implicit conversion, because a primitive conversion hides validation and a value conversion erases the domain type. Reading uses the wrapped value or its text form, and creation through a named creation path keeps every value under the validation the type declares.
provisions.example: A post title accepts only non-blank text up to 200 characters: blank or longer input fails creation, and two titles with the same text compare as equal.

provisions.heading: Use One Ubiquitous Language
provisions.evidence: Which Domain names match no term in the project glossary? Look at the Domain names beside `glossary.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A Domain name MUST match a term in the project glossary.
provisions.rationale: When code and specification share names, a reader moves between them without translation. A business action named `Publish` in the glossary is not `SetStatus` in code, because the second name hides which business action ran. The glossary holds each term meaning, labels per language, rejected words, and broader and narrower links; records cite the terms they use, following `litespec/core/domain-model#define-every-behavior-term-in-the-glossary`.

provisions.heading: Use Stateless Domain Services for Ownerless Rules
provisions.evidence: Which domain services hold state, take non-Domain values, or reach persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or a provider? Look at each domain service and its calls.
provisions.statement: A domain service MUST be stateless, accept and return Domain values, and perform no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call.
provisions.rationale: Some calculations span concepts with no natural aggregate owner; forcing them into one aggregate couples it to another's data. A stateless service holds that calculation, accepting and returning Domain values with no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call. Application loads the aggregates, calls the service, and passes its result into aggregate behavior. A domain service is stateless and takes no port, so its tests are Domain tests. They sit beside the aggregate tests in the unit tests mirroring the module tree, with no harness, no substitute, and no fixture.
provisions.example: An order-pricing service takes order lines and a currency and returns their total as `Money`, with no domain repository, clock, logger, or provider client. Application supplies the lines and passes the returned total into aggregate behavior.

provisions.heading: Use These Domain Names
provisions.evidence: Which Domain names break the cited workspace naming provisions, or which state cases break the one kept form? Look at each Domain name.
provisions.statement: Name each Domain type from the aggregate root it belongs to, following the workspace naming provisions cited below.
provisions.rationale: Aggregate-prefixed names keep each type readable at its call site without its namespace. Aggregate-owned names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root`. Architectural suffixes follow `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`. Refusal names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`. A project names every state case in one form and keeps it.
provisions.example: A post title reads as `PostTitle` at its call site, and a published post state as `PostPublishedState`. The stack page states the declaration form each name takes.

provisions.heading: Declare Operation Metadata in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Which operations miss a stable `operationId`, authorization, request, success, or Problem Details metadata, typed results or `Produces` entries, or a summary? Look at each operation.
provisions.statement: An operation MUST declare a stable `operationId`, its authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and typed results or `Produces` metadata, and a summary.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients name their calls from `operationId`, so an unnamed or unstable operation breaks every client regeneration. Authorization and Problem Details metadata tell a client which policies apply and which failures to handle; without them the client guesses. Route-lambda comments never reach the contract, so the summary and description are declared explicitly. This provision binds `litespec/backend/api#declare-stable-operation-metadata-in-the-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Derive HTTP Statuses from Refusal Codes
provisions.evidence: Which refusal codes escape the one `IExceptionHandler`, or map outside their outcome-table status? Look at the WebApi global handler.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST map each refusal code to its HTTP status in one global handler.
provisions.rationale: The specification records each refusal with its stable `code` and no transport status, so the stack derives the status its transport needs. The handler uses ASP.NET Core `AddProblemDetails` with one `IExceptionHandler`: validation failures answer 400, missing targets answer through the operation's 404 policy, forbidden failures answer 403 or the declared 404 disclosure policy, conflicts and state rejections answer 409, and unexpected failures answer 500 with code `internal_error`. The derived `invalid-input` refusal answers 400 under the project's `refusals.invalidInput` code, and the derived `forbidden` refusal answers 403 or the declared 404 under the project's `refusals.forbidden` code. Known Domain exception types map individually, and a cancellation from a disconnected request is not reported as an application error. The outcome-to-status assignment lives in `litespec/backend/api#use-consistent-status-codes`; this provision binds it for .NET.

provisions.heading: Exclude MVC Controllers from the Stack
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2003` for a WebApi class deriving from `ControllerBase` or carrying `ApiController`.
provisions.statement: WebApi code MUST NOT route requests through MVC controllers or `ControllerBase`.
provisions.rationale: Controllers and endpoint classes route, filter, and map errors through different models. When both exist, a reviewer checks two mappings for every behavior, and error responses drift apart. One model means one place defines how requests reach handlers and how failures reach clients.

provisions.heading: Keep Program.cs as Composition
provisions.evidence: Which `Program.cs` files break the recorded composition order or miss a step? Look at `Program.cs`.
provisions.statement: `Program.cs` holds module registration, middleware order, endpoint discovery, health endpoints, OpenAPI, and host startup, ending with an empty partial `Program` class.
provisions.rationale: Middleware runs in registration order, so authentication registered after endpoints never runs. When one file shows the whole sequence, a reviewer sees the order at a glance; when registration scatters across files, a misplaced call hides. This file binds `litespec/backend/architecture#compose-each-process-explicitly` for WebApi.
provisions.example: The visible order is trusted forwarded headers, exception handling, transport security, authentication, authorization, endpoints, and then health. Forwarded headers appear only when the deployment boundary requires trusted proxies. OpenAPI and Scalar map only in Development.

provisions.heading: Mark Polymorphic Transport Models with Discriminators
provisions.evidence: Which data-bearing sets escape the abstract base record with one sealed record per case, or carry no discriminator under the generic provision? Look at each data-bearing set.
provisions.statement: A data-bearing set MUST map to an abstract base record with one sealed record per case, carrying the discriminator that `litespec/backend/api#mark-polymorphic-models-with-discriminators` requires.
provisions.rationale: A concrete base record cannot mark the discriminator as required, so a client could send a payload that names no case. This provision binds `litespec/backend/api#mark-polymorphic-models-with-discriminators` for .NET and adds no discriminator rule of its own.
provisions.example:
- Declare an abstract base record carrying `JsonPolymorphic` and one `JsonDerivedType` per case, on the type itself rather than in host options.
- Name the discriminator through `TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName`, using a name such as `type` or `outcome`.
- Complete discriminator metadata that the generator omits with a document or schema transformer.

provisions.heading: Place Endpoints in Their Use Case Folders
provisions.evidence: Which use case folders miss the endpoint, request and response models, or mappings named for the use case? Look at each use case folder.
provisions.statement: Place each endpoint with its request and response models and mappings flat in its use case folder inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Transport types take the names their boundary roles assign under `litespec/backend/api#name-transport-types-by-their-boundary-role`, and transport mapping lives in WebApi under `litespec/backend/application#keep-mappings-at-the-owning-boundary`. Response models carry the query's declared `include` groups. Transport types used by two or more use cases of one aggregate live in the aggregate WebApi folder, and those used by two or more aggregates in the module WebApi folder. Module nesting, including the single-aggregate flat form, follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.
provisions.example:
The endpoint layout is:

```text
{Product}.Modules/
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module
    WebApi/
      PostLinks.cs                  transport types two or more Posts use cases name
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
        CreateDraftEndpoint.cs
        CreateDraftRequestModel.cs
        CreateDraftResponseModel.cs
        CreateDraftApiMappings.cs
      GetPost/
        GetPostEndpoint.cs
        GetPostResponseModel.cs
        GetPostApiMappings.cs
  Customers/                        two aggregates: use cases nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
    CustomerAccounts/
      UseCases/
        RestrictAccount/
          RestrictAccountEndpoint.cs
          RestrictAccountRequestModel.cs
          RestrictAccountApiMappings.cs
    Consents/
      UseCases/
        GrantConsent/
          GrantConsentEndpoint.cs
          GrantConsentRequestModel.cs
          GrantConsentApiMappings.cs
{Product}.WebApi/
  Errors/
    GlobalExceptionHandler.cs
    ProblemDetailsApiMappings.cs
  Security/
    CurrentActor.cs
  OpenApi/
  Program.cs
```

provisions.heading: Use One Endpoint per Operation
provisions.evidence: Which mapped routes escape one `IEndpoint` type converting input, dispatching, and mapping the result? Look at the endpoints in the use case folders.
provisions.statement: A WebApi endpoint MUST implement `IEndpoint`, map one route operation, convert input to an Application message, dispatch through its mediator, and map the result.
provisions.rationale: When one class owns one route, a reviewer finds the input mapping, the dispatch, and the result mapping for that route in one place, and no route drifts into a second pattern unnoticed. Without that rule, operations share classes or helpers, and a change to one route silently affects another. This provision binds `litespec/backend/api#map-one-operation-per-endpoint` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Bind Command Handlers to Load, Call and Stage
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2012` for a handler that throws a forbidden refusal or takes the authorization guard, `LS2013` for an audit call that reads the message, `LS2014` for a find followed by a create, and `LS2015` for a store inside a loop.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST load or create one aggregate through its repository, call one domain method on it, stage it, and return the result.
provisions.rationale: The handler body has three steps: the load or creation, the one domain call, and the stage. A required load uses the throwing `GetByIdAsync` and an optional lookup uses the nullable `FindBy...Async` under `litespec/backend/dotnet/domain#keep-repository-interfaces-in-domain`. The message carries the pipeline-stamped timestamp as `HandledAt` under `litespec/backend/application#take-one-timestamp-per-message` (see `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#bind-the-pipeline-to-the-pinned-litebus-apis`), so the handler stamps decisions without reading a clock. Validation, authorization, idempotency, audit, holds, and the commit are pipeline stages; messages, provider calls, and writes to other aggregates run in event handlers after the commit under `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#dispatch-declared-effects-through-their-entry-points`. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates is the one exception: the handler loads, calls, and stages each aggregate its `changes` names, one method each. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage` and `litespec/backend/application#load-a-required-record-or-refuse-it` for .NET, where `GetByIdAsync` and `FindBy...Async` are the forms.

provisions.heading: Bind the Pipeline to the Pinned LiteBus APIs
provisions.evidence: Which pipeline positions lack their pinned LiteBus API? Look at the command pipeline composition.
provisions.statement: An Application MUST compose its command pipeline through the LiteBus APIs this provision names for commit, authorization, audit, fault classification, delivery, event staging, and the timestamp.
provisions.rationale: One pinned binding per position keeps every project's pipeline identical. The commit runs through `commands.UseMartenUnitOfWork()`, which registers the LiteBus `IUnitOfWork` at `HandlerPriorities.UnitOfWork`, so the pipeline commits once under `litespec/backend/dotnet/persistence#commit-once-in-the-command-pipeline`. Authorization runs through a guard derived from `LiteBus.Messaging.Abstractions.DeclarationGuard<TMessage, TValue>`, reading the declaration from the message definition under `litespec/backend/application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline`. Audit runs through `AuditDeclaration.Audited(...).WithTargetFrom<TCommand>(...).WithReasonFrom<TCommand>(...)` in an `IAuditDefinition<TCommand>`, declaring the target and reason beside the message under `litespec/backend/application#declare-audit-values-beside-the-message`. Fault classification runs through `UseFaultRefusalClassifierInstance(new PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier(map))`, mapping each store fault to its refusal under `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`. Delivery runs through `outbox.EnablePerHandlerDelivery()`, reaching each handler separately under `litespec/ext/outbox#deliver-each-event-to-each-handler-separately`. Event staging runs through `outbox.StageCollectedEvents()`, staging the facts `IDomainEventCollector` collected in the same commit as the aggregate change. The timestamp runs through `IExecutionContext.HandledAt`, stamping each message once for the handler to read as `HandledAt` under `litespec/backend/application#take-one-timestamp-per-message`.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Declared Effects Through Their Entry Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for a dispatch no record declares; each event handler dispatches sends through the messenger port, calls through its external-system port, and runs through `ICommandMediator`, after the commit.
provisions.statement: An event handler MUST dispatch each declared `sends` effect through the messenger port, each declared `calls` effect through its external-system port, and each declared `runs` effect through `ICommandMediator`, after the commit that stored the fact it answers, while the aggregate raises each declared `emits` effect as a domain event the outbox stages in the same commit.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes its aggregate and returns; it dispatches nothing. The aggregate raises its facts, and the outbox stages them in the same commit through `outbox.StageCollectedEvents()` (see `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#bind-the-pipeline-to-the-pinned-litebus-apis`). After that commit, an event handler answers each fact through its entry point: the messenger port for `sends`, its external-system port for `calls`, and `ICommandMediator` for `runs`. An `inline` `runs` entry states whether it shares the caller's transaction. A scheduled or manual job dispatches through the same entry points. Each handler gets its own delivery under `litespec/ext/outbox#deliver-each-event-to-each-handler-separately`, so one failing handler retries alone. An undeclared dispatch fails `effect-undeclared`, whatever its entry point. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Query Handlers Free of Repositories
provisions.evidence: Which query handlers take a repository, skip `IQuerySession`, or stage, store, delete, or dispatch? Look at each query handler; `dotnet build` reports LS2011 for a repository in a query handler and LS2012 for a forbidden refusal or the authorization guard.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST take no repository and stage, store, delete or dispatch nothing.
provisions.rationale: A read path acts on no invariant, so a repository in a query handler loads an aggregate the query has no write to justify. The handler projects through the read session under `litespec/backend/dotnet/persistence#query-through-iquerysession`. A read that writes makes retries and caching unsafe; an audited read is the pipeline's work, not the handler's. `dotnet build` reports a repository in a query handler as `LS2011`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#project-queries-directly` and `litespec/backend/application#keep-query-handlers-free-of-writes` for .NET.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query projects its rows through `IQuerySession`, taking no repository and staging nothing.

provisions.heading: Report Input Problems as Validity
provisions.evidence: Which validators report outside `Validity`, or skip member, code, or message, or leak HTTP status? Look at each validator.
