provisions.statement: A validator MUST report its findings as Validity, with each ValidationFailure carrying a member, a code, and a message, and no HTTP status.
provisions.rationale: Every validator for the message runs, and the pipeline merges the findings before it refuses the request, so the caller fixes the whole form at once. The member tells the caller which input failed, the stable code lets a client branch on the reason, and the message explains the problem in words safe to show. Validity values come from the pinned mediator's abstractions, named in `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#use-the-pinned-mediator-entry-points`, so every project reports the same shape. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#report-input-problems-as-validity-findings` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Run Reactions in Dedicated Handlers
provisions.evidence: Which reactions escape one handler class with their record's mark in the module `UseCases/On{Fact}` folder? Look at each reaction in its module `UseCases/` folder.
provisions.statement: A reaction MUST run in one class carrying one mark naming its reaction record.
provisions.rationale: One class per reaction answers the trigger the record names in `triggeredBy` and dispatches only through its `effects` entries. The class carries the mark `reaction/<module>.<name>` in the declared style, so the stack reader links it without guessing. It lives in the `On{Fact}` folder inside its module `UseCases/` folder under `litespec/workspace/naming#group-event-handlers-by-the-fact-they-handle`, beside every other handler of the same fact. It never writes an aggregate directly: a reaction that needs a write runs a command. It honors the record's `reads`, its idempotency, and its `onFailure`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#keep-reaction-implementations-explicit` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Run Scheduled Jobs as Hosted Operations
provisions.evidence: Which scheduled or manual jobs escape one marked hosted operation honoring selection, batch size, lease, and cursor? Look at each such job.
provisions.statement: A scheduled or manual job MUST run as one hosted operation carrying one mark naming its job record.
provisions.rationale: The hosted operation lives in its module Jobs folder with the scheduling concerns and registers on the declared execution host. It honors its record's selection, batch size, lease, and cursor, runs its commands once per item, and records its evidence where the record states. A `manual` job states its `runsWhere` and its guard and touches no aggregate. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#run-each-job-within-its-declared-selection` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Use the Pinned Mediator Entry Points
provisions.evidence: Which dispatch sites bypass `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` or `IQueryMediator.QueryAsync`, or use an unpinned LiteBus version? Look at each dispatch site.
provisions.statement: Dispatch a command through `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` and a query through `IQueryMediator.QueryAsync`, from the LiteBus version the manifest pins.
provisions.rationale: One pinned library means every dispatch site in every project reads the same way, and an agent finds all callers of a message with one search. A project that replaces the default still keeps commands and queries on separate entry points, because that separation is required by `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-commands-and-queries-through-separate-entry-points` and no replacement removes it.

provisions.heading: Use the Use Case Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Which use case folders miss message, result, validator, or handler files named for the use case, or which event handlers escape their module `UseCases/On{Fact}` folder? Look at each use case folder.
provisions.statement: Place each use case flat in a folder named for its use case inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate, with the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates a use case from its use-case identifier without searching. Type names derive from the use-case identifier with the architectural suffix, so `use-case/spending.submit-expense` owns `SubmitExpenseCommand` under `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`. Only a use case or a handled fact gets a folder below its `UseCases/` folder: any other type sits flat in the layer folder that owns it under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`, and a handled fact folder takes the `On{Fact}` name with its marked handler classes under `litespec/workspace/naming#group-event-handlers-by-the-fact-they-handle`. Each result type carries one case per result, and each refusal carries the refusal `code` from its result record. A query result type carries one member per declared `include` group, and each result part is named after its result under `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result`.
provisions.example:
The use case folder layout is:

```text
{Product}.SharedKernel/
  Application/                      product plumbing: pipeline positions, clock, failures, validation
    Pipeline/                       the pipeline own stages, and nothing else
      ApplicationPipeline.cs
      AuthorizationGuard.cs
    Clock/
      IClock.cs
    Failures/
      ResourceNotFoundException.cs
      UseCaseForbiddenException.cs
      UseCaseConflictException.cs
    Validation/
      ValidationErrors.cs
{Product}.Modules/
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module: use cases sit in the module UseCases folder
    Application/
      IPostArchive.cs               a port several Posts use cases name
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
        CreateDraftCommand.cs
        CreateDraftCommandResult.cs
        CreateDraftCommandValidator.cs
        CreateDraftCommandHandler.cs
        CreateDraftEndpoint.cs
        CreateDraftRequestModel.cs
        CreateDraftResponseModel.cs
      GetPost/
        GetPostQuery.cs
        GetPostQueryResult.cs
        GetPostQueryValidator.cs
        GetPostQueryHandler.cs
      ListPosts/
        ListPostsQuery.cs
        ListPostsQueryResult.cs
        ListPostsQueryResultItem.cs
        ListPostsQueryValidator.cs
        ListPostsQueryHandler.cs
      OnPostPublished/              event handlers of one fact: one marked class per reaction
        NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler.cs
        IPostPublicationNotifier.cs a port one event handler names
  Customers/                        two aggregates: use cases nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
    CustomerAccounts/
      Application/
        CustomerAccountScopeLookup.cs aggregate-owned, so it sits with the aggregate
      UseCases/
        RestrictAccount/
          RestrictAccountCommand.cs
          RestrictAccountCommandHandler.cs
    Consents/
      UseCases/
        GrantConsent/
          GrantConsentCommand.cs
          GrantConsentCommandHandler.cs
```

Module and aggregate order, including the single-aggregate flat form, follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. A use case file takes its layer from its role suffix under `litespec/backend/dotnet/architecture#keep-closed-folder-sets-at-every-level`.

provisions.heading: Follow Declared Module Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Which module references name a module outside their owner dependsOn, or close a dependency cycle? Look at the cross-module references beside the module records.
provisions.statement: A module MUST reference only modules its record names in dependsOn.
provisions.rationale: The dependsOn list states which modules a module may know, so an undeclared edge is a boundary the design never allowed. The rule covers code references and record links alike, and the graph stays acyclic.

provisions.heading: Follow Layer Direction in Every File
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1001` for a Domain type naming an outer-layer type and `LS2018` for an Application or WebApi type naming a type outside its layer.
provisions.statement: A type MUST reference only the layers its own layer allows under the layer table of [Backend Architecture](../architecture.md#the-four-layers).
provisions.rationale: Layers are roles played by folders and use case files, whatever project holds them. A file takes its layer from its folder and, inside a use case folder, from its role suffix. Global usings import namespaces for every file, so the rule reads them too and they hide coupling from nothing. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#point-dependencies-inward` for .NET.
provisions.example: Domain touches no Application Infrastructure or WebApi type and none of the persistence web mediator logging and injection namespaces. Application touches no Infrastructure or WebApi type and no ASP.NET Core type. WebApi touches no Domain type outside typed identifiers and shared-kernel values and no repository.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Types in Their Layer Folders
provisions.evidence: Which commands queries results handlers validators or ports sit outside their Application folder or their Contracts kind folder? Look at the Application and Contracts folders beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: An application MUST place commands queries results handlers validators and module ports in Application folders and cross-module contracts in the sorted kind folders of its Contracts folder.
provisions.rationale: One use case stays flat in its folder, with its command query result handler validator endpoint and transport models side by side. Types used by two or more use cases of one aggregate live in the aggregate Application folder, types used by two or more aggregates in the module Application folder, and product-wide plumbing in the shared kernel Application folder. A module publishes its typed identifiers in `Contracts/Identifiers/`, its refusals in `Contracts/Exceptions/`, its integration events in `Contracts/IntegrationEvents/` and its cross-module ports in `Contracts/Ports/`, so the public surface of a module stays visible at the module.

provisions.heading: Keep Closed Folder Sets at Every Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-folder-drift` for a folder outside its closed set or naming no declared record.
provisions.statement: Each level of the shared kernel and modules projects MUST hold only the folders the closed set table in this section allows.
provisions.rationale: A closed set refuses the catch-all folder by construction: anything outside the table has no home and review refuses it. Product-wide plumbing lives in the product layer folders and cross-module contracts in each module Contracts folder, while `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers` decides between a use case folder and the aggregate module and product layer folders. Module folders mirror record homes: use cases sit in `UseCases/` folders, reactions in `On{Fact}/` folders beside the module use cases, and jobs in the module `Jobs/` folder.
provisions.example:
| Level | Allowed folders |
|:---|:---|
| Shared kernel project root | `Domain/`, `Application/`, `Infrastructure/`, `WebApi/` |
| Modules project root | `Composition/`, one per declared module |
| Module | `Contracts/`, `Domain/`, `Application/`, `Infrastructure/`, `WebApi/`, `UseCases/`, `Jobs/`, one per declared aggregate |
| Module `Contracts/` | `Identifiers/`, `Exceptions/`, `IntegrationEvents/`, `Commands/`, `Ports/` |
| Module `UseCases/` | one per declared module use case, one `On{Fact}/` per reaction |
| Aggregate | `Domain/`, `Application/`, `Infrastructure/`, `WebApi/`, `UseCases/` |
| Aggregate `UseCases/` | one per declared use case |
| Use case, `On{Fact}/` | Files only |

```text
{Product}.SharedKernel/
  Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
{Product}.Modules/
  Composition/
  Organizations/
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/  Exceptions/  IntegrationEvents/  Commands/  Ports/
    Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
    Teams/
      Domain/          Team.cs  TeamState.cs  ITeamRepository.cs  Events/  Exceptions/
      Application/     types used by two or more Team use cases
      Infrastructure/  TeamRepository.cs
      WebApi/          transport types used by two or more Team use cases
      UseCases/
        CreateTeam/    use case, flat: Command, Result, Handler, Validator, Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel
    UseCases/
      ReadTeamDirectory/        a use case no single aggregate owns
      OnTeamMemberRemoved/      a reaction
    Jobs/
```

provisions.heading: Keep Composition in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Which service registration calls sit outside `Program.cs` and the host registration modules? Look at the registration calls.
provisions.statement: Keep service registration in `Program.cs` and host registration modules.
provisions.rationale: Domain and Application declare abstractions for the hosts to implement. A registration call inside either layer makes the abstraction depend on the thing it abstracts, inverting the dependency direction. Each module registers its own Infrastructure types in its module Infrastructure folder, and `Program.cs` calls each module entry point in one visible order. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#keep-service-registration-in-hosts` for .NET.
provisions.example:
One registration entry point per module plus product plumbing has this shape:

```text
AddOrganizationsInfrastructure(...)
AddTeamsInfrastructure(...)
AddWebApi(...)
```

`Program.cs` keeps their call order visible. The WebApi entry point owns Problem Details, authentication, authorization, endpoint discovery, and OpenAPI.

provisions.heading: Keep Host Endpoints in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Which host endpoints without a handler sit outside their host project, or lack their mark? Look at the host endpoints beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: Each host endpoint without a handler MUST live in its host project.
provisions.rationale: Protocol endpoints, static assets, and development-only tooling have no use case folder to sit beside, so the host keeps them. Each still carries its mark, and the placement check accepts a host endpoint in the host.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementation Types Internal
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2001` for an implementation type that is not `internal sealed`.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, endpoint
provisions.statement: A handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, or endpoint implementation MUST be declared `internal sealed`.
provisions.rationale: A public type is an offer to every assembly, so an implementation left public invites callers it was never written for. Messages, results, markers, and ports stay public only when another assembly uses them; handlers, validators, and implementations stay `internal sealed`. Assembly scanning reads internal types through the one public marker, so it never justifies widening visibility. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#keep-implementation-types-hidden` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Use Case Folders Isolated
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2019` for a use case folder naming a type in another use case folder, other than one whose outermost type ends in `Command`, `Query`, `CommandResult` or `QueryResult`.
provisions.artifact: use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, endpoint, reaction
provisions.statement: A use case folder MUST reference no type in another use case folder, except the message and result of a use case it runs.
provisions.rationale: A use case folder holds one use case flat, so a reference between two such folders couples two slices that change for different reasons. A reaction or a use case that runs another use case sends that use case's command or query and reads its result, which is the published way in, so those types stay nameable. A type named by two use cases belongs in the aggregate module or shared kernel layer folder that holds every consumer naming it, under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. The rule applies to files and to global usings alike.

provisions.heading: Mirror Modules Aggregates and Use Cases in One Namespace Tree
provisions.evidence: Which types miss the product module aggregate use case namespace or name one outside its folder? Look at the namespaces beside the folders in the shared kernel and modules projects.
provisions.statement: Every type in the shared kernel and modules projects MUST live in the namespace tree that starts with the product name and follows the folders below the project root.
provisions.rationale: The namespace reads like the folder path, so `Claimwick.Spending.Expenses.UseCases.SubmitExpense` names the product module aggregate and use case without a map. Namespaces follow folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`, so a reader moves from a Domain aggregate to its handler its repository and its endpoint by name alone. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The Expenses aggregate of the Spending module fills one branch:

```text
Claimwick.Modules/Spending/Expenses/Domain/Expense.cs
Claimwick.Modules/Spending/Expenses/UseCases/SubmitExpense/SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.cs
```

The handler above lives in namespace `Claimwick.Spending.Expenses.UseCases.SubmitExpense`.

provisions.heading: Reach Another Module Only Through Contracts
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2020` for a module reference naming another module type outside its Contracts folder.
provisions.statement: A module MUST reach another module only through types its Contracts folder publishes.
provisions.rationale: The Contracts folder is the public surface of a module, sorted by kind: typed identifiers in `Identifiers/`, the refusals of rules other modules enforce in `Exceptions/`, integration events in `IntegrationEvents/`, the commands and queries other modules send with their results in `Commands/`, and ports that other modules call in `Ports/`. Domain may name the typed identifiers and refusals; ports and integration events stay outside Domain. A module that needs another module data reads it through a read port in the owner `Contracts/Ports/` folder that returns contract results keyed by typed identifier, or answers with its own query; it loads no foreign aggregate or repository. A command changes only its own module aggregates, and an act on another module aggregate runs as that module use case, dispatched or triggered by an integration event. A reaction to another module fact subscribes to the published integration event and never to the domain event.

provisions.heading: Separate the Shared Kernel from the Modules
provisions.evidence: Which projects sit outside the shared kernel, the modules project and their hosts, and does the shared kernel reference the modules project? Look at the solution file and the project references.
provisions.statement: Use a `{Product}.SharedKernel` project for what every module builds on and a `{Product}.Modules` project for the modules, with WebApi and optional Worker hosts, at every size.
provisions.rationale: The modules project then holds only business code and module slices, so a reader opening it sees the modules of the product and nothing else, and one use case stays in one tree instead of spreading across layer projects. The shared kernel names no module, so a change to one module never touches it, and the build refuses a shared kernel type that reaches into a module because the shared kernel project does not reference the modules project. Hosts stay separate projects, because two hosts can run the same modules.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/api/src/{Product}.SharedKernel/
apps/api/src/{Product}.Modules/
apps/api/src/{Product}.WebApi/
apps/api/src/{Product}.Worker/     only when background work needs its own process
```

provisions.heading: Use One Public Assembly Marker
provisions.evidence: Does the modules project expose one public static assembly marker, and does any other project expose one it needs not? Look at each project for its marker.
provisions.statement: Expose one public static assembly marker in the modules project for host endpoint discovery and scanning.
provisions.rationale: Scanners and the host need an assembly reference, and without a marker developers make handlers public to supply one. One public static marker in the modules project gives the host and the scanners their reference while every handler stays internal.

provisions.heading: Centralize .NET Build Settings
provisions.evidence: Does `apps/api/Directory.Build.props` set the manifest target framework with nullable types, implicit usings, and warnings as errors? Look at that file.
provisions.statement: `apps/api/Directory.Build.props` MUST set the target framework of the manifest .NET stack release, and enable nullable types, implicit usings, and warnings as errors.
provisions.rationale: When each project sets its own framework, nullability, usings, and warnings, one project silently builds under weaker rules and its warnings go unread. One file owns those settings, so a change applies to every project and review sees it in one diff.

provisions.heading: Centralize NuGet Versions
provisions.evidence: Does `apps/api/Directory.Packages.props` enable central management with the manifest pins, and which project files carry versions? Look at the central file beside the project files.
provisions.statement: `apps/api/Directory.Packages.props` MUST enable central package management and carry an exact version within each manifest pin.
provisions.rationale: A version written in a project file is invisible to the manifest that owns it, and two projects drift to two versions of one package. With central management, project files name packages only, and one file carries the exact version within each pin, so an upgrade touches one place.

provisions.heading: Commit the Tool Manifest
provisions.evidence: Which local tools that a documented command invokes escape the root `.config/dotnet-tools.json` pin, including the Stryker.NET runner? Look at the tool manifest.
provisions.statement: The root `.config/dotnet-tools.json` MUST pin every local .NET tool that a documented command invokes.
provisions.rationale: A tool installed by version range resolves differently on two machines, and a build that passes locally fails in CI. Pinning every tool a documented command invokes means local and CI runs use one version; when a tool ships in the manifest's .NET release, its pin matches that release. The manifest pins the Stryker.NET runner that `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines` names.

provisions.heading: Set the SDK Floor at the Workspace Root
provisions.evidence: Does the root `global.json` set the manifest major release's first feature band with `latestFeature` roll-forward? Look at the root `global.json`.
provisions.statement: The root `global.json` MUST set the first feature band of the manifest .NET major release as its SDK version and roll forward with `latestFeature`.
provisions.rationale: The first feature band of the manifest's major release is the lowest SDK that builds the workspace, and `latestFeature` roll-forward lets a later feature band of the same major release build it too. A newer major release needs a workspace change, so a local machine and CI stay on one major line. The compiler and its analyzers ship with the SDK, so a different SDK can still build different output within that line; the floor sets the minimum, not identical output. The manifest names the major release; `Directory.Build.props` sets its target framework.

provisions.heading: Define the Shared Domain Contracts Once
provisions.evidence: Which shared Domain contracts repeat, or which `DomainException` or `AggregateRoot<TId>` break their declared shape? Look at the shared contracts.
provisions.statement: Declare the shared Domain contracts once in the shared kernel Domain folder and reuse them across every module.
provisions.rationale: Every module raises events, throws domain exceptions, and identifies aggregates, so each shared contract declared twice becomes two contracts that drift. Declaring `IDomainEvent`, `DomainException`, `IStronglyTypedId`, `Entity<TId>`, `IAggregateRoot`, and `AggregateRoot<TId>` once in the shared kernel Domain folder gives every module the same mechanics. Generic handling constrains its parameters with `IAggregateRoot`, as in `IRepository<T> where T : IAggregateRoot`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#reuse-the-shared-domain-contracts-across-modules` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Document Every Public Domain Contract
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1011` for a public Domain type or member without XML documentation.
provisions.statement: Every public Domain type and member MUST carry XML documentation stating the business constraint, result, or failure it represents.
provisions.rationale: A public Domain member is a business promise, and its XML documentation is where a reader learns the constraint, result, or failure it represents. A summary that restates the member name adds nothing; a mutation method names its source states, resulting state, protected invariant, and recorded event. Without that, callers infer the contract from the implementation and miss the rule. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#describe-every-public-domain-contract-in-documentation` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Implement Domain Services as Stateless Classes
provisions.evidence: Which domain services hold state, take non-Domain parameters, or call a provider? Look at each domain service.
provisions.statement: A domain service MUST be a stateless sealed class accepting and returning Domain values.
provisions.rationale: Some calculations span concepts with no natural aggregate owner, and a stateless service holds that calculation with no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call. Application loads the aggregates, calls the service, and passes its result into aggregate behavior. The service carries a mark naming its rule, so the builder links it to the rule it computes. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#use-stateless-domain-services-for-ownerless-rules` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Clock Reads and Random Values Out of Domain
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1009` for a clock, randomness, or identifier read in Domain.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST NOT read a clock, a random source or a new `Guid`, so every such value arrives as an argument.
provisions.rationale: `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `TimeProvider`, `Random`, `RandomNumberGenerator` and `Guid.NewGuid` or `Guid.CreateVersion7` return a different value on each call, so a Domain method that reads one cannot be tested with a fixed value. Receiving each value as an argument keeps every Domain call a pure function of its inputs. The Application layer obtains each value through its owned port and passes it in. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#pass-nondeterministic-values-into-domain` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Free of Outer-Layer Concerns
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1001` for Domain code naming an outer-layer type.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST reference only the .NET base class library and product-owned Domain types.
provisions.rationale: A package reference is a direction: once Domain names a persistence or web type, business rules start depending on the framework instead of the framework depending on them. Keeping Domain to the base class library and product-owned types means a provider change cannot reach business behavior. Infrastructure registers persisted discriminators and mappings, so Domain carries no serialization attribute. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#keep-domain-independent-of-outer-layers` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Double and Float Out of Exact Quantities
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1008` for a `double` or `float` type in Domain.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST NOT declare a `double` or `float` for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality.
provisions.rationale: `double` and `float` represent most decimal fractions only approximately, so two amounts that read as equal compare as different. The shared `Money` object holds a `decimal`, and a rate applied to a `Money` amount is a `decimal` too. The analyzer reports the declaration in Domain that breaks this form. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#keep-binary-floating-point-out-of-exact-quantities` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep ID Representations Aligned at Every Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which identifiers break the same UUID text form across Domain, persistence, transport, and client boundaries? Look at one identifier in each boundary form.
provisions.statement: Represent an identifier the same way in Domain, persistence, transport, and generated clients.
provisions.rationale: An identifier crosses every boundary in the table below, and each boundary that invents its own text form forces converters at both ends. One UUID text form everywhere means a value copied from a log, a route, or a JSON payload parses at the next boundary without translation. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#align-id-representations-at-every-boundary` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Repository Interfaces in Domain
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1010` for a repository interface exposing a query surface.
provisions.statement: A repository interface MUST expose only aggregate and Domain types for exactly one aggregate root, without `IQueryable`, a session, or a generic CRUD surface.
provisions.rationale: One repository per aggregate keeps the write boundary aligned with the consistency boundary: the interface loads and stages complete aggregates of its own type, and nothing else. `GetByIdAsync` throws `{Aggregate}NotFoundException` for a required load, so handlers repeat no null check; a nullable `FindBy...Async` is reserved for lookups where absence is normal. A flow that finds a record or creates it is two use cases that the boundary owning the flow chooses between, following `litespec/backend/application#implement-one-outcome-path-per-command`. `IQueryable`, sessions, and generic CRUD surfaces would leak query shaping and provider behavior into Domain, so the interface exposes none of them. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#expose-repositories-for-one-aggregate-only` for .NET. This interface is the write side only. Reading for a Query uses a Read Model owned by Application and shaped by Infrastructure, and that path declares no Domain interface. A repository that gained a projection method would put query shapes in Domain, which is the coupling this layer exists to prevent. A `store` aggregate owns no repository interface; its port carries the state its owner holds.

provisions.heading: Make Money and Decimal Rules Explicit
provisions.evidence: Which monetary amounts escape the `decimal` inside the shared `Money` object with amount and currency? Look at each monetary amount.
provisions.statement: A monetary amount MUST use `decimal` inside one shared `Money` value object carrying an ISO 4217 currency code and serializing as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`.
provisions.rationale: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly, so money computed in `double` drifts by cents. The shared `Money` object keeps a `decimal` amount with an ISO 4217 currency code, and the owning module record defines supported currencies, scale, rounding, sign rules, and cross-currency arithmetic. Infrastructure maps that precision explicitly, and a use case fixed to one currency accepts an amount alone while stating that currency in its record. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#model-money-with-exact-decimal-values` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Changing Root Method with One Use Case
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5003` for a root method carrying other than one use-case mark, and `LS5002` for a mark on a reading or private method.
provisions.statement: A root method that changes state MUST carry exactly one `<implements>` mark naming its use case.
provisions.rationale: The mark is the XML documentation tag that ties a method to the use case whose act it performs, so the builder and the analyzer read the same link. A reading or private method performs no act and carries no use-case mark, which `LS5002` reports. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#give-each-use-case-its-own-act` for .NET; the model check on the same rule stays on that generic provision.

provisions.heading: Model Child Entities as Sealed Classes
provisions.evidence: Which child entity declarations escape the sealed class deriving from `Entity<TId>` or creation through root methods? Look at each child entity.
provisions.statement: A child entity MUST be a sealed class deriving from the project-owned `Entity<TId>`.
provisions.rationale: The base supplies typed identity and identity equality, so the child declares its own data and behavior only. The root creates, finds, and changes its children through business methods, and a child exposes no mutable state outside the root. A child is a design choice inside its aggregate: it appears in code and the glossary, never as a record. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#keep-child-entities-inside-the-aggregate-boundary` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Every Aggregate Lifecycle with State Records
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1003` for an aggregate with no `State` property, `LS1004` for a state case left unsealed, and `LS1013` for a switch that leaves a sealed state case to its discard arm.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST expose its lifecycle only through one `State` property backed by an abstract `{Aggregate}State` record with sealed per-state records.
provisions.rationale: An enum, status string, boolean flag, parallel nullable field, or computed state cannot carry state-specific data. State records hold each state's data, aggregate methods own the transitions, and even a one-state aggregate defines its hierarchy so later states have a home. The C# compiler does not check that a switch over the hierarchy covers every sealed case: a switch expression needs a discard arm to compile without warning CS8509, and a sealed case with no arm of its own reaches that discard arm at run time. `LS1013` reports a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm, and tests cover the discard path for a case added later. The sealed set matches the aggregate's declared `states`, which is the link the builder follows. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-aggregate-lifecycle-with-state-types` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Every Closed Set of Domain Values Without Enums
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1002` for an enum declared in Domain and `LS1013` for a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST model every closed set as an abstract record base with sealed cases exposing one stable `Code`, converting labels through `FromCode`.
provisions.rationale: An enum is a named integer: it carries no case data, admits undefined values through a cast, and forces parallel fields when a case later gains data. A record hierarchy carries each case's data in its own sealed record, and a boundary converts a label through `FromCode` instead of `ToString`, so an unrecognized label becomes a validation failure rather than a silent default. The C# compiler does not check that a switch over the hierarchy covers every sealed case: a switch expression needs a discard arm to compile without warning CS8509, and a sealed case with no arm of its own reaches that discard arm at run time. `LS1013` reports a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm, and tests cover the discard path for a case added later. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-closed-set-of-domain-values-as-a-closed-type-hierarchy` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Value Objects as Records
provisions.evidence: Which value objects escape the immutable record with static creation and no base type? Look at each value object.
provisions.statement: A value object MUST be an immutable C# record with no base type.
provisions.rationale: Immutability with comparison by complete value lets two instances with the same data stand in for each other. The type exposes no setter and no implicit conversion, and creation through a named static method keeps every construction path under the validation the type declares. A value object containing a collection implements content equality and a matching hash for its declared ordering rule, copying incoming collections and returning read-only views. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#use-immutable-value-objects-for-domain-concepts` and `litespec/backend/domain#define-collection-value-semantics-explicitly` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Raise Immutable Domain Facts
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1007` for a domain event that is not an immutable record.
provisions.statement: A domain event MUST be a public immutable record named `{Aggregate}{PastFact}Event` implementing `IDomainEvent`, carrying business data only and one mark naming its event record.
provisions.rationale: The `{Aggregate}{PastFact}Event` name tells a reader which aggregate raised the fact without opening the file. The event carries business data only: typed identifiers and the values its reactions need. It carries no aggregate, session, service, mutable collection, or exception, because a mutable payload lets a reaction observe state that changed after the fact. Envelope identity, such as message and causation identity, lives on the published integration event that carries the fact outside the process. Its `Classification` comes from the event record its mark names, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/stack#generate-runtime-values-from-the-records`. Only the aggregate root raises events, through `RaiseDomainEvent` on the shared base. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#raise-immutable-facts-as-domain-events` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Reject Business Violations with Domain Exceptions
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1005` for a throw outside a `DomainException` subclass and `LS1006` for a domain exception that is misnamed or open.
provisions.statement: A rejected business rule MUST throw a `DomainException` subclass named `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception`, carrying the refusal `code` and one mark naming its rule.
provisions.rationale: One exception type per rule puts the stable code and the message in the type, and its `Code` comes from the refusal result its rule names, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/stack#generate-runtime-values-from-the-records`. The call site passes only domain values and two rules never share a type by accident. A shared rule exception with caller-supplied codes lets any caller invent a code and lets unrelated rules merge silently. An invariant rule is checked in the root's factory and methods, and a precondition rule is checked in the use-case validator or the root's method. Each exception's code equals the refusal `code` on the result record it answers. Names lead with the aggregate root and follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`; this provision owns the one-type-per-rule shape and the code each type carries. Domain throws no `InvalidOperationException`, `ArgumentException`, validation, HTTP, or provider exception for a business rejection, and carries no transport status. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#reject-business-violations-with-dedicated-refusals` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Use Strongly Typed Version 7 Identifiers
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1012` for an `Id` struct outside the strongly typed form, or a raw `Guid` as an aggregate identity.
provisions.statement: An aggregate identity MUST be a `readonly record struct` wrapping one version 7 `Guid`, declaring no implicit conversion, primitive alias, or public parameterless creation path.
provisions.rationale: A bare `Guid` parameter accepts any identifier, including an empty one and one meant for another aggregate. The typed struct rejects `Guid.Empty` and the struct default in every factory, implements `IStronglyTypedId` and `IParsable<TId>`, and declares no implicit conversion or parameterless creation, so a wrong identifier fails at the boundary. New values arrive from the caller: a factory takes its identifier as an argument, and a method that needs several takes a generator. Domain reads no clock and calls no static source of time or randomness, which keeps business behavior deterministic and testable. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#identify-aggregates-with-strongly-typed-version-7-values` for .NET. When two callers generate the same value, persistence rejects the duplicate key and the operation fails on the same path as any other write conflict, with the violation mapped to the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`.

provisions.heading: Use the Domain Layer Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Which aggregate Domain folders break the states events exceptions and concepts layout, or hold a typed identifier another module names? Look at each Domain folder beside its Contracts folder.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate Domain folder its states, events, exceptions, and concepts in the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate Domain folder holds everything one aggregate owns in the files the layout names, so a reader finds the full aggregate in one place. Namespaces follow the folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`, and each file sits at the lowest folder holding its consumers under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. A typed identifier that another module names lives in its owner `Contracts/Identifiers/` folder, and shared values live in the shared kernel `Domain/` folder with the exceptions of the rules they enforce, which take the product as their home, such as `rule/claimwick.amount-is-never-negative`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#organize-a-module-by-aggregate-and-concept` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The Domain layer folder layout is:

```text
{Product}.SharedKernel/
  Domain/                         shared kernel: AggregateRoot, Entity, IAggregateRoot, IDomainEvent, IStronglyTypedId, DomainException
{Product}.Modules/
  Posts/                          one aggregate whose name matches the module: kept flat in the module folder
    Domain/
      Post.cs
      PostTitle.cs
      IPostRepository.cs
      States/
        PostState.cs
        PostDraftState.cs
        PostPublishedState.cs
        PostArchivedState.cs
      Events/
        PostCreatedEvent.cs
        PostPublishedEvent.cs
      Exceptions/
        PostIdentityRequiredException.cs
        PostAlreadyPublishedException.cs
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/
        PostId.cs                 only when another module names it; else beside Post.cs
  Shipping/                       one aggregate whose name differs from the module, with a domain union in a concept folder
    Shipments/
      Domain/
        Shipment.cs
        ShipmentId.cs
        IShipmentRepository.cs
        Outcomes/
          ShipmentOutcome.cs
          ShipmentDeliveredOutcome.cs
          ShipmentReturnedOutcome.cs
          ShipmentLostOutcome.cs
        States/
          ShipmentState.cs
          ShipmentPendingState.cs
          ShipmentDispatchedState.cs
          ShipmentDeliveredState.cs
        Events/
          ShipmentOutcomeRecordedEvent.cs
  Customers/                      more than one aggregate: one plural folder per aggregate
    CustomerAccounts/
      Domain/                     namespace Shop.Customers.CustomerAccounts.Domain
        CustomerAccount.cs
        CustomerAccountId.cs
        ICustomerAccountRepository.cs
        States/
          CustomerAccountState.cs
          CustomerAccountClaimedState.cs
        Events/
          CustomerAccountRestrictedEvent.cs
    Consents/
      Domain/                     namespace Shop.Customers.Consents.Domain
        Consent.cs
        ConsentId.cs
        IConsentRepository.cs
        States/
          ConsentState.cs
          ConsentGrantedState.cs
        Events/
          ConsentGrantedEvent.cs
```

Each aggregate repository interface stays with the aggregate it loads. Module and aggregate folders keep the same names at every layer, per `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

provisions.heading: Use the Project Aggregate Root Contract
provisions.evidence: Which aggregate root declarations escape the sealed class deriving from the project-owned `AggregateRoot<TId>`? Look at each root declaration.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST be a sealed class deriving from the project-owned `AggregateRoot<TId>`, taking identity and event mechanics from that base.
provisions.rationale: One project-owned base gives every aggregate the same identity and event mechanics: typed identity, a pending event collection, protected recording, and clearing. The root is a sealed class, so no behavior extends an aggregate by inheritance. The root carries a mark naming its aggregate record, so the builder links the record by that mark. A shared base that also owned timestamps, audit, tenancy, lifecycle, or persistence would force every aggregate to carry behavior most never need. The base carries the aggregate version only as persistence metadata that Domain never reads or sets. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#take-identity-and-events-from-the-project-root-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Assert Observable Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Which BDD scenarios assert no response, read, event, record, or other observable outcome? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD scenario MUST assert a response, later read, durable event, audit record, or other observable outcome.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that runs requests without asserting proves only that nothing threw. Asserting a response, a later read, a durable event, an audit record, or another observable outcome shows the public boundary achieved the expected behavior.

provisions.heading: Avoid Routine Scenario Duplication
provisions.evidence: Which unit or validation tests repeat as a duplicate BDD scenario? Look at the narrower suites beside the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A test author MUST NOT duplicate every unit or validation test as a BDD scenario.
provisions.rationale: A unit test fails at the exact rule and runs in milliseconds; the same test duplicated as a BDD scenario fails at a public boundary after a full setup. Duplication slows the suite and moves the failure away from its cause, so routine behavior stays in its narrower tests.

provisions.heading: Drive Public Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which step definitions call outside the HTTP API and the declared public boundaries? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step MUST call the HTTP API or another declared public system boundary.
provisions.rationale: A step that calls the HTTP API or another declared public boundary proves what a caller can observe. A step that reaches past the boundary depends on implementation details, so a refactoring breaks the scenario without breaking the behavior.

provisions.heading: Exclude Production Internals
provisions.evidence: Which step definitions resolve a repository, handler, session, or the production service provider? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step definition MUST NOT resolve repositories, handlers, sessions, or the production service provider.
provisions.rationale: Resolving a repository, handler, session, or the production service provider runs the behavior without the boundary the scenario claims to verify. The scenario then passes while the public path stays untested, so step definitions resolve none of them.

provisions.heading: Group Feature Classes by Module
provisions.evidence: Which feature classes sit outside module folders without a documented grouping? Look at `Acceptance.Tests` beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Group feature classes under module folders in `Acceptance.Tests`.
provisions.rationale: A scenario filed by business module sits beside the vocabulary it exercises, so a reader finds every example of one module in one folder. A flat or technically grouped suite scatters them.

provisions.heading: Isolate Scenario Execution
provisions.evidence: Which scenarios fail alone or in another order, or which runs skip the state reset? Look at the acceptance suite runs.
provisions.statement: The acceptance suite MUST reset database state between scenarios and avoid scenario-order dependencies.
provisions.rationale: State left by one scenario becomes a hidden precondition of the next, and the suite passes only in one order. Resetting database state between scenarios removes that coupling, so any scenario runs alone or in any order.

provisions.heading: Keep Steps Vocabulary-Scoped
provisions.evidence: Which reusable step sets serve more than one business vocabulary without a documented scope? Look at each reusable step set beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep step definitions narrow and reusable only within one business vocabulary.
provisions.rationale: A step reused across vocabularies, such as a generic success step, means something subtly different in each place and couples unrelated modules to one definition. Steps narrow to one business vocabulary keep their meaning exact.

provisions.heading: Limit Database Assertions
provisions.evidence: Which direct database assertions name no documented durable boundary? Look at each direct database assertion in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD scenario MUST use direct database assertions only for a documented durable boundary.
provisions.rationale: The database is an implementation detail, so asserting its rows couples the scenario to storage shapes. A direct assertion is allowed only for a documented durable boundary, such as an outbox record, where the stored row is itself the promised evidence.

provisions.heading: Limit Scenario Context
provisions.evidence: Which scenario context objects hold more than scenario state without a documented use? Look at the scenario context beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Store values for one scenario in a scenario context object.
provisions.rationale: One context object holding the scenario's own values keeps shared state visible and small. Resolving services from it turns it into a service locator that hides what the scenario depends on.

provisions.heading: Mark Pull-Request Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Which pull-request subsets grow beyond their stated bound or lose their owner? Look at the marked subset beside the proves claims.
provisions.statement: Mark the small pull-request subset separately from the proves claim, with a critical test trait on the LightBDD scenario.
provisions.rationale: The critical trait selects the small subset whose failure stops a release, for fast pull-request feedback. The marking stays separate from the proves claim, which records scenario proof rather than release gating. A marking that every scenario carries selects nothing, so the subset keeps a stated size bound and an owner who keeps it there.

provisions.heading: Own Scenario Data
provisions.evidence: Which BDD scenarios borrow identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, or expected state? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: Each BDD scenario MUST own its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that borrows identifiers or state prepared elsewhere breaks when that other setup changes. Owning its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state keeps each scenario self-contained and runnable alone.

provisions.heading: Preserve Scenario Failures
provisions.evidence: Which hooks skip awaiting setup or cleanup, or replace the original scenario failure? Look at each hook in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD hook MUST await asynchronous setup and cleanup without replacing the original scenario failure.
provisions.rationale: Setup and cleanup are asynchronous, and an unawaited hook leaves the next scenario running against a half-reset database. A hook that throws during cleanup can also replace the scenario's own failure, hiding the real cause. Awaiting both without replacing the original failure keeps the evidence trustworthy.

provisions.heading: Prove a Scenario from Every BDD Scenario
provisions.evidence: Which BDD scenarios lack one `proves` claim naming their scenario? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: Every BDD scenario MUST carry one `proves` claim naming the scenario it proves.
provisions.rationale: A scenario pairs one `given` situation and `when` action with the `then` result they lead to, and the proves claim is what ties the BDD scenario to that record. The claim names it, the steps call the proved use case, and the assertion checks its result; without the claim, the model builder cannot tell which scenario the BDD scenario proves. A LightBDD scenario carries the claim as a proves mark on the scenario method, in the style the project declares. The model builder reads proves marks on C# methods, so a Gherkin feature file would not count as proof and would state each scenario twice beside its scenario record.
provisions.example: `/// <proves>scenario/cancel-order.canceling-twice-is-refused</proves>` traces a cancellation BDD scenario to its scenario record.

provisions.heading: Select Shared Critical Examples
provisions.evidence: Which BDD scenarios trace to no cross-layer example the team discusses in business language? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A test author MUST create a BDD scenario only when business-language form improves shared understanding of cross-layer behavior.
provisions.rationale: A scenario costs maintenance on every behavior change, so the suite earns its keep only where business-language form improves shared understanding of cross-layer behavior. Each selected scenario gives product, domain, engineering, and testing discussions one executable example instead of four retellings.

provisions.heading: Translate Business Phrases
provisions.evidence: Which step definitions skip the typed test-driver call? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step definition MUST translate a business phrase into a typed test-driver call.
provisions.rationale: HTTP calls, JSON shapes, and assertion mechanics in a step definition hide the business phrase the scenario promises. Translating each phrase into a typed test-driver call keeps the scenario readable while the driver owns the boundary mechanics.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Dependencies Narrow
provisions.evidence: Which Application project files reference beyond the permitted abstractions and the one read boundary? Look at the Application project file.
provisions.statement: Application MUST reference only LiteBus command and query abstractions, required read abstractions, and needed Microsoft abstractions, plus the `IQuerySession` read boundary.
provisions.rationale: Application coordinates; Infrastructure hides technology. A provider package in Application makes the coordination layer depend on the technology it was meant to stay free of. The Statement names the one permitted read boundary; everything else provider-shaped stays out. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/dependencies#keep-application-free-of-provider-packages`.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Package-Free
provisions.evidence: Which Domain project files reference a package beyond the base class library? Look at the Domain project file.
provisions.statement: The Domain project MUST reference no package beyond the .NET base class library.
provisions.rationale: A package in Domain makes business rules depend on a framework, a provider, or a messenger. Marten, LiteBus, ASP.NET Core, injection, serialization, and logging packages all stay outside, so Domain builds on the base class library alone. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/dependencies#keep-domain-dependency-free`.

provisions.heading: Keep .NET Production and Test Projects Separate
provisions.evidence: Which production or test project files, or solution files, sit outside their fixed address? Look at `apps/api/`.
provisions.statement: Production projects MUST live under `apps/api/src/` and test projects under `apps/api/tests/`, with the solution directly under `apps/api/`.
provisions.rationale: Production under `apps/api/src/` and tests under `apps/api/tests/` make a test dependency reaching production visible in the path itself. The solution sits directly under `apps/api/`, beside both. A workspace AppHost is the one production project outside `src/`, placed by `litespec/backend/dotnet/workspace#place-a-workspace-apphost-beside-the-applications-it-runs`. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/structure#keep-production-and-test-code-separate`.
provisions.example:
The baseline tree is:

```text
apps/api/
  {ProjectName}.slnx
  Directory.Build.props
  Directory.Packages.props
  src/
    {ProjectName}.Domain/
    {ProjectName}.Application.Abstractions/
    {ProjectName}.Application/
    {ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
    {ProjectName}.WebApi/
    {ProjectName}.Worker/             when background work needs a host
    {ProjectName}.AppHost/            when an orchestration host runs the API alone
    {ProjectName}.ServiceDefaults/    when a local orchestration host is used
  tests/
    {ProjectName}.Architecture.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Integration.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Acceptance.Tests/   when size is large
    {ProjectName}.Domain.Tests/       optional unit tests
    {ProjectName}.Application.Tests/  optional unit tests
```

Worker is conditional on the extension that runs background work. Acceptance.Tests is required when `size` is large and optional otherwise. Domain.Tests and Application.Tests are optional in both sizes. `AppHost` and `ServiceDefaults` are local hosting and diagnostics projects rather than application layers. An application that orchestrates its local dependencies another way ships neither and records no departure for their absence.

provisions.heading: Keep One Application Assembly
provisions.evidence: Which command, query, result, validator, handler, or event handler files escape the Application project, or which cross-module contracts escape Application.Abstractions and the merged Application? Look at the Application project files beside the shared contracts.
provisions.statement: An application MUST place commands, queries, results, validators, handlers, event handler classes, and module-owned ports in one Application project, and cross-module contracts in Application.Abstractions, or in Application where the project merges them under `litespec/backend/dotnet/ext/layer-projects#use-five-application-projects`.
provisions.rationale: Splitting Application into Write, Read, Contracts, and event-handler assemblies would buy a deployment boundary the stack never uses, and every use case would pay for it with a project reference to cross. The separation this stack keeps is the one [Fowler describes as CQRS](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html): the command and query models differ, while one assembly holds them. Event handlers live in Application `On{Fact}` folders of the aggregate whose records they change; job host classes live in Worker or Infrastructure with the scheduling concerns, under `litespec/backend/architecture#declare-the-execution-host-for-work-that-outlives-a-request`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Test Projects the Size Requires
provisions.evidence: Which solution trees miss Architecture or Integration test projects, or add Acceptance outside size large? Look at `apps/api/tests/` beside the declared size.
provisions.statement: A backend solution MUST hold exactly the test projects its size requires: Architecture and Integration for small, adding Acceptance for large.
provisions.rationale: The required suites match the size: Architecture and Integration for small, adding Acceptance for large. Unit test projects stay optional in both sizes, and Acceptance stays optional for small. An Acceptance project without the executable BDD extension is an unnamed baseline project: select the extension, or name the project for what it actually is. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/backend/testing#keep-the-test-suites-the-size-requires`.
provisions.example:
A test suite can contain:

```text
{ProjectName}.Architecture.Tests/
{ProjectName}.Integration.Tests/
{ProjectName}.Acceptance.Tests/
```

A small solution holds the first two; Acceptance appears when the executable BDD extension activates.

provisions.heading: Mirror Modules in Folders and Namespaces
provisions.evidence: Which projects miss one folder and namespace per module, or name one outside its module? Look at the module folders and namespaces in every project.
provisions.statement: Every project MUST give each module one folder and namespace.
provisions.rationale: The folder name derives from the module identifier, so `module/spending` owns the `Spending` folder in every project, and the namespace follows the folder under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`. The same module names in every layer let a reader move from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint without a map. This provision states the five-project form of the module organization that `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` states for the module layout.
provisions.example:
The `Spending` module owns one folder in every project, and each namespace follows its folder:

```text
Claimwick.Domain/Spending/Expenses/Expense.cs
Claimwick.Application/Spending/Expenses/SubmitExpense/SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.cs
```

The handler above lives in namespace `Claimwick.Application.Spending.Expenses.SubmitExpense`.

provisions.heading: Run LiteSpec.Analyzers in Every Application Project
provisions.evidence: Which layer project files miss `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin with `PrivateAssets="all"`? Look at each layer project file.
provisions.statement: Reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin, with `PrivateAssets="all"`, from every Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi project.
provisions.rationale: The analyzers report a breach of a .NET provision in the editor and the build, at the line that breaks it, with a link to the provision. Without them, a breach surfaces only in review, if at all. The package is a development dependency: it adds nothing to the built assemblies, so Domain stays package-free at run time. `LS2016` reports a pipeline-owned collaborator in a handler constructor; its default list covers the LiteBus unit of work, idempotency store, and outbox, and a project adds its uniqueness claim service. [Check .NET code with the analyzers](../../../analyzers/check-dotnet-code-with-the-analyzers.md) sets it up, and [Analyzer rules](../../../analyzers/README.md) lists what each rule reports.
provisions.example:
```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="LiteSpec.Analyzers" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
```

provisions.heading: Use Five Application Projects
provisions.evidence: Which projects sit outside the five baseline projects, the merged small layout, or the allowed hosts and Worker? Look at the solution file beside the declared project size.
provisions.statement: Use Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi as the five baseline projects at every size, with a small project merging Application.Abstractions into Application and hosts and a Worker project as allowed extras.
provisions.rationale: `Application.Abstractions` holds the contracts that more than one module names: the pipeline's own positions, the cross-module ports, the transport-neutral failures, and the published integration events. It references Domain and the required LiteBus module abstractions, and nothing else, so no type in it can name a use case, a handler, or a module. That refusal is why it is a project rather than a folder. A folder inside Application cannot decline what a developer puts in it, and the folder that tries becomes the place every unplaced type goes. A small project with few cross-module contracts may merge them into Application, trading that protection for one less project. An implementation never belongs there. The project name states the test, and a type that cannot pass it belongs to a module under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. Hosts support local hosting and diagnostics. They are hosts rather than layer projects. A Worker project hosts background work under `litespec/backend/architecture#create-a-worker-project-when-background-work-needs-its-own-process`.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Domain/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Application.Abstractions/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Application/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.WebApi/
```

provisions.heading: Use the Domain Module Layout
provisions.evidence: Which Domain module folders break the one plural folder per aggregate with states, events, exceptions, and concepts? Look at each module folder.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate a folder named with its plural root name, holding its states, events, exceptions, and concepts in the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate folder holds everything one aggregate owns in the files the layout names, so a reader finds the full aggregate in one place. Namespaces follow the folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`, and each file sits at the lowest folder holding its consumers under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/backend/domain#organize-a-module-by-aggregate-and-concept`.
provisions.example:
The Domain module layout is:

```text
{ProjectName}.Domain/
  Shared/
    AggregateRoot.cs
    Entity.cs
    IAggregateRoot.cs
    IDomainEvent.cs
    StronglyTypedIds/
      IStronglyTypedId.cs
    Exceptions/
      DomainException.cs
  Posts/                          one aggregate whose name matches the module: kept flat in the module folder
    Post.cs
    PostId.cs
    PostTitle.cs
    IPostRepository.cs
    States/
      PostState.cs
      PostDraftState.cs
      PostPublishedState.cs
      PostArchivedState.cs
    Events/
      PostCreatedEvent.cs
      PostPublishedEvent.cs
    Exceptions/
      PostIdentityRequiredException.cs
      PostAlreadyPublishedException.cs
  Shipping/                       one aggregate whose name differs from the module, with a domain union in a concept folder
    Shipments/
      Shipment.cs
      ShipmentId.cs
      IShipmentRepository.cs
      Outcomes/
        ShipmentOutcome.cs
        ShipmentDeliveredOutcome.cs
        ShipmentReturnedOutcome.cs
        ShipmentLostOutcome.cs
      States/
        ShipmentState.cs
        ShipmentPendingState.cs
        ShipmentDispatchedState.cs
        ShipmentDeliveredState.cs
      Events/
        ShipmentOutcomeRecordedEvent.cs
  Customers/                      more than one aggregate: one plural folder per aggregate
    CustomerAccounts/               namespace Shop.Domain.Customers.CustomerAccounts
      CustomerAccount.cs
      CustomerAccountId.cs
      ICustomerAccountRepository.cs
      States/
        CustomerAccountState.cs
        CustomerAccountClaimedState.cs
      Events/
        CustomerAccountRestrictedEvent.cs
    Consents/                       namespace Shop.Domain.Customers.Consents
      Consent.cs
      ConsentId.cs
      IConsentRepository.cs
      States/
        ConsentState.cs
        ConsentGrantedState.cs
      Events/
        ConsentGrantedEvent.cs
```

Each aggregate-specific repository interface stays with the aggregate it loads. Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi use the same module and per-aggregate folder names, per `litespec/backend/dotnet/ext/layer-projects#mirror-modules-in-folders-and-namespaces`.

provisions.heading: Use the Endpoint Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Which endpoint folders miss the endpoint, request and response models, or mappings named for the use case? Look at each endpoint folder.
provisions.statement: Place each endpoint in a folder named for its use case under its module and aggregate, with the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Transport types take the names their boundary roles assign under `litespec/backend/api#name-transport-types-by-their-boundary-role`, and transport mapping lives in WebApi under `litespec/backend/application#keep-mappings-at-the-owning-boundary`. Response models carry the query's declared `include` groups. Module nesting, including the single-aggregate flat form, follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.
provisions.example:
The endpoint layout is:

```text
{ProjectName}.WebApi/
  Endpoints/
    Posts/                          single aggregate whose name matches the module
      CreateDraft/
        CreateDraftEndpoint.cs
        CreateDraftRequestModel.cs
        CreateDraftResponseModel.cs
        CreateDraftApiMappings.cs
      GetPost/
        GetPostEndpoint.cs
        GetPostResponseModel.cs
        GetPostApiMappings.cs
    Customers/                      two aggregates: operations nest under each aggregate
      CustomerAccounts/
        RestrictAccount/
          RestrictAccountEndpoint.cs
          RestrictAccountRequestModel.cs
          RestrictAccountApiMappings.cs
      Consents/
        GrantConsent/
          GrantConsentEndpoint.cs
          GrantConsentRequestModel.cs
          GrantConsentApiMappings.cs
  Errors/
    GlobalExceptionHandler.cs
    ProblemDetailsApiMappings.cs
  Security/
    CurrentActor.cs
  OpenApi/
  Program.cs
```

provisions.heading: Use the Operation Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Which operation folders miss message, result, validator, or handler files named for the use case, or which event handlers escape their `On{Fact}` folder? Look at each operation folder.
provisions.statement: Place each operation in a folder named for its use case under its module and aggregate, with the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Type names derive from the use-case identifier with the architectural suffix, so `use-case/spending.submit-expense` owns `SubmitExpenseCommand` under `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`. Only a use case or a handled fact gets a folder: any other type sits flat in the folder that owns it under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`, and a handled fact's folder takes the `On{Fact}` name with its marked handler classes. Each result type carries one case per result, and each refusal carries the refusal `code` from its result record. A query result type carries one member per declared `include` group, and each result part is named after its result under `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result`.
provisions.example:
The operation layout is:

```text
{ProjectName}.Application.Abstractions/     contracts more than one module names
  Clock/
    IClock.cs
  Failures/
    ResourceNotFoundException.cs
    UseCaseForbiddenException.cs
    UseCaseConflictException.cs
  Validation/
    ValidationErrors.cs
{ProjectName}.Application/
  Pipeline/                         the pipeline's own stages, and nothing else
    ApplicationPipeline.cs
    AuthorizationGuard.cs
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module: operations sit directly under the module
    IPostArchive.cs                 a port several Posts use cases name
    CreateDraft/
      CreateDraftCommand.cs
      CreateDraftCommandResult.cs
      CreateDraftCommandValidator.cs
      CreateDraftCommandHandler.cs
    GetPost/
      GetPostQuery.cs
      GetPostQueryResult.cs
      GetPostQueryValidator.cs
      GetPostQueryHandler.cs
    ListPosts/
      ListPostsQuery.cs
      ListPostsQueryResult.cs
      ListPostsQueryResultItem.cs
      ListPostsQueryValidator.cs
      ListPostsQueryHandler.cs
    OnPostPublished/   event handlers of one fact: one marked class per reaction
      NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler.cs
      IPostPublicationNotifier.cs   a port one event handler names
  Customers/                        two aggregates: operations nest under each aggregate
    CustomerAccounts/
      CustomerAccountScopeLookup.cs aggregate-owned, so it sits with the aggregate
      RestrictAccount/
        RestrictAccountCommand.cs
        RestrictAccountCommandHandler.cs
    Consents/
      GrantConsent/
        GrantConsentCommand.cs
        GrantConsentCommandHandler.cs
```

Module and aggregate order, including the single-aggregate flat form, follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

provisions.heading: Use the Project Reference Graph
provisions.evidence: Which project files add a reference outside the permitted edges of the graph table? Look at each project file beside the graph table.
provisions.statement: A project reference MUST follow the graph in the table in this section and add no other edge.
provisions.rationale: An undeclared reference lets a layer reach past its boundary, and review has no ground to refuse what no graph forbids. The table names every permitted edge, so composition stays in the hosts and each project names only the layers its job needs. A small project merged under `litespec/backend/dotnet/ext/layer-projects#use-five-application-projects` has no Application.Abstractions row; its remaining rows still bind. This provision states the project form of the layer graph that `litespec/workspace/dependencies#follow-the-declared-dependency-graph` declares.
provisions.example:
| Project | may reference |
|:---|:---|
| Domain | None |
| Application.Abstractions | Domain |
| Application | Domain, Application.Abstractions |
| Infrastructure | Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application |
| WebApi | Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure |
| Worker | Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure |
| AppHost | Deployable host projects through Aspire resource references |
| Test projects | Only production projects and test support needed by their test category |

`WebApi` references Infrastructure for composition in `Program.cs`. Endpoint implementations take their dependencies from Application abstractions, not from Infrastructure repositories, sessions, or provider clients.

provisions.heading: Use This Baseline Package Ownership
provisions.evidence: Which baseline package references sit outside the project the ownership table assigns? Look at each package reference beside the ownership table.
provisions.statement: Assign each baseline package to the owning layer named in the table in this section.
provisions.rationale: Without an owner, a package lands in the project that first needs it and spreads from there. The table assigns each baseline package to its one owning project, so review can refuse it anywhere else. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/dependencies#assign-each-baseline-package-to-its-owning-layer`.
provisions.example:
| Project | Direct package groups |
|:---|:---|
| Domain | None |
| Application.Abstractions | Required LiteBus module abstractions only |
| Application | Required LiteBus module abstractions; `Marten` for the selected `IQuerySession` read boundary; Microsoft abstractions used by public ports |
| Infrastructure | `Marten`; LiteBus registration modules. Provider, resilience, service discovery, and configuration packages required by implemented adapters |
| WebApi | JWT Bearer [REDACTED], ASP.NET Core OpenAPI, build-time OpenAPI generation, Scalar, and required LiteBus mediator abstractions |
| Worker | LiteBus registration modules; the provider, resilience, and configuration packages its hosted operations need |
| ServiceDefaults | Health checks, service discovery, HTTP resilience, and OpenTelemetry registration and instrumentation |
| AppHost | Aspire AppHost and resource hosting packages |
| Domain.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, and FsCheck |
| Application.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, and NSubstitute for outside providers and the clock |
| Integration.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, test host, Testcontainers PostgreSQL, and the Microsoft.Testing.Platform report and coverage extensions |
| Architecture.Tests | xUnit v3 and assertions |
| Acceptance.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, the behavior runner its extension selects, test host, and the report and coverage extensions |

Application.Tests run each handler against the real repositories on the test database. A test substitutes only the outside providers and the clock, as `litespec/quality/testing#use-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack` requires.

Test projects reference xUnit v3 and run on Microsoft.Testing.Platform. The consumer `global.json` sets `"test": { "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform" }`, because the .NET 10 `dotnet test` command refuses the VSTest mode for these projects. Domain.Tests carries FsCheck at the 3.6.0 pin `litespec.manifest.yaml` states for the property tests that `litespec/backend/testing#prove-every-calculation-with-property-tests` names and the model-based tests that `litespec/backend/testing#prove-every-aggregate-with-a-model-based-test` names.

The example adds a package to the narrowest owning project. A central version entry does not authorize every project to reference that package. Conditional packages such as LightBDD, SignalR, and WireMock are referenced only after their extension activates. The manifest pins no architecture-test library; a project that wants one adds it with owner approval.

provisions.heading: Use This Infrastructure Layout
provisions.evidence: Which Marten configuration, repository, commit, or serialization files sit outside the one Infrastructure persistence folder? Look at the persistence files.
provisions.statement: Place Marten configuration, repositories, commit behavior, and serialization under one Infrastructure persistence folder.
