provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for a grant outside permission, self, anonymous, and system, and `reference-unknown` for a permission no record defines.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its grant as a permission, a self grant, anonymous, or system.
provisions.rationale: The grant is the check the call passes: a permission for role-held action, a self grant for action on records the caller owns, anonymous for open calls, and system for work with no caller. A grant outside these four forms gives the checker no stated check to enforce, and each caller invents its own test.
provisions.example: `permission/manage-copies` for staff work, `self(permission/read-loans)` for a reader reading their own loans, `anonymous` for a public catalog, and `system` for a self-checkout handler acting for the device.

provisions.heading: Grant Permissions Through Roles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a role with no `allows` entry, and `permission-orphan` for a permission allowed by no role.
provisions.statement: A role MUST name the permissions it allows in `allows`.
provisions.rationale: The allows list is the middle of the chain: it joins the actors that hold the role to the use cases that cite its permissions in their grants. The role lives in Intent and the permission lives in Behavior, so `allows` is a declared down-link. A role that names no permission grants nothing, so every use case its holders run breaks the chain at the middle link.
provisions.example: `role/employee` allows `permission/submit-expense`, which the submit use case cites in its grant.

provisions.heading: Keep Access Records in Their Homes
provisions.evidence: Which access records sit outside the homes their type names? Look at the actor, role, permission, entry point, and external system homes.
provisions.statement: An access record MUST live in the home its type names.
provisions.rationale: One home per type tells a reader where to open a record and tells the book where to render it. A record kept anywhere else looks written while readers open the home and find nothing there.

provisions.heading: Keep Permission Lists to Entries
provisions.evidence: Which module permissions files carry an explanation file? Look beside each permissions file for a `.md` file with its name.
provisions.statement: A module permissions file MUST hold entries only.
provisions.rationale: The file holds entries only: each permission is one row with its fields, and prose around them would restate the meanings the entries already carry. A file with entries only stays readable as a list even as entries grow.

provisions.heading: Name Every Actor with Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an actor without `kind` and `field-invalid` for a kind outside person and organization.
provisions.statement: An actor MUST name its kind in `kind`.
provisions.rationale: The kind tells a reviewer whether a human or an organization stands behind the actor, which decides who answers for what it does. Without the kind, a reviewer assigns responsibility without knowing who stands behind the actor. Software stands behind no actor.
provisions.example: An employee actor carries `person`, and the library as a lending party carries `organization`.

provisions.heading: Prove Hierarchies Derived Trust and Delegation with Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Which hierarchy, trust, or delegation patterns lack an allowed and a refused scenario? Look at the scenarios on the use cases that carry the pattern.
provisions.statement: A hierarchy, derived trust, or delegation pattern MUST prove its allowed and refused calls with scenarios.
provisions.rationale: Patterns compose the same access parts into wider reach, so prose alone cannot show where the wider grant stops. Scenarios that walk an allowed call and a refused call pin the boundary as checked facts, and the checker confirms each one through the public boundary.
provisions.example: A delegation story shows an assistant acting for a manager succeeding, and the same assistant acting without delegation ending in the derived forbidden result.

provisions.heading: Record a Delegated Grant Inside One Tenant as a Role Assignment
provisions.evidence: Which delegated or temporary grants inside one tenant lack a role assignment with `validFrom` and `validUntil` on an aggregate the access model reads, or lack their own granting and revoking use cases? Look at the assignments beside the actor holds and the use cases that act under them.
provisions.statement: A delegated or temporary grant inside one tenant MUST be recorded as a role assignment with a validity window in `validFrom` and `validUntil`, held on an aggregate the access model reads and granted and revoked by its own use cases.
provisions.rationale: Inside one tenant, delegation changes who holds a role for a time, not which grant forms exist. Recording the assignment with its window on an aggregate the access model reads gives the authorization guard one stated source for the deputy, the role, and the dates, and the granting and revoking use cases make the start and the end reviewable acts. A use case acting under the assignment declares its permission as usual, so no new access form appears. The tenancy extension adds only the cross-tenant form of delegation; it adds no form inside one tenant.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, a manager delegating team management to a deputy for 2026-12-20 to 2027-01-05 is recorded as an assignment of the manager role to the deputy with `validFrom` of 2026-12-20 and `validUntil` of 2027-01-05, granted by its own grant use case and ended by its own revoke use case. The manage use case acting under it still declares `permission/manage-team`.

provisions.heading: Record Every Role Hold with Its Scope
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `role-orphaned` for a role held by no actor.
provisions.statement: An actor that acts through a role MUST record the hold in `holds`.
provisions.rationale: The hold is the grant: without it, the actor and the role sit on separate pages with no stated connection, and no reviewer can tell what the actor is allowed to do. The scope bounds each grant, so one role grants platform reach to one actor and self reach to another.
provisions.example:
```json
"holds": [{ "role": "role/employee", "scope": "self" }]
```

provisions.heading: Remove a Target That Must Be the Caller
provisions.evidence: Which use cases with a self grant name a caller-owned target in their inputs without a self declaration the guard enforces, or compare the caller with a target in a handler? Look at the inputs and handlers beside the self grants.
provisions.statement: A message whose target must be the caller MUST carry no target and act on the caller, or declare a self grant that the authorization guard enforces.
provisions.rationale: A target that must equal the caller is a value the caller could forge: each handler would compare it with the verified identity, and each comparison is authorization logic in a handler. Carrying no target leaves nothing to forge, and the call acts on the caller from verified claims. Where the target must stay on the message, a self grant states the scope beside the use case, and the guard enforces it.
provisions.example: "My loans" lists the signed-in reader's loans and takes no reader id.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Grant to Its Tenant Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for a tenant scope outside own, cross, public, and none.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its tenant scope as own, cross, public, or none.
provisions.rationale: The tenant scope bounds which tenant data the call may touch: own stays inside the caller tenant, cross reaches across tenants, public works beyond tenant boundaries, and none touches no tenant data. Without the scope, a read inside one tenant and a read across all tenants look the same, and the widest reach hides in the narrowest grant.
provisions.example: An expense report names `own`, a staff search across tenants names `cross`, a public catalog names `public`, and a health check names `none`.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Role
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a role without `scope` and `field-invalid` for a scope outside kebab-case form.
provisions.statement: A role MUST name its scope in `scope`.
provisions.rationale: The scope bounds what the role reaches: the same permission allows platform-wide action in one grant and own-record action in another. Without a named scope, every grant reads as product-wide, and the narrowest grant gets the widest reach.
provisions.example: A scope of `team` bounds the role to one team, while `platform` bounds it to the whole product.

provisions.heading: State Every Permission with Its Meaning
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission without `meaning`.
provisions.statement: A permission MUST state what it allows in `meaning`.
provisions.rationale: The meaning is the one sentence a reviewer reads to decide whether the grant fits the role: a name alone carries no boundary. Two permissions with the same name pattern and no meanings drift into overlapping grants that no audit can separate.
provisions.example: `permission/submit-expense` carries "Submit an expense for reimbursement."

provisions.heading: State the Scope of Every Permission
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission entry without `scope`.
provisions.statement: Each permission MUST state the scope at which a role grants it.
provisions.rationale: A grant without a named reach is decided in code: each check looks up the reach beside the permission list, and code then holds a second list of permissions.
provisions.example: `permission/manage-copies` carries `scope: platform`, the same level as the librarian role that grants it.

provisions.heading: Use Three Conventional Scope Levels
provisions.evidence: Which role scopes fall outside platform, tenant, and self without a recorded project convention? Look at `scope` on each role page.
provisions.statement: Use `platform`, `tenant`, and `self` as role scopes.
provisions.rationale: Three levels cover the grants most products need: product-wide administration, tenant-wide operation, and action on one's own records. A project with different boundaries names its own levels, and every role still carries exactly one scope.

provisions.heading: Write a Summary on Every Actor and Role Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `prose-missing` for an actor or role page without `summary`.
provisions.statement: An actor or role page MUST carry a `summary` field.
provisions.rationale: The `summary` states in plain sentences who the party is and what the grant is for, which the fields alone do not say. A reviewer meets the story first and the fields after, so the grant reads as a decision rather than a row.

provisions.heading: Write a Summary on Every External System Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `prose-missing` for an external system page without `summary`.
provisions.statement: An external system page MUST carry a `summary` field.
provisions.rationale: The `summary` states in plain sentences what the outside system does for the product, which the message lists alone do not say. A reviewer meets the relationship first and the messages after, so the dependency reads as a decision rather than a row.

provisions.heading: Advise Without Gating
provisions.evidence: The agent output records findings as advice with evidence, with decisions left to the owner.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST report its findings as advice with evidence, never as a decision.
provisions.rationale: Decisions belong to the owner: the pull request that changes a record is its review. An agent that records a decision spends authority it was never given. Advice with evidence lets the owner decide faster without moving the decision to the agent.

provisions.heading: Apply Guidance Precedence
provisions.evidence: The design applies the project departure, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply the project departure, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order.
provisions.rationale: Overlapping guidance is normal: a project departure narrows a shared provision, an extension replaces a baseline default, and a stack page refines its area page. Without a fixed order, two agents resolve the same overlap differently and the workspace drifts. The order puts the most local decision first, so the broader baseline fills only the gaps it leaves.

provisions.heading: Escalate Decisions That Specify Forbids
provisions.evidence: Each figure the owner sets that the change needs sits in an owner question or a backlog item, not in an agent-written decision.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT decide a figure the owner sets.
provisions.rationale: The Specify rule reserves the figures the owner sets for Intent, because each one binds the product to buyers, markets, or law; the [Intent page](intent.md) states the Specify boundary. An agent that picks a figure silently takes a decision that belongs to the owner. Each undecided figure becomes a question to the owner with a recommendation, or a backlog item.
provisions.example: A setting needs a default queue cap; the agent raises a question to the owner with a recommendation instead of writing the default into the record.

provisions.heading: Follow the Local Pattern Before the Model Query
provisions.evidence: The change touches no permission carrying `risk` and names the local pattern it followed.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST run the model query before a change that touches a permission carrying `risk`, and MAY rely on neighboring code otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A small edit with no risk behind it does not need the full record set: the neighboring files already show the decided shape. Requiring a model query for every small change would slow ordinary work without adding information. A change touching a permission that carries `risk` keeps the full query, because the query shows the risk a one-line change would otherwise miss, and it costs seconds.
provisions.example: A spelling fix in a setting page reads the sibling setting, then edits without querying the model.

provisions.heading: Inspect Existing Work Before Editing
provisions.evidence: `git status` output precedes the edits, with user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output untouched.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST read `git status` before editing and preserve user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output.
provisions.rationale: A working tree can hold the user's own uncommitted edits, untracked files, and generated output from an unrelated task. An agent that edits without looking overwrites or deletes work outside its scope. Reading `git status` first marks that work as untouchable.

provisions.heading: Inspect Local Examples After Standards
provisions.evidence: The change names the neighboring files that shaped it after the standards.
provisions.statement: Inspect neighboring consumer files after loading applicable standards.
provisions.rationale: Standards state the required shape, while neighboring files show the names, folders, and idioms this project chose for it. An agent that skips them writes compliant but foreign-looking code that the next edit rewrites.

provisions.heading: Keep Agent Working Files Under Agents
provisions.evidence: Every agent working file sits under `.agents/` or the path the working-files convention names.
provisions.statement: Keep agent working files under `.agents/`, with tracked `skills/` and `records/` folders and ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.rationale: Agent work with no agreed home lands beside authored records, where it pollutes review, or vanishes with the session, where nobody can audit it. The split keeps durable work in `skills/` and `records/` and machine-local work in the ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.example:
```text
.agents/
  skills/
  records/
  delegate/
  scratch/
```

provisions.heading: Keep the Agent Protocol Current
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `agent-protocol-drift` (level S) when the region differs from what `render` would write, `agent-protocol-missing` (level S) when `AGENTS.md` holds no region, and `skill-drift` (level S) when a project-scope skill copy differs from what the carried release generates.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep its agent protocol region and its project-scope skill copies equal to what its LiteSpec release generates.
provisions.rationale: The region carries the commands and rules every session loads first. A stale region points agents at an old release, an old selection, or commands that changed, while the tool output stays current. The project-scope skill copies carry the same procedure to tools that load skills on demand. A stale copy points at the same old release. The release template plus the project file regenerate the region and the project-scope skill copies in one command, so drift is always fixable. Global copies live outside the project and stay outside the check. Settled by [decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol](decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol) and [decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill](decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill).
provisions.example: Claimwick upgrades its LiteSpec release and runs `litespec model render`; the region in its `AGENTS.md` and its project-scope skill copies match what the new release generates.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Extensions
provisions.evidence: The change names each extension loaded before editing inside its boundary.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST load selected project extensions and selected applicable local extensions before editing code or prose inside the extension's boundary.
provisions.rationale: An extension replaces baseline guidance inside its boundary. An agent that edits there without loading the extension follows the baseline the extension replaced, and the change contradicts the project's own selection.
provisions.example: A change to the cached catalog reads the selected caching extension before touching the code its boundary covers.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Provisions Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Which judgment provisions that `litespec rules --since <base>` listed lack a judged answer in the completion report? Compare the rules output with the report.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST run `litespec rules <path>` before editing a file and answer each judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` lists before reporting done.
provisions.rationale: Provisions are only usable when retrieved by situation: the query returns what governs the change, grouped by strength, with project conventions and departures merged in. `litespec rules <...> --full` adds rationale and example when a statement is not enough. Settled by [decision/0038-narrow-rules-output-per-file-and-change-set](decision/0038-narrow-rules-output-per-file-and-change-set).
provisions.example: `litespec rules use-case/spending.submit-expense` returns the provisions that govern the change, grouped by strength.

provisions.heading: Make Coherent Scoped Changes
provisions.evidence: Every changed artifact traces to the authorized request.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST make the smallest coherent change that satisfies the authorized request.
provisions.rationale: A change that stops at code and skips its records, tests, or operating evidence leaves the workspace claiming behavior nothing proves. A change that sprawls past the request drags unrelated files into review. The smallest coherent change keeps the records, code, tests, and evidence that belong together in one reviewable unit.

provisions.heading: Name Judged Provisions in the Completion Report
provisions.evidence: Which judged provisions lack a how in the completion report? Look at the provisions beside the report.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name each provision the agent judged and how it judged it.
provisions.rationale: The report shows which required provisions, defaults, and advisory provisions the change met and the judgment for each, so the owner checks the reasoning without re-reading the change. A provision the query returned but the report skips is a judgment nobody can check.
provisions.example: The report names each returned provision with its judgment: followed, replaced by a named convention, or parked by a departure.

provisions.heading: Protect Proofs from Implementation Edits
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check --since <ref>` reports `proof-hash-drift` as advisory for each scenario whose proving test method changed since the base while the scenario did not.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT delete, skip, or weaken a test that proves a scenario, or change its expected values, unless the scenario changed in the same change; it reports a test it believes is wrong instead of editing it.
provisions.rationale: A proof that changes with the implementation stops proving the decided behavior and starts restating the code. The proof ledger records each scenario's hash and the hash of each test that proves it, so `model check --since` can report, as an advisory finding, each scenario whose proving test changed while the scenario did not. Hashing the proving test method rather than its file keeps an unrelated edit in the same file from reporting a change. Settled by [decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests](decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests).
provisions.example: A handler change makes a proving test fail; the agent reports the failing test and the mismatch instead of changing the expected value to fit the new result.

provisions.heading: Raise Open Figures to the Owner
provisions.evidence: Which open figures lack an owner question with a recommendation or a backlog item? Look at the owner questions and the backlog board beside the change.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST raise each open figure to the owner with a recommendation, or place it on the backlog board.
provisions.rationale: A figure without a recommendation asks the owner to research from nothing, while a recommendation gives a default to accept or correct. Grouping figures by subject lets the owner answer one set at a time. A figure never becomes a silent agent decision or code written on a guess.
provisions.example: Two open figures land in one owner question set, each with a recommendation.

provisions.heading: Read the Full Record Before Changing a Boundary
provisions.evidence: Each file generation or boundary change cites the full record it matched.
provisions.statement: Read the full record, the record file with its explanation file, before generating a file, changing a public boundary, or choosing between patterns.
provisions.rationale: Generating a file or changing a public boundary from a summary risks baking a paraphrase into a contract. The full record carries the exact fields, links, and wording the new surface matches. A small edit that follows an existing local pattern can rely on neighboring code instead.

provisions.heading: Replace Only Declared Conventions
provisions.evidence: Each convention replacement resolves to a recorded local convention in the project documentation.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply a replacement for a convention only when the project documentation records that replacement.
provisions.rationale: Conventions exist to be replaced, but only through a recorded decision. An undocumented local preference that silently replaces a baseline default looks identical to a mistake, so the next agent fixes it back. The recorded convention keeps the replacement visible and reviewable.

provisions.heading: Restrict Unapproved Side Effects
provisions.evidence: An approval covers each package, migration, authentication, public API, production data, release, spending, or state-changing outside call the change makes.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT act without approval on packages, migrations, authentication, a public API, production data, releases, spending, or outside calls that change state.
provisions.rationale: The listed changes alter project boundaries beyond an ordinary implementation edit: they move money or data, open security boundaries, or change state outside the repository. None of them can be judged from the task text alone, so the task authorizer approves each one before the agent acts.

provisions.heading: Search the Provisions Before Recording a Decision
provisions.evidence: Which technical decisions restate a choice a provision already makes? Compare each decision with the `rules` output for its subject.
provisions.statement: Query `litespec rules` for the decision's subject, and where a provision makes the choice, follow that provision instead of recording a decision.
provisions.rationale: Many technical choices are already decided: a provision names the shape, the baseline, or the boundary the code follows. A decision that restates such a choice splits authority between the provision and the record, and the two drift. Searching first keeps one home for each decided choice.
provisions.example: An agent about to record how Claimwick declares integration edges queries `litespec rules` for the subject; the provision declares every edge in a record, so the code follows it and no decision is recorded.

provisions.heading: Select Task Context
provisions.evidence: The completion report names the model query that selected the cited records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST query the project model for the records that cover the request, and read the query output, before editing.
provisions.rationale: Without the query, an agent reads either too little and invents the missing rules, or half the repository and buries the task in unrelated guidance. The query returns the smallest record set that covers the request, with the links the builder joined between records, so the agent starts from decided Intent.
provisions.example: `litespec model query use-case/spending.submit-expense` returns the use case with its rules, results, and scenarios.

provisions.heading: Stop on Unresolved Conflict
provisions.evidence: The stopped work quotes the conflict with both provision IDs and paths.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stop when applicable provisions disagree without declared precedence and quote both provision IDs and paths.
provisions.rationale: When two provisions disagree and no precedence decides, any continuation invents a compromise neither provision states. Stopping with both provision identifiers and paths hands the decision to a person with exactly the evidence the decision needs.

provisions.heading: Take Expected Values from the Scenario
provisions.evidence: Each test's expected values match the scenario's Then, with none taken from a code run.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST take a test's expected values only from the scenario's Then, never from running the code.
provisions.rationale: Expected values read from a passing run restate what the code already does, so the test stays green while behavior drifts. The scenario's Then states the decided intent, which makes the test check the behavior rather than copy it.
provisions.example: A scenario whose Then names a total of `42.50` keeps `42.50` as the asserted value even when the code returns `42.51`: the mismatch fails the test instead of updating the expectation.

provisions.heading: Verify Refusals and Calculations Against Held-Back Examples
provisions.evidence: The check log shows refusal and calculation example rows withheld during implementation and run after.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST verify a refusal or calculation implementation against example rows held back from the agent that wrote it.
provisions.rationale: An agent that sees the examples while implementing fits the code to the rows instead of the rule. Held-back rows turn the examples into an independent check: the implementing agent works from the rule and the scenario, and a later check runs the withheld rows against the result.
provisions.example: The implementing agent writes a discount calculation from its rule and scenario; a later check runs the withheld example rows against the result.

provisions.heading: Write Pages Below Decided Intent
provisions.evidence: Each written page traces to a decided Intent record, with no invented promise.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST write every page below decided Intent.
provisions.rationale: Intent holds the decided promises, and everything below those decisions is written by agents: Behavior records, code, and tests that carry the decisions down. An agent that invents promises writes commitments nobody decided, while an agent that waits for dictation wastes the reading the owner gives to finished work. Writing below decided Intent keeps authorship with the agent and decisions with the owner.
provisions.example: Given a requirement for expense reimbursement, an agent writes the use case, its scenarios, and the handler without asking what the promise means.

provisions.heading: Attach Examples to Their Provisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_EXAMPLE_LABEL`, `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION`, or `REFERENCE_EXAMPLE_DECLARATION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An informative example MUST belong to its provision or to a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates.
provisions.rationale: An example floating free of its provision reads as a second rule: readers obey the illustration instead of the obligation. Belonging to its provision, or to a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates, marks it as illustration.

provisions.heading: Cite Owned Content Instead of Copying It
provisions.evidence: Which passages restate content another page owns? Compare repeated passages with the owning page.
provisions.statement: A page MUST link to content another page owns instead of restating it.
provisions.rationale: A copy drifts from its source with the next unrelated edit, and readers follow the stale one. One home for each fact keeps every reader on the current text. A link to a record names its identifier, not its file.

provisions.heading: Define Each Glossary Term Under Its Heading
provisions.evidence: Which glossary entries open with something other than the definition, or carry a Term line? Look in `docs/reference/glossary.md`.
provisions.statement: A glossary entry MUST hold its definition in the paragraph under its term heading.
provisions.rationale: The heading anchor already carries the term identifier, so a `Term` line repeats it. Lines after the definition name the record layer, established aliases, the source, and rejected synonyms where they exist.

provisions.heading: Exclude a Sequence Number from the Identifier
provisions.evidence: Which identifiers carry a sequence number? Look at the provision IDs the change adds.
provisions.statement: A provision ID MUST NOT contain a sequence number.
provisions.rationale: A counter orders a provision among its siblings and says nothing about what it requires. Words name the obligation; numbers would renumber every sibling on each insertion and break citations for no gain.

provisions.heading: Exclude Cross-Release Compatibility Work
provisions.evidence: Which pages promise migration, mapping, or alias between releases? Look at the release material the change adds.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec repository MUST NOT publish a compatibility guarantee, migration path, deprecation period, or identifier alias between its own releases.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec is a pinned contract, not a running service: consumers adopt a release whole, on their own schedule. Compatibility guarantees, migration paths, deprecation periods, and identifier aliases between LiteSpec releases would promise a continuity the model does not offer. A consumer product keeps its own API compatibility, migration, deprecation, and rollback provisions for its own users.

provisions.heading: Exclude Generated Regions from Prose Checks
provisions.evidence: Which findings point inside generated-region fences? Look at the findings the checks report.
provisions.statement: An authoring check MUST skip every generated region.
provisions.rationale: A generated region holds tool output that no author wrote and no author can fix by editing the page. Checking it would fail pages for words outside author control and train writers to ignore diagnostics.

provisions.heading: Exclude Historical Transition Material
provisions.evidence: Which active files carry history-specific paths, aliases, or migration material? Look at the files the change adds.
provisions.statement: Current standards material MUST NOT contain history-specific paths, IDs, terms, aliases, replacement maps, release migration material, compatibility rules, or transition checks other than the generated provision identifier list in the changelog.
provisions.rationale: A snapshot that carries aliases, maps, migration notes, or transition checks for other releases forces every reader to learn releases they did not pin. The published snapshot states its own contract and nothing else. An extension's `Baseline Relationship` section names a provision it replaces inside this release, which is a current replacement rather than history. The changelog's generated list of added, removed and renamed provision identifiers states a fact about the release it ships in; it offers no alias, mapping or migration path, so it stands as the one exception this provision allows.

provisions.heading: Generate the Provision Diff for Each Release
provisions.evidence: Which changelog identifiers were typed by hand, or name an identifier that a comparison of the provision index at the previous tag with the provision index of the release does not produce? Look at the changelog entry beside the two provision indexes.
provisions.statement: The changelog for each LiteSpec release MUST list the provision identifiers the release adds, removes, and renames, generated from the provision index at the previous tag and the provision index of the release.
provisions.rationale: A consumer cites provision identifiers in code marks, records, and departures, so a release that removes or renames an identifier without naming it leaves every citation pointing at nothing with no way to find what changed. The generated list states a fact about the release it ships in and nothing more: it carries no alias, no replacement map, and no migration path, and no provision depends on an earlier release to state its own contract. Because the list derives from the two provision indexes, a tool generates it; a list typed by hand goes stale with the next provision edit. This provision is the exception to `litespec/core/authoring#exclude-historical-transition-material`, and it extends to no other history material.
provisions.example: `litespec-maintain changelog --from v3.0.0` writes the list into the changelog entry for a release, with `litespec/core/scope#claim-the-record-layers-the-project-uses` under Added when that provision first ships, and a major release lists each identifier it removes or renames under Removed and Renamed in the same entry.

provisions.heading: Give One Observable Fact One Mark Across Pages
provisions.evidence: Which shared facts carry different labels? Compare the verification lines that name one check, using the provision index.
provisions.statement: One observable fact MUST carry one mark across pages.
provisions.rationale: A fact checked by a tool on one page and judged by a person on another leaves each reviewer unsure which judgment holds.

provisions.heading: Identify Actionable Conventions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `CONVENTION_MISSING_DEFAULT`, `CONVENTION_MISSING_REPLACEMENT`, `CONVENTION_DEFAULT_SENTENCE`, `CONVENTION_REPLACEMENT_SENTENCE`, `CONVENTION_REPLACEMENT_DEVIATION`, or `PROVISION_RESTATES_HEADING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A Convention provision MUST follow the Convention contract this page defines.
provisions.rationale: A Convention heading under `## Conventions` makes each replaceable default traceable: a project cites exactly the default it replaces. Without the contract, defaults hide in prose and replacements cite paragraphs instead of identifiers.

provisions.heading: Keep a Pinned Release for as Long as It Serves
provisions.evidence: Which provisions oblige a move to a later release? Look at the Statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec release MUST NOT oblige a consumer to move to a later release.
provisions.rationale: Adoption is the consumer's decision. If a repository change could oblige a move, every LiteSpec edit would become a deadline for every consumer. Keeping any published release for as long as it serves decouples the consumer's schedule from the standard's.

provisions.heading: Keep Authored Prose ASCII-Safe
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PROSE_NON_ASCII` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST contain only ASCII unless code, data, or mathematical content requires another character.
provisions.rationale: Non-ASCII characters break in terminals, diffs, generated context, and plain-text tools: a curly quote becomes unreadable in one reader and a silent mismatch in another. ASCII prose renders the same everywhere the standard is read or checked.
provisions.example: Write a hyphen or a comma where a typographic dash would go.

provisions.heading: Keep Identifiers Out of Provision Headings
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_IN_HEADING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision heading MUST carry no identifier text.
provisions.rationale: The page path and the heading already state the identifier. An identifier written into the heading repeats it at best and contradicts it at worst, after a rename touches one and misses the other.

provisions.heading: Keep Principle Pages Free of Stack Detail
provisions.evidence: Which principle pages name stack detail? Look for framework, package, and language names in principle pages.
provisions.statement: A principle page MUST NOT name a framework, a package, or a language-specific construct.
provisions.rationale: Technology lives in stack pages, so a principle holds for every stack. A framework name in a principle binds every stack to one choice.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Intent to Three Sentences
provisions.evidence: Which Intent sections run past three sentences? Look at the Intent section of each page the change touches.
provisions.statement: An Intent section MUST hold at most three sentences.
provisions.rationale: The first sentence states the scope and boundary. The second states who applies the page and when. An optional third sentence relates the page to its neighbors.

provisions.heading: Map Provisions to Evidence
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_MISSING_ID`, `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_ID`, `VERIFY_ORDER`, or `VERIFY_HEADER` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST end its fields with exactly one verification line.
provisions.rationale: A provision with no verification line is a rule nobody checks: people assume a tool covers it while no tool was told. One line per provision, beside the rule it checks, makes each rule reviewable by a person or a tool.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Provision Checkable or Guidance
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `VERIFY_MISSING_ID` for a provision whose verification line opens with any other label.
provisions.statement: A verification line MUST open with `Checked by` for a provision a tool checks or `Reviewed for` for one a person judges.
provisions.rationale: The label tells a reader who judges the provision: a tool (`checkable`) or a person (`guidance`). Without it, a team automates a judgment call or hand-reviews what a command already proves.

provisions.heading: Match Strength to the Modal Word
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` confirms each Standards provision carries the modal its Strength line grades.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST carry the modal its Strength line grades.
provisions.rationale: The Strength line tells a reader how binding a provision is, and the modal in its Statement says the same thing in words: a required provision obliges with must or must not, while an advisory one suggests with neither. A permission on its own reads as optional advice under a required label, so a permission either joins the provision it relaxes or becomes an obligation. When the two disagree, each reader picks the one that suits the change, and the grade means nothing.
provisions.example: A required provision states that a use case declares its kind with must, while an advisory provision suggests a naming shape without it.

provisions.heading: Name Observable Evidence in Verification Lines
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_GENERIC_EVIDENCE`, `VERIFY_TEMPLATED_EVIDENCE`, `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_EVIDENCE`, `VERIFY_COMMAND`, or `CHECKED_BY_UNKNOWN` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A verification line MUST name the observable evidence and where the reviewer looks.
provisions.rationale: A line that restates its Statement sends the reviewer in a circle: the evidence confirms that the rule says what it says. Naming the artifact and its location turns the line into an instruction the reviewer follows.

provisions.heading: Name the Escape from Every Abstraction
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_MISSING_SECTION` diagnostic for a command page.
provisions.statement: A command page MUST state under `Underneath` what the command runs or the sentence `Nothing beneath this command is separately runnable.`.
provisions.rationale: A wrapper nobody can see through leaves a failure with no command to run by hand and no documentation tier to inspect. Stating what the command runs, or that nothing beneath it is separately runnable, gives every failure a next step.
provisions.example: A command with nothing separately runnable writes `Nothing beneath this command is separately runnable.` under `Underneath`.

provisions.heading: Name the Owning Page in the Identifier
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_PAGE_FILENAME` or `ID_DUPLICATE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision ID's page segment MUST be its page's path under `docs/` without the `.md` extension.
provisions.rationale: The page segment is the file a reader opens and the address the provision carries on the published site. Deriving it from the path keeps the identifier and the file from disagreeing.
provisions.example: `litespec/frontend/structure#mirror-the-backend-use-case-path-in-kebab-case` and `litespec/frontend/mobile/structure#organize-screens-by-module` are on two different pages.

provisions.heading: Name the Tool Rather Than the Mechanism
provisions.evidence: Which procedure steps lack a repository command? Look at the steps the change adds.
provisions.statement: A tutorial step or how-to step MUST name the repository command that performs it, where one exists.
provisions.rationale: A procedure that lists what a command already does becomes a second copy of that command's behavior. The copy drifts from the tool, and readers follow stale steps. Naming the repository command delegates the steps to the tool that performs them.
provisions.example: A step reads ``Run `./shop up` `` rather than listing the compose start, the readiness wait, and each process launch.

provisions.heading: Order Glossary Groups Alphabetically
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `GLOSSARY_ORDER` or `GLOSSARY_DEFINITION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Glossary groups MUST stand in alphabetical order, each opening with one intro sentence.
provisions.rationale: Groups in a fixed order with one opening sentence tell a reader where a term lives before any term is read. An unordered group hides its terms from a reader who guesses the wrong place, and a group without its sentence opens on terms with no shared context.
provisions.example: The code, product, and standard term groups open the glossary in that order, each with one sentence saying what its terms name.

provisions.heading: Place Each Stack Binding on Its Stack Page
provisions.evidence: Which shared pages carry stack-specific sections? Look for stack sections outside stack pages.
provisions.statement: A stack-specific section MUST live on its stack page rather than on a shared page.
provisions.rationale: Shared pages stay neutral across stacks. Each stack page carries its own bindings, so a reader finds one stack's detail in one place.

provisions.heading: Place the ID Under Every Provision Heading
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_LINE_MISSING` or `ID_LINE_MISMATCH` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision heading MUST be followed by an ID line holding the provision's identity.
provisions.rationale: A reader who cites a provision copies its ID from where the provision stands, instead of deriving a slug by hand or looking it up elsewhere. The ID line is the identity: a heading may change without changing it, so an ID line that reads differently from its heading still holds.
provisions.example: `### Keep Shared UI in One Package` on `docs/frontend/components.md` is followed by the ID line `litespec/frontend/components#keep-shared-ui-in-one-package`.

provisions.heading: Prefer Direct Action Headings
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `HEADING_ACTION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Start a Standard or Convention heading with a concrete action verb.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Release as a Complete Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` checks every page of the release in one run, and the manifest names one version for the whole contract.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec release MUST state every active provision without depending on an earlier release.
provisions.rationale: A consumer pins one snapshot and reads it as the whole obligation. Depending on another release would force the consumer to pin and read two contracts to know either. Stating every active provision in each release keeps one snapshot sufficient.

provisions.heading: Record a Setting as Reference
provisions.evidence: Which procedure-named settings lack a configuration page row? Look at the settings the change adds, beside the configuration pages.
provisions.statement: A configuration setting a reader can change MUST appear on a configuration page with its default, its scope, and what overrides it.
provisions.rationale: A setting introduced inside a procedure is found only by the reader who already knows which procedure mentioned it. A configuration page with the default, scope, and overrides puts every setting where a reader looks it up.

provisions.heading: Record the Reviewed LiteSpec Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `release-drift` when `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` names no release or a release other than the installed tool release.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record the LiteSpec release it adopts in `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` within `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A provision can gain force while keeping its ID, so a departure written against one release could otherwise apply to a rule nobody reread. Recording the adopted release in `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` makes adoption an explicit act and tells every reader which contract the project reviewed.

provisions.heading: Regenerate the Provision Index
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain provisions --check` exits zero.
provisions.statement: A standards change MUST leave `docs/reference/provisions.md` equal to the output of `litespec-maintain provisions`.
provisions.rationale: One generated page resolves every identifier to its heading and page, so a reader follows a citation in one step. It carries each provision's scope and strength, so the CLI reads one file instead of parsing every page. Regenerating it with `litespec-maintain provisions` on every standards change keeps the index and the pages from disagreeing.

provisions.heading: Restrict Normative Language to Standards and Conventions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PROSE_NORMATIVE_LOCATION` or `STANDARD_INFORMATIVE_NORMATIVE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A capitalized modal MUST appear only in a Statement, a Deviation, a Default, or a Replacement.
provisions.rationale: Obligation hides when it sits in Concepts, Rationale, or an example: a project replaces a default it saw nowhere in the labeled assertions. One location for every modal lets readers and tools find each obligation in the same place. A prohibition written as `cannot` and a rule written as `never` belong in the same labels.

provisions.heading: Route the Reader Before Listing Pages
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `INDEX_MISSING_ROUTING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A documentation root index MUST state which page style answers which reader question before its first navigation group.
provisions.rationale: A reader without a map from question to page opens both and trusts neither. Naming each style in the reader's terms before the first navigation group sends each question to the page that answers it.
provisions.example: A `Which Page Do You Want` section names each style in the reader's terms, one sentence each.

provisions.heading: Run Repeatable Authoring Checks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate`, `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` and `git diff --check` exit zero.
provisions.statement: A standards change MUST pass the repository validator, the test suite, and `git diff --check`.
provisions.rationale: The repository validator, the test suite, and `git diff --check` each catch what the others miss: structure, behavior, and whitespace. Passing all three on every standards change keeps the standard checkable by anyone who runs the same commands. The tools check every schema with LiteSpec's own evaluator, so running them needs no paid license, settled by [decision/0022-own-schema-evaluator](decision/0022-own-schema-evaluator) on the evidence in [research/schema-evaluator-evidence](research/schema-evaluator-evidence). The change report lists every skipped check with its reason. The [command index](../tools/README.md) and the [maintainer index](../maintain/README.md) name each check and its command. Settled by [decision/0035-bind-docs-to-tools-and-example](decision/0035-bind-docs-to-tools-and-example), which checks each tool fact the pages cite against the tools' own data.

provisions.heading: Split Extension Dependencies into Three Labeled Lines
provisions.evidence: Which Dependencies sections lack a labeled line? Look in each page under an `ext/` folder.
provisions.statement: An extension Dependencies section MUST carry the lines Packages, Related extensions, and Guides.
provisions.rationale: Fixed labels separate package needs from related extensions and guides. A line with nothing to name holds `None.`.

provisions.heading: State One Tier per Page
provisions.evidence: Which command pages mix mechanism into other sections? Look outside the Underneath section of each command page the change touches.
provisions.statement: A page MUST NOT describe both a command and the mechanism that command runs, outside an `Underneath` section.
provisions.rationale: A reader who wanted the command reads mechanism detail as noise, and a reader who wanted the mechanism reads the command wrapper as an obstacle. One documentation tier per page serves each reader, and the `Underneath` section holds the mechanism for the reader who asks for it.

provisions.heading: Use Controlled Capitalization
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_TITLE_CASE` or `PAGE_HEADING_CASE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A page MUST use Title Case for its title and every heading.
provisions.rationale: Titles and headings read as names in indexes, tabs, and search results. Title Case capitalizes every word except articles (`a`, `an`, `the`), coordinating conjunctions (`and`, `but`, `for`, `nor`, `or`, `so`, `yet`), and prepositions of four letters or fewer (`as`, `at`, `by`, `for`, `from`, `in`, `into`, `of`, `off`, `on`, `onto`, `over`, `per`, `to`, `up`, `upon`, `via`, `with`); the first and last words stay capitalized, and code, identifiers, and file names keep their own case.

provisions.heading: Use One Normative Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_MODAL_COUNT` or `STANDARD_MODAL_VOCABULARY` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST use exactly one listed capitalized modal and no other capitalized normative term.
provisions.rationale: Strength words work only when each one means exactly one thing. The provision contract defines the listed modals with their RFC meaning, so a reader knows whether a word obliges or suggests, and no second capitalized term sneaks in a different shade of obligation.

provisions.heading: Use One Term for One Concept
provisions.evidence: Which concepts appear under more than one name? Look at the terms the change adds, beside the glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST name each concept with its one glossary term.
provisions.rationale: A second name for one concept reads as a second concept: the reader hunts for a distinction the writer did not mean. One term per concept means each term is defined once and checked once. Settled by [decision/0018-one-record-language](decision/0018-one-record-language) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` or `ID_DUPLICATE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision ID MUST be `litespec/<page>#<slug>` as its ID line states it.
provisions.rationale: The page names the file and the ID line states the slug, so a citation resolves with no lookup table. One grammar for every identifier keeps citations writable by hand and checkable by tool. The ID line is the identity: a heading reword leaves it unchanged, and no two provisions share one.
provisions.example: `litespec/frontend/components#compose-composites-in-page-code` is the ID line under its heading on the frontend components page.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Page Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_MISSING_SECTION`, `PAGE_SECTION_ORDER` or `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An authored page MUST use the sections, in order, of its page style.
provisions.rationale: A fixed shape puts the authority, the context, the defaults, and the evidence in the same place on every page. Readers learn the shape once, and tools find each section without guessing. A page that invents its own order sends both searching. A record file carries its type's fields in canonical key order instead of sections.

provisions.heading: Validate Current Standards Material
provisions.evidence: Which validator inputs come from outside the working tree? Look at the paths the validator reads.
provisions.statement: The standards validator MUST evaluate only current standards material.
provisions.rationale: Each pinned release is a complete snapshot, so the validator judges the working tree alone. Reading history would let a provision pass on the strength of a release nobody pinned. Git history and the changelog give release context to readers outside validation.

provisions.heading: Write Atomic Standards Provisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_LABEL_INVALID`, `STANDARD_LABEL_ORDER`, `STANDARD_LABEL_DUPLICATE`, `STANDARD_SENTENCE_COUNT`, `STANDARD_MODAL_COUNT`, `STANDARD_MODAL_VOCABULARY`, `STANDARD_MISSING_DEVIATION`, `STANDARD_UNEXPECTED_DEVIATION`, `STANDARD_DEVIATION_NORMATIVE`, `STANDARD_DEVIATION_SENTENCE`, `STANDARD_MISSING_REQUIREMENT`, `STANDARD_REQUIREMENT_COUNT`, `STANDARD_UNLABELED_CONTENT`, or `PROVISION_RESTATES_HEADING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST follow the Standard contract this page defines.
provisions.rationale: One provision with one obligation has one authority, one identifier, and one verification line. A provision that bundles two obligations leaves a project half-compliant with no identifier for the half it missed.
provisions.example: `### Keep Business Invariants in Domain` owns one obligation about where invariants are enforced.

provisions.heading: Write None in an Empty Required Section
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_EMPTY_SECTION` or `PAGE_EMPTY_SECTION_TEXT` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A required section with nothing to say MUST contain only `None.`.
provisions.rationale: One fixed marker reads the same on every page and gives the validator one shape to accept.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Reaction and Job Edge in Effects
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job with no `effects` or with a top-level effect verb.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its edges in `effects`, with exactly one verb per entry.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job with no declared edge observes and never acts, while an edge outside `effects` hides behavior the checks never see. Declaring each edge in `effects` with exactly one verb of `runs`, `sends`, `emits`, or `calls` keeps every consequence of the reaction or job beside its trigger, under one grammar for every record that has edges, as the [use-cases page](use-cases.md) states.

provisions.heading: File Every Reaction and Job with the Module It Changes
provisions.evidence: Which reaction or job pages sit outside the module they change? Look at the reactions and jobs beside the modules whose records they change.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST live with the module whose records it changes, or with the module owning the notification it sends when it only sends.
provisions.rationale: Reactions and jobs filed by trigger scatter: one module behavior hides on a dozen trigger pages, and nobody sees the module whole. Filing each reaction and job with the module it changes keeps each module behavior in one place. Its event handler lives in that module's code in the `On{Fact}` folder inside the module `UseCases/` folder (`litespec/workspace/naming#group-event-handlers-by-the-fact-they-handle`). The trigger page shows reactions answering its event as a view derived from records.

provisions.heading: Guard Every Manual Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `job-guard-missing` (level G) for a manual job without `guard`.
provisions.statement: Each job with `kind: manual` MUST state the guard it runs under.
provisions.rationale: Work a person starts without a guard runs anywhere by anyone: a rehearsal harness touches production, a manual sweep runs twice. Stating the guard keeps person-started work inside its fence, beside where it runs in `runsWhere`.
provisions.example: The rehearse-payout job runs under the platform guard on the staging deployment.

provisions.heading: Keep Job Fields off Reactions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction carrying `kind`, `schedule`, `runbook`, `runsWhere`, `guard`, `cursor`, `selection`, `lease`, `batchSize`, `serviceLevel`, or `evidence`.
provisions.statement: A reaction MUST NOT carry `kind`, `schedule`, `runbook`, `runsWhere`, `guard`, `cursor`, `selection`, `lease`, `batchSize`, `serviceLevel`, or `evidence`.
provisions.rationale: Run fields describe work over time: the kind, the schedule, what each run selects, how many items per batch, the lock, where resume state lives, where it runs, the guard it runs under, the promised service level, and the evidence the run leaves. A reaction answers one event and carries none of that, so a run field on it claims a schedule the trigger never states. Settled by [decision/0015-automations-and-sagas](decision/0015-automations-and-sagas) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example: The send-due-notice reaction answers its event with no `selection` and no `guard`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Job for the Use Case It Runs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `job-name-invalid` (level G) for a job outside `<verb>-<what>` with the verb of a use case it runs.
provisions.statement: Each job MUST be named `<verb>-<what>` with the verb of a use case it runs.
provisions.rationale: A job selects items and runs one command for each, so naming it for that command lets a reader go from the schedule to the behavior in one step, as `litespec/core/language#name-each-record-by-its-types-name-form` states.
provisions.example: `job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds` runs `use-case/lending.expire-holds`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Reaction for Its Act and Its Trigger
provisions.evidence: Which reaction names hide their act or their trigger? Look at the reaction names beside their triggering events.
provisions.statement: Each reaction MUST be named `<verb>-<what>-on-<fact>` with a declared verb.
provisions.rationale: A reaction runs because something happened, and a name without its trigger hides why it runs: `send-due-notice` could fire on a borrow, a hold, or a reminder run. Naming the act and the fact lets a reader find every consequence of a fact by its name, as `litespec/core/language#name-each-record-by-its-types-name-form` states.
provisions.example: `reaction/lending.send-due-notice-on-loan-borrowed` answers `event/loan.loan-borrowed`.

provisions.heading: Point Reaction and Job Scenarios at the Run Result
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scenario-result-unknown` for a reaction or job scenario ending outside the run use case results.
provisions.statement: Each scenario on a reaction or job MUST end in a result of a use case its effects run.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job scenario ending anywhere else proves another behavior story: it walks the trigger and asserts an ending no run use case declares. Ending in a run use case result keeps the scenario a proof of the reaction or job consequence.

provisions.heading: Run Every Job from Its Declared Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `schedule-invalid` (level G) for a schedule neither an `every` duration, a `cron` expression, nor `at: startup`, and fails a job without its `kind` or a scheduled job without `schedule`.
provisions.statement: Each job MUST declare its `kind` of `scheduled`, `one-off`, or `manual` with its `schedule` where scheduled.
provisions.rationale: A job without a kind never runs or runs whenever its author remembered: reviewers see behavior with no moment attached. Naming the kind states when the job runs: the schedule with its `every` duration, `cron` expression and timezone, or `at: startup` for a run once at deployment start, `one-off` for work that runs once, or `manual` for work a person starts.
provisions.example: The expire-lapsed-holds job runs every six hours over open holds past their window.

provisions.heading: State the Failure Handling of Every Reaction and Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` fails a reaction or job with `onFailure` outside the one failure shape, and reports `record-invalid` for prose handling, a missing or malformed retry, and a malformed duration.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its `onFailure` in the one failure shape and its idempotency.
provisions.rationale: A failed reaction or job without handling retries forever or drops silently: notices double-send, holds never clear. Declaring `onFailure` states the failure shape beside the trigger: `mode` of `retry`, `skip-and-log`, or `discard`; `retry` with `maxAttempts`, `initialDelay`, `maxDelay`, and `backoff` of `exponential` or `fixed`; `then` of `dead-letter`; `deadLetter` carrying `after` with the action a person takes; `surfacesIn` naming the entry point showing the failure and `runbook` the recovery procedure. `retry` and `then` are required with `mode: retry`; `deadLetter`, `surfacesIn`, and `runbook` are optional. Delays and `after` are ISO 8601 durations, and prose handling is refused. The same shape serves every record and every effect entry. The idempotency mode, usually `state`, states how repeats collapse.

provisions.heading: Trigger Every Reaction from Its Declared Events
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reaction-trigger-unknown` (level G) for a trigger naming an unknown event, and fails a reaction without a `triggeredBy` list.
provisions.statement: Each reaction MUST declare the events it answers in `triggeredBy` as a list of `event/...` or `integration-event/...` ids.
provisions.rationale: A reaction without a trigger never runs or runs whenever its author remembered: reviewers see behavior with no moment attached. Naming the events states when the reaction fires: the domain or integration events it answers, one id or a list. A `skippedWhen` clause states when it skips.
provisions.example: The send-due-notice reaction answers the loan-borrowed domain event and runs the send-due-notice command.

provisions.heading: Write Every Runbook to Run or Recover
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a runbook page without `impact`, `prerequisites`, `procedure`, `verification`, `recovery`, or `escalation`.
provisions.statement: Each runbook MUST state its `impact`, `prerequisites`, `procedure`, `verification`, `recovery`, and `escalation`.
provisions.rationale: A runbook named by a job, a failure policy, or an alert is the answer a person opens under pressure: `impact` says what breaks, `prerequisites` say what to hold, `procedure` says each step, `verification` says how to confirm, `recovery` says how to undo, and `escalation` says who to call. A runbook missing one leaves the reader guessing at the worst moment.
provisions.example: The clear-stuck-reimbursements runbook states its impact on waiting expenses, its prerequisites, its procedure, its verification query, its recovery, and its escalation to the spending team.

provisions.heading: Write No Aggregate Directly from a Reaction or Job
provisions.evidence: Which reactions or jobs write an aggregate outside the use case they run? Look at the reaction and job effects beside the use cases.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST NOT write an aggregate except through the use case it runs.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job writing directly splits the write path: the same aggregate changes through a reviewed command and through an unreviewed reaction or job, each with its own guards. Running a small command keeps every write behind a use case with its access, consistency, results, and scenarios.

provisions.heading: Group Cross-Aggregate Rules by Theme
provisions.evidence: Which rule sets state no theme in `summary` without a recorded project convention? Look at the `summary` of each rule-set record file.
provisions.statement: Each rule-set record file holds the cross-aggregate rules of one theme, named in its `summary`.
provisions.rationale: Cross-aggregate rules share no aggregate to gather them, so an ungrouped rule set becomes a list of unrelated checks. One theme per rule set, stated in its `summary`, keeps each rule set reviewable as one decision about what holds across the domain.

provisions.heading: Illustrate Pages with Examples from the Cast
provisions.evidence: Which module, aggregate, and use-case explanation files lack an Example section from the cast where a walk would add to the records, without a recorded project convention? Look at the Example sections beside the module, aggregate, and use-case record files.
provisions.statement: Each module, aggregate, and use-case explanation file carries an Example section drawn from the example cast, removed where no walk adds to the records.
provisions.rationale: Every field states a rule, a state, or a mapping; none says when the behavior happens or who is under pressure while it does. An occasion drawn from the one shared cast lets a reviewer judge whether the behavior fits the world it serves, and lets readers carry the same people and figures from page to page.

provisions.heading: Keep Design Choices Out of the Records
provisions.evidence: Which record pages declare a child entity or value object as a record type? Look at the record types beside the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: Child entities and value objects MUST appear only in code and the glossary, never as records.
provisions.rationale: The records name what carries business meaning; the design inside an aggregate changes without changing that meaning. Recording each child and value as its own record would triple the tree while adding no decision a reviewer judges. Code and the glossary carry them, where builders and readers meet them.
provisions.example: Order lines live as a child of the order aggregate, and money as a value with its glossary entry; neither is a record.

provisions.heading: Depart from Advice Without a Record
provisions.evidence: Which departures name a provision of Strength advisory in their `covers`? Look at `covers` in each file under `.litespec/governance/departures/`.
provisions.statement: A project MAY depart from a provision of Strength advisory without recording a departure, since an advisory provision binds no project.
provisions.rationale: A provision of Strength advisory is experience applied with judgement, and [Provision Scopes](scopes.md) says it records nothing. A departure from it would name a rule the provision never made. A provision whose Statement says should takes this strength for the same reason.

provisions.heading: Record a Project-Wide Lowering as a Departure
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `analyzer-lowering-unrecorded` (level S) for a project-wide lowering in `.editorconfig`, `.globalconfig`, `<NoWarn>`, `#pragma warning disable` or `[SuppressMessage]` that no live departure covers.
provisions.statement: A project MUST record a departure for every analyzer rule it lowers or switches off in an `.editorconfig` that applies beyond one file.
provisions.rationale: A project-wide lowering in `.editorconfig` is a departure from the standard rather than a setting. A departure names the provision, the reason and the expiry date, so the lowering is dated and ends instead of staying silent.
provisions.example: A project that lowers LS5001 to a suggestion in its root `.editorconfig` records a departure whose `covers` names `litespec/core/system#point-code-and-tests-up-to-records`, the provision the rule enforces.

provisions.heading: Record Accepted Gaps as Departures
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `departure-expired` (level G) for a departure past its `expiresOn` date, and `departure-invalid` (level G) for a departure whose `covers` names a finding code no check emits, a code the model needs in order to load, or a provision or page the installed release does not ship.
provisions.statement: An accepted gap MUST live as a departure with an `expiresOn` date and an `exit`.
provisions.rationale: Missing work with no date is invisible: nothing reports it. A departure with an `expiresOn` date turns the same missing work into a dated promise. Its `covers` findings are covered until the date, the `exit` says how the gap closes, and `departure-expired` reports the departure after the date. Settled by [decision/0014-one-exception-record](decision/0014-one-exception-record) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example:
The running Claimwick example accepts that exporting expenses has no handler yet, so the gap lives as a departure in `.litespec/governance/departures/export-expenses-unimplemented.yaml`:

```yaml
type: departure
id: departure/export-expenses-unimplemented
title: Export Expenses Unimplemented
summary: Export waits for the finance file format.
covers:
  - use-case-unimplemented
subject:
  - use-case/spending.export-expenses
reason: Export waits for the finance file format.
exit: Exporting expenses has no handler yet. The gap closes when the finance file format lands and the export use case gains its handler.
expiresOn: 2027-06-01
```

The `use-case-unimplemented` finding is covered, and the run passes, until 2027-06-01, which satisfies this provision.

provisions.heading: Bind Every Atomic Write Group in Its Rule
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `atomic-group-drift` (level G) for an atomic use case whose `changes` differs from its rule's `binds`, and `atomic-group-invalid` (level A) for a group binding more than 4 aggregates.
provisions.statement: Each atomicity rule MUST name the aggregates it binds in `binds`.
provisions.rationale: An atomic write across aggregates stays allowed only through its rule: the rule states the group and why, such as an order without its hold overselling, and the use case commits exactly that group, as the [use-cases page](use-cases.md) states. A group above 4 aggregates is a coordination candidate, reported at level A.
provisions.example: The hold rule binds the hold and the copy aggregates, so a hold without its copy never stands.

provisions.heading: Compute Shared Values from One Calculation Rule
provisions.evidence: Which queries and commands computing one value cite different rules in `computedBy`? Look at the use cases beside the calculation rule.
provisions.statement: A value shown by a query and recorded by a command MUST cite the same calculation rule in `computedBy` on both use cases.
provisions.rationale: Two computations of one value drift: the screen shows one figure while the ledger records another, and each side cites its own code. Citing the same calculation rule on both use cases keeps one computation behind both faces. Code carries a mark naming the rule, and never the reverse.

provisions.heading: Connect Every State Through Transitions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `state-unreached` (level G) for a state reached by no transition, a creation included, and `transition-unknown` (level G) for a transition naming a missing state or use case.
provisions.statement: Each entity MUST list every allowed state change with its use case in `transitions`, including the creation that enters its first state.
provisions.rationale: States without transitions are a list of names with no path between them: a reviewer sees where an aggregate rests but never how it moves. Listing every allowed change with the use case that moves it shows the whole lifecycle beside the states, and leaves no state reachable only by a path no record names. The `state-unreached` and `transition-unknown` checks report a state no transition reaches and a transition naming a missing state or use case.

provisions.heading: Declare the Kind of Every Aggregate
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an aggregate page without `kind` or with an unknown kind.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST declare its kind: entity or store.
provisions.rationale: The kind decides what the page carries: an entity carries a lifecycle and a store carries an owner with no guarded invariant. Without the kind, a thing kept consistent reads the same as a table the product only holds.
provisions.example: The expense declares `kind: entity`, and the suppression list declares `kind: store`.

provisions.heading: Define Every Behavior Term in the Glossary
provisions.evidence: Which terms do the Behavior records name without a glossary entry stating their meaning? Look at the records beside the project glossary.
provisions.statement: Each term a Behavior record names MUST have a glossary entry stating its meaning.
provisions.rationale: Records and code share one language only when each word is defined once: a term used without an entry means whatever each reader guesses. The entry fixes the meaning, the rejected synonyms, and the wider and narrower terms, so reviewers and checks read the same word the same way.
provisions.example: The term `receipt` carries the meaning "proof of payment accepted for an expense" in the glossary, so every record naming a receipt means that proof.

provisions.heading: Freeze Every Commercial Data Value
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a commercial-data rule without `frozenWhen` or `retainedIn`.
provisions.statement: Each commercial-data rule MUST name when the value freezes in `frozenWhen` and where its retained facts live in `retainedIn`.
provisions.rationale: A price, fee, or rate read live changes under settled business: a refund follows today price instead of the price at sale. Naming when the value freezes pins each reading to its moment, and the retained link keeps the earlier values reachable for audit and dispute.

provisions.heading: Keep Cross-Aggregate Rules on a Rule Page
provisions.evidence: Which cross-aggregate rules sit outside a rule page? Look at the rule entries beside their aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A rule spanning aggregates MUST live as an entry on a rule page.
provisions.rationale: An aggregate page holds what one aggregate guarantees; a rule spanning aggregates guarantees what no single aggregate owns. Giving such rules their own page keeps each aggregate page a true account of its aggregate, and gathers the shared rules where a reviewer judges them together.

provisions.heading: Keep Model Invariants in Rules
provisions.evidence: Which setting pages hold a model invariant? Look at the settings beside the rules.
provisions.statement: A model invariant MUST live as a rule, never as a setting.
provisions.rationale: A setting tunes; a rule holds. An invariant filed as a setting reads as tunable, and a later operator tunes away what the model guaranteed. Keeping invariants in rules keeps what holds apart from what varies.

provisions.heading: Keep the Negation Word in the Rule Name
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-name-invalid` for a rule whose statement says `not`, `no`, `never`, or `cannot` while its name keeps no restricting word or uniqueness.
provisions.statement: A rule whose statement says `not`, `no`, `never`, or `cannot` MUST keep a restricting word in its name: `no`, `never`, `not`, `cannot`, `none`, `nothing`, `without`, `unless`, `non`, `refused`, `refuses`, `refusal`, `forbidden`, `blocked`, or `rejected`, a limit `only`, or a uniqueness `one-...-per-...`.
provisions.rationale: A name that drops the negation reads as its own opposite: a rule named `cancel-after-shipment` whose statement says "never" allows what it forbids. A restricting word keeps the name a true sentence a reviewer trusts without opening the statement, and `one-grant-per-account` already says what "an account never holds two grants" says. The `rule-name-invalid` check reports a rule whose statement negates while its name keeps no restricting word or uniqueness.
provisions.example: The rule reads `rule/order.cancel-never-after-shipment`.

provisions.heading: Leave States off Every Store
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a store aggregate carrying `states`.
