provisions.statement: A store MUST carry no states.
provisions.rationale: A store holds state no aggregate invariant guards, so a lifecycle on it promises what nothing guards: states claim a reviewed path while any writer moves the rows. The store names its owner instead, as `litespec/core/domain-model#name-the-owner-of-every-store` states, and staff actions on it stay ordinary use cases.
provisions.example: The suppression list declares `kind: store` with its owner and no states.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Term with Its Layer
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `glossary-invalid` for a glossary term without `layer`, and each behavior term lists the synonyms its readers know in `aliases`.
provisions.statement: Each glossary term MUST carry its record layer, intent, behavior, or implementation, with the established synonyms its readers know in `aliases`.
provisions.rationale: Business words, design words, and implementation words age on different clocks: a business term moves when the market moves, a design term moves when the model moves, and an implementation term moves when the code moves. The record layer tells each reader which clock the word follows, and the aliases let industry readers find LiteSpec own words without learning a second vocabulary first.
provisions.example: The term `refusal` carries `layer: behavior` with `aliases: ["rejection", "error"]`.

provisions.heading: Model Each Aggregate Lifecycle with States
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an entity page without `states` entries carrying a name and a meaning.
provisions.statement: Each entity MUST declare its lifecycle as `states` entries with a name and a meaning.
provisions.rationale: A bare state name tells a reviewer nothing: `rejected` without its meaning hides what rejection costs and allows. A name with a meaning makes each lifecycle step reviewable on the page, and gives `transitions` states worth connecting. An entity tracks what the thing is. A store carries no lifecycle, so it carries no states.
provisions.example: The hold queue entity declares `Requested`, `Ready`, `Collected`, `Cancelled`, and `Lapsed`, each with one sentence saying what the hold awaits or has received.

provisions.heading: Name Each Module After Its Capability
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate in this module serve the capability the module name states? Look at the aggregates beside the module name.
provisions.statement: Name each module after one capability the software offers, not after a company function or a catch-all, and split a module whose aggregates serve more than one capability into sibling modules.
provisions.rationale: Modules mark the areas of the bounded context, where a monolith would later split and how a reader finds a use case by module, then aggregate, then use case. A capability name keeps one module cohesive; a company function or a catch-all such as `platform`, `sales`, `operations`, or `misc` gathers unrelated aggregates that change for unrelated reasons. Splitting such a module into siblings keeps each module one capability with aggregates that serve it.
provisions.example: The finance module holds payout and ledger aggregates serving finance, while a misc module holding lending and catalog aggregates splits into lending and catalog siblings.

provisions.heading: Name Every Event in the Past Tense
provisions.evidence: Which event names read as an order rather than a completed fact? Look at the event entries beside their raising acts.
provisions.statement: Each domain event MUST be named in the past tense.
provisions.rationale: An event names a fact that completed, so the past tense tells a reader the business already moved: `submitted` reports, while `submit` orders. The past tense also pairs each event with the act raising it.
provisions.example: The expense aggregate raises `event/expense.submitted` for a completed submission.

provisions.heading: Name the Owner of Every Store
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a store aggregate page without `owner`.
provisions.statement: Each store MUST name its owning system or module in `owner`.
provisions.rationale: A store holds state no aggregate invariant guards, so nothing in the model explains who answers for its shape: a library-owned table, a suppression list, or a delivery log. Naming the owner puts one party behind it, and keeps staff actions on it as ordinary use cases instead of unwritten operations.

provisions.heading: Name the Refusal a Broken Rule Produces
provisions.evidence: Which guarded rules name no refusal in `refusal`? Look at the rule entries beside the results they refuse.
provisions.statement: Each rule whose breach refuses a use case MUST name the refusal in `refusal`.
provisions.rationale: A guarded rule without a named refusal leaves the ending unnamed: callers branch on a refusal the records never predicted. Naming the refusal ties the rule to the result the use case declares, so the breach and the ending stay one fact.

provisions.heading: Raise Every Event Through Its Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Which events leave from outside the root of their aggregate? Look at the aggregate code beside the event entries.
provisions.statement: Each event MUST be raised through its aggregate root.
provisions.rationale: The root is the one type through which outside behavior changes the aggregate, so it sees every change worth announcing. Raising each event there keeps the fact and its announcement in one step, and leaves no event announced for a change the aggregate never made.

provisions.heading: Release Every Reservation by a Named Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reservation-release-missing` for a reservation rule whose `releasedBy` names neither a use case nor `{ "mode": "never", "reason": "..." }` with its cost.
provisions.statement: Each reservation rule MUST name the use case releasing it in `releasedBy`, or `{ "mode": "never", "reason": "..." }` with its cost.
provisions.rationale: A held claim with no release is a leak: places, funds, or names stay locked past their need, and nobody owns freeing them. Naming the releasing use case states the end of the hold beside its start, and `{ "mode": "never", "reason": "..." }` with its cost admits a hold that truly lasts, with the price on record. Persistence claims the added keys and releases the removed ones in the commit that changes the aggregate (`litespec/backend/persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`). The `reservation-release-missing` check reports a reservation with no release.

provisions.heading: State Each Event with Meaning and Carries
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an event entry without `meaning` or `carries`.
provisions.statement: Each event MUST state its meaning and the facts it carries.
provisions.rationale: An event without a meaning is a name every reaction interprets alone; facts without a carries list are reconstructed from code at each reaction. Stating both on the entry lets each reaction trust what happened and what arrived with it.

provisions.heading: State Each Rule with Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a rule entry without `kind` or `statement`.
provisions.statement: Each rule MUST state its kind and its statement.
provisions.rationale: The kind decides how the rule is proved: an invariant on every change, a precondition before the behavior, a calculation through its examples, a cross-aggregate rule where aggregates meet, an atomicity rule naming its bound group, a reservation through its release, a commercial-data rule through its frozen value, a default through the value the model holds. A rule without a kind leaves each reader to prove it a different way, and the checks no place to confirm it.
provisions.example: `rule/expense.reimbursed-once` is an invariant stating "an expense is reimbursed at most once", checked on every reimbursement.

provisions.heading: State Every Module Dependency
provisions.evidence: Which modules rely on a module that `dependsOn` does not name? Look at the module pages beside the modules they rely on.
provisions.statement: Each module MUST name every module it depends on in `dependsOn`.
provisions.rationale: A module relies on the language and behavior of others, and each reliance shapes change: editing a module ripples into everything depending on it. Naming every reliance in `dependsOn` shows that ripple as data instead of leaving it for readers to reconstruct from prose.

provisions.heading: Tabulate Every Calculation with Examples
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `calculation-table-missing` for a calculation rule with no scenario examples table.
provisions.statement: Each calculation rule MUST be proven by a scenario carrying an `examples` table.
provisions.rationale: A calculation stated only as a sentence hides its edges: reviewers agree on the words while each pictures other numbers. An `examples` table shows those edges, and the scenario proving the rule pins them as checked facts. The `calculation-table-missing` check reports a calculation rule with no scenario `examples` table.

provisions.heading: Claim Every Notification Promise from a Requirement
provisions.evidence: Which notification claims lack a cited requirement? Look at the claims beside each notification.
provisions.statement: Each claim a notification makes MUST cite its requirement.
provisions.rationale: A message promising what no requirement holds is a promise no requirement states: the text assures a refund the policy never states. Citing the requirement behind each claim keeps every assured sentence a carried promise.

provisions.heading: Describe Every External System Operation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system operation without direction, timeout, timeout handling, response, or cache.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST describe its operations with direction, timeout, timeout handling, response, and cache.
provisions.rationale: An outside call without a declared shape fails by surprise: timeouts hang, retries double-charge, responses unparse. Describing each operation with its direction of `out` or `in`, its timeout with its timeout handling, its response, and its cache states the coupling beside the system. The `retries` prose states the retry behavior in words beside `onTimeout`. The retry count lives on the calling edge in `onFailure.retry.maxAttempts`. The system stands alone and names no actor.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Integration Event for Its Direction
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an integration event without direction, CloudEvents identity, typed payload, or trust.
provisions.statement: Each integration event MUST declare its direction, its CloudEvents identity, its typed payload, and the trust its readers place in it.
provisions.rationale: A published fact without a direction is read both ways: an outbound notice is answered as an order, an inbound claim is trusted as law. The direction, the CloudEvents type, source, and subject, the payload with classifications and types, and the trust of `trigger-only` or `payload` state what the fact is and how far readers follow it. Each payload field carries the field types use-case inputs use, as `litespec/core/use-cases#describe-every-use-case-input-with-origin-and-classification` states, and a money field carries an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, as the [Record Language](language.md) states. An event may name the `dataschema` URL its payload follows. An inbound event also declares its `correlation`; an outbound event declares its `translates` domain event and its optional `addresses`.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Notification with Audience Channel and Consent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `notification-sender-missing` for a notification no use case, reaction, or job sends, and fails a notification without its declared fields.
provisions.statement: Each notification MUST declare its template, addresses, channel, consent, frequency, dedup key, parameters, and locale.
provisions.rationale: A message without declared addresses and consent is sent on hope: the wrong actors receive it, the channel ignores consent, repeats annoy. Declaring the template with its parameters and locale, the addresses, the channel, the consent rule, the frequency of `once` or `per-attempt`, and the dedup key states the message beside its promise. Suppression lives on the notification in `suppressedWhen`, and suppression scenarios show the message sending nothing. The `notification-sender-missing` check reports a notification no use case, reaction, or job sends.

provisions.heading: Give Each Entry Point a Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an entry point without `kind` or `auth`.
provisions.statement: Each entry point MUST declare its kind and its `auth`.
provisions.rationale: A door with no kind is entered any way: a webhook is called as a page, a device as a browser. Declaring the kind of `browser`, `api`, `webhook`, `device`, `cli`, `mcp`, or `served-content` with its auth states how callers arrive and prove themselves.

provisions.heading: Give Every Browser Step a Screen
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `step-screen-missing` (level G) for a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves.
provisions.statement: Every journey step a use case serves through a browser or device entry point MUST be served by at least one screen.
provisions.rationale: A step a person achieves in a browser happens on some page. A step no screen serves is either carried by a page nobody recorded or not reachable at all, and the book cannot tell the reader where it happens. The pair sits side by side: `step-use-case-missing` names a step no use case serves, and `step-screen-missing` names a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves.
provisions.example: `journey/submit-and-reimburse#s1` is served by the expense form.

provisions.heading: Give Every Page Its Screen Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-unimplemented` (level S) for a screen no route marks, and `behavior-unrecorded` (level S) for a route with no mark or a mark naming no screen.
provisions.statement: Every route a browser or device entry point serves MUST be the implementation of exactly one screen record.
provisions.rationale: A page is where a person meets the product, and an unrecorded page offers use cases nobody reviewed as a page: what it lets someone start, which journey step it carries, which refusal it shows. One record per page, with one mark on the route, makes the page a reviewable promise and lets every other link (calls, results, journey coverage) be computed from it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's web route `/expenses` carries `implements: "screen/claimwick-app.expense-list"`, and `behavior/entry-points/claimwick-app/screens/expense-list.yaml` offers `use-case/spending.list-expenses`.

provisions.heading: Give Every Screen an Address or a Host
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a screen without exactly one of `address` and `host`.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST carry exactly one of `address` and `host`.
provisions.rationale: A route screen without an address is unreachable, and an overlay with one is two pages fighting over a route. An address places a screen on its route; a host places an overlay on the screen it opens on. Exactly one of the two leaves every page placed once.
provisions.example: The expense list carries the address `/expenses`; its confirm overlay names the expense list in `host` instead.

provisions.heading: Keep Notification Templates and the Template Store One Set
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `template-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared key the store the stack page names lacks, and `template-unrecorded` (level S) for a stored key no notification declares, in a project whose stack configuration names a template store.
provisions.statement: The `template` keys the notification records declare and the keys the project's template store holds MUST be the same set.
provisions.rationale: The template key is the one join between a notification's promise and the text a person receives. A declared key the store lacks fails at send time, and a stored template no notification declares is text nobody reviewed. The store is the stack's own file, so the check reads it where it is instead of copying the keys into a record. A notification whose body the sender composes at send time declares `template: none` and is left out.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `notification/spending.receipt-reminder` declares `template: receipt-reminder-manager`, and the template store holds `receipt-reminder-manager`.

provisions.heading: Match a Screen's Offers to Its Calls
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-offers-drift` (level S) for a screen whose `offers` and computed calls differ, naming each use case on one side only.
provisions.statement: A screen's `offers` MUST equal the use cases its route reaches through the generated client.
provisions.rationale: `offers` is the recorded promise of what a person can start on the page, and the calls are what the page really does. When the two differ, either the page grew a capability nobody recorded or the record promises one the page dropped. Comparing them on every run keeps the record honest without anyone re-reading the page.
provisions.example: The expense list offers `use-case/spending.list-expenses`, and its route calls `ListExpenses` through the generated client.

provisions.heading: Name Each Template for Its Subject, Event and Audience
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `template-key-invalid` (level A) for a template key ending in no name the notification declares in `addresses`.
provisions.statement: Each notification template key MUST read `<subject>-<event>-<audience>`, with the audience name the record declares in `addresses`.
provisions.rationale: A key naming its subject, its event and its audience tells each reader what the message is about and who receives it; a key naming none of the three hides both.
provisions.example: `receipt-reminder-manager` names the receipt, the reminder and the manager audience; `email-change-confirmation` names no audience and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Published Events in the Domain's Words
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `integration-event-name-invalid` (level G) for an outbound event named with an internal word.
provisions.statement: Each outbound integration event SHOULD be named for the business fact, without internal words.
provisions.rationale: An integrator reads the published name as the business fact; `staged`, `dispatch` or `outbox` describe the machinery that delivered it. A name carrying the fact travels across the boundary unchanged. The internal words are `staged`, `dispatch`, `dispatched`, `outbox`, `handler`, `queued`, `worker`, and `job`.
provisions.example: `expense-reimbursement-requested` names the requested reimbursement; `expense-reimbursement-staged` names the staging step and is reported.

provisions.heading: Publish Every Outbound Integration Event from Effects
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an emitted integration event no record declares in effects.
provisions.statement: Each use case, reaction, or job emitting an integration event MUST declare it in its effects as `emits`.
provisions.rationale: An emitted fact no edge declares is a hidden coupling: downstream readers depend on a promise the records never made, and the promise breaks without a diff. Declaring each emission as an `emits` effect states the coupling beside the behavior causing it. The `effect-undeclared` check reports an emitted event no record declares.

provisions.heading: Reach Every Inbound Integration Event Through a Webhook
provisions.evidence: Which inbound integration events lack a webhook entry point as their door? Look at the inbound events beside the entry points.
provisions.statement: Each inbound integration event MUST arrive through an entry point of kind `webhook`.
provisions.rationale: An inbound fact with no door is accepted anywhere: each handler invents its own intake, and trust scatters across the code. Arriving through a webhook entry point gives each inbound fact one door with one auth, where trust and correlation hold.

provisions.heading: Serve Only the Steps a Screen's Use Cases Serve
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-serves-drift` (level G) for a served step no offered use case serves.
provisions.statement: A screen's `serves` MUST name only journey steps that a use case it offers serves through a browser or device entry point.
provisions.rationale: A journey step is achieved through use cases, and a person reaches those use cases on a screen. Naming the step on the screen lets the book say where each step happens, and checking it against the offered use cases finds a screen claiming a step its use cases do not carry.
provisions.example: The expense form serves `journey/submit-and-reimburse#s1` because it offers `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, which serves that step.

provisions.heading: Serve Static Content Through Served Content
provisions.evidence: Which static scripts or legal texts sit outside served content, or lack path, content type, cache control, or versioning? Look at the static files beside the served-content entries.
provisions.statement: A static script or legal text MUST be served content with its path, content type, cache control, and versioning, never a use case.
provisions.rationale: A static file modeled as a use case invents behavior where none exists: results, scenarios, and handlers for bytes served unchanged. Serving it as content with its path, content type, cache control, versioning, and fulfilled requirements keeps content apart from behavior.

provisions.heading: Show Every Refusal a Screen Can Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-sentence-missing` (level A) for a refusal a screen can reach with neither a sentence in its frontend's `refusalDictionary` nor a browser test asserting its code.
provisions.statement: Every refusal a use case a screen offers can return MUST have a sentence in the refusal dictionary its frontend names in `refusalDictionary` or a browser test that asserts its code.
provisions.rationale: A refusal a person can trigger on a page is part of what the page says to them. Without a sentence, the person sees a code or a generic error; without a test, nobody knows what they see. Requiring one of the two only where a screen can reach the refusal avoids demanding sentences for refusals no person meets. Each frontend names its dictionary in its `frontends[]` entry, so the check reads that frontend's words rather than a convention.
provisions.example: The expense form offers `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, whose `spending.receipt-missing` refusal has a sentence in the dictionary the Claimwick web frontend names in `refusalDictionary`.

provisions.heading: Use Every Declared Template Parameter
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `template-param-drift` (level S) for a declared parameter whose placeholder, in the case the stack page states, appears in none of its template's texts.
provisions.statement: Every parameter a notification declares in `params` MUST appear as a placeholder in at least one of its template's texts.
provisions.rationale: A declared parameter is part of the message's promise: the order number in a confirmation, the name in a reminder. A parameter the template never uses is a promise the message does not keep, and it usually means the template was rewritten without the record.
provisions.example: `notification/spending.receipt-reminder` declares the parameter `submitterName`, and the `receipt-reminder-manager` template uses `{{SubmitterName}}`.

provisions.heading: Admit Only Outside Pains as Problems
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `problem-sufferer-invalid` for a problem whose primary sufferer is no person or organization outside the team; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a problem record file missing `affects`, `summary` or `statement`.
provisions.statement: A problem MUST name in `affects` a primary sufferer that is a person or organization actor outside the team building the product, and state the pain in `summary` and `statement` in fields.
provisions.rationale: A problem is a pain someone outside the team has today. The first `affects` entry is the primary sufferer, so who has the pain is the first fact a reader meets. `statement` states the sufferer, the condition and the consequence in one sentence, with the product never as its subject. `summary` states what the pain is in one paragraph: when it happens and what the person was trying to do, and never stands as a bare pointer to another page. What is no problem leaves for its own record: a solution in disguise becomes a feature, a worry about what might happen becomes a decision or a goal, an internal limit becomes a limit on the plan written outside Intent, a market fact becomes research, and a legal duty becomes a constraint.
provisions.example: In the library product, readers losing track of due dates is a problem whose primary sufferer is the reader. The library having too few staff for the summer is an internal limit and no problem.

provisions.heading: Answer Every Constraint
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a constraint record file missing a required field; the builder generates What It Requires from citing requirements.
provisions.statement: A constraint MUST state its `authority`, `readOn`, `kind`, `applies`, `appliesBecause`, and `summary` in fields, with What It Requires generated from the requirements that cite it.
provisions.rationale: An unanswered constraint is an outside rule the product can break unknowingly: a law, a regulation, or provider terms the team never examined. Recording each rule with its authority and applicability proves the team asked. The `kind` is technical, organizational, convention, or legal. `summary` states the rule in the authority's own words, `readOn` states when the outside rule was read, and What It Requires lists the requirements that cite the constraint, generated at build time. A fact learned from the world, such as the payout bank lengthening its settlement window, first lands as research with its source and date, then as a constraint.

provisions.heading: Cite Each Applying Constraint from a Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `constraint-unreached` for a constraint with `applies: true` that no requirement cites.
provisions.statement: A requirement MUST cite in `cites` each constraint with `applies: true` that binds it.
provisions.rationale: An applying constraint with no citing requirement has no answer the product keeps. Citing it ties the outside rule to the commitments that obey it, and What It Requires lists those commitments back. A constraint with `applies: true` that no requirement cites reports as `constraint-unreached` at check level G.

provisions.heading: Cite the Reasons of Every Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-cites-missing` for a requirement entry naming no reason in `cites`.
provisions.statement: Each requirement entry MUST name its reasons in `cites`.
provisions.rationale: The `cites` list holds any of goal, problem, feature, constraint, research, and decision, in no order of precedence. The feature holding the entry is the parent; the cited reasons are connections that explain why the commitment exists. A requirement that cites nothing reports as `requirement-cites-missing`.

provisions.heading: Define Each Recurring Capitalized Phrase
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `term-missing` for a capitalized phrase of two to four words named in three or more records that no glossary term defines.
provisions.statement: A capitalized phrase of two to four words named in three or more records MUST be defined by a glossary term.
provisions.rationale: A phrase used across records reads as a defined term whether or not any definition exists: readers and agents build on a meaning nobody wrote. Flagging the phrase while it is still cheap to define keeps the glossary equal to the words the records actually use.
provisions.example: A library phrase naming its first lending partners, used across goals and problems, takes a glossary term stating who those partners are, or the records stop using the phrase.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Journey
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a journey record file missing `summary`.
provisions.statement: A journey MUST state in `summary`, in up to four sentences, who walks, what starts the walk, what good looks like, and why it matters.
provisions.rationale: A journey page opens with its steps, so a reader landing on it cold learns the mechanics before the purpose. The summary states the walk in the walker's terms first, and the book renders it first on the page. `finishedWhen` stays the checkable end state; the summary carries the purpose no field checks.
provisions.example: The library journey to borrow and return describes a reader who holds a copy, starting at the shelf and ending with the copy back on its shelf, because a reader plans the next visit around the return.

provisions.heading: Explain Each Requirement in One Line
provisions.evidence: The one-line `rationale` on each requirement entry.
provisions.statement: Each requirement entry MUST explain its reason in a one-line `rationale`.
provisions.rationale: A commitment without its reason cannot be rejudged when the world moves: the reader finds what holds but not why. One line forces the reason into the open without inviting an essay. The feature carries the full story; the `rationale` carries the reason beside the commitment.

provisions.heading: Explain Every Problem in Four Sections
provisions.evidence: The four sections, in order, in each problem explanation file.
provisions.statement: A problem explanation file MUST carry Who Has It, What They Do Today, Evidence, and What Would Retire It, in that order.
provisions.rationale: The fields state who suffers; the explanation carries the cost, the one concrete occasion, the workaround in use, the evidence behind each claim, and what change in the world would retire the pain. A fixed order means a reader who learned one problem page finds each part on every problem page.
provisions.example: The library problem on due dates opens Who Has It with one reader at the desk with three overdue copies, and closes with What Would Retire It: readers holding their due dates without a paper list.

provisions.heading: Grade Problem Evidence by Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `problem-evidence-missing` for a problem with only assumed evidence or none. The builder writes `evidenceStrength` on each problem in the model.
provisions.statement: A problem MUST list each evidence entry with its `claim`, its `source` as a record id or a URL, its `readOn` date, and its `kind` as observed, reported or assumed, and carry at least one observed or reported entry.
provisions.rationale: Evidence states how anyone knows the pain is real: observed means a sufferer was watched, reported means a sufferer said it, and assumed means nobody outside the team has confirmed it. The strength of a problem is the strongest kind present, computed by the builder and never written, so it cannot drift from the entries. A problem resting on assumption alone, or on no entry, is unfinished work for the backlog until a sufferer is watched or heard.
provisions.example: The library problem of readers losing due dates carries a reported entry from the desk log, read on its date, so its computed strength is reported.

provisions.heading: Group Product Records by Module
provisions.evidence: The `.litespec/intent/` layout beside the project's recorded layout.
provisions.artifact: record:product, record:goal, record:problem, record:constraint, record:decision, record:research, record:actor, record:role, record:journey, record:module, record:feature
provisions.statement: Keep the product record at `.litespec/intent/product.yaml`, product-level goals, problems, constraints, decisions, research, actors and journeys in their folders under `.litespec/intent/`, and each module with its goals, problems, constraints, decisions, research and features under `.litespec/intent/modules/<module>/`.
provisions.rationale: A module folder keeps related pages together, so the pages of one product area sit side by side. One folder per kind keeps each record findable: goals, problems, features, constraints, decisions, research, journeys, and actors each have one home. A newcomer learns the layout once and predicts where the next record lives. A module names a product area, never the company, and each module folder names a module declared in Behavior.
provisions.example:
```text
.litespec/intent/
  product.yaml
  goals/
    <name>.yaml
  problems/
    <name>.yaml
  constraints/
    <name>.yaml
  decisions/
    <number>-<name>.yaml
  research/
    <name>.yaml
  actors/
    <name>.yaml
  journeys/
    <name>.yaml
  modules/
    spending/
      module.yaml
      goals/
        <name>.yaml
      problems/
        <name>.yaml
      constraints/
        <name>.yaml
      decisions/
        <number>-<name>.yaml
      research/
        <name>.yaml
      features/
        <name>.yaml
```

provisions.heading: Identify Every Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a requirement entry without identifier; `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a feature segment differing from its feature.
provisions.statement: Each requirement entry MUST carry one identifier `requirement/<feature>.<name>` naming its own feature.
provisions.rationale: An identifier lets a Behavior record name the commitment it fulfills and lets the model resolve the name. A commitment written only as prose cannot be traced from Intent to code. The feature segment names the feature holding the entry, and the feature is the parent by identifier containment. Proposed by [decision/0003-requirement-origin](decision/0003-requirement-origin) on the evidence in [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](research/intent-hierarchy-evidence), [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence), and [research/established-traceability-practice](research/established-traceability-practice).

provisions.heading: Keep Actors to People and Organizations
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an actor record file with a kind outside person and organization, or with no `belongsToTeam`; `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for such a kind.
provisions.statement: An actor MUST carry a `kind` of person or organization and state in `belongsToTeam` whether it belongs to the team building and running the product.
provisions.rationale: An actor answers for what it does, so software stands behind no actor: an external system stands alone as its own record, and internal machinery such as a reaction, a job, a transport or a renderer is never an actor. A person or an organization can hold a role, suffer a problem and walk a journey. `belongsToTeam` reads as a predicate that is true about the record, so a reader tells a team actor from a customer at a glance, and a problem can refuse a team sufferer.
provisions.example: The library reader is an actor of kind person with `belongsToTeam` false. The text gateway is an external system and no actor.

provisions.heading: Keep Behavior Out of Intent
provisions.evidence: Intent records under `.litespec/intent/` free of the detail the Statement names.
provisions.statement: An Intent record MUST NOT describe states, results, codes, transactions, edges, consistency modes, Behavior field names, or code.
provisions.rationale: An Intent record that names Behavior detail becomes a second specification, and it drifts from the first with the next Behavior change. Two specifications force every reader to ask which one the code follows. Behavior records own behavior and point up to the requirements and steps they serve, so each fact has one home.

provisions.heading: Keep Company Operation Out of Intent
provisions.evidence: Intent and Behavior records stating company operation beside the constraints and research that carry the binding facts.
provisions.statement: An Intent or Behavior record MUST state only behavior the application performs, data it holds, a refusal it raises at runtime, infrastructure it runs on, or a limit it enforces.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec specifies the product, not the company. Prices as an offer, markets, hiring, sales actions, launch calendars, company goals and founder concerns can be checked only against a bank account, a diary or a contract, so they sit outside the records a reader reviews as the product. A company fact that binds the product still enters: as a constraint when an authority or a limit binds the application, and as dated research when a choice rests on it. [The Software Test](#the-software-test) names what belongs for each record type: a goal states a software outcome, a problem states a user pain the software answers, a feature states a capability the software has, and a module names a product area, never a company function. Plan entitlements the software enforces stay, as settings and permissions; the price list as a company offer leaves.
provisions.example: A library holds its lending limit as a setting the application enforces, so the limit stays as Behavior. The membership price the library charges as an offer is a company fact: it enters only as dated research behind the decision that sets the limit.

provisions.heading: Keep Intent in Its Homes
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a record outside its home, a record type outside its allowed levels, and a link from another module to a module-local record, and `module-undeclared` for a folder under `intent/modules/` naming no declared module or a module folder without its module.
provisions.artifact: record:product, record:goal, record:problem, record:constraint, record:decision, record:research, record:actor, record:role, record:journey, record:module, record:feature
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST keep its product record at `.litespec/intent/product.yaml`, its product-level goals, problems, constraints, decisions, research, actors and journeys in their folders under `.litespec/intent/`, and each module with its goals, problems, constraints, decisions, research and features under `.litespec/intent/modules/<module>/`.
provisions.rationale: Intent split across notes and books gives no single answer to the question an agent asks before building. One home per kind, with the product record, goals, problems, constraints, decisions, research, actors and journeys at product level and each module with its goals, problems, constraints, decisions, research and features under its module folder, gives every reader one place to look. A second home for any kind starts a second truth about the product. The folder is the parent: product level holds only the product, actors, roles and journeys, module level holds only features with their requirements, and goals, problems, constraints, decisions and research sit at either level with the folder saying which. Each module folder names a module declared in Behavior, so one name runs through Intent, Behavior and code.

provisions.heading: Move Every Goal with a Journey or a Quality Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `goal-mover-missing` for a goal moved by no journey and no quality requirement.
provisions.statement: A goal MUST be moved by a journey serving it or by a quality requirement citing it.
provisions.rationale: A goal no journey serves and no quality requirement confirms names an outcome the product never touches: a company hope filed as a product goal. A journey serving the goal shows the walk that moves the counted outcome, and a quality requirement citing it states the measure that confirms the move. An outcome the system controls directly is a quality requirement, and an outcome only the company controls is no goal at all.
provisions.example: The library goal of faster pickup is moved by the borrow-and-return journey serving it; a goal of higher membership sales is moved by no journey and is no product goal.

provisions.heading: Name Each Sibling Problem or Merge It
provisions.evidence: Which problems share a sufferer and a feature yet name neither each other nor a merge? Look at the problems cited from each feature.
provisions.statement: Two problems with the same primary sufferer cited from the same feature MUST name each other or merge into one problem.
provisions.rationale: Two pains of one sufferer under one feature, written in different words, hide that they are one pain or two: one feature solves both halves, and the book lists the sufferer twice with no sign of the overlap. Naming the sibling states the split where a reader meets it; merging keeps one pain with one sufferer.
provisions.example: Two library problems of the reader cited from the borrowing feature, one on due dates and one on renewals, name each other, so a reader sees both before the feature solves either.

provisions.heading: Name Every Actor from a Journey, a Problem or an Access Position
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `actor-unused` for an actor named by no journey, problem or access position.
provisions.statement: Every actor MUST be named by a journey, by a problem in `affects`, or by an access position in `holds`.
provisions.rationale: An actor named by nothing is a party nobody suffers as, walks as or grants to: a leftover from a system or a machine promoted beside real people. Naming each actor from the walk it walks, the pain it suffers or the role it holds keeps the actor list equal to the parties the product serves.
provisions.example: The library reader is named by the borrow-and-return journey and by the due-date problem; the librarian is named by the holds of the librarian role.

provisions.heading: Name No Solution in a Problem Statement
provisions.evidence: Which problem statements name a product, a feature, or a solution? Look at the problem statements beside their sufferers.
provisions.statement: A problem `statement` MUST name no product, feature or solution.
provisions.rationale: A statement naming a solution files a missing feature as a pain: the reader accepts the answer before weighing the pain, and every alternative answer reads as off-topic. A statement naming the sufferer, the condition and the consequence leaves the answer to the feature that solves it.
provisions.example: "Readers lose track of due dates" names a pain. "Readers need a reminder dashboard" names a solution and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Product Decisions in One Numbered Sequence
provisions.evidence: Each decision file named `<number>-<name>.yaml` beside its matching identifier.
provisions.statement: Name each product decision `<four-digit number>-<name>.yaml` and use `decision/<four-digit number>-<name>` as its identifier.
provisions.rationale: One numbered sequence orders each decision by when the choice was proposed, giving every record a short stable name. The number counts as a word, so digits never stand alone in the identifier. Scattered names would force every citation to carry the full path.

provisions.heading: Order Each Journey Toward One Goal
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a journey record file missing its `actor`, `serves`, `summary`, `finishedWhen`, `steps`, or `betweenSteps`.
provisions.statement: A journey MUST walk one actor toward one goal through ordered steps, naming the goal record in `serves` and stating `betweenSteps` in fields.
provisions.rationale: A journey names its `actor`, its goal record in `serves`, its `finishedWhen`, and its ordered `steps`. One actor means a step names another actor only at a handoff; one goal means a walk with several goals splits into several journeys. The order shows how the steps join toward the goal, so a step that fits nowhere is visible. The journey names in `cites` the requirements it carries, and the use cases, reactions, and jobs that serve each step point up with `serves`. `betweenSteps` holds branch order only, and Example in the explanation file shows one concrete occasion. Proposed by [decision/0005-journeys-serve-a-goal](decision/0005-journeys-serve-a-goal) on the evidence in [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](research/intent-hierarchy-evidence), [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence), and [research/established-traceability-practice](research/established-traceability-practice).
provisions.example: The largest consumer held a 21-step journey with five actors, from creating the organizer to closing the books. Split by goal, it is four journeys: set up and sell an event; buy a ticket; admit the crowd; close the night.

provisions.heading: Perform Each Journey Step with an Actor or a System
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a journey step carrying both `actor` and `system`; `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for such a step or for a `system` naming no external system, job or reaction.
provisions.statement: A journey step MUST name at most one performer: another actor in `actor` at a handoff, or the external system, job or reaction in `system` when no person acts, and a step naming neither is performed by the walking actor.
provisions.rationale: A step performed by machinery forced a machine actor into Intent, where it sat beside real people and held no role. Naming the system record that performs the step keeps the actor list to people and organizations, and keeps the performing party one link away. A step naming both an actor and a system names two performers for one act.
provisions.example: In the library journey, the step that sends the overdue notice names the text gateway in `system`; the steps the reader walks name no performer.

provisions.heading: Reach Every Intent Record with Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `intent-unreached` for a record that reaches no Behavior.
provisions.statement: Each Intent record MUST reach Behavior through its stated path.
provisions.rationale: The folder fixes where a record sits. Reachability fixes that it leads to software. A goal reaches a journey or a quality requirement. A problem reaches a feature or a requirement that addresses it. A feature or a requirement reaches a use case, a journey or a quality scenario in Behavior. A constraint is answered by a requirement. Research is cited by a record that reaches Behavior. A decision decides a record that reaches Behavior. A record that reaches no Behavior is either unfinished work for the backlog or not software.

provisions.heading: Record Each Decision Option with Pros and Cons
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a decision option missing `pros` or `cons`.
provisions.statement: Each decision option MUST carry its `pros` and its `cons`.
provisions.rationale: A choice argued from options and evidence can be revisited on its merits; one argued from authority cannot. Each option carries its name with what speaks for it in `pros` and against it in `cons`, so the comparison sits in the entries instead of a prose section.

provisions.heading: Record Research with Read Sources
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a research record file without `question`, `conclusion`, or `sources`; `litespec model check` reports `explanation-missing` for a research record without Answer in its explanation file, `source-link-bare` for a bare URL, `source-key-unknown` for an unknown key, and `source-unused` for an unused source.
provisions.statement: A research record MUST state its `question`, state its `conclusion` in one sentence, list each source with its `key`, `url`, and `readOn`, and carry Answer in its explanation file.
provisions.rationale: A fact without its source cannot be rechecked when a decision depends on it. The read date shows when the outside fact was true, so a later reader knows whether to trust or refresh it. Research without sources and dates asks every later choice to rest on memory. The `conclusion` states in one sentence what the sources establish and what follows, so a decision can cite it as data. Each source carries its `key`, `url`, and `readOn`; the explanation cites a source with a reference link `[text][key]`, and a bare URL, an unknown key, or an unused source is a finding. Answer expands the `conclusion`: what the sources say, claim by claim, with the confidence behind each claim, and Notes on Sources holds what a later reader needs about each source. Observed provider behavior lands here too, cited and dated, before any constraint or requirement rests on it. Proposed by [decision/0009-research-states-its-conclusion](decision/0009-research-states-its-conclusion) on the evidence in [research/research-conclusion-evidence](research/research-conclusion-evidence).

provisions.heading: Restrict Requirement Fulfillment to Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-fulfillment-missing` for a requirement no Behavior record fulfills.
provisions.statement: A requirement MUST be fulfilled only from Behavior records.
provisions.rationale: The records that fulfill are rule, use case, reaction, job, notification, and setting. A journey names the requirements it shows in `cites`; it never fulfills, so a journey alone never clears an unfulfilled requirement. Behavior points up to the promises it keeps, and each promise traces down to the behavior that keeps it.

provisions.heading: Shape Each Decision Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a decision record file missing a required field; `litespec model check` reports `explanation-missing` for a decision without Context in its explanation file.
provisions.statement: A decision MUST state its `choice` and `consequences` in fields and carry Context in its explanation file.
provisions.rationale: Context in the explanation file states the choice, `choice` names the chosen option, and `consequences` states what follows, so each decision reads the same way. Decision in the explanation file expands the chosen option, and Evidence with Confidence holds the supporting material with its confidence where the choice rests on it. The `reopenedWhen` condition names what would reopen the choice, so a decision reopened by a condition rather than a date stays stable until the world actually changes. The `basedOn` link names the constraints and research behind it, and requirements only on a technical decision. The [model page](model.md) requires each product decision to name the records it settles in `decides`.

provisions.heading: Shape Each Module Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a module record file missing a required field.
provisions.statement: A module MUST state its `summary` and its `dependsOn` in fields.
provisions.rationale: The module names one product area of the bounded context, so Intent, Behavior and code share one name for one area. `summary` states what the area covers in one place, and `dependsOn` names the modules it builds on. A reader learns where each area sits once and finds its records under one folder. Cross-cutting work sits at product level, never in a module that borrows it.
provisions.example: The spending module covers expenses, receipts and the policy, with an empty `dependsOn` where it stands alone.

provisions.heading: State Each Exception with Its Fallback
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `except-fallback-missing` finding.
provisions.statement: A requirement that names an `except` condition MUST name its `fallback` requirement in the same entry.
provisions.rationale: An exception without a fallback leaves the reader at the exact moment the promise breaks: the product refuses with no stated alternative. The `condition` states in product words when the commitment does not hold, and `fallback` names the requirement that covers what happens then. The fallback carries no `except` of its own, so the chain stays one deep and every exception ends in a promise.
provisions.example: A reimbursed expense lands in the employee's account, never more than they spent. Except when the payout bank's settlement window has closed for that batch, with `fallback` naming the requirement that has finance repay the employee by other means.

provisions.heading: State Each Feature with Its Offering
provisions.evidence: Which features miss their offering, their solved problems, or their moved goals? Look at each feature record beside its problems and goals.
provisions.statement: A feature MUST state its `offering`, name the problems it solves in `solves`, and name the goals it moves in `advances`.
provisions.rationale: A feature names the problems it solves in `solves` and the goals it moves in `advances`, so each offer traces to a pain and an outcome. `offering` states what is in and what is out, so the scope of the offer is written where the links are. Proposed by [decision/0004-features-advance-goals](decision/0004-features-advance-goals) on the evidence in [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](research/intent-hierarchy-evidence), [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence), and [research/established-traceability-practice](research/established-traceability-practice).

provisions.heading: State Each Goal with Its Measure
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a goal record file missing a required field.
provisions.statement: A goal MUST state its `summary`, `statement`, `measure`, and `target` in fields.
provisions.rationale: A goal without a measure is a wish no check can confirm: the team cannot tell whether the product serves it. The `summary` states what the goal is in one paragraph, the `statement` names the outcome and why it matters, and `measure` and `target` name what is counted and the number aimed for. A goal carries no authority: it explains why features exist and never decides a conflict.

provisions.heading: State Each Problem with Its Evidence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a problem record file missing its `summary` or `statement`.
provisions.statement: A problem MUST state its `summary` and `statement` in fields, with its evidence graded under [Grade Problem Evidence by Kind](#grade-problem-evidence-by-kind).
provisions.rationale: A problem that names what its people face points to the pain its solution lifts. `summary` describes the pain in the people's own terms, and the graded evidence shows it is real. Problems without sufferers attract solutions nobody needs. The `affects` link names the actors who face it, so each pain traces to the people a solution must serve.

provisions.heading: State Each Quality Requirement as a Scenario
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a quality requirement missing `stimulus`, `environment`, `response`, `measure`, or `check`.
provisions.statement: A quality requirement MUST state the moment it holds for in `stimulus` and `environment`, what the product does in `response`, how that is measured in `measure`, and how that is confirmed in `check`, with `target`, `conditions`, `runsOn`, and `evidence` where they apply.
provisions.rationale: "Fast", "secure", or "always available" cannot be built to or checked. A quality requirement holds only for a moment that can happen: something arrives, under some condition, and the product answers within a measure. Written that way, it tells the builder what to design for and tells a test or a probe what to look for, and a later change in the moment (a bigger on-sale, a new attack) visibly reopens the target. The four fields follow the quality attribute scenario the architecture literature uses, so a reviewer can compare one target with another. The `check` names the probe or test that confirms the measure, and it is required where the requirement carries `measure`. The `target` names the number aimed for, `conditions` names what holds while measuring, `runsOn` names where the check runs, and `evidence` names what the run leaves behind; each applies where the confirmation needs it.
provisions.example: `requirement/expense-submission.month-end-submissions` has `kind: quality`, `stimulus` "Five hundred employees submit expenses in the last hour of the month", `environment` "Normal operation, one application instance down", `response` "Each submission is stored and acknowledged", `measure` "Share of submissions acknowledged within two seconds: at least 99 percent", and `check` "month-end acknowledgement probe".

provisions.heading: State One Product
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `product-count-invalid` finding, and `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for product fields outside the record schema.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST state exactly one product record at `.litespec/intent/product.yaml`, with `boundary`, `addresses`, and `summary`.
provisions.rationale: One product record gives every reader one answer to what the product is and who it serves. The `boundary` and `addresses` focus every later choice. Two product statements let each plan cite the one it prefers. `summary` states what the product is in one place.

provisions.heading: State Requirement Kind and Statement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a requirement entry without `kind` or `statement`, or a policy requirement without dated values.
provisions.statement: Each requirement entry MUST carry `kind` and `statement`.
provisions.rationale: The `kind` is functional, quality, or policy: what the product does, how well it does it, or what the business holds. A policy requirement carries its `values` with effective dates. The `statement` states the commitment in one testable sentence.

provisions.heading: State the Cost and Workaround of Every Problem
provisions.evidence: The cost and the workaround, each in the sufferer's own units or the word `unknown`, in Who Has It and What They Do Today of each problem explanation file.
provisions.statement: A problem MUST state what the pain costs its sufferer today and what the sufferer does instead, each in the sufferer's own units or the word `unknown`, in its explanation file.
provisions.rationale: A pain with no cost and no workaround is a slogan: no reader can tell a daily loss from a passing annoyance, and no feature can be judged against the price of standing still. The workaround shows the pain is real enough to work around, and why that workaround fails. Where nobody has priced the cost or named the workaround, `unknown` states the gap honestly. Who Has It states the cost and What They Do Today states the workaround, so the fields stay checkable and the context stays readable.
provisions.example: A reader who loses track of due dates pays late fees each month, and keeps a paper list of due dates, which fails when the list stays at home.

provisions.heading: State the Measure on a Counted Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a requirement carrying `measure` without `check` or a passing run, and for a statement naming a number with no `measure`.
provisions.statement: A requirement whose statement names a number MUST carry `measure`.
provisions.rationale: A number without its measure cannot be checked: the team cannot tell what is counted. The `measure` names what is counted. A requirement carrying `measure` needs a `check` and a passing run, and a statement naming a number with no `measure` reports at check level A.

provisions.heading: State When Each Journey Finishes
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a journey record file missing `finishedWhen`.
provisions.statement: A journey MUST state its observable end in `finishedWhen`.
provisions.rationale: A journey without a stated end can stop anywhere: the reader cannot tell a finished walk from an abandoned one, and serving records cannot tell done from dropped. `finishedWhen` states the observable end in one sentence, in product words.
provisions.example: `finishedWhen`: the employee holds the reimbursement.

provisions.heading: Treat Generated Research as Source Material
provisions.evidence: A research record or a decision behind each position built from generated records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST treat records generated outside `docs/` as source material until a research record or a decision states the claim.
provisions.rationale: Records generated outside `docs/` mix verified facts, inferences, and recommendations in one confident voice. Treating them as source material with no authority keeps a recommendation from being built as if someone decided it. A research record or a decision restates the claim before anything rests on it.

provisions.heading: Treat Tenant-Set Values as Data
provisions.evidence: Each `setBy: tenant` value stored as tenant data.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat a `setBy: tenant` value as tenant data.
provisions.rationale: Tenants choose their own values within the ranges Intent sets: a tenant holds its receipt threshold at EUR 25 by default within the EUR 0 to EUR 500 range. The requirement sets the range and the default, and each tenant's choice inside it is data. Treating tenant values as product values would bind every tenant to one tenant's choice.
provisions.example: The tenant sets a receipt threshold of EUR 50; the requirement covering threshold ranges already sets the range, so the threshold itself is data.

provisions.heading: Write Journey Steps as Sentences with Ids
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a journey step missing `id` or `statement`, or naming a use case.
provisions.statement: Each journey step MUST carry its `id` and its product sentence in `statement`, and name no use case.
provisions.rationale: A step written as a product sentence reads in journey detail with no Behavior knowledge: it states what a person experiences, not which handler runs. The `id` (`s1`, `s2`, and so on) gives Behavior a stable target: use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with `serves` to `journey/<name>#s1`. A step that names its use case drags Behavior into Intent and breaks the journey detail every time Behavior renames. The performer and the failure text are optional: a step names the walking actor only at a handoff in `actor`, or the system record performing it in `system` when no person acts, and carries `failure` where the walk can fail.
provisions.example: Step `s4` states `Finance reimburses the approved expense.` in `statement` and names no use case; `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` names `journey/submit-and-reimburse#s4` in `serves`.

provisions.heading: Cite Shared Provisions in Their Published Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A shared provision citation MUST use its published identifier.
provisions.rationale: A shared provision is cited across projects, so its identifier looks the same everywhere. The published `litespec/<page>#<slug>` form stays fixed, while project records use the type forms above.

provisions.heading: Exclude Declared Content Paths from the ASCII Check
provisions.evidence: Which non-ASCII prose sits outside the paths the project record declares? Look at the content files beside the declaration.
provisions.statement: An ASCII check MUST exclude only the natural-language content paths that the project record declares.
provisions.rationale: A product whose subject is another language carries that language in its content files, where a diacritic is part of a word rather than a styling choice. Excluding only the declared content paths keeps the check strict everywhere else: documents about that content stay in scope, so styled prose filed beside content still meets the check.

provisions.heading: Exclude the Compound That Names Another Concept
provisions.evidence: Which compounds use a rejected word to name another concept without being listed in the rejection's `except`?
provisions.statement: A glossary rejection MUST list, in `except`, every compound in which a rejected word names a concept other than the one the rejection is about.
provisions.rationale: A rejection matches a word, and a word can belong to more than one term: Claimwick rejects `docket` in favor of `receipt` for payment proof while a docket still names the shipping list. Without the `except` list, the check would force the project to rename an unrelated concept or drop a sound rejection.
provisions.example:
The exemption covers the compound only, so the bare word stays rejected.

```json
{ "word": "docket", "reason": "one word for a payment receipt and a shipping list",
  "scope": "^.litespec/domain/modules/spending/", "except": ["shipping docket"] }
```

provisions.heading: Follow the Identifier Form of Each Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for an identifier outside the form its type uses.
provisions.statement: A record identifier MUST follow the form the model states for its record type.
provisions.rationale: A reader who meets `use-case/spending.submit-expense` knows it is a use case in the spending module without opening it. If two types shared one form, a citation needs its surrounding page to make sense, and search returns the wrong records.
provisions.example: `event/expense.submitted` names an event of the expense aggregate.

provisions.heading: Keep Names an Outside Standard Fixes
provisions.evidence: Which fixed names were renamed to fit the grammar? Look at the Gherkin fields and CloudEvents attributes the change touches.
provisions.statement: Every name an outside standard fixes MUST stay exactly as that standard spells it.
provisions.rationale: A name an outside standard fixes belongs to that standard: renaming `given` to fit the word classes breaks every Gherkin reader. The grammar stays complete by exempting exactly these names instead of growing an exceptions list. Gherkin and CloudEvents names are the only exemptions.
provisions.example: A Claimwick scenario keeps `given`, `when`, and `then`, which the word-class table gives no class.

provisions.heading: Keep Wire Codes Stable
provisions.evidence: Which wire codes in the contract break the values deployed clients branch on? Look at the wire codes beside the deployed clients.
provisions.statement: A wire code MUST stay unchanged once clients read it.
provisions.rationale: Wire codes travel to deployed clients, which branch on their exact values. Renaming a code that clients already read breaks every deployed reader that compares the old value, with no record the reader opens to learn the new one.

provisions.heading: Name a Boolean as a Predicate
provisions.evidence: Which boolean fields read as something other than a predicate, or carry an `is` or `has` prefix? Look at the boolean fields the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every boolean field MUST read as a present-tense predicate that is true about the record when the value is true.
provisions.rationale: A boolean without a prefix reads as a fact about the record: `applies` says the constraint applies, and `recorded` says the entry is recorded. An `is` or `has` prefix adds a word that says nothing the value does not already say. The predicate form keeps every boolean readable in a sentence about its record.
provisions.example: Claimwick marks an applying constraint with `applies: true` instead of `isApplicable: true`.

provisions.heading: Name Commands as Verbs and Flags by What They Set
provisions.evidence: Which subcommands read as nouns, or which flags name something other than their mode or value? Look at the commands and flags the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every subcommand MUST read as a verb and every flag as the mode or value it sets.
provisions.rationale: A verb names what the command does, so `check` reads as an action before its arguments are weighed. A flag that names its mode or value reads the same way at every call site, and kebab-case keeps multiword flags writable without quotes. Stable exit codes let scripts tell a clean run from a blocking finding from bad arguments.
provisions.example: The release check runs as `litespec model check --release` and exits 1 on a blocking finding.

provisions.heading: Name Each Date by What It Marks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `FIELD_NAME_SHAPE` diagnostic for a date field.
provisions.statement: Every date field MUST end in `On` for a recorded date or carry a name that states what the date does.
provisions.rationale: A recorded date says when something happened or until when it holds: `readOn` says when an outside source was read, and `expiresOn` says when a departure ends. `effectiveFrom` opens a validity span. The shape tells a reader which dates record the world and which open a span.
provisions.example: A Claimwick constraint carries `readOn` with the date its authority was read, and a departure carries `expiresOn` with the date it ends.

provisions.heading: Name Each Field by Its Word Class
provisions.evidence: Which fields break their word class? Look at the field names the change adds, beside the word-class table.
provisions.statement: Every record field MUST use the name its word class gives it in the word-class table.
provisions.rationale: One grammar with no exceptions list means a reader who learned `cites` on a journey reads `cites` on a requirement without a second look. Each class answers one question about the field: whether it identifies, links, classifies, narrates, conditions, or reasons. Only names an outside standard fixes stand outside this grammar. Settled by [decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar](decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar) on the evidence in [research/field-naming-evidence](research/field-naming-evidence) and [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence).
provisions.example: The Claimwick journey `submit-an-expense` cites its goal in `cites` and states each step in `statement`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Finding Code by Subject and Problem
provisions.evidence: Which finding codes miss the subject-problem form or end in a word the problem-word table does not hold? Look at the finding codes the change adds, beside the problem-word table.
provisions.statement: Every finding code MUST read as `<subject>-<problem>` with the problem drawn from the problem-word table.
provisions.rationale: A code in subject-problem form tells a reader what the finding is about and what is wrong with it before the message is opened. A closed set of problem words, each with one meaning, keeps codes comparable across tools: one word for absent, one for expired, and no synonyms. The problem-word table holds each word with its meaning and an example.
provisions.example: A use case with no scenario takes the code `use-case-scenario-missing`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Record by Its Types Name Form
provisions.evidence: Which record names miss the name form of their type? Look at the identifiers the change adds, beside the record-name table.
provisions.statement: Every record name MUST use the name form the record-name table gives its type.
provisions.rationale: A name in the word class of what the record is tells a reader the type before the identifier is opened: a verb opens a use case, a noun phrase opens a goal, and a past participle opens an event. One name form per type keeps listings scannable and citations writable by hand. The record-name table holds the Intent forms beside the Behavior and governance forms.
provisions.example: Claimwick names the journey `submit-an-expense`, the use case `submit-expense`, and the setting `receipt-threshold`.

provisions.heading: Name Records with One to Six Words
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a name outside one to six lowercase hyphenated words.
provisions.statement: A name MUST carry one to six lowercase hyphenated words.
provisions.rationale: A short hyphenated name reads aloud in review and stays stable when the wording of the record changes. A long name gets shortened differently at each citation, and the shortcuts drift into competing names for one record.
provisions.example: `decision/0001-receipt-threshold` counts its number as one word.

provisions.heading: Record the Project Vocabulary as Data
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `glossary-invalid` for a glossary that fails the glossary schema.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record each term, its rejected synonyms, the scope of each rejection, and its mannered terms in the project glossary satisfying `schemas/glossary.schema.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A glossary column headed "Avoid" speaks to a reader and to nothing else: no tool can check it. A rule held as data reaches the reader and the validator alike, so the same rejection appears in prose guidance and in diagnostics.
provisions.example:
A rejection carries the scope that binds it, because a word that is right in one module is wrong in another.

```json
{ "id": "term/customer", "term": "customer", "meaning": "A person or company that buys.",
  "rejected": [{ "word": "client", "scope": "^domain/modules/orders/",
    "reason": "client names the API consumer" }] }
```

provisions.heading: Reject a Recorded Synonym Inside Its Scope
provisions.evidence: Which words on the page are synonyms the project glossary rejects for the scope the page sits in?
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST NOT use a synonym that the project glossary rejects for the scope the page sits in.
provisions.rationale: Term drift is invisible one page at a time and plain across a module: each page looks fine while the project slowly speaks two languages. The expensive case is a synonym that is a defined term elsewhere, because one word then names two things and every reader guesses which one.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Identifier Citation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a citation naming no written record.
provisions.statement: Every identifier citation MUST resolve to a written record.
provisions.rationale: A citation is a promise that a record exists at the other end. A citation that names nothing sends the reader searching for a record nobody wrote, so the model check fails it.

provisions.heading: Review Each Term for Its Lookalikes
provisions.evidence: Which terms differ from another term only in hyphenation, spelling, plurality, or a compound split? Look at the terms the change adds, beside the glossary.
provisions.statement: A project MUST resolve each pair of terms that differ only in hyphenation, spelling variant, plurality, or a compound split.
provisions.rationale: Two spellings of one concept split every search and every listing, and a reader cannot tell whether they name one concept or two. One spelling per concept keeps each term defined once and checked once. A hyphenated pair whose first part is a function word is two words side by side, not one compound split in two, so the check skips it: `a`, `an`, `as`, `at`, `by`, `in`, `of`, `on`, `or`, `to`, and `with`.
provisions.example: The notification `send-receiptreminder-confirmation` and the reaction `send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` name one concept with two spellings; the project picks one and renames the other. `send-on-line-notice` beside `send-online-notice` is not reported, since `on` opens no compound.

provisions.heading: State Mannered Terms Literally
provisions.evidence: Which mannered terms on the page stand where the glossary asks for the literal word?
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST NOT use a mannered term the project glossary lists.
provisions.rationale: A metaphor or stock phrase reads smoothly while hiding what the project means: each reader pictures a different act behind the same flourish. The glossary lists each mannered term with the literal phrase that carries its meaning, so the check points at the flourish and names the plain words to reach for.
provisions.example: The glossary lists `{ "term": "leverage", "instead": "use" }`, so prose reads "use the retry queue" rather than "leverage the retry queue".

provisions.heading: Use Every Identifier Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-duplicate` for an identifier used twice.
provisions.statement: A record identifier MUST name exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: An identifier used twice names two records at once, so every citation of it points both ways. One use per identifier keeps each citation single-valued.
provisions.example: Two records named `use-case/spending.submit-expense` leave the model check reporting the duplicate on the second record.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Record Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a record identifier outside the declared grammar.
provisions.statement: A consumer record identifier MUST be `type/home.name` in kebab-case, using the form the Project Model states for its type.
provisions.rationale: The type names the record kind and `home.name` names the owning module or set, so an identifier resolves with no lookup table. One grammar for every record kind keeps identifiers writable by hand and checkable by tool. The [Project Model](model.md) states the form each type uses, and the Identifier Forms section above states the name rules and checks.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` is a reaction owned by the spending module, and `journey/submit-and-reimburse#s2` is the second step of a journey.

provisions.heading: Write Each Finding Message as a Fact
provisions.evidence: Which finding messages instruct instead of stating a fact, or open without the subject and identifier? Look at the messages the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every finding message MUST state one present-tense fact that opens with the subject title and its quoted identifier.
provisions.rationale: A message that states a fact survives every reader: the terminal and the book both show what is true. Advice belongs in the finding table on the [model page](../tools/model.md), where it is written once beside the code instead of repeated in every occurrence. Analyzer diagnostics keep their `LS` numbers and follow the same message rule.
provisions.example: A journey step with no serving use case reports `Journey step 'book-a-room#s3' is served by no use case.`

provisions.heading: Write Each Kind of Text in Its Form
provisions.evidence: Which texts miss the form of their kind? Look at the statements, steps, and meanings the change adds, beside the text-kind table.
provisions.statement: Every project text MUST use the form the text-kind table gives its kind.
