provisions.rationale: Each kind of text has one reader and one job: a requirement promises, an event reports, and a runbook step instructs. One form per kind means the tense and voice tell the reader what the text does before a word is weighed. Record values stay in the third person, Intent chapter prose says `we` for the business, and nothing says `you`.
provisions.example: A Claimwick requirement states "An expense above the threshold waits for its approver."

provisions.heading: Write Each Value in the Value Style
provisions.evidence: Which statement, meaning, rationale, condition, failure, or title values miss the value style of their row? Look at the values the change adds, beside the value-style table.
provisions.statement: Every `statement`, `meaning`, `rationale`, `*Because`, `*When`, `condition`, `failure`, and `title` value MUST use the value style the value-style table states.
provisions.rationale: Values are read far more than they are written, in records, in the book, and in tool output. One written form per value means a period or a capital letter is never a styling choice but part of the value. The value-style table ends each row with the mechanical test the value meets. Settled by [decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values](decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).
provisions.example: A Claimwick journey step states "The traveller pays for the booking."

provisions.heading: Write in American English
provisions.evidence: Which words use British spelling? Look at the field names, enum values, and prose the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every field name and enum value MUST use American spelling.
provisions.rationale: One spelling per word keeps each term defined once and checked once: `license` in one record and `licence` in another split every search and every listing. American spelling is the project spelling for field names and enum values; prose spelling follows the [Writing Standard](writing.md). Each British form reads as a rejected word beside its American spelling.
provisions.example: Claimwick writes `license` and `pseudonymize` in field names, values, and prose.

provisions.heading: Write Quantities in Standard Units
provisions.evidence: Which quantities use free text or miss their unit? Look at the dates, durations, money values, and numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every quantity in a record MUST use an ISO 8601 date, an ISO 8601 duration, an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, or a number with its unit.
provisions.rationale: Free-text quantities hide behind local habits: one record writes `7 years`, another writes `seven years`, and a check matches neither. ISO dates, ISO durations, and ISO currency codes give every quantity one written form across records and tools. Prose keeps numbers readable by writing each with its unit.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds a room for `PT10M` and writes "95 percent of checkouts complete" in prose.

provisions.heading: Add Behavior Detail When Specifying Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `requirement-fulfillment-missing`, `record-link-missing`, `step-use-case-missing`, `erasure-undeclared`, or `setting-requirement-missing` finding across Behavior records.
provisions.statement: Behavior that fulfills an Intent record MUST add the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access the Intent record leaves unstated.
provisions.rationale: Intent promises outcomes in product words, and Behavior turns each promise into the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access that keep it. Only Behavior records fulfill a requirement (`litespec/core/intent#restrict-requirement-fulfillment-to-behavior`). Without that detail each implementer guesses the states and the access scope, and two guesses diverge. The checks `requirement-fulfillment-missing`, `record-link-missing`, `step-use-case-missing`, `erasure-undeclared`, and `setting-requirement-missing` report the gaps.
provisions.example: A reimbursement promise gains an entity with Approved and Reimbursed states, a refusal for an expense that is already reimbursed, and atomic consistency over one aggregate.

provisions.heading: Build Ahead of a Regulation Only Under Its Constraint
provisions.evidence: Which anticipatory behavior lacks a citing constraint, or blocks a release before the statutory date? Look at the regulation-driven Behavior records beside the constraint and its date.
provisions.statement: Behavior that anticipates a regulation with a deadline MUST follow that regulation's constraint.
provisions.rationale: A regulation with a deadline needs working behavior before its requirement exists, so the constraint carries the rule in the meantime. The release stays shippable until the statutory date, and only then does the missing behavior block it. Without this path teams either ship late or build the rule where no record owns it.
provisions.example: A privacy regulation that takes effect next year enters as a constraint with its statutory date, and the anticipatory behavior follows that constraint until the requirement exists.

provisions.heading: Enter World Facts as Cited Research or Constraints
provisions.evidence: Which world facts entered without a cited and dated research or constraint record? Look at the provider, regulation, and incident facts the change relies on.
provisions.statement: A fact learned from the world MUST enter Intent as research or a constraint that cites its source and date.
provisions.rationale: Commitments flow down, and facts from the world flow up: a provider's behavior, a regulation, or an incident enters Intent where people can weigh it. The citation and date show where the fact came from and when it held, so a later change rechecks the source instead of the memory.
provisions.example: An observed two-day payout settlement window enters as research, then as a constraint citing that research.

provisions.heading: Implement Only Declared Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, or `refusal-unimplemented` finding across the implementation.
provisions.statement: Implementation MUST add only the code shapes its stack pages fix and no observable outcome, edge, write, or access grant its Behavior records leave undeclared.
provisions.rationale: The stack pages fix the code shapes, so the handler, the repository call, and the published event each have one prescribed form. An observable outcome, edge, write, or access grant outside the records splits the project into a specification that says one thing and code that does another. The checks `behavior-unrecorded`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, and `refusal-unimplemented` report the excess, and analyzer `LS2012` reports a handler that authorizes itself.
provisions.example: A handler that returns a code no result declares fails `result-undeclared`; the fix declares the result or removes the code.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `use-case-scenario-missing` or `proves-unreached` finding across scenarios and tests.
provisions.statement: At large size, or with the `bdd` extension, each scenario MUST be proved by one test through the public boundary.
provisions.rationale: Small projects carry no scenarios unless the `bdd` extension switches them on, so the rule binds large projects and small projects with the extension. A scenario is the leaf of the record tree, so one test through the public boundary ties each leaf to running behavior. The checks `use-case-scenario-missing` and `proves-unreached` report the missing proof.
provisions.example: A large project carries a scenario for each refusal, and one test proves it through the public boundary.

provisions.heading: Raise Open Needs as Owner Questions or Backlog Items
provisions.evidence: Which unstated needs lack a question to the owner or a backlog item? Look at the added records from a lower record layer, beside the owner questions and the backlog.
provisions.statement: A need a lower record layer meets that the upper record layer leaves unstated MUST travel up as a question to the owner or a backlog item, never as code.
provisions.rationale: The lower record layer does not decide what the upper record layer left unstated, so the need travels up with its context instead of turning into a guess. A question to the owner settles what only an accountable person decides, and a backlog item holds the rest where it stays visible. The specification is closed: an agent builds what it states and nothing more.
provisions.example: A missing reimbursement policy becomes a question to the owner, not a rule the agent writes.

provisions.heading: Record Changed Provider Behavior as Observed Research
provisions.evidence: Which provider changes lack observed research and a citing constraint? Look at the provider facts the change relies on, beside the research records.
provisions.statement: A changed provider behavior MUST enter as research recording the observed behavior, then as a constraint citing that research.
provisions.rationale: The provider's behavior is a fact from the world, and research is where such facts enter. The constraint that follows cites the research, so the constraint carries its evidence. Code is not the source: a failed reimbursement in production points at the world, and the world is cited.
provisions.example: A payout provider that starts settling every two days instead of daily enters as research with the observed dates, and a settlement-window constraint cites that research.

provisions.heading: Send Commercial and Observable Figures to the Owner
provisions.evidence: Which figures the owner sets did Behavior fix without asking? Look at the settings and rules the change adds, beside the list of owner-set figures on the model page.
provisions.statement: Behavior that meets a figure the owner sets MUST send it to the owner instead of fixing it.
provisions.rationale: The [model page](model.md) holds the one list of figures the owner sets: prices, fees, rates, terms, markets, payers, retention periods, freshness, and figures that differ by tenant, market, or date. Each figure is a business choice, and only an accountable person makes it. An agent that fixed one would bury a commitment in a Behavior record nobody chose. The figure becomes a question to the owner or a backlog item, never a silent default.
provisions.example: A receipt threshold of EUR 25 waits for the owner instead of entering the setting silently.

provisions.heading: Write Each Layer from the Layer Above It
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded` finding for a refusal literal or a screen call to no endpoint, and reports `mark-missing` for a code element that carries no mark.
provisions.statement: Each record below Intent MUST be written from a record in the record layer above it.
provisions.rationale: Each record layer rests on the one above it: Behavior fulfills Intent, Implementation builds Behavior, and Proof proves Implementation. Derivation between records is part of that direction, so generic refusals derive from `access` and `input` without new records. An agent either writes the missing record above such code or removes the code, so the specification wins where Intent has spoken.
provisions.example: An agent that finds a guard in code with no record above it writes the requirement or rule, or removes the guard.

provisions.heading: Keep Provision Identifiers Stable Within a Major Version
provisions.evidence: Which provision identifiers did a minor release remove or rename? Compare the provision index at the previous tag with the provision index of the release, beside the changelog entry that lists the generated diff.
provisions.statement: A minor LiteSpec release MUST keep every provision identifier of its major version, adding provisions and rewording provision text without removing or renaming an identifier.
provisions.rationale: Consumers cite provision identifiers in code marks, records, and departures, and each citation is written against the major version the project pins. A minor release that removes or renames an identifier breaks those citations inside a version line the consumer took as stable, with no major release to signal the break. A major release may remove or rename identifiers, and the generated provision diff in its changelog lists every added, removed and renamed identifier, so a consumer moving across a major version finds each change in one place.
provisions.example: A release in the 5.x line adds `litespec/core/scope#claim-the-record-layers-the-project-uses` and rewords a neighboring provision; both keep their identifiers, so every mark and departure written against the 5.x line still resolves.

provisions.heading: List Every Stack Shape and Extension in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `EXTENSION_UNLISTED` for an extension page no manifest entry lists, `LAYER_UNREACHABLE` for a page no stack selection reaches, and `MANIFEST_ANALYZER_PIN` for an analyzer pin that differs from the analyzer project version.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec manifest MUST list every stack, shape, extension, and version pin the release carries.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the release record that tools read: stacks and shapes decide which pages apply, extensions decide which conditional bundles a project selects from, and pins decide which versions build. A stack, shape, extension, or pin the manifest omits is one no consumer selects and no tool resolves. Listing all of them in one file keeps the release reproducible from its tag.
provisions.example: The manifest lists the `cache` extension with its page path `docs/ext/cache.md` and its `local` activation scope.

provisions.heading: Mark the Tools with the Provisions They Follow
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `MARK_MISSING` for a class with a method and no `follows` mark in a source project under `apps/`, and `MARK_UNRESOLVED` for a `follows` or `proves` mark in a .NET project under `apps/`, outside its `Fixtures` folders, that names no provision in `docs/reference/provisions.md`.
provisions.statement: Every top-level class that declares a method in a .NET source project under `apps/`, and every test that verifies a provision, MUST name its provision in a mark: a `follows` mark on the class and a `proves` mark on the test.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec's own tools are technical classes: they serve no product record, and each exists because a provision requires a check, a reader, or a generator of its shape. A `follows` mark is the reverse index from that code to the provision, so a retired or renamed provision finds every class still built for it, and a `proves` mark finds the tests that keep its check honest. LiteSpec keeps the research and decisions behind its provisions as records under `docs/intent/`, in the shapes a consumer uses; its provisions remain its specification, and the marks point at them directly. The site under `apps/site` is TypeScript with no mark form in the maintainer tool, so it carries no marks.
provisions.example: The .NET scenario reader carries `/// <follows>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</follows>`, and the test that confirms a scenario driven through a shared probe step carries `/// <proves>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</proves>`.

provisions.heading: Publish a LiteSpec Release from a Tag
provisions.evidence: `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` fails `ReleaseVersionTests` when the changelog, the template, or either package version differs from the manifest version, and `.github/workflows/release.yml` refuses a tag that does not name the manifest version.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec release MUST carry the highest git tag in the manifest version, the changelog entry, the consumer template version, and the tool and analyzer package versions.
provisions.rationale: A git tag is the only durable artifact that names a release: branches move and files change, but the tag stays. Reading the current release from the highest tag gives maintainers, consumers, and tools one shared answer. Writing that version into the manifest, the changelog, the template, and the tool package in the same release keeps the four from disagreeing. Each release publishes the CLI as one native executable per platform, in the tool packages and in standalone archives, so the version reaches a consumer with or without .NET, settled by [decision/0021-native-command-line](decision/0021-native-command-line) on the evidence in [research/native-command-line-evidence](research/native-command-line-evidence).

provisions.heading: Record the Reasoning Behind Each Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `RECORD_SCHEMA`, `RECORD_ID_MISMATCH`, `RECORD_SOURCE`, `RECORD_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE`, or `RECORD_DECISION_UNCITED` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep the research and decisions behind each release as records under `docs/intent/`.
provisions.rationale: Provisions state obligations without the questions, sources, or conclusions behind them, so a later change cannot tell why a rule reads as it does. Settled by [decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records](decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records) on the evidence in [research/comparable-rationale-practice](research/comparable-rationale-practice).
provisions.example: Claimwick states its five-day reimbursement target in a provision, and the benchmark behind the number sits in a research record beside it.

provisions.heading: Replace Every Citation on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision rename MUST replace every citation of the old identifier in one change.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename changes the ID line, and the repository keeps no alias to catch stragglers. Every citation the rename misses names a provision that no longer exists, and readers follow it nowhere. Replacing all of them in one change keeps the repository resolvable at every commit. A heading reword leaves the identifier unchanged, so it needs no citation sweep.
provisions.example: Renaming a provision identifier changes its ID line and every citation together.

provisions.heading: State the Provision Lifecycle
provisions.evidence: Each provision sits in exactly one lifecycle state, with retired identifiers cited nowhere.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep each provision in exactly one of three states: draft, active, or retired.
provisions.rationale: The three states tell a maintainer what an identifier promises. An active identifier names a rule that holds and that its verification line says how to check. A retired identifier names nothing, so a citation to it is a defect rather than a reference. Without the lifecycle, a half-written provision and a removed one look identical to a cited one.
provisions.example: A provision is added in draft. When its verification line is written it becomes active. When its assertion is folded into a richer provision, the provision is retired.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Fact to LiteSpec Before the Book Shows It
provisions.evidence: Which facts does the book show that no record field, computed status or check defines? Look at the book beside the model output and the finding codes.
provisions.statement: A fact the book needs that LiteSpec does not define MUST become a record field, a computed status, or a check in LiteSpec before the book shows it.
provisions.rationale: Rendering the book is a probe: what it cannot show is a gap in the specification. Closing the gap in LiteSpec gives every project the fact, checked; closing it in the book gives one view an unchecked fact. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book needs to say that a refusal has no scenario, so LiteSpec gains a check for it, and the book shows that check's findings.

provisions.heading: Author One Slice at a Time
provisions.evidence: Behavior records show Intent above them through their `fulfills` and `decides` links.
provisions.statement: Authoring MUST complete one feature from problem to scenario before starting the next.
provisions.rationale: A feature worked from problem to scenario stays complete at every level: each record lands with the Intent above it already written. Parallel slices leave Behavior records resting on Intent nobody wrote yet.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Specification File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `explanation-orphaned` finding, and fails a `.yaml` file with no record type outside a declared unstructured path.
provisions.statement: Every file under the consumer documentation root MUST be a record file, an explanation file beside its record file, or a document, or sit under a declared unstructured path.
provisions.rationale: A file the validator leaves unclassified is skipped, and a skipped file looks sound: its errors stay hidden. Requiring every file to be a record file, an explanation, or a document, or to sit under a declared unstructured path, leaves no page unchecked. A directory index that owns no record uses the index style, and a `README.md` with no frontmatter is a document.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion in the Builder
provisions.evidence: Which features read below `verified`, and which children hold each one back? Look at `completion` on each feature in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST compute one completion stage for every requirement, use case, journey, feature and goal, and write it as `completion` with `stage`, `proof`, `heldBy` and `counts`, with a parent only as far as its weakest in-scope child and `heldBy` naming at most ten children at that stage.
provisions.rationale: Completion is a fact the builder can count from fulfillment, code and proof, so no record carries a shorthand saying how far it is. One ladder reads the same everywhere: `unfulfilled` when no Behavior record fulfills a record, `specified` when it is fulfilled and no code is found, `coded` when code is found for every in-scope child, and `verified` when every in-scope child is verified with fresh proof. When the model holds no test run, a coded record stays `coded` with proof `unknown`, so proof unknown never reads as a failure. A requirement a departure parks stays out of the stage and the counts and names itself in `heldBy`, so deferred work stays visible.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `feature/expense-submission` shows `coded` with proof `unknown` before any test run, held by the one requirement with no fulfiller; after a passing run proves every fulfiller, the same feature shows `verified` with no held-by entries.

provisions.heading: Compute Proof Statuses in the Builder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unimplemented`, `proves-unreached`, and `refusal-unimplemented` for a use case whose handler, proof, or refusal code is missing, and `proof-invalid` (level A) for a test that both passed and failed within the runs read.
provisions.statement: Coded, verified, tested, exercised, stale, flaky, and reachable MUST come from the builder, never from handwriting.
provisions.rationale: Handwritten state drifts: a record marked coded stays marked after its handler is deleted. Computed state cannot drift, because the builder re-derives it from handlers, routes, scenarios, and test runs on every run. A use case reads coded when a handler, reaction, job, or endpoint marked with it carries it out, verified when every scenario has a passing proof through the public boundary that is not stale, and stale when the scenario hash or the test-body hash differs from `.litespec/proof/proofs.json`. A requirement reads verified when everything fulfilling it is verified and its measure's check passes. A record reads tested when a passing test that asserts something links to it. A journey step reads exercised when a passing proof of a use case serves it. A proof reads flaky when its test both passed and failed within the runs read. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code: derivation from code into any other record is forbidden, and code-computed facts live in the book and the model output. Settled by [decision/0017-proof-that-holds](decision/0017-proof-that-holds) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example: A use case reads coded when its handler exists.

provisions.heading: Connect Across Modules Only Through Declared Dependencies
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-locality-invalid` for a record under a module that is linked from another module with no declared dependency or integration event.
provisions.statement: Within one layer, a record under a module MUST be linked from another module only along a declared module dependency or through an integration event.
provisions.rationale: A record linked from another module with no declared tie is not local: it belongs at product level. The declared dependency or the integration event names the tie, so the seam where a monolith would split stays visible. Links from one layer down to the next may cross modules, because that is how one capability spans modules.
provisions.example: A spending rule cited from the finance module with no `dependsOn` tie and no integration event between them is reported; the rule moves to product level or the modules declare the tie.

provisions.heading: Connect Every Behavior Record to Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-link-missing` for a use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting with neither `serves` nor `fulfills`, and `use-case-journey-missing` (level G) at large size for a use case that no reaction, job or other use case runs and that serves no journey step.
provisions.statement: A use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting MUST carry serves, fulfills, or both.
provisions.rationale: A use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting with no served journey step and no fulfilled requirement answers to nothing above it: no promise explains why it exists. Pointing up with serves or fulfills ties every behavior to the Intent that asks for it. `record-link-missing` fails a use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting carrying neither. A use case is background-only when a reaction or job runs it, so `use-case-journey-missing` skips it.

provisions.heading: Declare One Mark Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S) for a mark written in a form its language does not take.
provisions.statement: A project MUST write each C# mark in the one style that `marks` in `.litespec/project.yaml` declares, each TypeScript mark as a typed constant, and each operations mark as a comment.
provisions.rationale: Two styles in one language are two ways to do one job: a reader learns both, a check covers both, and a search for a record finds half its code. The C# style is a project choice made once, so every tool reads it from the project file and refuses the other style within C#. TypeScript and operations files have one form each, so a typed constant beside a C# documentation tag is two languages, not two styles. A code fix converts a mark to the form its language takes.
provisions.example: The Claimwick product declares `"marks": "xml"`, so its submit-expense handler carries a documentation tag naming `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, and an attribute naming the same use case is reported. Its use-case module carries the same identifier as a typed constant, and its deployment file carries its `follows` mark as a comment.

provisions.heading: Declare Size and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `size-type-missing` and `record-invalid` for a project missing its declaration or a required type.
provisions.statement: A project MUST declare its size and stacks.
provisions.rationale: Size decides which record types and test projects the checks require, while stacks decide which technology pages and checks apply. Without the declaration, the builder cannot tell a missing record from one the project never needed.
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example declares large with a server shape and two stacks.

provisions.heading: Declare Structured Specification Metadata
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for each record file and document frontmatter block that fails the record schema.
provisions.statement: Every record file and every document frontmatter block MUST satisfy the record schema for its declared type.
provisions.rationale: The record schema owns the field list of every record type and page style. A record file is one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`, holding no Markdown and no frontmatter fences. A document frontmatter block is YAML between two lines that hold only `---`, holding only the page style and its common fields. This page states the record types and their homes.
provisions.example:
A use-case record file opens with its identity fields.

```yaml
type: use-case
id: use-case/spending.submit-expense
title: Submit Expense
```

provisions.heading: Derive a Computed Fact Instead of Restating It
provisions.evidence: Which counts, censuses, or membership lists lack a source or command? Look at the numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: A specification MUST name the source or the command that produces any count, census, or membership list derived between records.
provisions.rationale: A restated number is right until the next unrelated edit changes the records it counts, and nothing reports when it goes stale. Naming the source or the command gives every reader the current figure instead of the figure from commit day. Derivation between records is allowed: generic refusals derive from `access` and `input`, and computed completion appears in the book and the model output only.
provisions.example:
A chapter states where its numbers come from rather than copying them.

```markdown
The figures below render from the retention schedule at build time.
```

provisions.heading: Explain Each Record Beside Its Record File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-orphaned` for a Markdown file under a record root with no frontmatter and no record file beside it.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST sit beside its record file with the same name and hold plain Markdown with no frontmatter.
provisions.rationale: The file name is the link: no field joins the two files, so a rename moves both and nothing else. Plain Markdown with no frontmatter keeps the explanation readable in any reader and tells every check to read fields from the record file only. The file opens with the record title and uses H2 sections, so each explanation has one shape.
provisions.example: `submit-expense.yaml` explains its Example and Notes in `submit-expense.md` beside it.

provisions.heading: Explain the Book from LiteSpec Definitions
provisions.evidence: Which explanations in the book are not a glossary definition or a record type question? Look at the book's explanations beside the glossary and the record type table.
provisions.statement: Every explanation the book shows MUST come from the glossary definition of the term or from the question its record type answers on this page.
provisions.rationale: The book explains itself so nobody needs a learning curve, and the explanation stays true only when it has one source. An explanation written for the book drifts from the definition the records follow. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book explains a departure with the glossary definition of Departure.

provisions.heading: Follow the Authority Order
provisions.evidence: Conflict decisions under `.litespec/intent/decisions/` name the higher record that won, in the order this page states.
provisions.statement: A conflict MUST resolve toward the higher authority.
provisions.rationale: Intent records outrank Behavior records: constraint over product, product over requirement, requirement over rule, rule over use case, use case over result, and result over scenario. The order settles a conflict without a meeting: a use case asking for behavior its rule forbids loses to the rule. Where Intent has spoken, the specification wins over code; where the specification is silent, an agent builds nothing, as the Authority section states. Goals, problems, features, journeys, actors, research, and prose carry no authority, so none outranks the ladder.

provisions.heading: Give Every Record One Parent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-parent-missing` (level G) for a record whose required parent is missing.
provisions.statement: Every record except the product MUST have exactly one parent from the Placement Table on this page.
provisions.rationale: A record with no parent has no place in the book, and a record with two parents appears twice. One parent per record puts every record exactly once: the container is the parent, so an entry sits under the record file that holds it, a scenario sits under its result, and a record file sits under its folder node. A requirement sits on its feature page, and types at product level sit under the product with no field written. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice.md).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `requirement/approval-reminders.receipt-over-threshold` sits on the `feature/approval-reminders` page under `intent/modules/spending/features/`; `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits beside its aggregate; and `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds` sits under `result/submit-expense.submitted`.

provisions.heading: Hold Module Rules in Rule Sets
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a rule in `module.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A module-level rule MUST live in a rule-set file under `behavior/modules/<m>/rules/`, never in `module.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The module record declares the module; rules are behavior and live with Behavior. A rule written into `module.yaml` hides behavior in a declaration no rule check scans.
provisions.example: A spending rule lives in a rule-set file under `behavior/modules/spending/rules/`; the same rule written into `module.yaml` is reported.

provisions.heading: Implement Each Mapped Behavior Record Behind a Mark
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `aggregate-unimplemented`, `reaction-unimplemented`, `job-unimplemented`, `external-system-unimplemented`, and `use-case-endpoint-missing` (level S) for a record no mark names, where `aggregate-unimplemented` fires only for an entity aggregate, and `use-case-unreached` (level A) for a browser use case no screen calls.
provisions.statement: Every entity aggregate, every reaction, job, and external system, and every use case reached through a `browser` or `api` entry point, MUST be named by a mark on the code element the marks table gives it.
provisions.rationale: A mark points up, so a check reading marks alone finds code nobody recorded but misses a record nobody built. Checking each record that the marks table maps to code from the top closes the loop in the other direction: an entity aggregate with no root, a reaction with no event handler, a job with no host, an external system with no port, and a use case people reach with no endpoint. A store has no root, so it needs no mark. A use case with no screen calling it is reported as an advisory finding, because whether a browser reaches it depends on the deployment.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted` has no event handler carrying its mark, so the check reports `reaction-unimplemented` and blocks.

provisions.heading: Keep Code Out of Intent and Behavior Fields
provisions.evidence: Which Intent or Behavior fields copy values from code? Look at the fields the change fills, beside the implementation.
provisions.statement: No field on an Intent or Behavior record MUST be filled from code.
provisions.rationale: Code implements Behavior, so a field filled from an implementation restates what already ships instead of stating the promise under review. A fact learned from the world enters Intent as research or a constraint, cited and dated, and a need the upper record layer does not state becomes a backlog item outside the repository. Derivation between records stays allowed.
provisions.example: A positivity guard found in a handler becomes a backlog item for a rule, while the code stays untouched until the rule lands.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Name Unique in the Product
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `name-duplicate` for a name segment that occurs twice in the product.
provisions.statement: Each name segment MUST stay unique in the product.
provisions.rationale: Short identifiers resolve with no lookup table only when each name means one record. Folders do not narrow uniqueness: two features with one name in two modules still collide everywhere the identifier is read.
provisions.example: Claimwick names one feature `approval-reminders`; a second feature with that name in another module is reported even though the folders differ.

provisions.heading: Keep Module Dependencies Free of Cycles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-dependency-invalid` for a module dependency cycle.
provisions.statement: Module `dependsOn` links MUST NOT form a cycle.
provisions.rationale: A dependency cycle says each module builds on the other, so neither has a seam to split along. The module order stays a directed graph with no cycle, like the effect edges.
provisions.example: Spending depends on finance and finance depends on spending, so the cycle is reported.

provisions.heading: Keep Rules and Targets Out of Technical Decisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-basis-missing` (level A) for a technical decision whose `basedOn` names nothing, and counts a quality requirement as fulfilled when a technical decision names it in `basedOn`.
provisions.statement: A technical decision MUST leave each rule the product obeys whatever its design to a constraint and each measurable target to a quality requirement, and name the ones it serves in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: A technical decision chooses one way among alternatives, and a better alternative may replace it tomorrow. A rule such as keeping personal data in the European Union, or a target such as answering checkout within two seconds, does not change when the library does: overriding it needs a business, legal, or organizational change. Written inside a decision, the rule disappears the day the decision is replaced, and nobody holds it as the promise it is. Kept in Intent, the rule and the target stand as the promises they are, the decision points up to them, and the chain runs unbroken from code through the decision to the constraint or requirement and the goal above it. A decision with no basis is advisory, level A, while a product decision that decides nothing blocks at level G: a technical choice among equal options may serve no rule or target yet and still govern the code that follows it, but a product decision that settles no record governs nothing.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps each receipt for the tax file because `constraint/tax-receipt-retention` requires it, and answers submissions quickly because `requirement/expense-submission.month-end-load` sets the target. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` names the constraint in `basedOn`, and `decision/0004-serve-receipts-behind-one-proxy` names the requirement in `basedOn`; neither the seven years nor the two seconds is written in a decision.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Check with Its Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a frontend whose reader is missing or failing, and prints the level beside each finding.
provisions.statement: Every check MUST carry its level and block or report as that level states.
provisions.rationale: The level tells a reader what a finding means: G reads records only and always blocks, S reads code through a stack reader and blocks only where the reader is qualified, and A reports, blocking only for the release-readiness findings under `--release`. `litespec model check` prints the level beside each finding, so a reader tells a blocking defect from an advisory finding at a glance. A missing required link is level G.

provisions.heading: Match Each Backend Mark to Its Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-folder-drift` (level S) for a handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root whose mark names a record outside its module and folder, and `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a code element, test, or folder outside the code folder its record's placement names.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, endpoint, reaction, job, aggregate
provisions.statement: A backend handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root MUST carry a mark naming a use case, reaction, job, or aggregate in the module and folder it sits in.
provisions.rationale: Copying a handler and forgetting its mark is the most common agent mistake, and the folder already says what the mark should be. A handler that sits in one use-case folder while naming another sends readers and checks to the wrong record. An aggregate method and a technical class carry the mark of the use case that calls them, which may sit in another module, so their folder says nothing about their mark. The frontend mirror already compares each mark with its module; the backend check applies the same comparison to handlers, endpoints, and aggregates.
provisions.example: A handler in `Booking/Holds/HoldRoom/` marked `use-case/booking.release-hold` is reported, because the folder holds `use-case/booking.hold-room`.

provisions.heading: Move Each Identifier with Its Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-folder-drift` for an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder.
provisions.statement: A record that moves to another module MUST change the module segment of its identifier and every citation in the same change.
provisions.rationale: The folder wins: an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder names a home the record left. Only identifiers whose first segment names a module change with a module move. A rule identifier keeps its home segment, because the segment names the aggregate or module the rule is about rather than the folder that holds it. A move between product and module level changes no identifier, so no citation changes.
provisions.example: Claimwick moves `use-case/spending.submit-expense` from the spending module to the finance module, so the use case becomes `use-case/finance.submit-expense` and every citation changes in the same change.

provisions.heading: Name Book Labels with LiteSpec Terms
provisions.evidence: Which book labels are neither a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, nor the reads-as phrase the Links table states for a connection? Look at the book beside the glossary and the Links table.
provisions.statement: Every label in the book MUST be a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or the reads-as phrase the Links table states for a connection.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec already names every concept once, for people and agents alike. A friendlier synonym in the book, such as promise for requirement, is a second word for one concept: the reader learns it, then meets the real word in the records and the checks, and has to translate. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: A use case page heads its results "Results" and its scenarios "Scenarios", never "Endings" and "Examples".

provisions.heading: Name the Lowest Record Each Test Proves
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a test that names no record or a record of a kind a test does not take.
provisions.statement: Every test MUST name in a `proves` mark the lowest record it verifies, from the kinds the marks table on this page lists for a test.
provisions.rationale: A test outside the record tree is either proof of something the specification forgot to state or a test that verifies nothing anyone promised. Naming the lowest record it verifies places each test: a scenario or rule for behavior, a quality requirement for how well the product behaves, a technical decision for a technical choice, an external system or integration event for an agreement with the outside, a provision for a structural rule the code must keep, and a project convention for a standing rule the code must keep. A test that verifies a choice no record states shows a missing record, which is written at the level where the choice lives, as safety-critical standards resolve derived requirements; a test that verifies nothing a record should state is deleted. Proof stays layered: only scenario and rule proofs verify a use case, and a passing test that asserts something links to a quality requirement, a technical decision, an external system, an integration event, or a provision marks that record tested, so "the adapter is right" never reads as "the promise is kept". A background use case is verified through the passing proofs of the use cases it serves. A browser success proof asserts the result sentence or the scenario Then text.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submit-expense acceptance test proves `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`; a load test of month-end submissions proves `requirement/expense-submission.month-end-load`; a receipt-rendering test proves `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf`; and the layering test that Domain references no persistence package proves `litespec/backend/architecture#point-dependencies-inward`.

provisions.heading: Name What Every Decision Decides
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-decides-missing` for a product decision with an empty `decides` field, and `decision-decides-duplicate` for two decisions deciding one record.
provisions.statement: Every product decision MUST name at least one record it settles in `decides`.
provisions.rationale: A decision that names nothing governs nothing. Naming at least one settled record gives the decision something to govern. A technical decision governs the code that follows it instead.

provisions.heading: Organize the Book by the Record Layers
provisions.evidence: Which book headings or groupings are not a record layer, a record type, or a record the identifier names? Look at the book's outline beside this page's record type table.
provisions.statement: The book MUST outline a project by the four record layers, with the governance records beside them, and place each record under the record its folder and links name.
provisions.rationale: The book is how people read the model, so it shows the model's own hierarchy. A reader who learns Intent, Behavior, Implementation and Proof in the book reads the same structure in the docs folder, in the model output and in every other LiteSpec project. An outline of the book's own invention is a second hierarchy to learn, and it drifts from the one the records keep. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice.md). Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits under Behavior, its module and its aggregate; its results under it; each scenario under the result it shows; and the handler that carries its mark under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Point Every Book Entry to Its Source
provisions.evidence: Which book entries lack a link to their file and line? Look at the book's record, code, test and finding entries.
provisions.statement: Every record, code element, test and finding the book shows MUST link to the file and line it comes from.
provisions.rationale: The book is where a reader notices what to change, and the source is where the change is made. A link to the file and line makes the next step one click, and it shows that every entry comes from a written record or from code, not from the book. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The submit-expense use case page links to `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/expense/submit-expense.yaml` at its first line, and its handler to the handler file at the class.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Integration Event from One Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `event-publisher-invalid` for an integration event with a second publishing module.
provisions.statement: An integration event MUST have exactly one publishing module.
provisions.rationale: An event with two publishers has two writers of one fact: readers cannot tell which module states it. One publishing module gives the fact one home, and every other module reads it through the event.
provisions.example: `integration-event/expense-submitted` is published from the spending module; a second publisher in the finance module is reported.

provisions.heading: Record Each Screen's Captures from the Gallery
provisions.evidence: Which screens with a route have no capture? Look at `captureState` `route-not-captured` on screen records in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST record each screen's captures from the gallery folders and file-name pattern the project file names, as `captures` with `path`, `theme`, `width` and `capturedOn`, and its `captureState` as `captured`, `route-not-captured` or `no-route`.
provisions.rationale: A reader judging a screen needs to see it, and a capture named by its route, theme and width is the copy the built screen makes. The route slug names the file the same way everywhere: the leading slash dropped, segments joined with a hyphen, a parameter reduced to its name, and the root route named `home`. A missing gallery folder captures nothing and fails nothing, so a project with no photography yet still builds its model.
provisions.example: The Claimwick web gallery holds `expenses--light--1440.png`, so `screen/expenses.list` at `/expenses` shows that capture at theme `light` and width 1440 with `captureState` `captured`; a screen with no address shows `no-route`.

provisions.heading: Record Each Technical Choice as a Decision
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-unimplemented` (level S) for a technical decision that no code element follows. It reports `decision-kind-missing` (level A) for a technical decision with no `kind`, `decision-scope-invalid` (level A) for a technical decision whose followers all sit in one module and each already carry an `implements` mark, and `decision-home-drift` (level A) for a technical decision kept at a level its followers do not match. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: whether any code follows a decision is known only across every project, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A technical choice of one of the six kinds that code follows and no LiteSpec provision makes MUST be a decision under `.litespec/implementation/decisions/` that at least one code element follows.
provisions.rationale: Why a pattern, a library, or a configuration value was chosen is the first thing a maintainer asks before changing it. Written in a comment, the answer drifts and no tool finds it. Written as a decision, it carries its options, what speaks for and against each, and what would reopen it, and every code element shaped by it names it in a `follows` mark. A choice a LiteSpec provision already makes needs no decision, because the provision is the record. The six kinds are provider, package, format, boundary, topology, and replacement, as the [decision records page](../reference/decision-records.md) states: a choice of no kind is not a decision. A choice of no kind states its reason in the class documentation, and the mark on the class names the record the class serves. Technical decisions sit under Implementation because they name technologies and code, which Intent never holds, and they share the numbered sequence of product decisions, so all decisions share one identifier space. Settled by [decision/0040-require-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice](decision/0040-require-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice).
provisions.example: Claimwick renders each receipt as a PDF file. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` weighs a PDF library against an HTML-to-PDF browser, chooses the PDF library, and names what reopens the choice: receipts no longer needing a downloadable file. The decision carries `kind: package`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Render Generated Regions from the Model
provisions.evidence: Which generated regions outside an index region render code-computed facts? Look inside the generated fences beside the book and the model output.
provisions.statement: A generated region renders only facts derived from records, and a `decision-index` or `departure-index` region also renders the computed follower facts its rows name.
provisions.rationale: A generated region sits inside a record page, so everything in it reads with record authority. Facts computed from code, such as coded and verified counts, describe the world rather than the promise, and rendering them beside records would lend them authority they do not hold. The book and the model output carry code-computed facts where readers meet them as computed. An index region is the exception: it lists the records beside it, so each row names the computed followers, concerns and flags the reader needs to read the list.

provisions.heading: Report Unverified Use Cases
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` (level A) for a use case whose scenarios are not all proved, and `litespec model check --release` blocks on it.
provisions.statement: A use case whose scenarios are not all proved MUST be reported as `use-case-unverified`.
provisions.rationale: Nothing blocks on an unverified scenario day to day, so the release gate would depend on someone reading the book. Reporting the use case keeps daily work loose, and `litespec model check --release` makes the finding block, so the release stays honest without slowing ordinary work.
provisions.example: Claimwick adds `use-case/spending.export-expenses` with two scenarios and one passing proof: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` for it and exits zero, and `litespec model check --release` blocks on it.

provisions.heading: Require an Explanation File for Article Types
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-missing` for an article type with no explanation file or with a required H2 section missing.
provisions.statement: A research or decision page MUST carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: An article is read as prose: the Answer of a research and the Context of a decision are what the reader comes for. The required sections keep each article complete: Answer for research, and Context, Options Considered, Decision, and What Would Reopen It for decision.
provisions.example: `research/approval-time-benchmarks` carries its Answer in `approval-time-benchmarks.md`.

provisions.heading: Require Explanation Files on the Layers a Project Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-missing` for a record page on a listed layer with no explanation file or with a required H2 section missing.
provisions.statement: A record page on a layer the project lists in `explanations.layers` MUST carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: A complex product needs every record explained for people who did not write it. The setting makes the explanation a gate instead of a habit.
provisions.example: Claimwick lists `intent` and `behavior` in `explanations.layers`, so its problem `problem/expenses-wait-weeks` carries `expenses-wait-weeks.md` with the sections Who Has It, What They Do Today, Evidence and What Would Retire It. A problem without that file, or without one of those sections, fails the check.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Page Link
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-unknown` for a link that resolves to no file and no written record identifier.
provisions.statement: Every Markdown link outside code in a record field, an explanation file, or a document MUST resolve to an existing file or to a written record identifier.
provisions.rationale: A link that points at a moved file or an unknown identifier reads as navigation and leads nowhere. A link whose target is a record identifier, with an optional `#<step-id>`, cites that record: link checks resolve it against the model's identifiers, citation checks count it, and the book links it to the record. Prose cites a record by its identifier, never by its file path.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt rule is cited as `[the receipt rule](rule/expense.approver-is-not-submitter)`.

provisions.heading: Rewrite Every Link on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec rename` leaves no citation of the old identifier, and `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An author MUST rename a record identifier with `litespec rename <old> <new>`, which rewrites every link.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename touches the record file, its explanation file, and every record that points at it. Rewriting every link in the same command leaves no citation pointing at the old name, so the repository stays resolvable at every commit. When the file name follows the identifier, both files move together.
provisions.example: `litespec rename use-case/spending.close-run use-case/spending.complete-run` updates the page and every citation together.

provisions.heading: Scaffold Pages and Reserve Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Which new pages lack a reserved identifier? Look for pages created without `litespec new`.
provisions.statement: An author MUST scaffold a new page with `litespec new <type> <id>`, which reserves its identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two agents working in parallel mint the same identifier when each writes a file by hand, and the collision surfaces only at merge time. Scaffolding reserves the identifier before any prose exists, so the second author learns the clash at creation and picks another name. For an article type the command also writes the explanation file, and for a document style it writes the document.
provisions.example: `litespec new reaction spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` creates the reaction record file with its reserved identifier.

provisions.heading: Serve Every Journey Step
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `step-use-case-missing` for a journey step with no serving use case, reaction, or job, beside `step-screen-missing` for a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves.
provisions.statement: Every journey step MUST have a serving use case, reaction, or job.
provisions.rationale: A step no use case, reaction, or job serves promises a moment the product never builds. Use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with serves, so each step id collects the behaviors that carry the walker through it. `step-use-case-missing` fails a step with no serving use case, reaction, or job. The pair sits side by side: `step-use-case-missing` names a step no use case, reaction, or job serves, and `step-screen-missing` names a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves.

provisions.heading: Show Only Computed Judgements in the Book
provisions.evidence: Which statuses, counts, orders or findings in the book does no builder output or check produce? Look at the book beside the model output.
provisions.statement: Every status, count, order and finding the book shows MUST be one the builder or a check computes.
provisions.rationale: The book is a view of the model, not a second authority. A judgement only the book makes, such as its own idea of what to do next, cannot be checked, cannot fail a build, and cannot be found by an agent reading the model output. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book orders features by the completion the builder computes.

provisions.heading: Split Record Fields from Explanation
provisions.evidence: Which explanation files state a fact a check reads? Look at each explanation file beside its record file.
provisions.statement: A fact a check reads MUST live as a field in the record file rather than in the explanation file.
provisions.rationale: Fields are checked; explanation prose is not. A fact a check reads that sits in prose is invisible to the check. The page explanation cites entries by identifier, so entries need no file of their own.
provisions.example: The submit-expense summary lives in the `summary` field of `submit-expense.yaml`, while why the flow reads well lives under Notes in `submit-expense.md`.

provisions.heading: Start Each Explanation File with Its Title
provisions.evidence: Which explanation files miss their H1 title or section content outside H2? Look at the explanation files beside the changed record files.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST open with one H1 title and section its content with H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: One shape puts the title and each section in the same place on every explanation. The H1 carries the record title, and each H2 carries one section from the table on this page or a free section; Notes take free `###` headings under their H2.

provisions.heading: State the Common Fields on Every Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record missing a common field.
provisions.statement: Every written record MUST carry its type, identifier, and title.
provisions.rationale: Type, identifier, and title are the fields every join needs. Without them on every record, the builder cannot connect decisions to requirements, scenarios to results, or records to terms, and the model falls apart into loose pages. A record adds `terms` when it uses glossary terms and `records` when it holds entries.

provisions.heading: State What Happens in Every Behavior Statement
provisions.evidence: Which rule statements, scenario steps, or result meanings hide their behavior behind a vague word? Look at the statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: A rule statement, scenario step, and result meaning SHOULD avoid words that hide behavior.
provisions.rationale: The vague words are handle, handles, handled, process, processes, manage, manages, various, etc., appropriate, appropriately, properly, as needed, and so on: each says that something happens without saying what. A reader cannot check a statement that hides its behavior, so each statement names the act in words a test could assert.
provisions.example: A scenario step reads "The member borrows the copy" rather than "The member handles the copy".

provisions.heading: Take Decision Numbers from One Sequence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-number-duplicate` for two decisions sharing one number.
provisions.statement: A decision number MUST come from one sequence across every home.
provisions.rationale: Product and technical decisions share one identifier space, so a number identifies one decision wherever it sits. `litespec new decision` takes the next free number, and no two decisions share it.
provisions.example: `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` is the fifth decision, whether it sits under Intent or under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Use One Metadata Carrier
provisions.evidence: Which pages carry field values outside the record file? Look at the explanation files beside the changed record files.
provisions.statement: A consumer page MUST use its record file as its only metadata carrier.
provisions.rationale: Two metadata carriers on one page disagree sooner or later: source links, paths, and evidence drift between the record file and the explanation file. One record file keeps every field a check reads in one place, while the explanation file beside it explains without stating a field value.

provisions.heading: Validate a Single Page Before Committing
provisions.evidence: The change report shows each touched page passing single-page validation before commit.
provisions.statement: An author MUST validate a single page before committing it.
provisions.rationale: Full validation walks the whole repository, which grows slow exactly when many authors commit often. A single-page check reports shape and link errors for the page at hand in seconds, so each commit arrives already sound.
provisions.example: The author validates the touched page, fixes the reported diagnostics, and commits only when the page passes.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record File in Canonical Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `format-drift` for a record file whose text differs from its canonical form.
provisions.statement: Every record file MUST match the canonical text the record writer produces for it.
provisions.rationale: One layout for every record keeps diffs small and readers on content: a change shows the moved fact, never reflowed prose or reordered keys. The tool owns the layout, so `litespec model format` rewrites every record file into canonical form and the check reports any file that differs.
provisions.example: A use-case file opens with `type`, `id`, and `title`, holds its own fields in schema order, and closes with `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Home
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `folder-invalid` for a folder outside the closed set of its layer and level, `module-undeclared` for a `modules` folder naming no declared module, and `record-placement-invalid` for a record outside its home.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every record in the home its type names.
provisions.rationale: One home per type tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. A record kept anywhere else is invisible to the checks that scan its home, so it looks sound while nothing validates it.
provisions.example: A decision lives at `.litespec/intent/decisions/0001-receipt-threshold.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Record File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record file that does not parse or whose top level names no record type or container page style.
provisions.statement: Every record page MUST live in one record file holding one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`.
provisions.rationale: One file per page tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. The mapping holds exactly the fields the schema defines for its type, with entries in `records`, so every record has one shape and the checks read every record the same way. A record kept anywhere else is invisible to the checks that scan its home. Settled by [decision/0020-records-in-yaml](decision/0020-records-in-yaml) on the evidence in [research/record-format-evidence](research/record-format-evidence).
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps `use-case/spending.submit-expense` in `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/expense/submit-expense.yaml`, with its results and scenarios in `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Links on the Record That Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a link whose target no record carries.
provisions.statement: A link MUST live as a field on the record it starts from, with the Links table stating how it reads in both directions.
provisions.rationale: One writing site keeps a link and its source in one edit: changing the source updates the link in the same change. Links written on the target instead would scatter each relationship across every page it touches. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice.md).

provisions.heading: Avoid Generic Boundary Names
provisions.evidence: Each changed boundary name carries the narrowest accurate business name, with no bare `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, or `service`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT use generic `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, or `service` names when a narrower name exists.
provisions.rationale: Names such as `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, and `service` say nothing about the business action, so unrelated responsibility collects behind them with every change. The narrower name keeps each boundary to the action it names.
provisions.example: A notifier named for post publication names its action; one named only `service` does not.

provisions.heading: Complete Work Before Merging
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports unreached records, such as `intent-unreached` and `constraint-unreached`, locally, and the pull-request check blocks on them.
provisions.statement: What merges MUST be complete.
provisions.rationale: A branch may be incomplete; what merges is complete. A record that must stay unreached past a merge carries a departure with `expiresOn`, which parks reachability for that record until it expires.
provisions.example: A use case with no endpoint stays on its branch until the endpoint lands or a departure with `expiresOn` parks it.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion from Code and Tests
provisions.evidence: Which records state their own completion? Compare the record fields with the completion the model computes.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT write completion by hand, because the model computes it from code, tests, and passing scenarios.
provisions.rationale: What a reader asks first is how much of a thing is coded and verified. Completion typed by hand turns the plan into a completion report that the next commit falsifies. The [model page](model.md) defines what the model computes.
provisions.example: The book shows a use case complete when its handler exists and its scenarios pass, with the model deriving that from the runs.

provisions.heading: Compute Nothing Above Implementation from Code
provisions.evidence: Which records above Implementation restate code instead of a decided promise? Compare each new record with the code beside it.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT compute a record above Implementation from code.
provisions.rationale: A record computed from code turns what exists into what is promised, so drift becomes the plan and the record restates what the code already does. Records above Implementation state decided promises, and code points up to the record it serves through a mark naming that record.

provisions.heading: Confine Atomic Consistency to Synchronous Edges
provisions.evidence: Which atomic use cases span an async edge? Look at the consistency and effects fields beside the changed use cases.
provisions.statement: Atomic consistency MUST NOT span an async edge.
provisions.rationale: An async edge crosses a commit boundary, so work past it can fail after the caller succeeded. Atomic consistency promises one shared outcome, which holds only while every edge stays synchronous.

provisions.heading: Cover Other Mechanisms with Extensions
provisions.evidence: Which mechanisms outside the favored set lack an extension? Look at the selected extensions beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: A mechanism outside modules, aggregates, domain events, use cases, reactions, and jobs MUST live in an extension.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec favors one set of mechanisms and states that choice openly instead of claiming neutrality. An extension states how its mechanism composes with the core fields, so a project that needs it selects one place that holds the whole contract.

provisions.heading: Derive Records Only from Records
provisions.evidence: Which derived values lack an authored source record? Trace each derived value to the record it cites.
provisions.statement: A record MUST take each derived value from another record.
provisions.rationale: Derivation between records keeps one authored source behind every value: the source changes once and each derived view follows. Generic refusals derive from access and input, and each view derives from the records it lists, so readers trace every derived value to the record that states it.

provisions.heading: End Every Effect Cycle in a Domain Event
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `effect-loop-invalid` finding on the changed records.
provisions.statement: An effect graph MUST NOT hold a cycle except through a domain event with a stated end condition.
provisions.rationale: A cycle without an end condition runs until something outside the records stops it, so no reader can state when the work finishes. Routing each cycle through a domain event with a stated end condition names the loop and its exit in the records the graph checks.

provisions.heading: Follow Intent Where It Has Spoken
provisions.evidence: Which code disagrees with a stated promise? Compare the changed code with the Intent records it serves.
provisions.statement: Behavior and Implementation MUST follow Intent where Intent states the promise.
provisions.rationale: Intent holds the decided promises, so Behavior that fulfills them and code that builds them keep one chain from promise to product. Where Intent states the promise, code that disagrees is the defect, and the fix changes the code.

provisions.heading: Keep Git as the Decision Record
provisions.evidence: Which changed records bypass their pull request? Look at the pull request behind the change.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat a record in the repository as decided, with the pull request that changes it as its review.
provisions.rationale: A record in git is the decision, and the pull request that changes it is its review. A record nobody wants is deleted, and git keeps who changed what and when. Records carry no history of their own.
provisions.example: A feature nobody wants is deleted from the repository; its history stays in git.

provisions.heading: Keep One Authored Source
provisions.evidence: Each fact on the changed pages traces to one authored record, with every other appearance derived from the model.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST author each record once in its home file and derive every other appearance from the model.
provisions.rationale: Two homes for one fact become two facts with the next edit: each copy changes on its own schedule while readers guess which one rules. Deriving every other appearance from the model keeps the authored record as the single place a change lands. Completion computed from the model stays true without anyone typing it by hand.

provisions.heading: Keep Tools Small
provisions.evidence: Which commands, checks, generated files, or packages lack an owner approval or a user? Look at the tooling the change adds beside its users.
provisions.statement: A command, check, generated file, or package MUST exist only while the owner approves it and something uses it.
provisions.rationale: Each command, check, generated file, or package adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts every later reader learns. A tool nothing uses is removed instead of kept beside its replacement. Settled by [decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker](decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker), [decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable](decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable) and [decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating](decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating), and the same rule removes project fields in [decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads](decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads).
provisions.example: A check nobody runs is removed with its command.
