provisions.heading: Locate Package Versions in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-version-drift` for a package whose version differs from its manifest pin, and `stack-invalid` for a named stack the manifest does not ship.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST resolve the standards-selected stack versions from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the version authority for the stack the standards select, so every consumer resolves the same tested combination. A version pinned in prose or remembered by an agent drifts from that authority with the next manifest change. Consumer dependencies still live in package manifests and lockfiles; only the standards-selected stack versions resolve from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Name Boundary Intent
provisions.evidence: Each changed boundary name states its business action.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST use business operation names, specific command and query mediators, and business-action external ports at boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Boundaries are where components meet and where future readers orient themselves. Business operation names, specific command and query mediators, and business-action external ports state the purpose at that meeting point. A precise name lets a newcomer place the interaction without opening either side.

provisions.heading: Prefer Direct Owned Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Each new abstraction names the boundary that justifies it, or the wrapping convention that permits it.
provisions.statement: Use a selected framework type directly inside the architecture layer that owns it until an architectural boundary exists.
provisions.rationale: Using a selected framework type directly keeps one concept where two would add nothing: the abstraction and what it hides. A project-owned abstraction earns its place for provider replacement, a test boundary, a stable domain concept, or an architecture boundary. Wrapping the framework everywhere else doubles the API the team maintains without isolating any real change.

provisions.heading: Prefer Local Code Until Reuse Is Real
provisions.evidence: Each new shared unit serves two real consumers under one accurate name, or the sharing convention permits it.
provisions.statement: Keep operation-specific code in its operation folder until two real consumers need the same precise behavior.
provisions.rationale: Operation-specific code kept beside its operation stays easy to change with the operation. Shared code needs a name and responsibility that stay accurate for both consumers, and the first consumer rarely knows what the second needs. Waiting for two real consumers means the shared unit covers behavior both actually need.

provisions.heading: Prove Enforceable Boundaries Mechanically
provisions.evidence: Each changed enforceable boundary names a reference, test, or lint rule that proves it.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST prove each enforceable boundary mechanically: a reference, visibility, an architecture test, a behavior test, or a lint rule.
provisions.rationale: A boundary stated only in prose holds until the first commit that ignores it. Mechanical proof, such as a reference, a visibility rule, an architecture test, a behavior test, or a lint rule, fails the build or the check the day the boundary breaks. Specifications then explain the decisions that need judgment, while tools guard the constraints that do not. Enforceable boundaries include project and package references, compiler visibility, permission guards, store constraints, and lint rules.
provisions.example: A project-reference test proves Domain has no Infrastructure reference.

provisions.heading: Record Stricter Edge Rules as Conventions
provisions.evidence: Which stricter edge rules lack a cited convention? Look at the project conventions beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: A project that keeps a stricter edge rule MUST record it as a cited convention.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec checks declared edges and leaves stricter taste to each project. A stricter rule recorded as a cited convention stays visible and checkable beside the records it constrains, instead of living as habit in a few heads.

provisions.heading: Require Current Complexity Activation
provisions.evidence: Each added package, project, wrapper, process, cache, queue, or pattern cites a current use case, decision, or requirement.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST add packages, projects, wrappers, background processes, caches, queues, or distributed patterns only for a current documented requirement.
provisions.rationale: Each package, project, wrapper, background process, cache, queue, or distributed pattern adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts every later reader must learn. A current use case, decision, or requirement names the activation criterion that justifies that cost. Preference and possible future need justify nothing, so speculative machinery stays out.

provisions.heading: State the Strength of Every Provision
provisions.evidence: Which provisions leave their strength or scope unstated? Look at the provisions the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST state whether it is required, a default, or advisory, and where it applies.
provisions.rationale: Strength words work only when each one means exactly one thing: an agent tells binding from advisory without a check existing. A check is an aid where one is cheap and sure, never the condition for a provision to exist.

provisions.heading: State Transaction Sharing on Every Inline Edge
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `record-invalid` finding on the changed inline edges.
provisions.statement: An inline edge MUST state whether it shares the caller's transaction.
provisions.rationale: Two inline edges that look alike run in one transaction or two, and the difference decides what a failure leaves behind. Stating the sharing on the edge keeps transaction honesty where the edge is declared.
provisions.example: An inline runs edge states `sharesTransaction: true`, so a failure in the use case it runs rolls back the caller.

provisions.heading: Take Every Name from the Intent Above It
provisions.evidence: Which act carries a different name in its use case, method, event, permission, route or screen label than the record above it states? Compare the names of one act across its record, its handler, its endpoint and its screen.
provisions.statement: Every layer below a record MUST carry the name that record gives an act, a name chosen for what the act does in the business.
provisions.rationale: A name is a claim about what happens. The right name comes from asking what the act really does, including how it can end, and the record that states the act decides it; the use case, the aggregate method, the event, the permission, the route and the screen label then repeat it. A check that reports two names for one act reports drift, not the answer: the fix brings every layer to the name the intent states, and the intent changes first when its own word is wrong. A rename made only to quiet a check, or a name kept in one layer while the others move, leaves one act with two names. Settled by [decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept](decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, finance staff send an approved expense's payout to the bank, and the bank can refuse it when the company account cannot cover it. The act is a submission, not a payment: the use case is `submit-payout`, the method `SubmitPayout`, the event `PayoutSubmitted`, the permission `submit-payout`, and the screen's button reads "Submit payout". A later command records whether the bank paid or refused.

provisions.heading: Treat Code Beyond Silent Intent as Evidence for an Owner Question
provisions.evidence: Which working code outside Intent lacks an owner question carrying it? Look at the owner questions beside the uncovered code.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat working code that Intent does not cover as evidence for a question to the owner, not as a defect to delete and not as a source to copy into Intent.
provisions.rationale: Silent Intent plus working code means a decision nobody recorded: deleting the code destroys behavior users rely on, and copying it quietly into Intent turns code into a promise nobody stated. A question carries the behavior to the owner with the code as evidence, and the answer lands in Intent first.
provisions.example: A positivity guard in code that no rule states becomes an owner question citing the guard, and the code stays until the answer lands in Intent.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record About the Software
provisions.evidence: Which records state company business instead of the software? Compare each new record with the code, results, tests, or infrastructure it translates into.
provisions.statement: Every record MUST state what the application does, holds, refuses at runtime, or runs on.
provisions.rationale: Goals, problems, features, research, and constraints all qualify when they translate into code, results, tests, or infrastructure. Running the company stays out; it enters only as a constraint or as dated research.
provisions.example: A goal that translates into payout code and tests qualifies; a sales target does not.

provisions.heading: Accept Every Retained Personal Data Class in Intent
provisions.evidence: Which pseudonymized, retained, or exempt personal or sensitive classes name no accepting requirement or decision? Look at `basedOn` on each data class.
provisions.statement: Each personal or sensitive data class kept with `pseudonymize`, `retain`, or `exempt` MUST name the Intent requirements or decisions accepting it in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: Keeping personal data past erasure is a business choice, not a technical default: the statute or the business accepts it, with the reason on record. Pseudonymized data stays personal data, so it needs the same acceptance as retained data. Naming those requirements or decisions in `basedOn` keeps the keeping reviewable where the promise lives.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Aggregate Data Field
provisions.evidence: Which aggregate data fields lack a meaning, a classification, or a data class? Look at `data` on each aggregate page.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST list its data fields with their meaning, classification, and data class in `data`.
provisions.rationale: Data without a classification is handled by guess: personal facts sit beside public ones with nothing marking which is which. A meaning with a classification of public, internal, personal, or sensitive tells every later reader how each field is handled, and the data class ties the field to its erasure position and its retention row. The fields live in `data` on the aggregate record file.

provisions.heading: Complete the Subject Export Before Erasure
provisions.evidence: The export-first classes show a completed export before each erasure run in the run evidence.
provisions.statement: A data class with `exportFirst` MUST complete the subject export before its erasure runs.
provisions.rationale: Erasure destroys the only copy of data the subject may still want: identity documents, message history, purchase records. Completing the export first gives the subject their data while it still exists, so erasure never destroys what the subject asked to keep elsewhere.
provisions.example: Claimwick makes finance download the tax-relevant data before a shredder runs, and refuses to shred when anything changed after that download.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Data Class with Its Erasure Position
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `erasure-undeclared` for a personal or sensitive field with no declared position and `retention-enforcement-missing` for a class nothing enforces.
provisions.statement: Each data class MUST declare its classification, its fields, its purpose, its erasure position, its basis, its retention period, and the enforcement that carries it out.
provisions.rationale: Erasure declared per field drifts: one field keeps a new position while its twin keeps the old one. Declaring the position once per class, with per-field exceptions beside it, keeps one decision in one place. The position is `erase`, `pseudonymize`, `anonymize`, `retain`, `exempt`, `tombstone`, `discard`, `cascade-only`, or `transferred`; the basis is `statute`, `business`, or `engineering`; the period is an ISO 8601 duration or `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }`; the enforcement is `reaction/...`, `job/...`, `record-expiry`, `store-ttl`, or `query-filter`. A pseudonymized class stays personal with its basis, and an anonymized class can no longer identify anyone. The `erasure-undeclared` check reports a personal or sensitive field with no declared position, and `retention-enforcement-missing` reports a class nothing enforces.
provisions.example: The submitter-contact class declares `personal`, `pseudonymize`, its purpose, and its accepting requirement, while the expense-ledger class declares `internal`, `retain`, a statutory seven years, and the finance expiry job.

provisions.heading: Discard Rows That Leave No Trace
provisions.evidence: The `onErasure` entries on the aggregate pages carry discard where no marker duty exists.
provisions.statement: A data class with no duty to keep a marker MUST use `onErasure: discard`.
provisions.rationale: A tombstone is still a row: it occupies storage, appears in counts, and invites readers to treat a gone subject as present. Where no reference and no audit needs the marker, deleting the row outright keeps the store honest.
provisions.example: Lago discards a customer: the profile is hidden and its relations end, while finalized invoices and credit notes stay as the ledger.

provisions.heading: Keep a Tombstone Where Deletion Stays Visible
provisions.evidence: The aggregate pages mark referenced-after-erasure classes tombstone with the marker fields each keeps.
provisions.statement: A data class whose rows outlive erasure as references MUST use `onErasure: tombstone` with the fields its marker keeps.
provisions.rationale: Some rows are referenced after they are gone: remote servers hold copies, audit trails cite row ids, and support tools link to deleted accounts. Erasing the row breaks those references, while keeping it breaks the erasure duty. A tombstone keeps the row id and the erasure date and drops every other field, so references resolve to a marker that says the subject is gone.
provisions.example: ZITADEL deletes a user by moving it to a terminal state and deleting its read-model rows while the events stay for audit, and Sentry writes a tombstone for a discarded issue so that later events for it are dropped at intake instead of stored again.

provisions.heading: Keep Tombstone Fields Minimal
provisions.evidence: The tombstone entries keep the row id and the erasure date, or the project lists wider fields with the rule behind each.
provisions.statement: A tombstone keeps the row id and the erasure date, and no other field.
provisions.rationale: Every field on a tombstone is data kept past erasure. The row id and the date satisfy references and audits, and anything wider needs its own rule.

provisions.heading: Move Data to Its Next Controller Instead of Erasing
provisions.evidence: The handed-over class entries name transferred with the receiver and the handover record.
provisions.statement: A data class handed to another controller MUST use `onErasure: transferred` with the receiver and the handover record.
provisions.rationale: Erasure is not the only end of custody: a branch closes and a successor takes its readers, a company is acquired, a contract moves to a new processor. The data survives under a new controller, so the record names the receiver and the handover both sides signed instead of a deletion that never happened.
provisions.example: A support tool sends a loan summary and the reader message to a hosted AI model to draft a reply; the position names the model provider, its region and its retention, and the product stores none of it.

provisions.heading: Purge Erased Data from Restored Backups
provisions.evidence: Which restore runbooks name no sweep job? Look at the restore runbooks.
provisions.statement: A restore runbook MUST name the sweep job that re-applies erasure after the restore.
provisions.rationale: A backup holds data as it was, including rows erased since: restoring it resurrects subjects the product promised to forget. The sweep job re-applies every erasure decided before the restore, so the restore brings the system back without bringing the erased data back with it.
provisions.example: The database restore runbook names `job/privacy.sweep-restored-erasure`, which runs before traffic returns and deletes every row erased since the backup.

provisions.heading: Record Which Duty Wins Each Conflict
provisions.evidence: The retention schedule rows name the winning duty with its basis.
provisions.statement: Each retention conflict MUST name the winning duty and its basis.
provisions.rationale: Keeping for audit and erasing for the subject collide on the same row: the invoice the statute keeps sits beside the name the subject erases. Silence lets each implementer pick a winner. Naming the winning duty with its basis keeps one decision where every reader finds it.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps the expense ledger for seven years under tax law while erasing the submitter contact. ZITADEL keeps its audit events while erasing the user they describe, under the same rule.

provisions.heading: Remove Child Rows Through Their Parent Only
provisions.evidence: The child class entries name cascade-only with the parent class, and the parent erasure tests clear the children.
provisions.statement: A data class erased only as a cascade from a parent erasure MUST use `onErasure: cascade-only` with the parent it follows.
provisions.rationale: Some rows have no subject of their own: line items belong to an invoice, receipt files belong to an expense, usage rows belong to a customer. A direct erasure request names the parent, never the child, so the child follows the parent's erasure and refuses a request addressed to itself.
provisions.example: Cal.com deletes a user by removing the account and letting the database cascade remove the rows that hang off it, with no retention schedule; a product at this rung declares cascade-only and names the cascade path.

provisions.heading: Require a Fresh Export After Changes
provisions.evidence: The erasure runs after mid-window edits show a fresh export completed first.
provisions.statement: Erasure under `unchangedSinceExport` MUST stop and ask for a fresh export when the data changed since the last export.
provisions.rationale: An export taken last month does not cover rows written yesterday. When the data changed since the last export, erasing on the stale copy destroys rows the subject never received. Stopping for a fresh export keeps the export-first promise true at the moment of erasure.
provisions.example: A reader who corrected their address after exporting it gets a fresh export first, and the erasure waits for it.

provisions.heading: Route Every External Erasure Through an Operation or Event
provisions.evidence: Which external systems declare no erasure call, forwarding event, or impossible reason with acceptance? Look at the external systems beside their erasure routes.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST declare its erasure as `{ "mode": "call", "operation": "external-system/<name>#<operation>" }`, `{ "mode": "event", "event": "integration-event/<name>" }`, or `{ "mode": "impossible", "reason": "..." }` with its acceptance.
provisions.rationale: Personal data forwarded to a processor without an erasure route stays there past erasure: the product forgets while the processor remembers. Declaring `{ "mode": "call", "operation": "external-system/<name>#<operation>" }` naming the operation, `{ "mode": "event", "event": "integration-event/<name>" }` naming the forwarding integration event, or `{ "mode": "impossible", "reason": "..." }` with its reason and its Intent acceptance states the route beside the system.

provisions.heading: Run One Sweep Job per Data Class
provisions.evidence: Each sweep job page covers one data class, or the project names the classes each job covers.
provisions.statement: Each sweep job covers one data class.
provisions.rationale: One sweep per class keeps the blast radius small: a broken sweep delays one class while the others complete. A shared sweep is one failure away from resurrecting every class at once.

provisions.heading: Schedule Every Data Class for Retention
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `retention-enforcement-missing` for a data class nothing enforces.
provisions.statement: Each data class MUST appear on the retention schedule with its purpose, basis, period, enforcement, and the requirement it cites where personal or sensitive.
provisions.rationale: Retention decided per aggregate scatters: one module erases in days what another keeps for years, and no page shows the whole. Listing every data class on one schedule with its purpose, basis, period, enforcement, processors with their forwarding and acceptance, and the conflict rule where keeping and erasing collide states the whole as rows a reviewer judges together. The schedule states the time limits of a record of processing. Personal or sensitive keeping cites its Intent requirement. The `retention-enforcement-missing` check reports a row nothing enforces.

provisions.heading: Scope Erasure to What the Subject Requested
provisions.evidence: The erasure use cases cite the request they answer and touch only the data it names.
provisions.statement: Erasure that answers a subject request MUST use `reach: requested` and touch only the data the request names.
provisions.rationale: A subject who asks to delete one order does not ask to delete the account, and a subject who asks to delete the account names everything. The requested reach ties the erasure to the request it answers, so a narrow request cannot widen into a broad deletion and a broad request cannot stop at one row.
provisions.example: A request naming one hold erases that hold and leaves the reader's other loans untouched.

provisions.heading: State the Erasure Sentence in Intent
provisions.evidence: The confirmation sentence in the Intent requirement stands before the release that shows it.
provisions.statement: The literal sentence the subject reads about an erasure MUST stand in Intent before the erasure ships.
provisions.rationale: The sentence on the confirmation screen is the promise: what goes, what stays, and for how long. Behavior cannot word it, because only the product team decides what the product promises. Stating it in Intent puts the exact sentence readers see beside the requirement it fulfils.
provisions.example: Mastodon shows on its account deletion form that content other servers have cached may persist, next to the promise that the account and its posts are removed; that sentence is the user-facing copy for a requested reach.

provisions.heading: Apply Release Access Controls
provisions.evidence: Which restricted release paths lack authentication or authorization? Look at the guards on each restricted path.
provisions.statement: A release with restricted access MUST provide authentication and authorization.
provisions.rationale: Restricted behavior without authentication accepts callers nobody identified, and without authorization it accepts actions nobody permitted. Both decisions call for a trusted identity and a declared permission before the behavior ships.

provisions.heading: Identify Immutable Release Artifacts
provisions.evidence: Which release records lack a source commit or artifact reference? Look at the record header beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST name source commit and immutable artifact reference.
provisions.rationale: The source commit names the verified input and the artifact reference names the deployed output. Together they bind the record to one build, so evidence from another build cannot stand in for it.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Contracts Stable
provisions.evidence: Which contract diffs hold timestamps, machine paths, or unstable order? Look at the generated diff beside each contract.
provisions.statement: A generated application contract MUST be stable and exclude timestamps, machine paths, and nondeterministic ordering.
provisions.rationale: Timestamps, machine paths, and unstable ordering make every regeneration look like a behavior change. Deterministic output keeps contract diffs reviewable, so a reviewer sees only the changes that matter.

provisions.heading: Keep Release Records Non-Authoritative
provisions.evidence: Which release records restate a specification or copy a scenario? Look at the record beside the linked specifications.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST NOT restate a specification or copy a scenario.
provisions.rationale: Specifications own behavior and scenarios. A release record that restates them becomes a second copy, and the copies drift until nobody knows which one holds. The record links outward instead.

provisions.heading: List Included Release Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which records omit an included journey, use case, or extension? Look at the behavior list on each release record.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST list included journeys, use cases, and selected applicable extensions.
provisions.rationale: The behavior boundary of an artifact is exactly its journeys, use cases, and extensions. Listing them tells operators and reviewers what the artifact contains and, by omission, what it does not.

provisions.heading: Qualify the Reader with Known Good and Known Bad Fixtures
provisions.evidence: Which gating S readers lack passing fixture runs? Look at the fixture results beside the stack reader.
provisions.statement: A stack reader MUST pass its known good and known bad fixtures before it gates with S checks.
provisions.rationale: An unqualified reader blocks on noise or passes on silence, and each mistake trains the team to ignore its findings. Passing a known good tree and reporting each planted defect in a known bad tree proves the reader sees what it claims before it blocks any change.
provisions.example: The .NET reader passes the clean tree and reports the planted undeclared write before its S findings block.

provisions.heading: Record Accepted Debt as a Departure
provisions.evidence: Which accepted debts lack a departure with an expiry date? Look at the departures beside each debt.
provisions.statement: Accepted debt MUST live as a departure record with an expiry date.
provisions.rationale: Accepted debt with no expiry date is forgotten work. A departure with an `expiresOn` and `exit` turns it into a dated promise whose findings are covered until the date and whose `departure-expired` reports after it. The [model page](model.md) states the departure shape.
provisions.example: Claimwick ships month-end export without its archive proof, so the debt lives as a departure with an `expiresOn` of 2027-03-01 and an `exit`; `departure-expired` reports it after that date.

provisions.heading: Record the Release Artifact
provisions.evidence: Which releases lack one record naming the immutable artifact? Look at the release records beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release MUST create one release record for its immutable artifact.
provisions.rationale: Evidence scattered across builds and reports answers no single question. One release record per immutable artifact binds every result to the exact output it proves.

provisions.heading: Regenerate Application Contracts
provisions.evidence: Which committed contracts differ from a fresh generation? Look at the contract diff beside the source change.
provisions.statement: A source change MUST regenerate OpenAPI and frontend API types when it changes their source contract.
provisions.rationale: OpenAPI and frontend API types derive from a source contract. A source change that leaves the committed copies stale ships clients built against a contract the server no longer honors.

provisions.heading: Report Verification Exactly
provisions.evidence: Which completion reports lack commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, differences, limits, or covered use cases? Look at the report beside the change.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name exact commands, outcomes, evidence scope, skipped checks, generated differences, scope limits, and covered use cases.
provisions.rationale: A vague report lets unrun checks hide among completed ones. Naming exact commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, and limits tells a reviewer precisely what the evidence covers and what it does not.

provisions.heading: Resolve Release Blockers
provisions.evidence: Which releases depend on an expired departure or an external claim without excluding the behavior? Look at the departures and claims beside the owning records.
provisions.statement: A release MUST settle every expired departure and every external claim it depends on, or exclude the affected behavior from every owning record.
provisions.rationale: An expired departure is a promise past its date, and an unverified external claim behind released behavior is a promise with unsettled terms: a provider fact, a law text, or a term nobody rechecked. Settling each one, or excluding the affected behavior from every owning record, keeps the Intent and release records agreeing on what shipped. `departure-expired` reports every expired departure.

provisions.heading: Run Backend Release Checks
provisions.evidence: Which backend changes lack a passing release build or suite result? Look at the build and suite reports beside the change.
provisions.statement: A backend change MUST pass the release build and the backend test suites.
provisions.rationale: The release build compiles the solution in release mode, catching the conditional and optimization-gated breaks a debug build hides. The architecture, integration, and acceptance suites the size requires prove architecture layering, wiring, and behavior in turn. Skipping any of them ships backend code the project's own suites do not fully prove.

provisions.heading: Run Boundary-Selected Checks
provisions.evidence: Which changes lack a passing result for a check their boundaries select? Look at the change report beside the boundary table.
provisions.statement: A release change MUST run every check selected by its changed backend, frontend, journey, Intent, Behavior, and extension boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Each boundary carries failures the others cannot see: frontend checks say nothing about migrations, and backend suites say nothing about rendered screens. Running every check the changed boundaries select keeps each change evidenced where its failure lives. A narrow category that passes alone certifies only part of the change.

provisions.heading: Run Consistency Checks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` exits zero when it reports no G finding, such as `record-invalid`.
provisions.statement: An Intent or Behavior change MUST pass the G checks with the book.
provisions.rationale: G checks read records only: shape, references, links, reachability, coverage, and the Behavior rules the check list names. Without them, a renamed record or a moved file silently breaks the references other pages rely on, and the book renders a graph that no longer holds. `litespec model check --since <ref>` blocks only on findings about records and code changed since `<ref>` and reports the rest, so an adopting project clears new findings first.

provisions.heading: Run Extension Checks
provisions.evidence: Which affected extensions lack their stated verification evidence? Look at the extension evidence beside the change.
provisions.statement: A selected project or applicable local extension MUST run its stated verification when affected.
provisions.rationale: An extension adds behavior, tests, and operating surface beyond the baseline. Its stated verification is the only evidence written for that surface, so skipping it releases extended behavior the baseline checks never examine.

provisions.heading: Run Frontend Release Checks
provisions.evidence: Which frontend changes lack a passing install, lint, type, test, or build result? Look at the frontend reports beside the change.
provisions.statement: A frontend change MUST run frozen installation, lint, type checking, tests, and production build checks.
provisions.rationale: Each step guards a different failure: frozen installation pins dependencies, lint and type checking catch static defects, tests prove behavior, and the production build proves the shipped bundle compiles. A frontend that skips one arrives at release with that whole class of defect unchecked.

provisions.heading: Run Journey Checks
provisions.evidence: Which journey changes lack passing journey tests? Look at the journey reports against the deployed boundary.
provisions.statement: A journey change MUST run its journey tests.
provisions.rationale: A journey change alters the connected path, so only a journey test through the deployed public boundary can prove it still reaches its outcome. Narrower suites keep passing while the journey itself breaks.

provisions.heading: State Each Release as a Complete Record
provisions.evidence: Which release records depend on an earlier record to be judged? Look at the record alone beside its links.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST state its complete behavior and evidence without depending on an earlier release record.
provisions.rationale: A release judged from fragments is judged by archaeology: the reader digs through other records to fill the gaps. A complete record lets one reader judge one release from one page, with no upgrade guide filling in.

provisions.heading: Store Release Records Together
provisions.evidence: Which release records sit outside `.litespec/releases/` without a recorded release path convention? Look at the release paths beside the convention.
provisions.statement: Keep release records under `.litespec/releases/`.
provisions.rationale: One folder for release records tells a maintainer where to find the evidence for any artifact. A record filed elsewhere looks missing while readers open the folder and find nothing there.
provisions.example: `.litespec/releases/2026-08-21.md` records one immutable artifact and its evidence.

provisions.heading: Verify Connected Journeys
provisions.evidence: Which completed journeys lack a passing test through the deployed boundary? Look at the journey tests beside each included journey.
provisions.statement: A completed journey MUST connect verified use cases to one observable outcome through a deployed public boundary.
provisions.rationale: Use cases that pass in isolation can still fail together: wiring, permissions, and data cross boundaries the isolated tests never touch. A journey test that runs verified use cases to one observable outcome through the deployed public boundary proves the connected path customers actually take.

provisions.heading: Answer the Constraints Question
provisions.evidence: `.litespec/project.yaml` states which outside constraints apply, or records an empty answer.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST state in `.litespec/project.yaml` whether any outside constraint applies to the project.
provisions.rationale: An outside rule the project never names is a law the product can break unknowingly. Recording the answer, even when it is empty, proves the team asked the question: an empty answer states that no outside rule binds the project. A later reader can then tell a project with no constraints from one that never looked.
provisions.example: A clinic booking system records that medical-device regulation does not apply to appointment scheduling.

provisions.heading: Claim Conformance Only When Every Applicable Provision Holds
provisions.evidence: `.litespec/project.yaml` names each claimed layer in `layers`, beside the selected size, shape, stacks, and extensions; each departure from a provision that applies to a claimed layer resolves to a departure record under `.litespec/governance/departures/`, and the checks that run for those layers pass.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST meet every provision that applies to each layer it claims in `layers` before claiming conformance to LiteSpec for those layers.
provisions.rationale: A conformance claim tells a reader that the whole part of the contract the project claimed holds, not only the parts the project chose to follow. A claim of `intent` and `behavior` takes in the provisions about the record model; a claim of `implementation` or `proof` also takes in the provisions that tie each layer to the records. A [departure](departures.md) outranks the provision or findings it covers while it stands, so a project that records each departure still meets this provision; a departure past its expiry date reports `departure-expired` and no longer outranks them. An unrecorded departure in a claimed layer breaks the claim for that layer and leaves any layer the project does meet untouched.
provisions.example: A consumer that claims all four layers with `litespec`, selects the dotnet stack and the caching extension, claims conformance when every page those selections apply holds and their checks pass, with each departure recorded. A consumer that claims `intent` and `behavior` claims conformance when the provisions about the record model hold, while its own code layout and tooling stay outside the claim.

provisions.heading: Claim the Record Layers the Project Uses
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file without `layers`, with a value other than those the table allows, or with a layer whose parent is not claimed.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST name in `layers` in `.litespec/project.yaml` each record layer it claims, with `litespec` or `own` for Implementation and Proof, leaving layers out only from the bottom.
provisions.rationale: Teams adopt LiteSpec in parts: the record model alone, records with marked code, records with acceptance tests, or all of it, and with their own architecture or test practice where they have one. Naming each layer lets every tool check exactly the part the team uses, so a missing test project is not a finding for a team that claims no Proof, and a team that keeps its own code layout still gets its marks checked. Leaving layers out from the bottom keeps every remaining link whole, because each layer points up to the one above it. Settled by [decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers](decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers).
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example claims all four layers with `litespec`. A product that marks its code in its own layout and proves no scenarios yet claims `intent`, `behavior` and `implementation: own`, and `model check` reports no `use-case-unverified` finding for it.

provisions.heading: Declare a Consumer That Has No Backend
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid` for a `client-only` project that names a backend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer with no server of its own MUST declare the `client-only` shape and record a decision naming the surfaces left without coverage.
provisions.rationale: The shape decides which backend pages still apply. A `client-only` product keeps a domain model, so it applies the backend architecture, domain, and application pages that the manifest lists under `shapes`. Persistence, the HTTP API, and API testing have no target without a server, and the decision names those uncovered surfaces. Adding a server only to obtain conformance contradicts `litespec/core/principles#require-current-complexity-activation`, which permits new machinery only for a current documented requirement.
provisions.example: `litespec/quality/ci#run-applicable-gates-on-every-pull-request` already permits skipping a gate whose surface does not exist, so a missing backend gate is a recorded consequence rather than an unexplained absence.

provisions.heading: Keep Every LiteSpec File Under One Folder
provisions.evidence: Which files created, read, or governed by LiteSpec sit outside `.litespec/`, or at the repository root? Look at the repository tree beside the project's `.litespec/` folder.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST hold every file LiteSpec creates, reads, or governs under one folder, `.litespec/`, at the repository root.
provisions.rationale: One folder with one name in every consumer makes the LiteSpec material identifiable at a glance: a reader, a tool, or an agent finds the whole contract in one place, moves or deletes it without hunting the tree, and keeps it apart from the application's code, tests, and infrastructure. Generated output inside it stays covered by its `.gitignore`, so a checkout never mixes committed records with built files. Every path in `.litespec/project.yaml` stays relative to the repository root, so moving the folder never rewrites the paths inside it, and a command finds the consumer by walking up from the working folder to the first folder that holds `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds its project file, glossary, example cast, and the Intent, Behavior, Implementation, Proof, and Governance folders under `examples/claimwick/.litespec/` (in a real consumer, at its repository root), beside its application code and tests, which keep their own places. An agent asked to read the contract opens that one folder instead of collecting a root project file, a documentation tree, a model folder, and a book folder from four places.

provisions.heading: Keep One Bounded Context
provisions.evidence: Module pages and `.litespec/project.yaml` name one business language and one deployment boundary, with no second of either.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST keep one business language and deployment boundary.
provisions.rationale: One business language and one deployment boundary keep every module, record, and use case in a single consistent model. Modules organize related language, models, use cases, and code without becoming independent services or bounded contexts. A second language or boundary splits the project into systems that the records, links, and checks can no longer hold together.
provisions.example: Posts, Authors, and Comments can be modules in one publishing context.

provisions.heading: Measure Capacity Before Expansion
provisions.evidence: Each added cache, replica, queue, or partition follows recorded load, latency target, and observed constraint, or a capacity convention.
provisions.statement: Record current load, latency target, and observed constraint before adding caches, replicas, queues, or partitioning.
provisions.rationale: Caches, replicas, queues, and partitioning each answer a different limitation, and only measurements show which one the project hit. Recording current load, the latency target, and the observed constraint before expanding proves the added capacity answers the observed limit. Expanding first and measuring later adds machinery that can hide the real bottleneck.

provisions.heading: Point Behavior Docs at the Behavior Root
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project record without `paths.behaviorDocs`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST set `paths.behaviorDocs` in `.litespec/project.yaml` to the folder that holds its Behavior records.
provisions.rationale: The builder joins records, queries, diffs, and the book from one declared root. A Behavior tree the project record never names is one the tools never see, so its records skip every check. One declared folder keeps authors and tools on the same tree.
provisions.example:
```yaml
paths:
  behaviorDocs: .litespec/behavior
```

provisions.heading: Record Selected Extensions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a selection without a criterion.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST list every selected extension in `selectedExtensions` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, each with its criterion.
provisions.rationale: The project record determines which extension boundaries apply to the project's work. Writing each selection with its criterion lets a later reader check whether the condition still holds. Without the record, extensions drift in through dependencies and prose while the checks apply a different set.

provisions.heading: Record Unsupported Scope Decisions
provisions.evidence: A project decision names each architecture outside the supported boundary the project adopts.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record a separate project decision for microservices, multiple contexts, native clients on a platform with no mobile stack, other platforms, event sourcing, active-active regions, or large pipelines.
provisions.rationale: Microservices, multiple contexts, native clients on a platform with no mobile stack, other platforms, event sourcing, active-active regions, and large pipelines each change the assumptions this page rests on: one language, one deployment, one API and database. A separate project decision records that the team saw the boundary and chose deliberately. Without it, the project drifts outside the supported scope while claiming its checks still apply.

provisions.heading: Select a Size, a Shape and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid`, when the project claims Implementation or Proof, for a shape whose backend stack count is wrong and a platform that names no frontend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST select a size, a shape, one stack per frontend, and one backend stack unless the shape is client-only or the project claims neither `implementation` nor `proof` in `layers`.
provisions.rationale: One size and explicit stacks tell every check which records and pages apply. The size decides which record types the project carries and which test projects prove them; each stack decides which technology pages and checks apply. Without the declaration, each agent infers the architecture from the directory tree, and two agents infer two architectures. A project that claims neither Implementation nor Proof may leave the stacks empty or absent, or name them for information alone, since no code reader runs for it; a project that claims either names the stacks the code reader and the checks govern.
provisions.example:
A project with one web frontend and no journeys selects small with the svelte stack; the running Claimwick example, with journeys, selects large.

The running Claimwick example declares large with a server shape and two stacks in `.litespec/project.yaml`:

```yaml
size: large
shape: server
stacks:
- dotnet
- svelte
layers:
  intent: litespec
  behavior: litespec
  implementation: litespec
  proof: litespec
```

The size selects the large record set, the shape selects a backend stack, and each stack selects its technology pages, which satisfies this provision.

The diagram shows size, shape and stacks and what each decides.

![Size, shape and stacks and what each decides: size, small or large, decides the record types and the test projects, with large adding goals, problems, features, journeys, and scenarios; shape, server or client-only, decides whether the project names a backend stack; stacks, one backend stack and one stack per frontend, decide the technology pages and the checks that apply.](../assets/diagrams/core-scope-selection.svg)

provisions.heading: Select Conditional Extensions Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Each entry in `selectedExtensions` carries a criterion that holds, and no applicable extension from the extension catalog stays unselected.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST select every extension whose activation criteria apply, and no extension whose criteria do not.
provisions.rationale: Conditional capabilities stay inactive until a documented product or engineering condition applies, so no project carries caching, messaging, or tenancy machinery it never justified. Selecting exactly the extensions whose criteria hold keeps the active rule set minimal and reviewable. The manifest's extension list is the closed set a project selects from, so there is no informal extension. Settled by [decision/0030-limit-the-jobs-extension](decision/0030-limit-the-jobs-extension) for the jobs extension, which keeps the subjects a small team follows.
provisions.example: Caching, durable messaging, and multitenancy are extensions; the extension index lists each with its activation criteria.

provisions.heading: Start with One API and Database
provisions.evidence: The topology holds one API deployable and one database, or a topology convention records what runs instead.
provisions.statement: Use one API deployable and one database.
provisions.rationale: One API deployable and one database keep the first architecture reviewable and operable by a small team. Each additional deployable or store adds deployment, data-consistency, and operations work that a project rarely needs at the start. A background job appears only when a process continues without an HTTP request.

provisions.heading: Write Every Hand-Written LiteSpec File in YAML
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file that is not `.litespec/project.yaml` or lacks `schemaVersion`; scope: the project file.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST write every LiteSpec file a person edits, the project file, the records, the glossary and the pattern catalog, in YAML that states its `schemaVersion` and names its schema in a first-line `# yaml-language-server: $schema=<url>` comment, while files that programs exchange, such as check results, the model and `--format json` output, stay JSON.
provisions.rationale: People write these files and review them in pull requests, so one syntax with comments and no brace noise keeps every edit readable, and one syntax across the folder means a reader learns it once. The schema comment gives an editor completion and validation without a key in the data, and `schemaVersion` tells a tool which shape the file holds. Programs gain nothing from YAML, so their output stays JSON, which every tool reads without a parser of its own. Settled by [decision/0023-every-handwritten-file-in-yaml](decision/0023-every-handwritten-file-in-yaml).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `.litespec/project.yaml` starts with the comment naming `https://litespec.dev/<version>/schemas/litespec-project.schema.yaml`, then `schemaVersion: 1`, and lists its layers, size, shape and stacks as YAML keys; its check results under `.litespec/proof/checks/` stay JSON files written by its harness.

provisions.heading: Declare the Page Scope
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_BLOCK` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Each page that owns provisions MUST declare its stack and concern in a `**Stack:**` line and a `**Concern:**` line directly under its title.
provisions.rationale: One block under the title tells every reader and tool which situation the page governs without reading further. A page without it leaves its provisions unfiled: retrieval cannot tell which change they govern, so it shows them everywhere or nowhere. Declaring both fields once keeps the page, not each provision, as the home of the common scope.

provisions.heading: Depart from a Rule Only Through a Recorded Departure
provisions.evidence: Which departures from a provision of Strength `required` name no provision, page or finding code, or give no reason? Look at the files under `.litespec/governance/departures/`.
provisions.statement: A project that departs from a provision of Strength `required` MUST record a departure whose `covers` names the provision, with a reason.
provisions.rationale: A rule binds every project it reaches: a silent departure claims conformance the project does not hold. The [departure record](departures.md) names the provision and the reason, and an expiry date marks a gap the team means to close, so the departure stays visible and ends instead of lingering.
provisions.example: Claimwick ships its weekend export without the review step, so it records a departure whose `covers` names the authorization provision and whose reason states the choice.

provisions.heading: Give Every Provision Its Layer and Trace
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_VALUE` diagnostic for a `layer` or `trace` value.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST carry the record layer of its page, or state its own layer as a `layer` field on its Applies to line when that layer differs from its page layer; a provision that ties its layer to the records states `trace: yes` on that line.
provisions.rationale: A tool that reports only the part of the record model a project claims reads the layer and trace of each provision from the provision index: a provision with no layer, or with a layer copied from its page, gives the tool no exact part to report. The page gives the default, one field states the exception, and the index carries the result beside the artifact, so no reader composes the layer by hand.
provisions.example: A provision about expense records on a page under `docs/core/` carries `any` from its page and states no field. A provision that requires code marks on the same page states `**Applies to:** layer: implementation; trace: yes`, and its index row carries `implementation` and `yes`.

provisions.heading: Name the Artifact of Every Provision on a Page That Names One
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_ARTIFACT` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: On a page where one provision names an `artifact`, every provision MUST name the kinds of file it governs, or `artifact: any` when it governs every file of its layer.
provisions.rationale: `litespec rules` matches a provision to a file by the kind of file it names. A provision that names none on a page of named kinds matches every file of the layer, so a handler receives the validator and port provisions beside its own and an agent reads provisions that do not govern the file in front of it.
provisions.example: On the application page, the provision for validators names `artifact: validator` and the provision for the whole application concern names `artifact: any`, so `litespec rules` on a command handler returns the second and leaves out the first.

provisions.heading: Record Each Replaced Default
provisions.evidence: Each choice against a provision of Strength default is recorded in the place its Replacement names.
provisions.statement: A project that chooses otherwise than a provision of Strength default MUST record its choice where the provision names.
provisions.rationale: A default holds until the project says otherwise in writing: without the record, a reader cannot tell a deliberate choice from a provision nobody read. The provision names the recording place in its Replacement, so each choice sits where its provision points. An advisory provision asks for no record, which is what sets the two strengths apart.
provisions.example: A project that keeps its pattern catalog outside the default path records the path in `paths.uiPatterns`, as the provision's Replacement names.

provisions.heading: State Applies to Only When Narrower
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_NARROW` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision MUST carry an Applies to line only when its scope is narrower than its page scope, its layer or trace differs from its page, or it marks its concern-wide scope with `artifact: any` on a page where another provision names a kind.
provisions.rationale: The page scope already governs every provision on it: repeating it on each provision doubles the homes for one fact, and the copies disagree at the next edit. An Applies to line that widens the page scope misfiles the provision under situations the page never governed. One line, only when narrower, at a different layer or trace, or marking the concern-wide scope beside a named kind, keeps retrieval exact.
provisions.example: On a page scoped to `concern: domain`, a provision for aggregates carries `**Applies to:** artifact: aggregate`, while a provision for the whole domain concern carries no line. On an application page where a provision names `artifact: validator`, a provision for the whole application concern carries `**Applies to:** artifact: any`. On a record-model page, a provision about marks carries `**Applies to:** layer: implementation; trace: yes`.

provisions.heading: Use Only Declared Scope Values
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_VALUE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A Scope block and an Applies to line MUST use only the stack, concern, artifact, layer, and trace values this page lists.
provisions.rationale: Retrieval matches situations to values: a value invented on one page matches nothing, so its provisions never surface for the change they govern. One closed vocabulary keeps every value comparable across pages. A new situation earns a value here first, then uses it on its page.
provisions.example: A provision about the expense aggregate narrows with `artifact: aggregate` rather than inventing `artifact: receipt`. A provision about marks on a record-model page states `trace: yes` rather than inventing a trace value.

provisions.heading: Apply the Complete Stack
provisions.evidence: The consumer file set covers every page in its stack folders, the folders above them, and their stackless subfolders.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting a stack MUST apply the pages in its folder, every folder above it, and their subfolders that hold no stack.
provisions.rationale: The stack is the unit of conformance: a consumer cannot claim a stack while silently omitting an applicable page. Applying the folder, every folder above it, and their stackless subfolders keeps inherited principles in force without restating them. A deeper page replaces only the provisions it names, so everything it leaves unnamed keeps applying.

provisions.heading: Declare Replacements
provisions.evidence: Each extension or departure names every baseline provision ID it replaces, with the rest staying active.
provisions.statement: An extension or a departure MUST name every baseline provision ID it replaces.
provisions.rationale: Naming every replaced provision ID draws the exact boundary of the change: everything unnamed stays active. A departure names the provision in `covers`, and `rules <path>` shows the departure in place of the provision. Without the list, a replacement silently widens its scope with each reading, and reviewers cannot tell which baseline provisions still bind the project.

provisions.heading: Keep the Stack Visible
provisions.evidence: `.litespec/project.yaml` names each selected stack, and the root `AGENTS.md` names the solution, applications, and commands.
provisions.statement: Name each selected stack in `.litespec/project.yaml` and the solution, applications, and commands in the root `AGENTS.md`.
provisions.rationale: Naming each selected stack in `.litespec/project.yaml` with the solution, applications, and commands in the root `AGENTS.md` lets an agent resolve the project placeholders directly. Inferring the selection from the directory tree fails whenever folders outnumber stacks or names overlap. Visible selection also tells a human reader what the project runs before opening any code.

provisions.heading: Use Manifest Version Pins
provisions.evidence: Each resolved SDK, framework, and package version matches its pin in `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST resolve every SDK, framework, and package version from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The manifest owns every pin, so resolving versions anywhere else produces builds the standard never described. A version copied from prose, an example, a package search, or agent memory drifts from the pin with the next edit. One resolution source keeps every consumer on the same tested combination.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Edge Between Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `effect-undeclared` or `effect-loop-invalid` finding across use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, and integration events, and reports `effect-unimplemented` (check level A) for a declared edge no code takes.
provisions.statement: Every edge between use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, integration events, and external systems MUST be declared in a record and checked.
provisions.rationale: The declared edges form the effect graph the checks verify: an undeclared edge is the defect, not the mechanism that carries it. The graph holds no cycles except through domain events with a stated end condition. An inline edge states whether it shares the caller's transaction, and atomic consistency spans no async edge. The [behavior page](behavior.md) states the edge fields, and the [layers page](layers.md) states how Implementation is checked against them.

provisions.heading: Deliver One Complete Use Case
provisions.evidence: The use case page with its behavior, persistence, entry points, tests, and operating records present.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST complete with behavior, persistence, entry points, evidence, and operating impact.
provisions.rationale: A use case is done only when a caller can run it and operations can support it: behavior, storage, entry points, automated evidence, and operating impact together. Accepting a thinner slice leaves the missing parts for later, and later rarely itemizes what shipped half-built. Placeholder work leaves the use case unimplemented. Multi-step product outcomes belong to a journey rather than stretching one use case across several goals.
provisions.example: A use case without its tests and operating records is not complete.

provisions.heading: Drive Work from Records
provisions.evidence: The change report listing the Intent and Behavior records the work started from.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST start behavior work from the Intent records and the Behavior records that own the behavior.
provisions.rationale: A prompt, ticket, chat message, or code comment can start work, but none of them holds the stated behavior. Starting from the owning records keeps the agent building what the records state, and keeps the records as the lasting statement of what the code does. Without this rule, each task reinterprets intent from its starting message, and the records drift from the code until nobody trusts either.

provisions.heading: Group Module Use Case Files by Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Each use case file under its module directory or its aggregate subdirectory.
provisions.statement: Group module use case files under a plural kebab-case aggregate subdirectory, each holding that aggregate's page; a module with one aggregate of the module's own name may stay flat.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate needs its own directory for its page and use cases, so grouping use case files under a plural kebab-case aggregate subdirectory gives every aggregate one home. A module with one aggregate of the module's own name may stay flat, avoiding a repeated segment such as `modules/products/products/`. The use case identifier stays `use-case/<module>.<name>`; only the directory changes.

provisions.heading: Keep Decision Authority with Accountable People
provisions.evidence: The change report naming the unknown fact, the person asked, and the record carrying the answer.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stop affected work and take to an accountable person an unknown fact that changes behavior, money, data, access, or recovery.
provisions.rationale: Agents meet unknowns in the middle of a task: an unknown access rule, an unclear retention limit, a missing recovery target. When the answer changes behavior, money, data, access, or recovery, only an accountable person can give it. Stopping and taking the question to that person keeps the choice visible instead of buried in code nobody stated. Accountable people decide outcomes, terms, policies, and criteria, and an agent contribution stays a proposal until one of them accepts it.

provisions.heading: Keep Operational and Security References Under Operations
provisions.evidence: Operating and security reference prose under `.litespec/implementation/operations/`, or the project documentation naming the replacement home.
provisions.statement: Keep operating and security reference prose under `.litespec/implementation/operations/`.
provisions.rationale: One home for operating and security reference prose means an on-call reader looks in `.litespec/implementation/operations/` first and finds the runbooks, limits, and inventories there. Scattering that prose across product and domain pages buries it where an incident never looks. Enforceable security and privacy rules still belong to their owning use case fields and rules, since those are what the code and tests prove.

provisions.heading: Point Code and Tests up to Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing`, `mark-unknown` and `mark-count-invalid` (check level S) for a code element with no mark, a mark naming no record of the type its element takes, or a handler marking other than one record.
provisions.statement: Every code element the marks table on the [model page](model.md) assigns a mark MUST carry one naming the record it serves, with each handler marking exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: The mark is the link from Implementation to Behavior and from Proof to the scenario it proves, in the two kinds the [model page](model.md) states: `implements` names the record served and `follows` names the choice followed. A folder or a type name only resembles the record, and a resemblance drifts with the next rename; a mark holds the identifier, so the checks, the analyzers and the editor follow the same link without guessing. One record per handler keeps each file answerable to one use case. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code, so the link points up and the records stay the authority.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense handler carries a mark naming `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense`, the `Reimburse` method on the expense root carries the same mark, and the reminder event handler carries a mark naming `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted`.

provisions.heading: Point Every Technical Class up to Its Record or Choice
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (check level S), and `dotnet build` reports `LS5001` and `LS5002`, for a technical class with no mark, an `implements` mark naming no Behavior record, or a `follows` mark naming no provision of the carried release, no decision, departure, or project convention, or a provision on a page the project's stacks do not apply.
provisions.statement: Every technical class the marks table on the [model page](model.md) names MUST carry at least one mark: an `implements` mark naming a Behavior record it serves, or a `follows` mark naming the LiteSpec provision, decision, departure, or project convention that shapes it.
provisions.rationale: Every class in the outer layers exists for a record or for a reason. An input validator or a read model serves one use case, and a repository serves one aggregate, so each names that record in `implements` like the handler beside it. Code that serves no record still exists for a reason: a provision requires it, a technical decision chose it, a departure allows it, or a project convention states it, and a `follows` mark names that reason by identifier. The named target is the reason for the shape the class carries, so review judges a `follows` mark by whether its target requires that shape. A reader asking why the command pipeline commits once, or why the repository stores documents, follows the link instead of guessing, and a check finds the code that still follows a deleted decision. A class may carry both kinds when it serves a record in a chosen way.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense validator carries `/// <implements>use-case/spending.submit-expense</implements>`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`, and the command pipeline's commit step carries `/// <follows>litespec/backend/persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once</follows>`. The payout bank port carries `/// <follows>claimwick/conventions#confirm-large-payouts</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Update Records with Behavior
provisions.evidence: The behavior change with its use case page, tests, product records, decision, journey, and operating records changed together.
provisions.statement: An observable behavior change MUST update its use case page, implementation, tests, product records, decision, journey, and operating records together.
provisions.rationale: Records map to current names and paths only when each behavior change carries them along. A change that moves code but leaves the use case page, the tests, or the journey behind splits the project into stated fiction and unstated fact. Updating the records in the same change keeps the change to behavior and the change to its description in one place.

provisions.heading: Use Established Technical Terms
provisions.evidence: Prose using aggregate, command, query, reaction, job, repository, projection, outbox, idempotency, and transaction with their accepted meanings.
provisions.statement: Use aggregate, command, query, reaction, job, repository, projection, outbox, idempotency, and transaction with their accepted technical meanings.
provisions.rationale: Names such as aggregate, command, query, reaction, job, repository, projection, outbox, idempotency, and transaction carry established meanings that developers and agents already share. Replacing one with a softer synonym hides the pattern and forces every reader to guess what the new word covers. When a term is unfamiliar, explain it and give an example instead of renaming it.

provisions.heading: Use Ordinary Capitalization in Prose
provisions.evidence: Prose writing module, aggregate, use case, journey, rule, event, and decision in lowercase outside names and identifiers.
provisions.statement: Write module, aggregate, use case, journey, rule, event, and decision as ordinary nouns in prose.
provisions.rationale: Lowercase module, aggregate, use case, journey, rule, event, and decision read as ordinary nouns, while exact record types and code types keep their declared capitalization. The contrast tells a reader whether a word names the concept or the artifact. Capitalizing both blurs that distinction on every page.

provisions.heading: Use the Docs Layout on the Model Page
provisions.evidence: The `docs/` tree matching the layout the model page states, or the project documentation naming the replacement layout.
provisions.statement: Use the docs layout the [model page](model.md) states under The Docs Layout, creating a directory only when its first real artifact exists.
provisions.rationale: One home for the docs layout means the folders and the record layers stay in one table. A second tree beside it drifts with the next reorganization, and readers follow the stale one.

provisions.heading: Bind Every Keyed Setting in One Marked Options Class
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unimplemented` (level S) for a keyed setting no options class marks, and `setting-key-drift` (level S) for a marked options class whose `SectionName` constant and property do not spell the setting's `key`.
provisions.statement: A setting with a `key` MUST be bound by an options class that carries an `implements` mark naming the setting and whose section and property spell the key.
provisions.rationale: The options class is where configuration becomes a typed value the code reads, so it is the code element that implements the setting. Marking it names the promise the class holds, and comparing its section name and property with the record's key finds the renamed section or the typo before the product starts with a default.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `SpendingOptions` declares `SectionName = "Spending"`, an `ApprovalReminderDelay` property, and `/// <implements>setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Bound Every Caller-Supplied Input Value
provisions.evidence: Which caller-supplied money or access inputs lack a cited bounding rule? Look beside each input with `origin: caller` on a money or access path.
provisions.statement: Each input value with `origin: caller` on a money or access path MUST cite the rule bounding it.
provisions.rationale: A caller-asserted figure on a money or access path is an open till: a replacement amount arrives negative, a quantity arrives absurd, and the code obliges. Citing the rule bounding it ties each such value to the guard holding it.
provisions.example: The replacement net amount cites the positivity rule bounding it.

provisions.heading: Connect Each Use Case to Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-link-missing` for a use case with neither `serves` nor `fulfills`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name a journey step in `serves` or a requirement in `fulfills`.
provisions.rationale: A use case serving nothing and fulfilling nothing is behavior nobody asked for: it ships without a promise behind it and stays when the promise changes. Naming a journey step or a requirement ties each behavior to the intent it carries. The `record-link-missing` check reports a use case with neither field, and `step-use-case-missing` reports a journey step no use case serves.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command serves `journey/submit-and-reimburse#s4` and fulfills `requirement/approval-reminders.single-reimbursement`.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Effect with One Verb and Its Timing
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an edge the records never declared and `effect-timing-invalid` for a command `sends` or `calls` effect with `inline` timing; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an effect entry without exactly one verb or its timing.
provisions.statement: Each effect entry MUST carry exactly one verb and its timing.
provisions.rationale: An edge no record declares is the defect: hidden calls between use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, integration events, and external systems. Declaring each edge with exactly one verb of `runs`, `sends`, `emits`, or `calls`, with its timing of `inline`, `after-commit`, or `async`, and its failure handling states every coupling as data. Timing is required on every use-case effect. On a command, a `sends` or `calls` effect carries `after-commit` or `async` timing, and an event handler runs the consequence after the commit. The `effect-undeclared` check reports an edge the records never declared.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command emits the reimbursed integration event after commit.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Query Output
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `query-output-missing` for a query with no declared output.
provisions.statement: Each query MUST declare its output in named `include` groups.
provisions.rationale: A query without a declared output returns whatever its author fetched: readers and screens guess the shape from code. Declaring the output in named groups with fields, classifications, the aggregates each group reads, and freshness states what readers receive, so the shape is reviewable before anything implements it. The `query-output-missing` check reports a query with no declared output.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query declares open and decided groups with `{ "mode": "immediate" }` freshness.

provisions.heading: Declare Paging on Every Collection Query
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `paging-undeclared` for a collection query with no paging.
provisions.statement: Each collection query MUST declare its paging with `mode` of `pages`, or `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its reason.
provisions.rationale: A collection without paging is a promise the data outgrows: the first hundred rows return, the next ten thousand time out. Declaring the order, the cursor or offset, and the default and maximum limits with `mode` of `pages` states the paging beside the read, and `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its reason states why a query returns one object. The `paging-undeclared` check reports a collection query with no paging.

provisions.heading: Derive Generic Refusals Instead of Writing Them
provisions.evidence: Which use-case pages write a generic forbidden or invalid-input refusal as a record? Look at the results on each use-case page beside the derived names.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST NOT write a generic forbidden or invalid-input refusal as a record.
provisions.rationale: Hand-written generic refusals multiply: hundreds of pages each declare their own forbidden, and each drifts in wording and code. Deriving them from the grant in `access` and the rules in `input` keeps one forbidden and one invalid input per use case, current with the grant: the builder derives `result/<use-case>.forbidden` and `result/<use-case>.invalid-input`. Scenarios point at the derived results without anyone writing them.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Use Case Input with Origin and Classification
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case input without name, meaning, or type, without `of` on an `id` or `choice` field, or with `of` on another type.
provisions.statement: Each use-case input MUST declare its name, meaning, type, origin, and classification.
provisions.rationale: An input without an origin is trusted on faith: caller-asserted values pass as verified claims, and money moves on an unchecked figure. Declaring the name, the meaning, the type from `text`, `integer`, `decimal`, `money`, `boolean`, `date`, `date-time`, `duration`, `email`, `choice`, and `id`, the origin of `caller`, `claim`, or `derived`, and the classification states what arrives, what it is, and how far to trust it. An `id` field names the record it refers to in `of`, and a `choice` field names its choices there; other types carry no `of`. `required` states whether the caller sends the field, and a money field carries an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, as the [Record Language](language.md) states. A type on each field lets the builder compare the records with the generated contract and lets agents generate the right code first time. Settled by [decision/0016-typed-contracts-and-privacy](decision/0016-typed-contracts-and-privacy) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).

provisions.heading: End Every Use Case in Named Results
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-success-missing` for a use case with no success result; each refusal entry on the use-case page carries its code.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its success result and every refusal with its code.
provisions.rationale: Callers branch on named endings: success, or one refusal with its stable code. A use case with no named success leaves readers guessing what good looks like, and a refusal without a code leaves each architecture layer reporting the same breach another way.
