The `use-case-success-missing` check reports a use case with no success result, and `result-undeclared` reports a code the records never declared.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares `reimbursed` with `spending.not-approved` and `spending.already-reimbursed`.

provisions.heading: Exercise Rules from Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Which scenarios show rules without naming them in `exercises`? Look at the scenarios beside the rules they walk.
provisions.statement: A scenario MUST name the rules it shows in `exercises`.
provisions.rationale: A rule proved only through a test mark hides which example walks it: readers open the rule and find no story. Naming the shown rules in `exercises` ties each example to the rules it walks, so every rule meets its stories.
provisions.example: A scenario walking a second hold on one copy names `rule/lending.one-hold-per-copy` in `exercises`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case a Command or Query Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case page without `kind` or with an unknown kind.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare one kind: command or query.
provisions.rationale: The kind decides what the use case is allowed to touch: a command changes, a query reads. A use case with no kind leaves each reader to allow it everything, and the checks no shape to confirm. When-X-do-Y behavior and work without a request are reaction and job records, as the [Automation page](automation.md) states.

provisions.heading: Grant Each Use Case Scoped Access
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case page without `access` carrying grant and tenant scope.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its grant and its tenant scope in `access`.
provisions.rationale: Access split across prose and code is widened silently: a new caller arrives, the grant stretches, and no record shows it. Declaring the grant of `permission/<name>`, `self(permission/<name>)`, `anonymous`, or `system`, and the tenant scope of `own`, `cross`, `public`, or `none` states who may act and how far the call reaches beside the behavior. The [Access page](access.md) states the grant forms and the tenant meanings, and the door the call arrives through states how the caller proved identity. The authorization guard enforces the grant (`litespec/backend/application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline`), and `LS2012` reports a handler that authorizes itself.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares the reimburse-expense permission with own tenant scope, reached through a session door, while the self-checkout scan declares a system grant through a device door.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Setting Default to a Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-requirement-missing` for a commercial, legal, or varying default with no cited requirement.
provisions.statement: Each setting MUST declare its value type, range, unit, setter, and bound behavior, with the requirement behind a commercial, legal, or varying default.
provisions.rationale: A default no requirement holds is a figure nobody stated: a price, a fee, a term, or a limit nobody decided. Declaring the value type, the range, the unit, the setter of product, operator, or tenant, and the bound behavior of `refuse`, `truncate`, or `degrade` states the tunable beside its promise, and a commercial, legal, or tenant-, market-, or date-varying default cites its requirement. The `setting-requirement-missing` check reports such a default with no cited requirement.
provisions.example: The receipt threshold declares money with a product-set default of EUR 25, refusing an expense above the line with no receipt, behind its requirement.

provisions.heading: Justify Every Wider Visibility
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `widening-cites-missing` for a widened include group with no cited requirement.
provisions.statement: Each include group visible to more roles than the aggregates it reads MUST cite the requirement widening it in `cites`.
provisions.rationale: A read showing more than the aggregates it reads is a quiet widening: roles see figures their own grants never allowed, and no requirement states the view. Citing the requirement in `cites` keeps the widening a decided choice, and `visibleWhen` states the condition where one narrows it. The `widening-cites-missing` check reports a widened group with no cited requirement.

provisions.heading: Keep One Kind per Verb
provisions.evidence: Which queries open with a changing verb, or which commands open with a reading verb? Look at the first word of each use-case name beside its kind.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST open with a verb of its own kind, or with an either verb.
provisions.rationale: The first word is the first thing a reader trusts. A query named `change-...` or a command named `read-...` makes every listing lie about what the use case may touch, and a reader stops trusting names at all. The baseline vocabulary gives each verb a kind of query, command, or either; an either verb opens either kind. A project records which of its domain verbs read; its other domain verbs open either kind.
provisions.example: `use-case/lending.list-loans` is a query and passes; `use-case/lending.answer-inquiry` opens either kind on an either verb and passes; `use-case/lending.read-overdue-count` declared as a command is reported, and so is `use-case/lending.change-copy` declared as a query.

provisions.heading: Keep the Effect Graph Free of Cycles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-loop-invalid` for a cycle with no stated end condition.
provisions.statement: The effect graph MUST hold no cycle except through a domain event carrying its end condition.
provisions.rationale: A cycle without an end condition runs until something breaks: a reaction runs a use case raising the event triggering the reaction. Forbidding cycles except through a domain event with a stated end condition keeps every loop a loop with an exit. The `effect-loop-invalid` check reports a cycle with no stated end.

provisions.heading: List Recorded Outcomes Inside Success Codes
provisions.evidence: Which success results with recorded outcomes list no `codes`? Look at the success results beside their use-case pages.
provisions.statement: Each success result with recorded outcomes MUST list them in `codes`.
provisions.rationale: A success hiding several recorded outcomes forces callers to guess: borrow and renew both succeed, but the due date and the analytics differ. Listing the closed codes inside the success states each recorded outcome beside the ending.
provisions.example: The checked-out result lists `borrow` and `renew`.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Lagging Query as Built Asynchronously
provisions.evidence: Which lagging queries lack `builtAsynchronously` with a bounded or advisory freshness and a lag scenario? Look at the queries beside the aggregates they read.
provisions.statement: Each query reading lagging aggregates MUST set `builtAsynchronously` with a `{ "mode": "bounded", "within": "..." }` or `{ "mode": "advisory", "authority": "..." }` freshness and a lag scenario.
provisions.rationale: A read built asynchronously without a mark is trusted as fresh: screens show yesterday figures as now, and nobody warned them. Marking the query, with a `{ "mode": "bounded", "within": "..." }` or `{ "mode": "advisory", "authority": "..." }` freshness and one scenario covering the lag, states the staleness beside the promise.

provisions.heading: Name a Use Case for the Act Its Aggregate Performs
provisions.evidence: Which command handlers call aggregate methods starting with neither the use-case verb nor `Request`? Look at the methods each command handler calls.
provisions.statement: Each command use case MUST share its verb with the aggregate method its handler calls.
provisions.rationale: The use case is the doorway into one aggregate act. A different word at the door and at the act means two meanings have merged, or the use case is misnamed, and each reader guesses which word tells the truth. A handler calling no aggregate method answers to no act, so queries and ports stay out of this rule. A command that records a request for work an event handler finishes after the commit, as `litespec/backend/application#call-external-systems-through-their-ports` requires, performs the request: its method starts with `Request` and passes.
provisions.example: `use-case/orders.void-order` whose handler calls `Abandon` is reported; the project renames the use case to the domain word, or the method and its event to `Void` and `OrderVoidedEvent`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Refusal Code for the State That Refuses
provisions.evidence: Which refusal codes fall outside `<module>.<noun>-<state>` or hide their state behind a vague word? Look at the refusal codes on each use-case page.
provisions.statement: Each refusal code MUST read `<module>.<noun>-<state>` and name the state, not the failure.
provisions.rationale: The code is a public contract; `invalid`, `failed` or `error` tell an integrator nothing to do. A code naming the state tells what holds and what to change. The prefix names the module that owns the refused state, which may differ from the module of the refusing use case, and a code built at run time from a key, such as the conflict for a lost uniqueness key, declares its template in `refusals.composed`.
provisions.example: `spending.receipt-missing` names the missing receipt; `spending.receipt-invalid` hides the state behind a vague word and is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Every Aggregate a Use Case Changes or Reads
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` for a write outside `changes` and `reference-unknown` for an unknown aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name every aggregate it changes in `changes` and every aggregate it reads in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A write no record names is invisible: the handler touches a second aggregate, the second aggregate changes, and no diff shows it. Naming every touched aggregate, including `store` aggregates, states the read and write footprint beside the behavior. The `write-undeclared` check reports a write outside `changes`.

provisions.heading: Name the Configuration Key of Every Operator Setting
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-key-missing` (level G) for a setting with `setBy: operator` and no `key`.
provisions.statement: A setting the operator sets MUST name its configuration path in `key`.
provisions.rationale: An operator setting reaches the product through configuration, so the record and the configuration meet at one path: the record states the default and the bounds, and the configuration names the value. Without the key, a renamed section silently falls back to a default nobody chose, and no reader can tell which configuration value a promise rests on. A setting a tenant or the product sets is held as data by an aggregate instead, and names no key.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay` is set by the operator and carries `key` `Spending:ApprovalReminderDelay`.

provisions.heading: Name the Entry Points That Reach Each Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a live use case that names no entry point and that nothing runs, and `reference-unknown` for a `reachedThrough` entry naming no entry point.
provisions.statement: Each use case a caller reaches from outside MUST name the entry points that reach it in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.rationale: A use case with no named door is reachable from anywhere or nowhere: readers cannot tell a public operation from an internal one. Naming the entry points shows how callers arrive at each behavior. A use case that only a reaction, a job, or another use case runs has no door of its own, and its `runs` edge already shows how it is reached.

provisions.heading: Name the Events Each Use Case Raises
provisions.evidence: Which use cases raise domain events that `raises` does not name? Look at `raises` beside each use-case page.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name the domain events it raises in `raises`.
provisions.rationale: An event raised but unnamed leaves reactions waiting: downstream behavior answers a fact no behavior admits raising. Naming the raised events ties each fact to the behavior announcing it.

provisions.heading: Name the Idempotency of Every Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use case without an idempotency mode or without the key, scope, or reason its mode needs; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a key with no `{field}` placeholder, a placeholder naming no input field, or a scope outside `tenant`, `account`, `login`, and `global`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its idempotency mode with the key, scope, or reason that mode needs.
provisions.rationale: A retried call without a stated idempotency runs twice: a double payout, a double loan, a double notice. Declaring the mode of `key`, `state`, or `not-pending`, with its key template and scope, states how repeats collapse; `none` carries the reason repeats cannot happen. The `key` templates `{field}` placeholders over the record's `input` field names, and the `scope` is `tenant`, `account`, `login`, or `global`. A reaction key names fields of the triggering event and a job key names fields of its run window instead, which the record does not list, so its placeholders are not checked. The self-checkout scan keys on `{nonce}` scoped to the login.

provisions.heading: Name the Result Each Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a scenario entry without `result`, and `scenario-result-unknown` for a scenario ending in an unknown result.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST name the result it ends in, written or derived.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that names no result illustrates behavior without asserting an ending: it reads well and proves nothing. Naming the result ties each example to the ending it walks toward, so every test knows what to assert. The `scenario-result-unknown` check reports a scenario ending in an unknown result.

provisions.heading: Name the Settings Each Use Case Reads
provisions.evidence: Which use cases read a setting that `reads` does not name? Look at the use cases beside the settings they read.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name the settings it reads in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A setting read by a use case no record names is a coupling readers cannot see: the tunable moves, the reader breaks, and no diff shows the pair. Naming the settings in `reads` beside the use case states the coupling where the reader lives, so each change to the range or default meets its readers. The setting's readers are computed as the inverse, never written. Settled by [decision/0012-use-cases-read-their-settings](decision/0012-use-cases-read-their-settings) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](research/behavior-containment-evidence) and [research/field-naming-evidence](research/field-naming-evidence).
provisions.example: The submit-expense use case names `setting/spending.receipt-threshold` in `reads`, so a move of the threshold meets the submission story.

provisions.heading: Name What a Use Case Acts on from the Model
provisions.evidence: Which use-case names carry no aggregate, declared part, or glossary term after their verb? Look at the words after the verb in each use-case name.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name, after its verb, an aggregate, a declared part, or a glossary term.
provisions.rationale: The noun groups behavior by the business record it changes; a free synonym hides which record that is and breeds a second word for the concept.
provisions.example: `use-case/lending.borrow-copy` names the copy aggregate, and `use-case/sales.add-line` names the declared line part; `use-case/lending.borrow-volume` names no model word and is reported.

provisions.heading: Order Every Refusal List by Precedence
provisions.evidence: Which refusal lists stand out of precedence order, or place a written refusal ahead of a derived one? Look at the refusal entries on each use-case page.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST list its refusals so the first match wins.
provisions.rationale: Two refusals matching one call need an order: without precedence, each architecture layer picks its own refusal, and callers branch on a different code per stack. The derived refusals come first, forbidden then invalid input, followed by the written refusals in the order the page lists them, so the first match is the one every architecture layer reports.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Written Result with a Scenario
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `result-scenario-missing`, level G for a success result and level A for a refusal.
provisions.statement: Each written result MUST be shown by at least one scenario of its use case.
provisions.rationale: A written result no scenario shows is an ending nobody proved: it reads on the page and is asserted in no test, so it drifts from the code with the next change. One scenario per result pins each ending as a checked fact, including the refusals a caller can meet.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares the `already-reimbursed` refusal, and a scenario walks an approved expense claimed twice to that refusal.

provisions.heading: Record Attempts Behind Recorded Refusals
provisions.evidence: Which refusals carrying `recorded: true` store no attempt with its reason? Look at the recorded refusals beside their use-case pages.
provisions.statement: Each refusal carrying `recorded: true` MUST store the attempt with its reason.
provisions.rationale: Some denials are forensics: a loan denial, a limit refusal, a fraud block. Storing the attempt with its reason keeps the evidence the business answers with, while a validating refusal such as a malformed code stores nothing.
provisions.example: The self-checkout scan records unknown, retired, and already-lent barcodes with their reasons, while a malformed scan stores nothing.

provisions.heading: Retire Refusal Codes with Their Replacements
provisions.evidence: Which refusal codes in use were renamed or reused instead of retired with a named replacement? Look at the refusal codes beside their results.
provisions.statement: A refusal code in use MUST be retired with its replacement named, never renamed or reused.
provisions.rationale: The code is a public contract; clients branch on it. Renaming a code in use silently breaks them, and reusing a retired code for another state sends old clients down the new branch. Retiring the code with its replacement named keeps every past refusal readable and every new client on the new code.
provisions.example: The retired `spending.receipt-missing` result names `spending.receipt-absent` as its replacement, and no later refusal reuses the old code.

provisions.heading: Share Scenario Setup in Background
provisions.evidence: Which use cases repeat shared setup across scenarios instead of holding it in `background`? Look at the givens beside each use-case page.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST hold the shared Given of its scenarios in `background`.
provisions.rationale: Every scenario repeating the same setup buries the step that differs: readers reread one Given on each story. Holding the shared Given once in `background` leaves each scenario its own situation, action, and assertion.
provisions.example: `background` holds that the employee has a session and one submitted expense awaits approval, and each approval scenario starts there.

provisions.heading: Start Every Use Case with a Declared Verb
provisions.evidence: Which use-case names open outside the baseline vocabulary and the recorded project verbs? Look at the first word of each use-case name.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST start with a verb from the baseline vocabulary or the domain verbs the project records as conventions.
provisions.rationale: One verb per meaning keeps use cases findable: `read` versus `get` and `change` versus `update` stop competing when every project starts from one closed baseline vocabulary and adds only its domain verbs. A shared first word groups related behavior in every listing, and a retired synonym points at its replacement instead of spreading silently. When the act verb is in neither list, the author first records it as a convention in the same change, and then scaffolds the use case. `litespec new` scaffolds a use-case page without checking its verb, so the convention lands before the scaffold rather than after a refusal from the scaffold command. A project never redefines a baseline verb. No tool checks the verb: a reviewer checks that a use-case name starts with a baseline verb or a recorded project verb, and that a retired synonym is replaced.
provisions.example: The project records `borrow` and `check-in` as domain verbs, so `use-case/lending.borrow-copy` and `use-case/lending.check-in-copy` pass, `use-case/lending.list-loans` passes on the baseline vocabulary, and `use-case/lending.update-copy` is told to use `change`.

provisions.heading: State the Audit Position of Every Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a command without an audit level and target or an exemption with its justification.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST declare its audit level and target, or its exemption with its justification.
provisions.rationale: An unaudited change with no exemption is a gap nobody admitted: money moves, holds lapse, and no record says who asked. Declaring the level of `required`, `optional`, or `none` with its target, or the exemption with its justification, states the audit beside the change. A level of `none` is not audited; async work audits at request time.

provisions.heading: State the Consistency of Every Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `consistency-cites-missing` for an atomic multi-aggregate write with no `cites`, `atomic-group-drift` for `changes` differing from the bound group, `atomic-group-invalid` (level A) for a group above 4 aggregates, and `atomic-group-duplicate` (level A) for a command saving more than one atomic write group.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its write consistency in `consistency`.
provisions.rationale: Consistency left unsaid defaults to hope: a multi-aggregate write is read as atomic until it fails halfway. Declaring the mode states the promise: `atomic` commits every write in `changes` as one group, `per-record` commits each write on its own, and `compensated` names the undo of each write. An atomic write across aggregates cites its `atomicity` rule in `cites`, and `changes` holds exactly the aggregates the rule binds; a group above 4 aggregates is reported. Atomic consistency never spans an `async` edge. The [Domain Model page](domain-model.md) states the `atomicity` rule. The `consistency-cites-missing` check reports an atomic multi-aggregate write with no `cites`, `atomic-group-drift` reports `changes` differing from the bound group, and `atomic-group-invalid` reports a group above 4 aggregates.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares atomic consistency citing the reimbursed-once rule, while the self-checkout scan declares per-record consistency across its attempts.

provisions.heading: State the Transaction Sharing of Every Inline Call
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an inline `runs` effect without `sharesTransaction`.
provisions.statement: Each inline `runs` effect MUST state whether it shares the caller transaction in `sharesTransaction`.
provisions.rationale: An inline call without a stated transaction is a coin toss at failure: the caller rolls back while the issued work stands, or the reverse. Stating whether the call shares the caller transaction makes the failure shape reviewable beside the edge.

provisions.heading: State the Unit of Every Quantity Setting
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unit-missing` (level A) for a numeric or duration setting declaring no `unit`.
provisions.statement: Each setting whose value is a number or a duration MUST declare its `unit`.
provisions.rationale: A number without a unit is a guess: minutes read as seconds, a count reads as money. Declaring the unit states the measure beside the value.
provisions.example: The retry backoff declares `unit: seconds`; a timeout with `valueType: duration` and no unit is reported.

provisions.heading: Write Every Scenario in Given When Then
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a scenario entry without `given`, `when`, or `then`.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST state its `given`, `when`, and `then`.
provisions.rationale: The three steps separate the situation from the action and the action from the assertion: collapsing them blurs what was true, what moved, and what the test checks. Stating all three keeps each example readable by a person and provable by a test.
provisions.example:
```json
{
  "type": "scenario",
  "id": "scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds",
  "title": "Submitting with a receipt succeeds",
  "given": "An employee paid for a train ticket and kept the receipt.",
  "when": "The employee submits the expense with the receipt.",
  "then": "The expense is submitted.",
  "result": "result/submit-expense.submitted"
}
```

provisions.heading: Write Prose on Every Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `prose-missing` for a use case without `summary`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST carry `summary`.
provisions.rationale: A use case states what it is in one paragraph, so a reader landing cold learns the act before its fields. The steps live under What Happens in the explanation file beside a command, where they stay readable without a shape a check must parse.
provisions.example: The submit-expense summary states that an employee files a work expense for approval, and its What Happens section walks validation, storage, and the approver notice in order.

provisions.heading: Apply Plain Mechanics
provisions.evidence: Which pages use British spelling, drop the serial comma, spell out a measured quantity, shorten a prose date, or carry a contraction inside a record? Look at the prose the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every page MUST use American spelling, the serial comma, numerals for numbers of 10 and above and for every quantity with a unit, ISO dates in fields and long-form dates in prose, straight quotes, and ASCII characters only.
provisions.rationale: One mechanical form per fact keeps every search, diff and listing exact: `license` in one page and `licence` in another split every lookup, and a curly quote or a typographic dash renders differently in terminals, generated context and plain-text tools. Numerals for measured quantities keep a count scannable beside its unit, while small counts in prose stay words a reader absorbs without stopping. An ISO date in a field sorts and checks as data; the same date in prose reads "2 November 2026", in the order a person says it. Contractions belong on documentation pages, where the voice is a person explaining; records hold none, because a record states a fact in its shortest checkable form. ASCII prose follows `litespec/core/authoring#keep-authored-prose-ascii-safe`.
provisions.example: Claimwick prose writes "The tenant keeps receipts for 7 years, files them by month, quarter, and year, and closes the period on 2 November 2026." The field beside it holds `2026-11-02`.

provisions.heading: Comment on Why, Not What
provisions.evidence: Which comments restate the code, hold commented-out code, or recount how the code arrived? Look at the comments and API summaries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every code comment and API summary MUST state why the code is as it is or what the code cannot express, with no commented-out code and no history.
provisions.rationale: The code already states what it does, so a comment that restates it adds words a maintainer must keep true without adding knowledge. The reason a boundary exists, the constraint a caller must respect, or the failure a member reports is what the next reader cannot recover from the code alone. History belongs in the commit that made the change, where a reader looking for it finds it; commented-out code is history with no commit to explain it. An API summary states the contract first: what the member does, what it needs, what it returns, and which failures belong to the contract, in the form the stack's pages state.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler comment states why the approval check runs before the payout call. It names no step the code below it already shows, and holds no earlier version of the call.

provisions.heading: Compare Real Options in Each Decision Record
provisions.evidence: Which decision records name no real alternative, compare options on different points, recount the discussion, or omit what would reopen the choice? Look at the decision records the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every decision record MUST compare its real options on their merits in Context and Options Considered, then state the chosen outcome and what would reopen it.
provisions.rationale: A decision record exists for a reader who was not there when the choice was made, and that reader needs the forces, the alternatives and the consequences, not the discussion that produced them. Options compared on the same points let a later reader rejudge the choice when the world moves; a record that names only the winner forces the whole argument to run again. What would reopen the choice belongs in the record beside the choice, so a stable decision stays stable until the named condition holds. Any option singled out from the decision carries its own sentence saying why it stands apart.
provisions.example: A Claimwick decision compares a receipt threshold of EUR 25 with EUR 50 on refusal rate and approver load, chooses EUR 25, and names a refusal rate above the stated bound as what would reopen it.

provisions.heading: Give Each Explanation File Its Fixed Sections
provisions.evidence: Which explanation files miss a fixed section, reorder the list, or open without their H1 title? Look at the explanation files beside the records the change adds, beside the explanation-section table.
provisions.statement: Every explanation file MUST use the fixed sections of its record type, in the order the explanation-section table gives, with the record title as its one H1.
provisions.rationale: A fixed section list answers the same questions on every record of one type, so a reader who learned one problem page reads the next without relearning where the evidence sits. Each list answers what a cold reader needs: who has the need, why it matters, what good looks like, and what the record connects to. A problem earns four sections because its reader judges a pain: who has it, what they do today, the evidence for it, and what would retire it. Free sections may follow the fixed ones; they never replace one.
provisions.example: The Claimwick problem explanation for waiting expenses runs Who Has It, What They Do Today, Evidence, What Would Retire It. The evidence stands in its own section instead of inside a pointer to another page.

provisions.heading: Give Each Paragraph One Idea
provisions.evidence: Which paragraphs carry two ideas, wrap across hard line breaks, or list items that are not parallel? Look at the explanation files and documents the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every paragraph in an explanation file or document MUST carry one idea, on one line in Markdown, with a list only where the items are truly parallel.
provisions.rationale: A paragraph that holds a rule, an exception and a fallback in one block forces the reader hunting for one of them to untangle all three. One idea per paragraph puts each fact where a scanning reader finds it, and one line per paragraph keeps diffs readable, so a changed sentence shows as one changed line. A list drawn from prose that is not parallel hides the reasoning that connects its items; connected reasoning stays in prose, and only parallel items become a list.
provisions.example: The Claimwick decision explanation gives What Would Reopen It its own paragraph. A reader looking for what would reopen the choice finds that paragraph without reading the example above it.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Record Sentence Within Twenty-Five Words
provisions.evidence: Which record statements or summaries carry a sentence past 25 words? Look at the statements and summaries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every sentence in a record `statement` or `summary` MUST hold at most 25 words.
provisions.rationale: A record sentence carries one fact a builder implements, and a sentence past 25 words usually carries two facts joined by a comma, so the reader weighs both at once or misses the second. Twenty-five words is the longest sentence a reader parses once, and the bound is mechanical, so a check counts it the same way on every record. A longer explanation belongs in the explanation file, split into sentences that each carry one fact.
provisions.example: "Employees wait three weeks for reimbursement while approvers batch decisions monthly." The sentence holds 11 words and one fact.

provisions.heading: Open Each Summary with Who and What Is at Stake
provisions.evidence: Which summaries open with a pointer, a field name or background instead of who and what is at stake? Look at the first sentence of each one the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every `summary` MUST restate who it concerns and what is at stake in its first sentence, with any pointer to another page after that content.
provisions.rationale: This field is the lead a cold reader meets in the book, before any field table or link. A first sentence that restates who and what is at stake lets that reader judge the record without opening its links; a bare pointer such as "described on the launch page" gives them nothing to judge and breaks the moment the pointed page moves. A pointer that follows the content helps the reader who wants more; a pointer that replaces the content helps no one.
provisions.example: A Claimwick problem `summary` opens "Employees wait three weeks for reimbursement while approvers batch decisions monthly." Who waits and what it costs stand in the first sentence, and any link follows after it.

provisions.heading: Put the Actor First
provisions.evidence: Which sentences open with a thing instead of an actor, use the passive voice, or promise in the future tense? Look at the statements and summaries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every sentence in a record MUST name its actor as its subject, in the active voice and the present tense.
provisions.rationale: A sentence that opens with its actor states who does what before the reader reaches the verb, and the present tense states what holds today rather than what a plan intends. Passive and future forms hide the actor or promise a behavior no record states. Second person belongs only on tutorial and how-to pages, where the reader is the actor; records stay in the third person, as the text-kind table on the [Record Language](language.md) page states.
provisions.example: Claimwick writes "Finance reimburses the due expense." The actor Finance opens the sentence, and the present tense states what holds.

provisions.heading: State Each Statement Without Modal Words
provisions.evidence: Which record statements carry a modal word or a second sentence? Look at the statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record `statement` MUST hold one sentence in the present tense with no modal word.
provisions.rationale: A statement states what holds, as a fact a builder implements. A modal word such as must, should, shall, may, can or will turns the fact into an intention, a permission or a promise, and each reader grades its strength differently. One sentence keeps one commitment per statement, so a change to one commitment changes one statement. The value style on the [Record Language](language.md) page states the same form; this provision states the prose reason and the check covers every record type.
provisions.example: Claimwick states "An expense above the threshold carries a receipt." The sentence states what holds, with no modal word grading it.

provisions.heading: Use Literal Words
provisions.evidence: Which titles or sentences use a metaphor, a stock phrase or an undefined term where a literal phrase exists? Look at the titles and first uses the change adds, beside the glossary.
provisions.statement: Every title and sentence MUST use the literal word for what it names, with each term defined on first use or linked to the glossary.
provisions.rationale: A metaphor reads smoothly while hiding what the project means: each reader pictures a different act behind the same flourish, and a metaphor title hides its subject in every list that shows it. A literal phrase names the act itself, so no reader has to decode it. Each concept keeps its one glossary term, as `litespec/core/authoring#use-one-term-for-one-concept` states; this page adds only that a term a cold reader may not know is defined where it first appears or linked to its glossary entry.
provisions.example: A Claimwick problem is titled "Expenses Wait Weeks for Reimbursement". The title names the wait and the delay literally, with no figure of speech to decode.

provisions.heading: Write Each Changelog as a Release Comparison
provisions.evidence: Which entries inventory files or work, bury their condition or action, or describe a former behavior outside the changelog? Look at the entries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every changelog entry MUST state the present behavior, who it affects and what the reader does, comparing with the previous release only inside the changelog.
provisions.rationale: A changelog serves a reader deciding whether to upgrade and a reader checking what changed after upgrading, and both need the observable change, its condition and the required action, never an inventory of the work. Stating the present state first lets every other page describe what is true today without carrying a former behavior; the changelog is the one place where the comparison with the previous release belongs. A breaking change, a removal and a security fix each state what stops working, who is affected, and the replacement or action, in the entry itself rather than behind a link.
provisions.example: A Claimwick changelog entry states "Submitting an expense without a receipt above the threshold is refused. Employees attach the receipt before submitting." The behavior, the reader and the action stand in the entry.

provisions.heading: Write Each Documentation Page as One Kind
provisions.evidence: Which pages mix two jobs, open with background instead of their kind's opening, or state no reader and purpose in their first lines? Look at the opening lines of each documentation page the change adds, beside the documentation-kind table.
provisions.statement: Every documentation page MUST do one of the four documentation jobs, open as that kind opens, and state its reader and its purpose in its first lines.
provisions.rationale: A tutorial that stops to explain a trade-off loses the reader mid-path, and a reference page that teaches leaves the reader hunting for the value they came to look up. One job per page puts each fact where its reader looks for it, and the opening tells a reader from a search result within two sentences whether this page answers their question. A README earns its first screen the same way: what the folder holds, who reads it, and where each reader goes next, before any file list. The page styles and their sections live in the [Authoring Standard](authoring.md); this provision states the prose each kind opens with.
provisions.example: A Claimwick how-to page opens "Remind an approver who has held an expense past three business days." The reader and the one problem solved stand before the first step.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record Title in Title Case
provisions.evidence: Which record titles fall outside Title Case, end in a period, or run past eight words? Look at the titles the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record title MUST use Title Case, carry no final period, and hold at most eight words.
provisions.rationale: A title is the record's name in book lists, outlines, tabs and search results, so it reads as a name, never as a sentence: Title Case capitalizes every major word and lowercases a, an, the, and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet, as, at, by, in, of, off, on, per, to, up, via, with, from, into, over and than unless the word stands first or last. One casing rule for every title is the only casing rule a check enforces the same way everywhere; mixed casing makes two records of one kind read as two kinds. Eight words keeps the whole title on one scannable line in a list while leaving room for the longest form, a problem clause naming who and the pain. LiteSpec headings follow the same casing under `litespec/core/authoring#use-controlled-capitalization`.
provisions.example: The Claimwick requirement title reads "Expense Above Threshold Carries Receipt", five words in Title Case with no final period.

provisions.heading: Write for the Reader Who Arrives Cold
provisions.evidence: Which records, sections and pages open with a pointer, a code or a field name instead of who and what is at stake? Look at the first sentence of each page the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record, explanation section and documentation page MUST open by naming who it concerns and what is at stake, before any pointer to another page.
provisions.rationale: Most readers land on one page from a list, a search result or a link, with nothing read before it. A page that opens with its subject and its stake answers that reader on its own; a page that opens with a pointer sends the reader elsewhere before it has given them anything. The tone throughout is a product explaining itself plainly: plain words, checkable facts and honest roles, with no selling and no decoration.
provisions.example: A Claimwick problem opens "Employees wait three weeks for reimbursement while approvers batch decisions monthly." A reader who has opened no other page knows who waits and what it costs them.

provisions.heading: Assert Structure and Never Wording
provisions.evidence: Which mediated query scenarios assert exact words instead of fields, codes, and cited sources? Look at the scenario assertions.
provisions.statement: A scenario for a model-mediated query MUST assert the output structure and never its wording.
provisions.rationale: Model wording shifts between runs: the same facts arrive in different sentences. A scenario asserting exact words fails on a paraphrase, while a scenario asserting structure, fields, codes, and cited sources passes on every true answer.
provisions.example: The scenario asserts the answer carries `orderId` and one cited source, not the sentence around them.

provisions.heading: Bound Tool Calls per Query
provisions.evidence: Which mediated queries state no per-run tool-call bound, or exceed it in the run tests? Look at the query definitions beside the run tests.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST bound how many tool calls one run makes.
provisions.rationale: A model in a loop calls tools until the budget or the patience runs out. A bound on calls per run caps the cost and the latency up front, so one curious run cannot spend the month's budget.
provisions.example: The support answer query allows eight tool calls per run and refuses the ninth.

provisions.heading: Name the Closed Tool Set
provisions.evidence: Which mediated queries call a tool outside their closed tool set? Look at each query's tool set beside the tool calls its tests record.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST name the closed set of tools the model calls.
provisions.rationale: A model with an open tool set invents tools, reaches past its grant, and surprises every review. A closed set names exactly what the model touches, so the grant, the tests, and the audit all read the same list.
provisions.example: The support answer query names `orders.lookup` and `docs.search` as its only tools.

provisions.heading: Pin a Deterministic Stub in Proof
provisions.evidence: Which mediated query tests call a live model instead of the pinned stub version? Look at the test configuration beside the stub version.
provisions.statement: Proof for a model-mediated query MUST run against a deterministic stub pinned by version.
provisions.rationale: A live model answers differently each run, so a test against it proves nothing twice. A deterministic stub pinned by version answers the same way every run, so Proof checks the product's handling instead of the model's mood.
provisions.example: The support answer tests run against `stub-answers v4`, which returns one fixed tool trace per prompt.

provisions.heading: Record Every Model Run
provisions.evidence: Which run log entries lack a prompt hash, the tools called, or an outcome, with no other evidence named in the AI documentation? Look at the run log.
provisions.statement: Each model run writes its prompt hash, the tools called, and the outcome to the run log.
provisions.rationale: Production answers need after-the-fact review: what was asked, what the model touched, and what came back. The run log holds the three without storing full prompts.

provisions.heading: Record Provenance in the Output
provisions.evidence: Which mediated query answers lack the model, the tools called, or the sources read? Look at the provenance on each answer.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST return provenance naming the model, the tools called, and the sources read.
provisions.rationale: An answer without provenance cannot be checked: nobody knows which model wrote it, which tools fed it, or which sources back it. Provenance names the three, so every answer carries its own audit trail.
provisions.example: The answer returns `model: support-7, tools: [orders.lookup], sources: [order-8841]`.

provisions.heading: Refuse Unknown Tools
provisions.evidence: Which mediated query tests allow a run to call a tool outside the closed set? Look at the refused-run tests.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST refuse a run that calls a tool outside its closed set.
provisions.rationale: Models drift: a prompt tweak or a version change can add a call nobody declared. Refusing the run at the first unknown tool keeps the closed set closed in production, not just on paper.
provisions.example: A run that calls `billing.refund` outside its set is refused before the call leaves the product.

provisions.heading: Add a Correcting Record
provisions.evidence: Which corrections edit history instead of adding a referencing record? Look at the correction records.
provisions.statement: A correction to the trail MUST be a new record that references the earlier one.
provisions.rationale: An edited history carries no evidential value, because the reviewer cannot tell a correction from a cover-up. A new record that references the earlier one keeps both visible: the mistake and its fix. The trail then shows its own repairs instead of hiding them.

provisions.heading: Anchor the Audit Chain Outside Its Own Store
provisions.evidence: Which stores publish no checkpoint outside operator reach? Look at the checkpoint destination and the threat model.
provisions.statement: An audit store SHOULD publish a periodic checkpoint of its chain head to a destination that the store's own operators cannot rewrite.
provisions.rationale: A chain proves that records agree with each other, but anyone holding the store can recompute the whole chain and keep it agreeing. A checkpoint held somewhere the operators cannot rewrite fixes the chain as it stood at that moment. A later recomputation disagrees with the checkpoint, which exposes it.
provisions.example: The checkpoint is the chain head and its record count, published at a stated interval. A separate append-only destination, a timestamping authority, and a transparency log each qualify.

provisions.heading: Audit Async Work at Request Time
provisions.evidence: Which deferred runs write their audit record at run time instead of request time? Look at the audit rows beside the requesting calls.
provisions.statement: Work that runs after its request MUST write its audit record at request time.
provisions.rationale: The actor, the origin, and the grant exist when the request arrives; the later run carries worker identity under system auth, which says nothing about who asked. Writing the record at request time ties the attempt to the caller who made it. A record written when the background run starts would attribute every scheduled and deferred act to the worker instead of the requester.

provisions.heading: Audit Reads of the Trail
provisions.evidence: Which completed trail reads produced no audit record? Look at the trail read path.
provisions.statement: A read of the audit trail MUST itself produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Reading the evidence is itself a sensitive action: the trail shows who did what across the whole product. A read that writes no record leaves the reviewer outside the trail. Recording each read puts the reviewer inside the same accountability as everyone else.

provisions.heading: Commit a Success Record with Its Business Change
provisions.evidence: Which succeeded records commit outside their business transaction? Look at the success write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `succeeded` outcome MUST commit in the same database transaction as the change it describes.
provisions.rationale: One transaction makes the action and its evidence inseparable: the change commits with its record or neither commits. Separate writes admit both an unrecorded action and a record of a rolled-back action. Either one leaves the trail disagreeing with the data it describes.

provisions.heading: Cover the Required Audit Categories
provisions.evidence: Which required categories have no selection entry? Look at the declared selection beside the eight listed categories.
provisions.statement: An audit selection MUST include authentication, authorization denial, grant change, monetary action, tenant configuration, personal-data read, bulk export, and background-process change.
provisions.rationale: Each listed category answers a question a security review, a customer, or a supervisory authority asks after an incident: who signed in, who was refused, who changed a grant, who moved money, and the rest. A trail that omits a category has no answer when that question arrives. The list fixes the floor so no project discovers the gap during its first review.

provisions.heading: Declare Audit Selection Beside the Command
provisions.evidence: Which Commands lack the declaration attribute with its action, target kind, category, and reason selector, or the recorded local convention? Look at the Command types.
provisions.statement: Declare the action, target kind, category, and reason selector as an attribute on the Command type, beside the use-case `audit` field.
provisions.rationale: The declaration stays with the code it describes, so a review reads both at once. The use-case page carries the audit position or exemption, and the attribute carries the action, target kind, and category the producer writes. The reason selector names the message field that carries the reason value, so the pipeline reads the declared reason without handler help. A selection kept in a separate file drifts from the Commands it names.

provisions.heading: Declare Audit Selection on Every Command
provisions.evidence: Which command use cases lack an audit position or an exemption with its justification in their `audit` field? Look at the use case pages.
provisions.statement: Every command use case MUST declare its audit position in its `audit` field, or declare an exemption with its justification.
provisions.rationale: An audit selection that lives only in code is invisible: a reader cannot tell an unaudited command from an audited one whose call is missing. The `audit` field states a level of `required`, `optional`, or `none` with its target, or an exemption with its justification, so each omission becomes a visible statement. A level of `none` means the command is not audited. `litespec/core/use-cases#state-the-audit-position-of-every-command` states the field, and review reads the selection instead of hunting for missing calls.
provisions.example: A storefront browse command declares an exemption because a public catalog read is not a sensitive action.

provisions.heading: Emit Audit Records at the Mediation Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which audit writes run inside handlers instead of the mediation pipeline? Look at the producer stages and the handler code.
provisions.statement: An audit producer MUST run in the mediation pipeline stages that dispatch the Command.
provisions.rationale: Only the pipeline stages that dispatch the Command observe the whole attempt, including attempts the handler never reaches. An audit call inside the handler misses every attempt that throws before it and every refusal the pipeline makes. The pipeline is therefore the one place that records all three outcomes.
provisions.example: A pre-handler opens the audit scope, a post-handler closes it as `succeeded`, and an error handler closes it as `denied` or `failed`.

provisions.heading: Enforce Append-Only Through Storage Privilege
provisions.evidence: Which writing accounts hold update or delete on the audit store? Look at the granted store privileges.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST refuse update and delete through the privileges granted to the writing account.
provisions.rationale: An audit store that relies on absent code paths stays append-only until someone writes the missing path. Revoked privileges refuse update and delete no matter what the code attempts. A reviewer verifies a privilege in the database instead of auditing every line for a missing write.
provisions.example: The application account holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the audit table. It holds neither `UPDATE` nor `DELETE`.

provisions.heading: Exclude Derived Audit Trails
provisions.evidence: Which trail writes derive from events, triggers, or capture? Look at the producer source.
provisions.statement: An audit trail MUST NOT be derived from domain events, database triggers, or change data capture.
provisions.rationale: Domain events, triggers, and change data capture describe committed state change. They carry no refused attempt, no use-case identity, and no request origin, which are the fields a reviewer reads. A trail derived from them answers what changed and never who attempted it.

provisions.heading: Exclude Indiscriminate Auditing
provisions.evidence: Which audited categories lack a recorded selection reason? Look at the declared selection.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT audit every Command without a recorded selection.
provisions.rationale: A trail that records every Command buries the sensitive action inside routine traffic, and the reviewer who has to read it stops reading. Volume then defeats the review the trail exists to support. A recorded selection keeps the trail small enough to read.

provisions.heading: Exclude Personal Data Beyond Actor Identity
provisions.evidence: Which records contain personal data beyond pseudonymous actor and target identifiers? Look at the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain personal data other than the pseudonymous identifier of the actor and the target.
provisions.rationale: A record holding a name, an address, or a message body turns retention into an erasure conflict: the law asks for deletion and the trail asks for keeping. Pseudonymous identifiers keep the record meaningful while the mapping lives, and erasable once the mapping goes. The record then survives erasure instead of fighting it. A pseudonymous identifier is still personal data where the party holding it can reverse it. That is the position [the EDPB states](https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-012020-processing-personal-data-context-art-6-1). The identifier is therefore safe inside the tenant that owns the mapping. It is a disclosure when it leaves that tenant.
provisions.example: An audit export crossing a tenant boundary replaces each identifier with one derived for that export. The receiving party then cannot join the records back to a subject.

provisions.heading: Exclude Secrets and Payment Data
provisions.evidence: Which records contain a secret or a payment instrument value? Look at the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a secret, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, or a payment instrument value.
provisions.rationale: The trail is retained, widely readable, and append-only, which is the worst combination for a secret: retention extends the exposure and append-only removes the repair. A credential or payment value written once stays readable for the whole retention period. Secrets and payment values therefore travel in the systems built to hold them, never in the trail.

provisions.heading: Exclude State Snapshots
provisions.evidence: Which records contain before or after state copies? Look at the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a copy of the state before or after the audited change.
provisions.rationale: The domain event stream already holds each change under its own retention. Copying before and after state into the trail duplicates that storage and widens every record with data the reviewer did not ask for. The trail adds the actor and the reason value, which nothing else holds, and leaves the change itself to the stream.

provisions.heading: Give the Trail a Read Path
provisions.evidence: Which trail reads lack an access grant or a declared filter? Look at the trail read use case.
provisions.statement: An audited system MUST provide a trail read as a use case with its access grant, filtered by tenant, actor, action, target, and outcome.
provisions.rationale: A trail no use case reads is storage, not a control. The read path is a use case with its own access grant: the actor holds a role at a role scope, the role allows the permission, and the grant permits the read. Tenant, actor, action, target, and outcome filters keep each reader inside the records they may see.

provisions.heading: Keep Audit Infrastructure in One Location
provisions.evidence: Which audit parts live outside the documented location or the recorded local convention? Look under `Infrastructure/Auditing/`.
provisions.statement: Keep the audit record, its store, the producer, and the integrity job under `Infrastructure/Auditing/`.
provisions.rationale: The record, the store, the producer, and the integrity job form one evidence mechanism. One Infrastructure location keeps that mechanism reviewable as a whole instead of scattered across the codebase.

provisions.heading: Provide Tamper Evidence
provisions.evidence: Which records lack the chained SHA-256 hash over the canonical serialization? Look at the stored chain values.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST chain each record to its predecessor with a SHA-256 hash over a canonical serialization of both.
provisions.rationale: The hash chain detects an edit and a removal, because a changed or missing record breaks every value after it. Detection is the obligation: it lets a reviewer prove the trail is intact. Prevention at a higher cost is not required. The algorithm is named because two implementations that each choose their own cannot verify each other. A verifier written later cannot recompute a chain whose algorithm no one recorded. Canonical serialization is named for the same reason. A hash over a serialization that reorders fields verifies nothing.
provisions.example: The chain value is `SHA-256(previousHash || canonical(record))`, where `canonical` sorts object members and uses one fixed encoding for every timestamp and number.

provisions.heading: Publish a Copy to the Security Platform
provisions.evidence: Which published copies leave the local store non-authoritative, or bypass the recorded local convention? Look at the delivery path.
provisions.statement: Publish a copy of each record to an external security platform through the outbox, and keep the local store authoritative.
provisions.rationale: Delivery is at-least-once, while evidence needs one durable source. The local store stays authoritative for accountability and the published copy serves detection, so a lost copy never corrupts the evidence.

provisions.heading: Publish Unsuccessful Write Failures
provisions.evidence: Which deployments publish no write failure count for the unsuccessful path? Look at the published metrics.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST publish the write failure count of its unsuccessful-outcome path.
provisions.rationale: The separate connection for unsuccessful records accepts a rare lost record when the process dies between the refusal and the write. Continuous loss is a defect, not bad luck, and only a published count separates the two. The deployment publishes that count so monitoring tells rarity from breakage.

provisions.heading: Record a Bulk Read Inside Its Own Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which above-threshold queries produced no record with the subject count? Look at the bulk query paths.
provisions.statement: A query returning personal data for more subjects than its declared threshold MUST produce an audit record, inside one tenant or account boundary as well.
provisions.rationale: The cross-boundary rule catches a disclosure to the wrong party, but it misses an export of every record a party may read one at a time, which is the shape a copied dataset has. A query above the declared threshold therefore writes a record even inside one boundary. [Article 30 of the GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/) asks what categories of data were processed and by whom, and an unrecorded bulk read answers neither.
provisions.example: A project records the threshold in the adoption decision. A list endpoint whose page size can exceed it audits the read with the subject count rather than the subjects.

provisions.heading: Record Bulk Export
provisions.evidence: Which exports produced no record naming the requested scope? Look at the export paths.
provisions.statement: An export that returns a set of records to a caller MUST produce an audit record naming the requested scope.
provisions.rationale: Bulk extraction is the highest-consequence read in most products: one call moves a dataset across the boundary. Naming the requested scope states what left the system. Without it, the project learns the shape of a leak from the party that received it.

provisions.heading: Record Delegated Administrative Access
provisions.evidence: Which support-grant actions lack the grant marker? Look at the records of actions under administrative grants.
provisions.statement: An action that an actor takes under an administrative or support grant MUST record that the grant was used.
provisions.rationale: Support staff act inside customer data under a grant, and without a marker their actions read exactly like customer actions. The marker makes a no-silent-access commitment demonstrable: every supplier-side action says so on its own record. A reviewer who cannot separate the two cannot verify the commitment.

provisions.heading: Record Every Attempt Outcome
provisions.evidence: Which records lack a succeeded, denied, or failed outcome? Look at the outcome column.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an outcome of `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed`.
provisions.rationale: A trail of successes is a change history, not evidence. The refused attempt carries the security signal, and the failed attempt carries the operating signal. Three outcomes keep both signals in the same trail as the successes they qualify.
provisions.example: `succeeded` names a committed change, `denied` names a refused authorization, and `failed` names a permitted attempt that did not complete.

provisions.heading: Record Failed Audited Attempts
provisions.evidence: Which permitted attempts that threw produced no failed record? Look at the error paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An audited action that the actor was permitted to take and that did not complete MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: A permitted attempt that throws is neither a success nor a refusal, and without a record it vanishes entirely. Writing it separates an operating defect from an access problem: failures cluster around broken behavior, denials cluster around missing permission. Support reads that split before it reads the logs.

provisions.heading: Record Personal-Data Reads
provisions.evidence: Which cross-boundary personal-data queries produced no record? Look at the query paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: A query returning personal data across a boundary MUST produce an audit record, defining the account boundary in the adoption decision where tenancy is absent.
provisions.rationale: A read changes no state and therefore leaves no other trace, so a disclosure without a record cannot be investigated. The audit record on a cross-boundary personal-data query states who read whose data and when. Where tenancy is absent, the adoption decision defines the account boundary the rule watches.

provisions.heading: Record Refused Authorization
provisions.evidence: Which refused authorizations produced no denied record? Look at the refusal paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An authorization decision that refuses an audited action MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Repeated refusal is the first indicator of a compromised or probing account, and no other record holds it: nothing changed, so nothing else was written. Each refusal therefore writes its own record. A trail without refusals shows an attacker who never failed.

provisions.heading: Record the Audit Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Which adoption decisions lack categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, or records entry? Look at the adoption decision behind the audited Commands.
provisions.statement: An audit adoption decision MUST record its audited categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry.
provisions.rationale: Which actions to audit, how long to keep them, and how to protect them are policy choices, so the project declares them once in the adoption decision. A reviewer reads the declared policy before reading the implementation instead of reconstructing it from the code, which would give two reviewers two different policies.

provisions.heading: Record the Operation Trace Identity
provisions.evidence: Which records lack the trace identifier of their operation? Look at the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry the trace identifier of the operation that produced it.
provisions.rationale: The audit record states what was attempted, and the diagnostic log states what the software did while attempting it. The trace identifier joins the two, so an investigation moves from evidence to detail in one step. Without it, the investigation stops at the audit record and reconstructs the rest by time.

provisions.heading: Record the Refusal Code on an Unsuccessful Attempt
provisions.evidence: Which denied or failed records lack the refusal code? Look at the unsuccessful audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST carry the refusal `code` that the attempt produced.
provisions.rationale: A refused permission and an exhausted precondition need different responses, but both look like failure without a code. The refusal `code` tells the reviewer which one the attempt produced. It also lets trend queries count one kind of refusal across the whole trail.

provisions.heading: Record the Request Origin
provisions.evidence: Which request-produced records lack origin, client, or request identifier? Look at the inbound-request audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record produced from an inbound request MUST carry the request origin address, the client description, and the request identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two records naming one account state nothing about location. The same account acting from two countries within one minute states that the account is compromised, but only when each record carries origin, client, and request identifier. The request identifier further joins the record to the exact request in the diagnostic log.

provisions.heading: Record the Required Audit Fields
provisions.evidence: Which records lack actor, action, target, outcome, business time, record time, or tenant? Look at the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST contain actor, action, target, outcome, business time, record time, and tenant, fixed where the tenancy extension is absent.
provisions.rationale: Actor, action, target, outcome, the two times, and the tenant together answer who attempted what, against whose data, with what result, and when. Business time states when the action happened and record time states when the evidence was written, so a delayed write stays visible as a delay. A record missing any of them leaves the accountability question half answered.

provisions.heading: Reject an Undeclared Command
provisions.evidence: Which Commands build or start with no audit position or exemption? Look at the build or startup gate.
provisions.statement: An automated check MUST fail when a Command declares neither an audit position nor an exemption, with a composition refusal at startup satisfying this rule.
provisions.rationale: The next Command is written by someone who did not read this page. Only an automated gate catches it: the build or startup fails while the declaration is missing. A selection that depends on every author remembering is a selection with holes.

provisions.heading: Remove the Identity Mapping on Erasure
provisions.evidence: Which erasures leave the actor mapping or delete audit records? Look at the erasure handling and the retained rows.
provisions.statement: An erasure request MUST remove the mapping from actor identifier to person and retain every audit record.
provisions.rationale: Erasure asks that the person stop being identifiable, while accountability asks that the record stay. Removing the mapping from identifier to person satisfies both: the record keeps its evidential value and no longer points at anyone. This works only because the record holds no other personal data.

provisions.heading: Restrict Handler Contribution to Determined Values
provisions.evidence: Which handler contributions repeat the declared target or reason value, the actor, action code, or timestamp? Look at the handler audit calls.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST contribute only the audit values that the handler alone determines.
provisions.rationale: The declaration beside the message already fixes the audit target and the reason value the message carries, as `litespec/backend/application#declare-audit-values-beside-the-message` requires, so the pipeline records both on every outcome, including a denial. Only the handler knows the values it learns while running, such as a generated target identity or a reason value composed from loaded state. Letting the handler write the rest invites a second copy of each field that drifts from the first.
provisions.example: A create handler contributes the identity it generated. It contributes no actor, action code, timestamp, or value the message already carries.

provisions.heading: Retain Each Category for Its Declared Period
provisions.evidence: Which records outlive the declared retention of their category? Look at the stored rows beside the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST delete a record after the retention period declared for its category.
provisions.rationale: Each category declares its retention in the adoption decision, and the deployment deletes records when that period ends. Deletion on schedule keeps retention defensible: kept data has a declared reason and nothing kept lacks one. An indefinite period is the hardest retention to defend and the easiest to correct at design time.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Record to Its Tenant
provisions.evidence: Which records on tenant-owned data lack the tenant identity? Look at the tenant column.
provisions.statement: An audit record describing an action inside tenant-owned data MUST carry the identity of that tenant.
provisions.rationale: The tenant is the filter for every read of the trail: each customer reads its own records and no one else's. A record without a tenant identity serves an internal reviewer and no customer. Scoping every record at write time keeps that filter exact.

provisions.heading: Stage the Audit Write Before the Business Commit
provisions.evidence: Which audit stages run after the business commit stage? Look at the pipeline stage order.
provisions.statement: An audit producer that stages a success record MUST run before the pipeline stage that commits the business transaction.
provisions.rationale: A success record staged after the commit reaches a transaction that is already closed, so the write has nowhere to land. The producer therefore runs before the pipeline stage that commits. Pipeline priority states that order explicitly instead of leaving it to registration order.

provisions.heading: State the Action as Use-Case Identity
provisions.evidence: Which action values name something other than the invoked use case? Look at the action column beside the use case pages.
provisions.statement: An audit `action` MUST use the identity of the use case that the actor invoked.
provisions.rationale: A reviewer who reads an action value opens the specification of that use case to learn the intended behavior. A separate action vocabulary needs a mapping to those specifications, and the mapping drifts as both sides change. Reusing the use-case identity keeps record and specification joined with no mapping to maintain.
provisions.example: `catalog.add-product` names both the use case and the audited action.

provisions.heading: Store the Trail Beside the Business Data
provisions.evidence: Which trails live outside the business database or the recorded local convention? Look at the audit store and its privileges.
provisions.statement: Store audit records in the business database, under a separate account holding `INSERT` and `SELECT` privileges.
provisions.rationale: One database provides the atomic success write the transaction rules depend on. A separate account holding only `INSERT` and `SELECT` provides the append-only guarantee.

provisions.heading: Use a Closed Actor Set
provisions.evidence: Which actor values fall outside the five actor kinds? Look at the actor column, with devices and processes mapped.
provisions.statement: An audit actor MUST be one of `person`, `company`, `provider`, `system`, or `guest`.
provisions.rationale: An absent actor collapses three answers into one: a scheduled process acted, a device acted, or no one recorded the actor, and only the third is a defect. The five kinds separate them: a device maps to the person whose account authorized it, with the device as the client description, and a named process maps to `system`. A free-text actor would let each writer spell the same actor differently and break every actor filter.
provisions.example: A warehouse handheld records the person actor whose account authorized it. The origin record names the device.

provisions.heading: Use a Fixed Category Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: Which category values fall outside the eight-value vocabulary or the recorded local convention? Look at the declared selection.
provisions.statement: Classify each audited action as `authentication`, `authorization-denial`, `grant-change`, `monetary-action`, `tenant-configuration`, `personal-data-read`, `bulk-export`, or `background-process-change`.
provisions.rationale: The category drives retention and the review query. A free-text value defeats both, because each writer spells the same category differently.

provisions.heading: Verify the Integrity Chain on a Schedule
provisions.evidence: Which deployments run no scheduled chain verification with an alert? Look at the integrity job and its alerts.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST verify its integrity chain on a recurring schedule and raise an alert on a break.
provisions.rationale: Tamper evidence nobody checks proves nothing: a break sits in the store until someone looks. Scheduled verification turns the chain into a standing claim the deployment re-proves on each run. The alert carries the break to an operator instead of waiting for the next review.

provisions.heading: Version the Audit Record Shape
provisions.evidence: Which records lack an explicit schema version? Look at the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an explicit schema version.
provisions.rationale: A retained record outlives several shapes of the application that wrote it. An explicit version lets a later reader parse each record in the shape it was written in. Without it, every shape change forces a rewrite of retained evidence.

provisions.heading: Write an Unsuccessful Record Outside the Failed Transaction
provisions.evidence: Which denied or failed records roll back with their transaction? Look at the unsuccessful write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST be written on a connection that the failing transaction does not roll back.
provisions.rationale: A denied or failed attempt ends with its transaction rolling back, which would take a record written inside it. The record therefore travels on a connection the rollback does not touch. The evidence of a refusal outlives the refusal itself.

provisions.heading: Avoid Unbounded Key Locks
provisions.evidence: Which lock schemes grow one entry per key without bound? Look at the lock state under high-cardinality keys.
provisions.statement: A cache implementation MUST NOT create an unbounded per-key lock inventory.
provisions.rationale: Per-key locks trade duplicate refresh for memory, and the trade needs a ceiling. Untrusted or high-cardinality keys create one lock entry each, which exhausts memory under attacker-chosen or runaway keys. A bounded lock scheme sheds that state instead of growing it.

provisions.heading: Bound Cache Refresh Work
provisions.evidence: Which caches refresh without bound on concurrent misses? Look at the refresh path under concurrent load.
provisions.statement: A cache implementation MUST bound simultaneous refresh work when concurrent misses could overload its source.
provisions.rationale: When a popular entry expires, every concurrent miss can trigger its own refresh and flood the source the cache was protecting. Bounding simultaneous refresh work holds that flood to what the source tolerates. Request coalescing and jittered expiry are two ways to meet the bound.
