provisions.example: One request refreshes a key while concurrent callers await the same bounded work.

provisions.heading: Compose Cache Keys from Result Inputs
provisions.evidence: Which keys miss the data-shape version, a result-affecting input, or the tenant or actor partition? Look at the key construction.
provisions.statement: A cache key MUST include its data-shape version, every result-affecting input, and applicable tenant or actor partition.
provisions.rationale: A key missing the data-shape version serves old shapes to new callers after a deploy. A key missing a result-affecting input serves one caller's answer to a different request. Tenant or actor partition keeps one party's results away from another's.
provisions.example: `post-summary:v2:tenant-42:post-17` identifies a versioned, tenant-scoped result.

provisions.heading: Define Cache Invalidation
provisions.evidence: Which cached values lack expiry, invalidating events, an owner, or failure behavior? Look at the invalidation contract of each cache.
provisions.statement: A cached value MUST define expiry as a setting record, invalidating write events, an invalidation owner, and behavior after invalidation failure.
provisions.rationale: Every cached value goes stale, and the only choice is whether the project decides the behavior up front or discovers it during an incident. Expiry, invalidating write events, an owner, and failure behavior state how long staleness lasts and who fixes it when invalidation fails. A cache without that contract serves stale data on a schedule nobody chose.

provisions.heading: Define Cache Outage Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which caches lack a documented source fallback or degraded response? Look at the outage behavior of each cache.
provisions.statement: A cache outage MUST use the source when capacity permits or return a documented degraded response.
provisions.rationale: Cache infrastructure fails like any other dependency. The outage behavior states whether callers fall back to the source or receive a documented degraded response, so an outage degrades the product on purpose instead of by accident.

provisions.heading: Emit a Signal for Each Degraded Cache Path
provisions.evidence: Which cache paths share one counter across miss, error, and degraded response? Look at the emitted metrics.
provisions.statement: A cache path MUST emit a metric distinguishing a cache miss, a cache error, and a degraded response.
provisions.rationale: A fallback that works is invisible. An outage runs until someone notices the source load instead. The three cases need different responses: a miss is normal, an error is an infrastructure fault, and a degraded response is a product behavior change. One counter for all three answers none of them.
provisions.example: The metric carries the cache name and the outcome, following [the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) for the client it wraps.

provisions.heading: Exclude Unsafe Cache Key Material
provisions.evidence: Which keys contain a secret, unbounded input, or unhashed personal data? Look at the key construction.
provisions.statement: A cache key MUST NOT contain a secret, unbounded raw input, or personal data that is not already a hash.
provisions.rationale: Keys appear in diagnostics, metrics, and provider administration tools. That copies the value into a store no one classified. An email address in a key is a personal-data record in the cache provider's key space. It sits outside every retention and erasure path the project defined. [Data minimization](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-5-gdpr/) applies to an identifier as much as to a field.
provisions.example: A per-account cache key carries the account's opaque identifier. A key that carried the address instead is replaced by a hash of it, and the entry is bound to the account that owns it.

provisions.heading: Keep Source Data Authoritative
provisions.evidence: Which required business data lives authoritatively in the cache? Look at the source of record beside the cached copy.
provisions.statement: A cache implementation MUST keep required business data authoritative in its source of record.
provisions.rationale: The cache holds a derived copy that the system can drop at any time. Required business data stays authoritative in its source of record, so losing the cache loses speed and nothing else. A cache that owns the only copy turns every cache outage into data loss.

provisions.heading: Place Cache Access at an Outer Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which cache access lives inside Domain, or outside the recorded local convention? Look at the cache call sites.
provisions.statement: Place cache access in Infrastructure or a frontend data boundary.
provisions.rationale: Cache access lives in Infrastructure or a frontend data boundary, behind a port the use case owns when Application needs one. Domain code takes no cache dependency, so business rules read the same with or without a cache. A cache concern inside Domain would couple every rule to the cache's presence.

provisions.heading: Prefer Bounded Staleness
provisions.evidence: Which long expiries lack a measured staleness and operating-cost decision? Look at the expiry beside the invalidation cost.
provisions.statement: A cache owner SHOULD use a short expiry when precise invalidation costs more than recomputation.
provisions.rationale: Precise invalidation costs design and code, while a short expiry costs one recomputation per window. When recomputation is cheaper, a short expiry bounds staleness without the machinery. A longer expiry then needs a measured decision that says the extra staleness is worth its saving.

provisions.heading: Record a Manual Cache Invalidation
provisions.evidence: Which manual clears lack a record naming actor, invalidation scope, and reason? Look at the invalidation runs.
provisions.statement: A manual invalidation MUST produce a record naming actor, invalidation scope, and reason, as an audit record in its category when the audit extension is selected.
provisions.rationale: A manual clear changes what every later caller sees and leaves no trace in the data itself. Investigating a stale-read report afterward means knowing whether someone already cleared the entry. [Article 30 of the GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/) treats an administrative action over personal data as processing that has a record.
provisions.example: A command that clears one tenant's cached price list records the tenant, the operator, and the incident it was run for.

provisions.heading: Record Accepted Cache Staleness
provisions.evidence: Which cached queries lack a bounded freshness object with its duration on their output? Look at the served query beside each cache.
provisions.statement: A cached query MUST state its accepted staleness as a `freshness` object with `mode` of `bounded` and its duration in `within`.
provisions.rationale: Accepted staleness is the contract each caller relies on: it states how stale a read may be before it counts as a defect. The served query states it as `{"mode": "bounded", "within": "PT5M"}` on its output, so the cache and the query share one bound that is reviewed with the use case.

provisions.heading: Record Measured Cache Need
provisions.evidence: Which cache proposals lack observed query, load, latency, cost, or target? Look at the proposal behind each cache.
provisions.statement: A cache proposal MUST record its observed query, representative load, latency, source cost, and target.
provisions.rationale: A cache costs invalidation, capacity, and recovery work for as long as it lives. The proposal records the observed query, load, latency, cost, and target so a reviewer weighs that cost against measured gain. A cache added without measurements stays until someone pays to remove it.

provisions.heading: Remove Unjustified Caches
provisions.evidence: Which caches stay past measurements that do not justify their operating cost? Look at the owner reviews beside the operating cost.
provisions.statement: A cache owner MUST remove a cache when measurements do not justify its operating cost.
provisions.rationale: Traffic shifts and sources get faster, so a cache that paid for itself last year can cost more than it saves today. The owner re-checks the measurements and removes the cache when they do not justify its operating cost. A cache nobody owns stays forever, and its invalidation bugs stay with it.

provisions.heading: Assign Operation IDs
provisions.evidence: Which independent-consumer operations lack a deliberate operationId? Look at the OpenAPI document.
provisions.statement: Every operation exposed to an independent consumer MUST have a deliberate `operationId`, except an endpoint whose shape a specification outside the project fixes.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients turn each `operationId` into a method name, and tools use it to reference the operation. A deliberate identifier keeps those names stable and meaningful. An endpoint whose shape an outside specification fixes is exempt, because the project does not own that contract.
provisions.example: An OAuth redirect endpoint, an OIDC discovery document, a provider webhook receiver, and a well-known resource each carry a shape the other party defines.

provisions.heading: Assign Versioned Operation IDs
provisions.evidence: Which new versions reuse the operation ID of a changed contract? Look at the versioned OpenAPI documents.
provisions.statement: A new API version MUST assign a new operation ID when its operation contract changes.
provisions.rationale: The new version needs its own contract names so the retained version keeps its own. A new `operationId` for each changed operation separates the two. Sharing one identifier across versions would let the new contract rename the old one.

provisions.heading: Classify Breaking Contract Changes
provisions.evidence: Which removed, renamed, narrowed, retyped, or authentication changes lack a breaking verdict? Look at the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify removal, rename, required input, narrowed value, response, status, or authentication changes as breaking.
provisions.rationale: A consumer can depend on any element of the contract: a field it reads, a status it branches on, an authentication scheme it implements. Removing, renaming, narrowing, or retyping any of them breaks the consumer that depended on it. Calling each such change breaking routes it to versioning instead of silent release.

provisions.heading: Classify Compatible Additions
provisions.evidence: Which optional additions lack a record of why existing behavior stays? Look at the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify an optional field, endpoint, or query parameter as compatible when existing clients retain behavior.
provisions.rationale: An optional field, endpoint, or query parameter asks nothing of existing callers: they send and interpret the same values as before. Classifying these as compatible keeps routine growth cheap. Treating them as breaking would version the API for changes nobody has to adopt.

provisions.heading: Classify Independent-Consumer Changes
provisions.evidence: Which independent-consumer contract changes lack a classification? Look at the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify each contract change that affects an independently deployed consumer.
provisions.rationale: Every contract change reaches consumers the project does not deploy. Classifying each one decides whether consumers need a new version, a review, or nothing at all. An unclassified change ships the decision to consumers as a surprise.

provisions.heading: Classify Integration Event Changes
provisions.evidence: Which integration-event changes lack a breaking, compatible, or needs-review verdict? Look at the event reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify each integration-event change as breaking, compatible, or needing consumer review under `litespec/ext/compat#classify-breaking-contract-changes`, `litespec/ext/compat#classify-compatible-additions`, and `litespec/ext/compat#review-exhaustive-consumer-changes`.
provisions.rationale: An integration event is a contract with consumers the project does not deploy, so its changes need the same verdicts as HTTP contract changes. Reusing the contract classification keeps one meaning of breaking, compatible, and needs-review across both surfaces. A separate event verdict would let one change read as compatible for events and breaking for HTTP.

provisions.heading: Diff Release Contracts
provisions.evidence: Which changes skipped the local or continuous integration diff against the baseline? Look at the local runs and the CI runs.
provisions.statement: The project MUST compare the current OpenAPI document with the selected supported baseline, both locally and in continuous integration.
provisions.rationale: The diff against the supported baseline runs both locally and in continuous integration. The local run catches a breaking change while it is cheap to rework. The CI run catches it when the local run was skipped.

provisions.heading: Exercise Generated Consumers
provisions.evidence: Which first-party clients skip compiling or exercising the changed contract? Look at the client test runs.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST test each first-party generated client against the changed OpenAPI document, with each client compiling and exercising its changed operations.
provisions.rationale: A structural diff compares documents; it never compiles a client. Testing each first-party generated client against the changed document compiles it and exercises its changed operations. The client's compiler and its exhaustive switches catch the breaks the diff cannot see.

provisions.heading: Gate New Error Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Which added error outcomes break existing consumers on unknown codes? Look at the consumer error handling.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST add an error outcome only when existing consumers safely handle an unknown code.
provisions.rationale: A new error outcome reaches consumers written before it existed. Adding it only when existing consumers handle an unknown code safely keeps old clients working against the new contract. An outcome old clients cannot parse turns their error path into a crash.

provisions.heading: Keep Baseline References Immutable
provisions.evidence: Which baselines move, or live outside the recorded local convention? Look at the baseline references.
provisions.statement: Store each supported baseline beside its contract owner or under an immutable retained-release reference.
provisions.rationale: A diff proves nothing when its comparison target can move. Baselines beside their contract owner or under an immutable release reference stay fixed. A mutable baseline lets a breaking change hide by moving the target.

provisions.heading: Keep Problem Details Codes Stable
provisions.evidence: Which Problem Details codes changed across compatible versions, or outside the recorded local convention? Look at the versioned error surface.
provisions.statement: Keep Problem Details error codes stable across compatible versions.
provisions.rationale: Consumer error handling branches on these codes for years. Keeping them stable across compatible versions lets that handling survive routine releases. A renamed code forces every consumer to update its failure path for no behavior gain.

provisions.heading: Preserve Stable Error Codes
provisions.evidence: Which removed or reassigned stable codes lack a breaking verdict? Look at the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify removal or reassignment of a stable Problem Details code as breaking.
provisions.rationale: Consumers branch on stable Problem Details codes the way they branch on statuses. Removing or reassigning a code breaks that branch while the status stays green. Treating the code as breaking keeps error handling stable across versions.

provisions.heading: Publish Deprecation Context
provisions.evidence: Which operations scheduled for removal are missing from the consumer changelog? Look at the consumer `CHANGELOG.md`.
provisions.statement: A public operation scheduled for removal MUST appear in the consumer `CHANGELOG.md`.
provisions.rationale: Headers announce the removal on the operation, but consumers plan from release notes. The consumer `CHANGELOG.md` names each operation scheduled for removal in the one place consumers already read. A deprecation missing from the changelog reaches only the consumers that inspect headers.

provisions.heading: Record Breaking Behavior Changes as Decisions
provisions.evidence: Which breaking Behavior changes past production lack a decision naming their consumer impact? Look at the decisions.
provisions.statement: After production, a breaking Behavior change MUST travel as a decision naming its consumer impact.
provisions.rationale: A breaking change past production breaks promises consumers release against, so the decision states the impact: which consumers break, what they must change, and when the old shape leaves. A developer review alone cannot accept breaking what the product promised.

provisions.heading: Record Deprecation Conditions
provisions.evidence: Which deprecations lack a sunset date, a replacement, or recording before removal? Look at the deprecation decisions.
provisions.statement: A deprecation decision MUST record the sunset date and replacement operation, with nothing removed before the decision is recorded.
provisions.rationale: A deprecation decision records the sunset date and the replacement operation, so each consumer knows when to move and where to go. Nothing is removed before the decision is recorded. A removal without a recorded replacement strands the consumer that depended on the old operation.

provisions.heading: Record Version Retirement
provisions.evidence: Which retirements lack affected consumers, a deadline, a removal condition, or recording before removal? Look at the versioning decisions.
provisions.statement: A versioning decision MUST name each affected consumer, the deadline, and the removal condition, with the decision recorded before any removal.
provisions.rationale: A removal touches consumers the project does not control, so the decision names each affected consumer, the deadline, and the removal condition. Recording happens before any removal, while the plan can still change. An unrecorded retirement removes first and notifies whoever complains.

provisions.heading: Reject Breaking Diffs Without Authorization
provisions.evidence: Which breaking diffs passed without a new version or a recorded decision? Look at the CI runs.
provisions.statement: Continuous integration MUST fail a breaking diff unless a new API version or a recorded consumer decision authorizes it.
provisions.rationale: A breaking diff that fails CI stops until a new API version or a recorded consumer decision authorizes it. The failure forces the compatibility decision before release, while versioning is still possible. A warning nobody has to answer authorizes nothing.

provisions.heading: Resolve Uncertain Classifications Safely
provisions.evidence: Which unclear changes shipped as compatible without consumer review? Look at the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify an unclear contract change as breaking and require consumer review.
provisions.rationale: A structural diff cannot prove every change compatible: some changes need a person to judge their effect on consumers. Classifying the unclear ones as breaking routes them to consumer review instead of release. The cost of a needless review is smaller than the cost of a broken consumer.

provisions.heading: Retain Compatible Operation IDs
provisions.evidence: Which compatible changes renamed the operationId? Look at the OpenAPI diff.
provisions.statement: A compatible API change MUST retain the existing `operationId`.
provisions.rationale: A compatible change promises existing consumers keep working. Renaming the `operationId` breaks that promise for every generated client and every stored operation reference. The identifier stays until a new version takes over.

provisions.heading: Retain Release Baselines
provisions.evidence: Which releases lack a retained OpenAPI baseline? Look at the release artifacts.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST store each release OpenAPI document as a retained baseline artifact.
provisions.rationale: Each release stores its OpenAPI document as an immutable baseline. Later changes diff against it instead of against memory or a mutable file. Without a retained baseline, the project cannot prove what changed between two releases.

provisions.heading: Retain Supported Versions
provisions.evidence: Which previous versions left before their support window? Look at the deployed versions beside the declared window.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST keep the previous version available for its declared support window.
provisions.rationale: A consumer the project does not deploy moves on its own release cadence. The declared support window states how long the previous version stays available for that move. Removing it early strands consumers that kept to the published plan.

provisions.heading: Retire Integration Events with Notice
provisions.evidence: Which retired event versions left before their support window or without notice? Look at the retirement records beside the event consumers.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST retire an integration event version only after its declared support window with a deprecation notice to its consumers.
provisions.rationale: A retired version strands every consumer still reading it, so the declared support window states how long the version stays available and the notice tells consumers when to move. Retiring early or silently turns a planned removal into an outage for the consumers that kept to the published plan.

provisions.heading: Review Exhaustive Consumer Changes
provisions.evidence: Which added enum values or discriminator cases shipped without consumer review? Look at the consumer reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST require consumer review for an added enum value or polymorphic subtype.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients often switch exhaustively over enum values and discriminator cases. A new value that the server sends reaches a client with no branch for it, which rejects a valid response. Consumer review checks that each client handles the new case before it ships.

provisions.heading: Signal Planned Public Removal
provisions.evidence: Which operations scheduled for removal lack a deprecation signal? Look at the public operations.
provisions.statement: A public operation scheduled for removal MUST expose a documented deprecation signal.
provisions.rationale: Consumers discover a planned removal only when the API tells them. A documented deprecation signal, such as `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers, announces the removal on the operation itself. A removal with no signal arrives as an outage to every consumer that missed the release notes.

provisions.heading: Store Current OpenAPI Source
provisions.evidence: Which current OpenAPI artifacts live outside the documented path or the recorded local convention? Look at `apps/api/openapi/`.
provisions.statement: Store the current source artifact at `apps/api/openapi/{ProjectName}.json`.
provisions.rationale: Source generation and contract review both need the current OpenAPI artifact. One predictable path keeps generation, review, and the diff reading the same file. A second copy drifts from the first.

provisions.heading: Treat Errors as Contracts
provisions.evidence: Which type, code, field-code, or status changes shipped outside versioning? Look at the versioned error surface.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST treat Problem Details type, code, field-error codes, and documented statuses as versioned contract elements.
provisions.rationale: Error handling is consumer code: it branches on Problem Details type, code, field-error codes, and documented statuses. Versioning those elements with the contract keeps error handling working across releases. An error shape that changes outside versioning breaks the consumer's failure path, which is the path least tested.

provisions.heading: Treat Removed Behavior Fields as Breaking
provisions.evidence: Which removed output fields, refusal codes, or integration-event payload fields lack a breaking verdict? Look at the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify removal of a query output field, a refusal code, or an integration-event payload field as breaking.
provisions.rationale: Consumers read query output fields, branch on refusal codes, and parse integration-event payloads, so a removed field breaks every consumer that relied on it while the route stays green. Calling each such removal breaking routes it to versioning and notice instead of silent release.

provisions.heading: Use One Diff Tool
provisions.evidence: Which local runs or CI runs use a different diff tool than the recorded local convention? Look at the local runs and the CI runs.
provisions.statement: Use the same OpenAPI diff tool in local verification and continuous integration.
provisions.rationale: The local run and CI have to agree on what breaking means. One diff tool in both places gives one classification for each change. Two tools disagree on edge cases and teach developers to distrust the check.

provisions.heading: Version Breaking Contracts
provisions.evidence: Which breaking contracts ship without a new route or media-type version? Look at the versioned API surface.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST use a new route or documented media-type version for a breaking contract.
provisions.rationale: Breaking changes need a boundary: a new route or a documented media-type version. Both contracts then serve at once, and each consumer moves on its own schedule. Without the boundary, one contract serves two incompatible expectations.

provisions.heading: Version Breaking Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Which breaking event changes ship without a new version beside the retained one? Look at the integration event versions.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST carry a breaking integration-event change in a new event version beside the retained version.
provisions.rationale: Outside consumers move on their own release cadence, so the breaking change ships beside the retained version instead of replacing it. Each consumer moves to the new version on its own schedule. Without the retained version, one event serves two incompatible expectations.

provisions.heading: Apply HTTP Version Preconditions
provisions.evidence: Which versioned HTTP operations miss a strong persistence-derived ETag or an If-Match requirement on writes? Look at the versioned endpoints.
provisions.statement: An HTTP operation requiring a caller version MUST return a strong persistence-derived `ETag` and require `If-Match` on writes.
provisions.rationale: The caller reads the current state with its strong persistence-derived `ETag` and sends it back in `If-Match` on the write. The server compares what the caller saw with what is stored. The round trip carries the version through HTTP headers instead of a second contract field.
provisions.example: A current `ETag` permits the write; a changed entity version rejects it.

provisions.heading: Bound Expired-Record Cleanup
provisions.evidence: Which expired-record cleanup runs outside a bounded maintenance process? Look at the cleanup jobs.
provisions.statement: An idempotency owner MUST remove expired records through a bounded maintenance process.
provisions.rationale: Expired keys accumulate without cleanup, and cleanup without bounds steals capacity from live work. A bounded maintenance process removes expired records within fixed limits on rate and batch. The store stays small without starving the application.

provisions.heading: Canonicalize Request Fingerprints
provisions.evidence: Which fingerprints miss canonical input, route identity, or actor identifier, or include credentials or the client key? Look at the fingerprint derivation.
provisions.statement: An idempotency implementation MUST derive its fingerprint from canonical mapped command input, route identity, and the authenticated actor identifier, excluding credentials and the client key.
provisions.rationale: The fingerprint decides whether two requests under one key carry the same intent. Canonical mapped command input, route identity, and the authenticated actor identifier make equivalent requests produce one value. The actor identifier is in the fingerprint because two actors can present the same client key, and a fingerprint without it would replay one actor's stored response to another. The credential that proved the actor stays out: a cookie and a signature each change between two requests the rule treats as equal.

provisions.heading: Compare Expected Aggregate Versions
provisions.evidence: Which caller-version comparisons run outside the transaction carrying their change? Look at the conflicting-write paths.
provisions.statement: An implementation MUST compare the caller-supplied version with the stored version in the same transaction as the change.
provisions.rationale: The caller-supplied version marks which write the caller saw, and the stored version marks what the database holds. Comparing the two in the same transaction as the change detects a competing accepted write against the same state, through the selected persistence model. A comparison outside the transaction races the commit it claims to guard.

provisions.heading: Declare Applicable Headers
provisions.evidence: Which applicable operations lack the idempotency header in the generated OpenAPI, with no recorded header-declaration convention naming how contracts expose it? Look at the generated OpenAPI document beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Declare the idempotency header as required on each applicable HTTP operation.
provisions.rationale: Each HTTP operation that accepts a client key declares the header as required. Generated API contracts then expose the requirement to every client author under `litespec/backend/api#publish-precise-complete-schemas`. An undeclared header reaches only the callers who read the implementation.

provisions.heading: Declare Replayed Transport Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Which idempotent use cases list no stored statuses and headers for replay? Look at the idempotent use case pages.
provisions.statement: An idempotent use case MUST list the statuses and headers stored for replay.
provisions.rationale: A completed retry reproduces the stored statuses and headers instead of the live ones. The declared list states which statuses and headers the store holds. A reviewer reads the list to learn exactly what a retry can return.

provisions.heading: Define Concurrent Retry Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which idempotent use cases leave concurrent-request behavior undefined? Look at the idempotent use case pages.
provisions.statement: An idempotent use case MUST define whether a concurrent request waits, reports in-progress, or returns a stable conflict.
provisions.rationale: An identical request can arrive while the first is still running. The use case states whether the concurrent request waits, learns the work is in progress, or receives a stable conflict. Without one documented result, each implementation invents its own and callers handle all of them.

provisions.heading: Delay Irreversible Provider Calls
provisions.evidence: Which irreversible provider calls run before their business transaction commits? Look at the idempotent operation paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST NOT perform an irreversible provider call before its business transaction commits.
provisions.rationale: A provider call that cannot be undone follows the commit. A call made before commit fires even when the transaction then rolls back. The business change would vanish while its external effect stands.

provisions.heading: Discard Failed Replay State
provisions.evidence: Which failed pre-commit requests leave a business change or a completed replay record? Look at the failure paths.
provisions.statement: A failed pre-commit idempotent request MUST leave neither the business change nor a completed replay record.
provisions.rationale: A request that fails before commit changed nothing, so it leaves neither the business change nor a completed replay record. A leftover completed record would replay success for work that never happened. Clean state lets a later retry perform the operation for the first time.

provisions.heading: Document Write Conflict Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which conflicting-write use cases lack conflicts, invalid state, winner behavior, or caller response? Look at the use case pages.
provisions.statement: A conflicting-write use case MUST document conflicting operations, invalid combined result, expected winner behavior, and user-visible conflict response.
provisions.rationale: Version coordination exists to protect one invariant. Naming the conflicting operations, the invalid combined result, the expected winner, and the caller-visible response states which invariant that is. An implementation without that document cannot tell a conflict it has to reject from contention it has to absorb.

provisions.heading: Enforce Key Uniqueness
provisions.evidence: Which idempotency stores lack the unique constraint on tenant, actor, operation, and client key? Look at the idempotency store schema.
provisions.statement: An idempotency store MUST enforce a unique constraint on tenant, actor, operation, and client key.
provisions.rationale: Two concurrent requests can arrive with the same key before either commits. The unique constraint on tenant, actor, operation, and client key admits one winner and rejects the other at the store. Application code alone cannot order two requests that arrive together. A project without the tenancy extension uses one fixed tenant value.

provisions.heading: Exclude Unsafe Replay Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Which replays return authentication failures, transient failures, cookies, hop-by-hop headers, tokens, or secrets? Look at the replayed responses.
provisions.statement: An idempotent implementation MUST NOT replay authentication failures, transient server failures, `Set-Cookie`, `Cache-Control`, `Vary`, `Expires`, `Age`, hop-by-hop headers, tokens, or secrets.
provisions.rationale: Authentication failures and transient server failures describe one exchange rather than the accepted result, so replaying them answers a new request with an old failure. Tokens, secrets, cookies, and hop-by-hop headers each belong to the exchange that produced them. The caching headers are computed for the response that produced them: replaying them hands a later caller freshness instructions from an earlier moment. [RFC 9111](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9111) makes each one a property of the exchange rather than of the result, so the replayed response computes its own.

provisions.heading: Hide Provider Version Values
provisions.evidence: Which transport models expose a provider-specific version value outside the ETag? Look at the public transport models.
provisions.statement: An HTTP API MUST NOT expose a provider-specific version value in another contract field.
provisions.rationale: The `ETag` is the one contract field that carries the persistence version. A provider-specific version leaked into another field gives callers a second version to depend on. Hiding it keeps the coordination behind one boundary the project can change.

provisions.heading: Keep Idempotency Persistence in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Which idempotency persistence or transaction handling sits outside Infrastructure, with no recorded idempotency-store convention naming where its state lives? Look at the idempotency store code beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Keep idempotency persistence and transaction handling in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: Idempotency state lives in provider transactions guarded by store constraints. That machinery belongs in Infrastructure, where provider details live. Application and Domain stay free of the store mechanics behind their operations.

provisions.heading: Limit Version Checks
provisions.evidence: Which caller-version requirements lack a documented conflicting-write case? Look at the versioned operations beside the conflicting-write documents.
provisions.statement: An implementation MUST NOT require a caller-supplied version without a documented conflicting-write case.
provisions.rationale: Every stored aggregate already carries a baseline version that the store compares at commit, so the version itself needs no document. Requiring the caller to supply a version adds a rejection path the caller has to handle: a missing or stale caller version refuses an otherwise valid write. The conflicting-write document stays the gate for that caller burden: no case, no caller-version requirement.

provisions.heading: Map Failed Expected Versions
provisions.evidence: Which failed expected versions miss the 409 Problem Details response or its stable code? Look at the conflict responses.
provisions.statement: An HTTP API MUST map a failed expected version to status 409 Problem Details with a stable code.
provisions.rationale: A caller that loses a version race retries: re-read, re-apply, re-send. Status 409 with a stable Problem Details code names the loss as a conflict, distinct from validation and authorization failures. Without the stable code, the caller guesses which failure it met.

provisions.heading: Map Replay Responses at the API Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which replay response mappings sit outside the API boundary, with no recorded replay-mapping convention naming where they live? Look at the replay mapping code beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Keep replay response mapping at the API boundary.
provisions.rationale: Replaying a stored result means rebuilding its statuses and headers. Those are transport concerns, so the mapping lives at the API boundary. Application code then deals in operation results, never in wire shapes.

provisions.heading: Protect Fingerprint Source Data
provisions.evidence: Which idempotency stores keep original sensitive request content that support never needs? Look at the fingerprint store.
provisions.statement: An idempotency implementation MUST store a cryptographic hash when support does not require original sensitive request content.
provisions.rationale: The fingerprint needs to compare requests, not to show what they contained. A cryptographic hash preserves the comparison while the original sensitive content stays out of the store. Support keeps original content only where it needs the original to help.

provisions.heading: Reject Conflicting Key Reuse
provisions.evidence: Which reused keys with a changed fingerprint miss the documented rejection? Look at the key-reuse paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST reject reuse of one key with a different request fingerprint.
provisions.rationale: A key reused with a different request fingerprint names two different intents under one key. Accepting both would replay the first intent's result for the second intent's request. Rejecting the reuse keeps one key bound to one intent.

provisions.heading: Reject Silent Overwrites
provisions.evidence: Which conflicting accepted writes silently replace the winner? Look at the conflict outcomes.
provisions.statement: An implementation MUST NOT silently overwrite a conflicting accepted change.
provisions.rationale: A conflicting write that silently replaces the accepted change destroys work another caller committed. The losing caller never learns its change is gone. Rejecting the conflict instead hands the caller the facts it needs to reconcile.

provisions.heading: Reload Concurrent Winners
provisions.evidence: Which losing concurrent requests with a matching fingerprint miss the reload and replay of the winner? Look at the concurrent retry paths.
provisions.statement: A losing concurrent idempotency request MUST reload and replay the winning record when its fingerprint matches.
provisions.rationale: The unique constraint admits one winner among concurrent same-key requests. A losing request whose fingerprint matches reloads the winning record and replays its result. The loser then returns the accepted outcome instead of an error for work that succeeded.

provisions.heading: Replay Completed Results
provisions.evidence: Which completed idempotent retries return other than the original response status and body? Look at the replay paths.
provisions.statement: A completed idempotent retry MUST return the original response status and body.
provisions.rationale: The first attempt performed the state change, and the retry performs it no second time. Returning the original response status and body gives the retry the accepted result. The caller sees one execution no matter how many times the network retried.

provisions.heading: Restrict Replay Data
provisions.evidence: Which stored replay fields serve no accepted result callers reproduce? Look at the replay store.
provisions.statement: An idempotent implementation MUST store only safe response fields required to reproduce an accepted result.
provisions.rationale: The store holds what a retry needs to reproduce the accepted result and nothing more. Each extra field widens the sensitive data held under the key's retention. A field that serves no replay need stays out.

provisions.heading: Retain Safe Retry Keys
provisions.evidence: Which keys expire before the documented safe retry time? Look at the retention settings beside the idempotent use cases.
provisions.statement: An idempotency owner MUST NOT expire a key before callers can safely retry.
provisions.rationale: Callers retry inside a documented window after an uncertain response. A key expired inside that window is gone when the retry arrives, so the retry executes as new work. Retention covers the whole window the project promises.

provisions.heading: Return Precondition Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Which versioned operations return a wrong status or code for a missing If-Match or a stale version? Look at the precondition responses.
provisions.statement: An HTTP API MUST return 428 `precondition_required` for missing `If-Match` and 409 `version_conflict` for stale versions.
provisions.rationale: A missing `If-Match` and a stale version are different caller mistakes with different fixes: send the version, or re-read and retry. Status 428 `precondition_required` names the omission and 409 `version_conflict` names the stale version. One code for both would leave the caller guessing which fix applies.

provisions.heading: Route Required External Effects Durably
provisions.evidence: Which required external effects use neither the outbox nor a documented provider idempotency contract? Look at the idempotent operation paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST use the outbox extension or a documented provider idempotency contract for required external effects.
provisions.rationale: A required external effect has to survive retries without duplicating. The outbox extension delivers it durably after commit, or a documented provider idempotency contract lets the provider absorb the replay. An effect with neither path fires once per retry.

provisions.heading: Run Idempotency in the Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Which idempotent operations run idempotency outside a pipeline stage after authorization and validation, before the handler? Look at the pipeline stage order.
provisions.statement: Idempotency MUST run as a pipeline stage after authorization and validation, before the handler.
provisions.rationale: Authorization and validation run first, so a denied or invalid attempt neither consumes a client key nor replays a stored result. The handler runs after, so a replayed key returns the stored response without executing the handler again. Any other order either spends keys on attempts the pipeline would refuse or executes work the store already accepted.

provisions.heading: Scope Client Keys
provisions.evidence: Which idempotent operations scope their client key to less than tenant, authenticated actor, and operation? Look at the keyed operations.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST scope its client key to the tenant, authenticated actor, and operation.
provisions.rationale: A client key alone proves nothing about who sent it: two callers can pick the same key. Scoping the key to tenant, authenticated actor, and operation stops one caller's key from replaying another caller's operation. A project without the tenancy extension uses one fixed tenant value.

provisions.heading: Set Key Retention
provisions.evidence: Which key retentions miss the caller retry window or the business risk? Look at the setting record beside the idempotent use case.
provisions.statement: An idempotency owner MUST record key retention as a setting record set from the caller retry window and business risk.
provisions.rationale: A key that expires too early turns a legitimate retry into duplicate business work. Retention therefore spans the caller retry window plus the business risk of a late duplicate. The setting record states that span where reviewers and operators read it.

provisions.heading: Store Idempotency State Atomically
provisions.evidence: Which idempotent operations store fingerprint, state, response, or expiry outside the business transaction? Look at the keyed write paths.
provisions.statement: An idempotent operation MUST store its fingerprint, state, response status, response body, and expiry with its business change in one provider transaction.
provisions.rationale: The fingerprint, state, response status, response body, and expiry describe the accepted change, so they commit with it in one provider transaction. One transaction leaves neither a completed record without its change nor a change without its replay record. A retry then replays exactly what the first attempt accepted.

provisions.heading: Use the Standard Idempotency Header
provisions.evidence: Which applicable operations accept no `Idempotency-Key` within its bounds, with no recorded client-key convention naming the header and value bounds? Look at the operations beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Use `Idempotency-Key` for HTTP commands that accept client keys, bounded to 255 characters of visible ASCII.
provisions.rationale: The `Idempotency-Key` header makes client-key behavior recognizable at the HTTP boundary. [The IETF draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/) leaves the value opaque, so a server stores whatever a client sends. The 255-character visible-ASCII bound stops an unbounded key from becoming an unbounded store entry and keeps control characters out of log lines.

provisions.heading: Bound Tenant Rule Runs per Period
provisions.evidence: Which stored instances carry no monthly run cap, with no cap scheme named in the customer rules documentation? Look at the stored instances and that documentation.
provisions.statement: Each tenant instance states a monthly run cap taken from the catalog default.
provisions.rationale: One tenant's runaway rule can starve every other tenant's automation. A monthly cap from the catalog default bounds the damage, and the tenant raises it by asking instead of by accident.

provisions.heading: Isolate Hook Failures from the Trigger
provisions.evidence: Which hook tests show a trigger outcome change when the endpoint fails? Look at the hook tests.
provisions.statement: A hook MUST leave its trigger's outcome unchanged when the customer endpoint fails.
provisions.rationale: The trigger's work is done before the hook fires: the invoice is paid, the expense is reimbursed. Failing the trigger because a customer endpoint timed out punishes the product for a stranger's outage. The hook records its own outcome and retries on its own schedule.
provisions.example: A hook call that times out is retried three times and then logged as failed, while the paid invoice stays paid.

provisions.heading: Record the Customer Rules Catalog
provisions.evidence: Which catalog triggers, conditions, or actions have no record? Look at the catalog records.
provisions.statement: Each trigger, condition, and action in the customer rules catalog MUST be a record.
provisions.rationale: The catalog is the product's promise surface: every tenant rule is built from it. Each entry as a record pins what it does, what it costs, and what it refuses, so tenant rules compose from parts the team stands behind.
provisions.example: The action `invoice.send-reminder` is a record stating its rate cap and its suppression rule.

provisions.heading: Refuse Unknown Catalog Entries
provisions.evidence: Which instance tests accept an entry outside the catalog, or refuse it without the current catalog? Look at the instance tests.
provisions.statement: An instance naming a trigger, condition, or action outside the catalog MUST be refused.
provisions.rationale: A renamed or retired entry lingers in old instances, and a crafted request can name entries that never existed. Refusing unknown entries keeps every running rule inside the catalog instead of executing a name nobody defined.
provisions.example: An instance naming the retired trigger `expense.submitted` is refused with the catalog's current trigger list.

provisions.heading: State What a Hook May Not Assume
provisions.evidence: Which hook records omit the ordering, timing, or payload bounds their endpoint leaves unassumed? Look at each hook record.
provisions.statement: Each hook MUST state its may-not contract: the ordering, timing, and payload bounds the customer endpoint never assumes.
provisions.rationale: What the contract omits, customers invent: they assume order, instant delivery, and payloads that never grow. The may-not contract closes those gaps up front, so a hook that fires twice or arrives late breaks no promise.
provisions.example: The hook `invoice.paid` states that deliveries may repeat, may arrive out of order, and carry no line-item detail.

provisions.heading: State What a Hook May Rely On
provisions.evidence: Which hook records omit the payload, retries, timeout, or signature their customer endpoint relies on? Look at each hook record.
provisions.statement: Each hook MUST state its may contract: the payload, retries, timeout, and signature the customer endpoint relies on.
provisions.rationale: A customer endpoint is built by strangers against the hook's word. The may contract states the payload shape, the retry count and spacing, the timeout, and the signature, so the endpoint is written against facts instead of guesses.
provisions.example: The hook `invoice.paid` states three retries spaced a minute apart, a ten-second timeout, and an HMAC signature header.

provisions.heading: Treat Tenant Rules as Data
provisions.evidence: Which tenant rule instances are stored as records? Look at the catalog records and the tenant storage.
provisions.statement: A tenant rule instance MUST live as tenant data, not as a record.
provisions.rationale: Tenants write thousands of rules the team never sees, and recording each one would halt both sides. The catalog carries the records instead: instances compose only catalog entries, so the unrecorded part is the composition, never the parts.
provisions.example: A tenant's rule `remind overdue invoices every Monday` is stored data, while its trigger, condition, and action each point at catalog entries.

provisions.heading: Version Catalog Entries
provisions.evidence: Which catalog entries carry no version, or which stored instances cite none? Look at the catalog records and the stored instances.
provisions.statement: Each catalog entry MUST carry a version that instances cite.
provisions.rationale: Catalog entries evolve: a condition gains an operator, an action changes its payload. Versions pin each instance to the behavior it was composed against, so an entry upgrade never silently rewrites running tenant rules.
provisions.example: The condition `order.total-above` moves from version 3 to version 4, and existing instances keep running version 3 until the tenant re-saves.

provisions.heading: Accept Every Shipped Package License Explicitly
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-license-unknown` (level S) for a direct package whose license the project does not accept and no `admits` entry names.
provisions.statement: Every direct package in the project's generated bill of materials MUST carry a license the project accepts in `dependencies.licenses`, or one its `admits` entry names.
provisions.rationale: A copyleft or commercial license binds the product the day the package ships, and a license nobody accepted is found at an audit rather than at the change that brought it. Listing the accepted licenses once, and naming any other on the admitting decision, keeps the license choice a decision with a person's name on it.
provisions.example: Claimwick accepts `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, and `BSD-3-Clause` in `dependencies.licenses`, so a direct package under `AGPL-3.0-only` that no decision admits is reported.

provisions.heading: Apply OCI Release Labels
provisions.evidence: Which release images miss OCI source, revision, version, or created-time labels? Look at the built images.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST include OCI source, revision, version, and created-time labels.
provisions.rationale: Source, revision, version, and created-time labels in the OCI standard form connect each image to the commit and release that produced it. An incident responder reads the running image's labels and opens the exact source. Images without labels force that join through guesswork.

provisions.heading: Apply the Documented Defaults
provisions.evidence: Which consumer workflow files match no jobs-table job and name, with no workflow-layout convention naming another arrangement? Look at the workflow files beside the jobs table.
provisions.statement: Keep one workflow per job the jobs table lists and use the job names the jobs table states.
provisions.rationale: One workflow per job keeps each gate readable, runnable, and skippable on its own. When containerized integration tests or browser tests join CI, they join as jobs the table names rather than as hidden steps inside another job, so the selection rules and the branch protection keep working unchanged.

provisions.heading: Ask Only Unanswered Questions
provisions.evidence: Which worker questions repeat answers the brief gives? Look at the worker questions beside the brief.
provisions.statement: A worker MUST ask no question its brief answers.
provisions.rationale: The brief answers the questions the agent handing off the work already settled. A worker that re-asks them spends a round trip on a reading failure. Questions stay for what the brief leaves genuinely unanswered.

provisions.heading: Attach Dashboard Links to Production Objectives
provisions.evidence: Which production objectives in the book lack a link to their dashboard? Look at the objective pages in the book.
provisions.statement: Each production objective MUST link to its dashboard in the book.
provisions.rationale: The book states intent while dashboards show production truth, and the link joins them: a reviewer clicks from the objective to the numbers behind it. Copying numbers into the page instead would freeze production truth at commit time.

provisions.heading: Build from the Workspace Root
provisions.evidence: Which image builds that need shared inputs do not start from the workspace root, with no build-context convention naming another context? Look at the image build commands.
provisions.statement: Build images from the workspace root when shared project or package files are required.
provisions.rationale: Shared project and package files sit above any one application, so the build starts from the workspace root to reach them. The Dockerfile excludes what the build does not need, including unrelated secrets. A narrower context would copy shared inputs into each build or miss them.

provisions.heading: Build Release Images in Stages
provisions.evidence: Which release images miss multi-stage builds or pinned base-image digests? Look at the Dockerfiles.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST use multi-stage builds and pinned base-image digests.
provisions.rationale: Build tooling has no place in a runtime image: each compiler and package cache widens the attack surface of every deployment. Multi-stage builds leave that tooling in the build stage. A pinned base-image digest fixes the exact reviewed base, so a rebuild months later starts from the same bytes.

provisions.heading: Close Incident Departures Within Seven Days
provisions.evidence: Which incident fixes lack a departure, or carry an expired one? Look at the departure records beside each fix.
provisions.statement: A production incident fix that ships before its records are updated MUST carry an incident departure expiring within seven days.
provisions.rationale: A production incident ships its fix at once. The incident departure records what shipped and why, and the records are updated before it expires. An expired departure is a blocking finding, so the gap stays visible until the records close it.

provisions.heading: Copy Only Runtime Files
provisions.evidence: Which runtime images carry files outside the declared runtime manifest? Look at the image file listing beside the declared runtime manifest.
provisions.statement: A runtime image MUST contain only files required to run the deployed application.
provisions.rationale: Every file in the runtime image ships to every replica and waits for an attacker to read it. Copying only the files the application needs keeps the image small to transfer and to inspect. Each extra file is cost with no runtime purpose.

provisions.heading: Cover Every Quality Requirement with an Alert or a Check
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `quality-alert-missing` (level G) for a quality requirement that no alert rule names in its `requirement` label, whose `check` matches no measured-check or check result the model read, and that no departure covering `quality-alert-missing` lists in its `subject`.
provisions.statement: Every quality requirement that is not retired MUST be named by at least one alert rule or check result, or covered by a departure.
provisions.rationale: A quality requirement nobody watches is a promise checked only when a customer notices it broken. An alert names it to watch production, and a check result, from a measured check or a drill, names it through its `check` to show it was measured before release; a requirement that cannot be watched yet says so as a departure with a reason, an exit and an expiry date, instead of passing silently.
provisions.example: `requirement/expense-submission.month-end-submissions` is named by the alert `submission-acknowledgement-slow` and by the k6 result its `check` names.

provisions.heading: Cover the Baseline Alert Set
provisions.evidence: Which of the five baseline failures (readiness failures, unexpected HTTP errors, release-flow latency, PostgreSQL outages, and failed deployments) lack an alert? Look at the alert rules.
provisions.statement: Baseline coverage MUST include sustained readiness failures, unexpected HTTP errors, release-flow latency, PostgreSQL outages, and failed deployments.
provisions.rationale: Five failures end a release when nobody observes them: readiness that never recovers, HTTP errors the code did not expect, a slowing release flow, a lost database, and a deployment that failed partway. Naming them as the minimum coverage keeps a team from declaring alerts only for the failure it just survived.

provisions.heading: Declare Writable Paths and Limits
provisions.evidence: Which deployments miss declared writable paths or CPU and memory setting records? Look at the deployment manifests beside the setting records.
provisions.statement: A deployment MUST declare writable paths and record CPU and memory bounds as setting records.
provisions.rationale: Declared writable paths name the mutable storage the application needs, and CPU and memory bounds as setting records cap what one deployment may consume. The bounds protect the node's capacity from one hungry replica. The declarations also tell the next reader what the application was sized for.

provisions.heading: Define Actionable Baseline Alerts
provisions.evidence: Which baseline alerts omit an owner, threshold, window, severity, or runbook? Look at each alert rule.
provisions.statement: A baseline alert MUST declare owner, threshold, evaluation window, severity, and runbook before a production release.
provisions.rationale: Each declared field answers one failure mode: - An alert with no owner waits for somebody to adopt it. - An alert with no threshold or evaluation window fires on noise. - An alert with no severity waits in the wrong queue. - An alert with no runbook asks its receiver to invent the response. Declaring all five before production makes each alert answerable the first time it fires.

provisions.heading: Define Backup and Restore Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which release documentation omits a backup owner, schedule, retention, encryption, location, restore command, or recovery objective? Look at the release documentation.
provisions.statement: A release MUST document backup owner, schedule, retention, encryption, location, restore command, and recovery objectives.
provisions.rationale: A backup is only as good as its restore: without a named owner, a schedule, a retention bound, encryption, a location, a restore command, and recovery objectives, nobody knows what is kept, who restores it, or how much loss is accepted. Writing all seven down before production data arrives leaves nothing to decide during the incident.

provisions.heading: Enforce the Supply-Chain Gate
provisions.evidence: Which supply-chain reports lack scan, pin, inventory, or license evidence, or a departure covering each unhandled high-severity advisory? Look at the supply-chain report beside the artifact.
provisions.statement: CI MUST enforce the supply-chain gate on every pull request.
provisions.rationale: When a new advisory names a component and a version range, the team must answer one question fast: does any running release contain it. Without a component inventory beside the artifact, that answer means rebuilding the dependency graph of a commit somebody has to find first. [NIST SP 800-218](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-218/final) states the practice, and the frozen lockfile the build resolved is what the inventory is generated from. OSV-Scanner matches dependencies against OSV.dev advisories and Gitleaks scans for leaked secrets, so advisories and secrets each have one evidence tool.
provisions.example: The build job that produces the artifact generates the inventory from the same frozen lockfile. It stores the inventory beside the artifact, under the release version.

provisions.heading: Exclude Build Material from Runtime Images
provisions.evidence: Which runtime images contain source, tests, package caches, or local configuration? Look at the runtime image contents.
provisions.statement: A runtime image MUST NOT contain source, tests, package caches, or local configuration.
provisions.rationale: Source, tests, package caches, and local configuration serve the build and never the running application. Carrying them into production leaks internals to anyone who pulls the image. Secrets stay out under `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data`.

provisions.heading: Exclude Build Timestamps from Contracts
provisions.evidence: Which published OpenAPI documents or generated clients contain a build timestamp? Look at the generated contracts.
provisions.statement: A published OpenAPI document or generated client MUST NOT contain a build timestamp.
provisions.rationale: A generated-at field or a build-time comment changes the OpenAPI document and generated clients on every build. The diff then reports change where no contract changed, which buries real breaks. Contracts carry version identity instead of build time.

provisions.heading: Exclude Environment Configuration from Images
provisions.evidence: Which release images contain environment-specific configuration? Look at the release image contents.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST NOT contain environment-specific configuration.
provisions.rationale: One immutable image deploys unchanged into staging and production. Environment values baked into the image break that promise: the tested bytes and the deployed bytes differ. External values keep the image identical everywhere it runs.

provisions.heading: Exclude Insecure Frontend Secret Carriers
provisions.evidence: Which frontend image builds use `ARG`, copied environment files, or image layers for secrets? Look at the frontend image builds.
provisions.statement: A frontend image build MUST NOT use `ARG`, copied environment files, or image layers for secrets.
provisions.rationale: `ARG` values, copied environment files, and image layers all persist into the image history. A secret delivered through any of them stays readable to anyone who pulls the image. Secrets stay out of layers under `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data`.

provisions.heading: Exercise a Restore Before the First Production Data
provisions.evidence: Which operations logs lack a restore rehearsal on representative data before the first production data? Look at the operations log entries.
provisions.statement: A project MUST rehearse a restore on representative data before its first deployment holds production data.
provisions.rationale: Backups fail in ways only a restore reveals: a missing key, a wrong permission, a dump the new version cannot read. Rehearsing on representative data before production data arrives finds those failures while they cost nothing. The first restore attempt is the wrong time to learn the backup cannot restore.

provisions.heading: Exercise Every Runbook Before Release
provisions.evidence: Which required runbooks lack a dated rehearsal in the operations log? Look at the operations log entries.
provisions.statement: Each required runbook MUST carry a dated rehearsal in the operations log before a production release, with restore rehearsed on representative data.
provisions.rationale: A runbook is a claim until somebody runs it: steps go stale, commands change, permissions lapse. A dated rehearsal in the operations log proves each required runbook still works against the current system. The restore rehearsal is the one `litespec/ext/delivery#exercise-a-restore-before-the-first-production-data` requires.

provisions.heading: Hold Back Example Rows from the Implementing Worker
provisions.evidence: Which refusal or calculation implementations were checked only against rows the worker saw? Look at the held-back rows and the check runs.
provisions.statement: An agent handing off work MUST check a refusal or calculation implementation against example rows held back from the worker that wrote it.
provisions.rationale: Example rows given to the implementing worker become the values the implementation is tuned to pass, so the check proves nothing. Rows held back stay an independent verdict: the agent handing off the work runs them after the worker finishes, and the implementation passes or fails on unseen cases.

provisions.heading: Keep a Canonical Job Graph
provisions.evidence: Which consumer workflows use job names or responsibilities the jobs table does not state? Look at the workflow files.
provisions.statement: Consumer CI MUST use the job names and responsibilities the jobs table on the [Continuous Integration page](../quality/ci.md) states.
provisions.rationale: The release job reruns the table's jobs by name, and the branch protection settings require them by name. When a consumer renames a job or moves its checks elsewhere, those references point at a job that no longer exists, and the gate stops checking without failing. Fixed names and responsibilities keep every reference resolving to the checks the table states.

provisions.heading: Keep a First-Release Readiness Record
provisions.evidence: Which pre-release consumers lack dated rehearsals, green gates, or a rehearsal owner? Look at the readiness record beside the project.
provisions.statement: A consumer before its first production release MUST keep a readiness record with dated rehearsals, green gates, and a rehearsal owner.
provisions.rationale: A release record binds evidence to one artifact, so a product with no artifact yet has nothing to record in one. The readiness record instead states what proves the product may take data: dated rehearsals, green gates, and a rehearsal owner who owns the backup and restore rehearsal.

provisions.heading: Keep Deployment Descriptors Together
provisions.evidence: Which deployment descriptors sit outside one `deploy/` tree, with no deployment-layout convention naming another arrangement? Look at the repository layout.
provisions.statement: Keep compose files, proxy configuration, the environment example, database setup, observability, DNS records, alert definitions, service definitions, and bootstrap scripts under one `deploy/` tree.
provisions.rationale: Deployment spreads across compose files, proxy configuration, environment examples, database setup, observability, DNS records, alert definitions, service definitions, and bootstrap scripts. Scattered across the workspace, one of them is always the file nobody finds during an incident. One `deploy/` tree keeps every descriptor where the operator looks first.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Alert Threshold to Its Requirement's Measure
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `alert-threshold-drift` (level A) for an alert rule whose own text carries none of the decimal numbers its requirement's `measure` names.
provisions.statement: An alert rule MUST state every number its requirement's `measure` names in its own expression or threshold.
provisions.rationale: The requirement's measure is the agreed target, and the alert is the one place it is enforced at runtime. A measure that says two seconds and an alert that fires at five drift apart silently, because nobody re-reads the alert when the requirement changes. Comparing the numbers is a coarse check, since a measure is prose, so it advises rather than blocks.
provisions.example: `requirement/expense-submission.month-end-submissions` measures "at least 99 percent within two seconds", and its alert's expression compares the 0.99 quantile against 2.

provisions.heading: Keep Mutable Data External
provisions.evidence: Which mutable data lives inside a container filesystem? Look at the application storage design.
provisions.statement: A containerized application MUST keep mutable data outside its container filesystem.
provisions.rationale: The platform recreates replicas at will: deploys, scaling, and node failures each replace containers with fresh ones. Mutable data kept inside the container filesystem dies with its replica. External storage keeps the data alive across every recreation.

provisions.heading: Keep Rollback Executable
provisions.evidence: Which rollback runbooks omit their artifact reference, command, compatibility, data condition, expand-and-contract sequence, or, for a container release, the previous image digest? Look at each rollback runbook.
provisions.statement: The rollback runbook MUST state the previous artifact reference, command, configuration and schema compatibility, data recovery condition, and the expand-and-contract sequence for destructive schema work, and name the previous image digest for a container release.
provisions.rationale: Rollback is written during the incident if it is not written before it, and an incident is the worst time to work out which artifact was live, which command restores it, and whether the schema still fits. Stating the previous artifact reference, the command, the configuration and schema compatibility, the data recovery condition, and the expand-and-contract sequence keeps each answer ready. For a container release the runbook names the previous image digest, which names one immutable image where a tag alone could have moved since the release went out. Rollback is a required runbook, so `litespec/ext/delivery#exercise-every-runbook-before-release` rehearses it.

provisions.heading: Keep Scripts at the Root
provisions.evidence: Which bootstrap, release, or CI helper scripts sit outside root `scripts/`, with no project documentation naming its own script layout? Look at the repository layout.
provisions.statement: Keep bootstrap, release, and CI helper scripts under root `scripts/`.
provisions.rationale: Bootstrap, release, and CI helper scripts serve the whole workspace, so the root `scripts/` folder keeps them where every caller looks. An application-specific script may stay inside its application when no other workspace calls it.

provisions.heading: Limit Container Privileges
provisions.evidence: Which deployments keep a writable filesystem or unnecessary capabilities where the application permits the limits? Look at the deployment manifests.
provisions.statement: A deployment MUST use a read-only filesystem when the application permits it and drop unnecessary capabilities.
provisions.rationale: A read-only filesystem and dropped capabilities shrink what a compromised process can do next: no writes outside declared paths, no privileged calls it never needed. The limits apply where the application permits them. Each kept capability is an action an attacker inherits.

provisions.heading: Match Every Shipped Package to Its Pin
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-version-drift` (level S) for a direct package whose version is outside its manifest pin.
provisions.statement: Every direct package in the project's generated bill of materials that the manifest pins MUST ship within its pin: a stable release of the pinned major, or the exact version where the manifest pins one.
provisions.rationale: The bill of materials (SBOM) is the computed list of what ships, so it is the one place a pin can be checked against instead of trusted. A version outside its pin carries a major's breaking changes, or a prerelease's behavior, that the release never reviewed. The bill is generated, so the fact stays written once, and a record per package would rewrite hundreds of facts on every update.
provisions.example: Claimwick's bill of materials sits at `.litespec/proof/sbom/api.spdx.json`, the project file names that folder in `paths.sbom`, and a direct `pkg:nuget/Marten` at 10.0.0 is reported because the manifest pins `9.x`.

provisions.heading: Meet Release Readiness Gates
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check --release` blocks on `use-case-unverified`.
provisions.statement: A release MUST show green G checks, verified scenarios, and green S checks where the reader is qualified.
provisions.rationale: The three parts prove the three risks are closed: G checks prove the record graph holds, verified scenarios prove each behavior through the public boundary, and S checks prove the code matches the records where a qualified reader exists. A release missing any part ships with that risk unjudged. `litespec model check --release` makes the release-readiness findings block, so the gate is a command.
provisions.example: A reimbursement release shows green G checks, every scenario verified, and green S checks on the .NET reader.

provisions.heading: Name Every Runbook from an Alert, Job, Reaction or Failure Policy
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `runbook-unused` (level A) for a runbook record that no alert label, job, reaction or failure policy names.
provisions.statement: Every runbook record MUST be named by at least one alert, job, reaction or failure policy.
provisions.rationale: A runbook nobody names answers no failure: an alert, a job, a reaction or a failure policy is the caller that sends a person to the procedure, and without that link the procedure waits undiscovered while the failure it answers is handled from memory. Naming each runbook from at least one caller keeps every procedure reachable from the event that needs it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's job `send-event-change-notices` names `runbook/clear-stuck-notices` in its `runbook` field, so the procedure is reachable from the work that needs it.

provisions.heading: Name the Requirement and Runbook on Every Alert
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `alert-link-missing` (level S) for an alert rule in the files `paths.alerts` names whose `requirement` label is missing or names no quality requirement, or whose `runbook` label is missing or names no runbook.
provisions.statement: Every alert rule MUST carry a `requirement` label naming the quality requirement it measures and a `runbook` label naming the runbook that answers it, both as record identifiers.
provisions.rationale: An alert is the runtime half of a quality requirement: it fires when the measure the requirement promises is breached, and the runbook says what a person does next. Written as a file path or left out, the link is a string no tool follows, so an alert can outlive its requirement, a requirement can lose its last alert, and a renamed runbook breaks silently. Record identifiers in the alert's own labels keep the link in the file the alert lives in, in the syntax its tool already reads, and let the model check both ends. A baseline alert also carries its window and severity, as `litespec/ext/delivery#define-actionable-baseline-alerts` states.
provisions.example: Claimwick's alert rule `submission-acknowledgement-slow` carries `requirement: requirement/expense-submission.month-end-submissions` and `runbook: runbook/slow-submissions` in its labels.

provisions.heading: Place Dockerfiles Beside Deployables
provisions.evidence: Which deployable applications keep no Dockerfile beside them, with no dockerfile-layout convention naming where Dockerfiles live? Look at each application folder.
provisions.statement: Keep one Dockerfile beside each deployable application.
provisions.rationale: One Dockerfile beside each deployable application keeps the image definition with the project that defines its runtime output. A reader finds the build next to the code it ships. A shared folder of Dockerfiles separates each build from its owner.

provisions.heading: Point Each Operations File at Its Decision
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a file in `paths.operations` with no `follows` mark and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming no decision, departure, or provision, and counts the file toward `decision-unimplemented`.
provisions.statement: Every deployment, proxy, host, and CI workflow file the project lists in `paths.operations` MUST carry a `follows` mark naming the technical decision, departure, or provision it carries out.
provisions.rationale: Operations files hold choices as load-bearing as code: the proxy's security headers, the backup schedule, the gates a pull request passes.
