provisions.rationale: Restore and administration queries reach records normal queries cannot see, so they need a path of their own with checks of their own. Without the named path, a privileged read hides inside normal query code and inherits normal authorization, which grants too much to too many callers.

provisions.heading: Authorize Lifecycle Changes
provisions.evidence: Which lifecycle operations change the record before checking their documented authorization? Look at each operation's authorization check.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle operation MUST apply its documented authorization.
provisions.rationale: Deleting or restoring the wrong record harms a customer or breaks a legal duty, so each lifecycle operation checks that the actor may perform it.

provisions.heading: Bound Purge and Archive Work
provisions.evidence: Which purge and archive runs fail to resume after interruption within declared bounds, or show no progress? Look at the purge and archive tests.
provisions.statement: A purge or archive operation MUST be resumable, bounded, cancellation-aware, and observable.
provisions.rationale: A purge or archive job can run for hours across millions of rows, and a deployment, a failure, or an operator stops it midway. Resumable, bounded, cancellation-aware work restarts where it stopped instead of from the beginning, and observable progress tells the operator whether it moves or stalls.

provisions.heading: Default to Hard Delete
provisions.evidence: Which deletions with no retention or restore requirement keep the row past the delete transaction? Look at the delete transaction code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST use hard delete when no accepted retention or restore requirement applies.
provisions.rationale: When no use case needs the data back, removing the row deletes the least and keeps the least: no hidden state, no filtered queries, no purge job to write and watch. A team that keeps deleted rows just in case pays for retention without a requirement and answers subject-access exports with data it promised to delete.
provisions.example: An expense deleted without a retention duty removes the expense row in the delete transaction.

provisions.heading: Define Post-Deletion References
provisions.evidence: Which specifications omit post-deletion behavior for references, exports, or unique constraints? Look at each specification's deletion section.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle specification MUST define post-deletion behavior for cross-aggregate references, exports, and unique constraints.
provisions.rationale: Other records can point at the deleted one, exports can carry its values, and a unique value such as an expense reference number can become available again. When the specification stays silent, each developer guesses: one nulls the reference, another keeps it, and a duplicate value slips through or a report breaks. Writing the behavior down gives every reference, export, and constraint one answer.

provisions.heading: Define Relational Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which relational implementations omit columns, query filters, partial indexes, migrations, or named filter behavior? Look at each relational implementation.
provisions.statement: A relational lifecycle implementation MUST define columns, query filters, partial indexes, migrations, and named filter behavior.
provisions.rationale: A relational table keeps retained rows beside active ones, so the team states which columns mark the state, which query filters hide retained rows, which partial indexes keep active values unique, which migrations add all of it, and what each named filter means. Without those choices, a unique constraint blocks a legitimate reuse or a query returns rows the lifecycle retired.

provisions.heading: Define Storage Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which document implementations omit document state, filtered queries, indexes, purge transformations, or contract evolution? Look at each document implementation.
provisions.statement: A Marten lifecycle implementation MUST define document state, filtered queries, indexes, purge transformations, and contract evolution.
provisions.rationale: A document store keeps whatever the aggregate writes, so the team states how each lifecycle state lands in the document: which state the document carries, which queries filter it, which indexes serve those queries, how a purge rewrites the document, and how the contract changes when the shape does. Without those choices, the business transition lands in storage by accident and each query invents its own filter.

provisions.heading: Exclude Inactive Records from Normal Reads
provisions.evidence: Which normal queries return deleted or archived records? Look at the query filters beside the active state.
provisions.statement: A normal query MUST exclude deleted or archived records.
provisions.rationale: An employee browsing expenses expects live data: deleted and archived records in that list confuse the employee and leak data the lifecycle retired. Normal queries therefore read only the active state, while the named privileged paths serve the records outside it.

provisions.heading: Exclude Persistence-Only Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which lifecycle transitions run through persistence filters or property setters alone? Look at the transition code and the persistence filters.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle rule MUST NOT rely only on persistence filters or property setters.
provisions.rationale: A query filter or a property setter runs without the business checks: it filters rows in storage while the aggregate never learns the transition happened. The product then enforces lifecycle in two places that disagree, and a new query that skips the filter exposes data the lifecycle retired.

provisions.heading: Keep Archive Records Module-Owned
provisions.evidence: Which archive records sit outside their owning module, with no shared archive area the project keeps? Look at the module folders.
provisions.statement: Keep archive records under the owning module.
provisions.rationale: The module that defines what the record means also defines what its archive means and who may read it. An archive kept elsewhere sits under two modules, and its access checks drift from its home module.

provisions.heading: Model Lifecycle Operations in Domain
provisions.evidence: Which aggregates lack a delete, archive, or restore method where those operations apply? Look at each aggregate's methods.
provisions.statement: A Domain aggregate MUST expose delete, archive, and restore as explicit behavior when those operations apply.
provisions.rationale: Delete, archive, and restore change what the business promises about a record, so the aggregate owns them the way it owns any rule: one method per operation, with the checks beside the change. When the operation lives anywhere else, two callers implement it two ways and the checks drift apart.

provisions.heading: Model Retained Lifecycle States
provisions.evidence: Which retained records lack a business reason or a named state transition? Look at each retained record beside its state transitions.
provisions.statement: A soft-deleted or archived record MUST have a business reason and explicit state transition.
provisions.rationale: A record that stays after deletion or moves to an archive still affects the product: it appears in some reads, skips others, and can return. A named state with a named transition shows that behavior in the aggregate itself, so a reader sees which transitions exist and which checks each one runs. Without the transition, the retained data is a row the code treats specially in scattered places.
provisions.example: `Archive` changes aggregate state after the authorization and audit checks succeed.

provisions.heading: Name Soft-Delete Timestamps
provisions.evidence: Which soft-delete timestamps use another column than `deleted_at_utc`, with no other column named in the documentation? Look at the schema columns.
provisions.statement: Use `deleted_at_utc` when a soft-delete timestamp is required.
provisions.rationale: One name for the deletion timestamp lets every reader and query recognize it on sight: the event and the unit remove the two guesses a reviewer otherwise makes.

provisions.heading: Preserve Legal-Hold Data
provisions.evidence: Which retention runs delete held data past its retention date? Look at the retention run code beside the hold records.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST preserve data under legal hold.
provisions.rationale: A legal hold suspends the duty to delete: the named data stays until the hold releases, even when its retention date passes. A retention job that ignores the hold destroys evidence the organization had a duty to keep.

provisions.heading: Record Lifecycle Scope
provisions.evidence: Which lifecycle records omit classification, retention, deletion trigger, hold, export, restore, or backup? Look at each lifecycle record.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle record MUST name classification, retention, deletion trigger, hold, export, restore, and backup.
provisions.rationale: A lifecycle record names every choice the team makes about a record's lifetime in one place: what kind of data it is, how long it stays, what triggers deletion, and how holds, exports, restores, and backups behave. Without that record, the choices scatter across tickets and memory, and a deletion runs before anyone checks the retention bound. Retention bounds live in setting records.

provisions.heading: Record Retention Progress
provisions.evidence: Which retention runs persist no progress for the next run to resume from? Look at the retention run code.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST record its progress.
provisions.rationale: A retention run can stop midway through millions of rows, and recorded progress tells the next run where to resume. Observable progress tells the operator whether the job moves or stalls.

provisions.heading: Record the Release of a Legal Hold
provisions.evidence: Which legal-hold releases lack an actor, data covered, reason, or resumed retention? Look at the release records.
provisions.statement: A legal-hold release MUST record actor, data covered, reason, and resumed retention: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A hold suspends the duty to erase, and releasing it resumes that duty from a date the team can name. Without a release record, nobody can state when the suspension ended, so a subject's [erasure request](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) has no answer date and the next retention run cannot tell which data is deletable again. The record also tells the retention job exactly which data resumed which retention date.
provisions.example: A release record names the hold, the release date, and the retention date the covered data carries.

provisions.heading: Reject Hidden Lifecycle Flags
provisions.evidence: Which lifecycle transitions run through a storage-only flag instead of explicit behavior? Look at the transition code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST NOT use a hidden boolean as its sole lifecycle behavior.
provisions.rationale: A boolean column that only the storage layer reads can flip without running the business checks: no authorization, no audit entry, no named transition a reviewer can find. The record then looks deleted in one query and active in another, depending on which filter the query remembered. An explicit lifecycle operation keeps the flag, where one exists, as an effect of the transition rather than the transition itself.

provisions.heading: Separate Query-Shaped History
provisions.evidence: Which query-shaped histories sit on an aggregate, with no read model the project keeps for them? Look at the aggregate code beside the read models.
provisions.statement: Use a separate read model when archived history is query-shaped instead of an aggregate invariant.
provisions.rationale: History kept for display, such as a list of past expenses, constrains nothing the aggregate protects, so it lives cheaper as a read model beside the record. Folding it into the record widens the transaction boundary for data no invariant needs.

provisions.heading: Test Provider Lifecycle Paths
provisions.evidence: Which lifecycle tests skip the normal and lifecycle query paths on the selected provider? Look at the lifecycle tests.
provisions.statement: A selected persistence provider MUST test normal and lifecycle query paths.
provisions.rationale: Filters, indexes, and migrations behave differently per provider, and a filter that works on documents can fail on tables. Tests that read through both the normal path and the lifecycle path on the selected provider catch the difference before a customer does.

provisions.heading: Avoid Catalog-Only Locale Claims
provisions.evidence: Which shipped locales come from outside the locale decision, or from catalog files that do more than translate? Look at the shipped locales beside the locale decision.
provisions.statement: A product MUST NOT infer supported locales from catalog files alone.
provisions.rationale: A catalog file proves only that someone wrote translations; it says nothing about routes, fallback, selection, or detection. A product that counts locales by counting files announces a language its routes cannot serve and its fallback never reaches.

provisions.heading: Avoid Duplicate Localized URLs
provisions.evidence: Which localized content items serve from more than one indexable URL? Look at the served URLs of each content item.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST NOT publish multiple indexable URLs for the same localized content.
provisions.rationale: When two addresses serve the same language, search engines split the page's rank between them and canonical links point two ways. One indexable address per language keeps search, sharing, and caching pointed at the same page.

provisions.heading: Complete or Fall Back Catalog Values
provisions.evidence: Which locales lack a required key with no declared fallback to resolve it? Look at each locale catalog beside the fallback chain.
provisions.statement: Each supported locale MUST contain required keys or use its declared fallback.
provisions.rationale: A missing translation with no declared fallback becomes a runtime surprise: the interface shows a key, an empty string, or the wrong language, and nobody chose which. The declaration states the fallback locale and what a missing key does at build time. A key missing from the default locale fails the build. No fallback exists for it, and the interface renders its identifier. A key missing from a non-default locale reports a warning and falls back. Shipping one untranslated string costs less than blocking a release on it.
provisions.example: A catalog check runs in the frontend lint gate. The two outcomes are visible before review, not in a browser.

provisions.heading: Define One Locale Route Shape
provisions.evidence: Which locales reach the application through a route shape other than the documented one? Look at the route definitions.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST define one documented locale route shape.
provisions.rationale: Users, links, crawlers, and caches all address a localized page, and one route shape gives each language one predictable address. A path segment is the default shape: it gives every localized page a distinct address that links, crawlers, and cache entries can each name. A cookie or header shape serves every locale from one address instead, so a shared cache and a search index each see only one of them. A product with no public pages, whose locale belongs to the signed-in account, documents one of those shapes instead of inventing a fourth.
provisions.example: `/nl/orders/42` places the locale in the documented path segment, so a crawler and a shared cache each address one language.

provisions.heading: Follow the Validation Message Grammar
provisions.evidence: Which validation messages omit the field label, the fault, or the accepted input, or use technical wording? Look at the validation messages in each locale.
provisions.statement: A validation catalog MUST state the field label, what is wrong, and what is accepted, without technical wording.
provisions.rationale: A validation message that names the field, the fault, and the accepted input tells the user how to fix the entry in any language, while a message with only one of the three leaves the user guessing. The three-part shape holds across languages; each language's sentence pattern lives in the labels of the field's glossary term and the language's writing page.
provisions.example: The glossary term for a field carries the sentence pattern for each supported language.

provisions.heading: Format Values with Active Locale
provisions.evidence: Which dates, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, or relative times bypass the active-locale formatters? Look at the formatting calls.
provisions.statement: A localized interface MUST format dates, times, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, and relative time by active locale.
provisions.rationale: Dates, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, and relative time each follow the user's conventions, and a date the user misreads becomes a missed appointment or a wrong payment. The platform supplies all of them. [The `Intl` namespace](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl) has `DateTimeFormat`, `NumberFormat`, `PluralRules`, `ListFormat`, and `RelativeTimeFormat`. Each one carries the locale data the browser already ships. A project-written formatter for any of these is a second locale database that no one updates. Its plural rules are wrong for the first language with more than two forms.
provisions.example: Create one formatter instance per locale and reuse it. Construction is the expensive part.

provisions.heading: Handle Unavailable Locale Segments
provisions.evidence: Which unsupported or missing locale segments fail to redirect under the documented product policy? Look at the redirect tests.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST redirect unsupported or missing locale segments according to product policy.
provisions.rationale: Readers mistype addresses and follow stale links, so a locale segment can name a language the product never shipped or omit the segment entirely. Without a documented policy, each route answers differently: one shows the default language, another shows an error, and a crawler indexes both as content.

provisions.heading: Keep Locale Selection Explicit
provisions.evidence: Which requests carry the locale in ambient request state instead of the URL or a documented session preference? Look at the request handling for the locale.
provisions.statement: Keep locale selection in the URL or documented session preference.
provisions.rationale: A locale stored in the URL or a documented session preference travels with the request, so any developer can see which language a page serves and link to it. An implicit global locale hides in process state, where one request can read another's language and no link reproduces the page.

provisions.heading: Keep Stable Error Codes Locale-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Which stable API error codes differ across locales? Look at the error code values in each locale's responses.
provisions.statement: A stable API error code MUST NOT change by locale.
provisions.rationale: Integrations and support tools match on the error code, and a code that changes per language forces every consumer to list every translation before handling one failure. The code stays fixed while the human-readable message beside it translates.

provisions.heading: Localize Public Presentation Content
provisions.evidence: Which public metadata, form labels, validation messages, or user-safe errors render outside the active locale? Look at each rendered page.
provisions.statement: Public metadata, form labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors MUST follow the active locale.
provisions.rationale: A Dutch page with an English title, English form labels, or an English error tells the user the translation stopped halfway and tells a search engine the page serves two languages. Metadata, labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors follow the active locale with the page around them.

provisions.heading: Name Messages by Meaning
provisions.evidence: Which catalog keys are source-language sentences, or lack a semantic name citing a glossary term? Look at the catalog keys.
provisions.statement: A locale catalog MUST use semantic keys that cite glossary terms rather than source-language sentences.
provisions.rationale: A key that copies the English sentence breaks its meaning the day English rewords it: every other language still points at the old sentence. A semantic key names the intent instead, citing the glossary term that holds the word's labels per language, so wording changes in any language without disturbing the key.
provisions.example: `orders.cancel.confirmation` identifies intent without copying the English sentence.

provisions.heading: Preserve Locale-Neutral Business Data
provisions.evidence: Which domain values or API contracts carry locale-specific text outside an explicitly localized exchange? Look at the domain values and contracts.
provisions.statement: Domain values and API contracts MUST remain locale-neutral unless a use case explicitly exchanges localized content.
provisions.rationale: An expense state or a price stored in Dutch breaks the moment an English speaker opens it, and an API contract that shifts per language forces every consumer to negotiate wording before reading data. Business values and wire contracts stay in one neutral form, and only the interface translates them for display. A use case that genuinely exchanges localized content, such as a product description the merchant writes per language, names that exchange explicitly.

provisions.heading: Record Supported Locale Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which locale decisions omit supported locales, the default locale, the fallback chain, user selection, or browser detection? Look at the locale decision record.
provisions.statement: A localization decision MUST list supported locales, default locale, fallback chain, user selection, and browser detection.
provisions.rationale: Locales, default, fallback, selection, and browser detection interact: each catalog, route, and formatter reads the same contract, so the team writes it once before building any of them. Without the contract, each part guesses a different fallback and the product answers each missing translation differently.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Shown Identifier
provisions.evidence: Which shown codes render as raw codes instead of glossary labels, outside user-facing reference numbers? Look at the rendered screens.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST resolve every closed-set code it renders to its glossary label and never render the raw code, excluding user-facing reference numbers.
provisions.rationale: A code such as a refusal ground or a billing state is a contract value built for systems, while the glossary label beside it is copy built for users. A screen that renders the raw code shows one untranslated fragment in an otherwise translated page and forces the user to decode it. Resolving every shown code keeps the whole screen in the user's language, except reference numbers the user quotes back.
provisions.example: A shipment row shows the glossary label for `shipment-delayed` in the active locale.

provisions.heading: Split Catalogs by Module When Needed
provisions.evidence: Which catalogs split before measured size calls for it, with no feature split the project chose from the start? Look at the catalog files beside the size measurements.
provisions.statement: Split catalogs by module only when catalog size requires it.
provisions.rationale: Small catalogs read better whole: one file per locale shows every key at a glance and survives a rename without cross-file edits. Splitting waits until measured size, such as slow loads or conflicting edits, proves one file no longer serves.

provisions.heading: Store User-Facing Copy in Catalogs
provisions.evidence: Which user-facing copy sits in source code instead of the locale catalogs? Look at the source files for literal copy.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST store user-facing copy in locale catalogs.
provisions.rationale: Copy in source code reaches translators only through developers, and each wording change becomes a code change with a review, a build, and a deployment. Catalogs hold every user-facing sentence in one place per locale, so translators edit wording while developers edit behavior.

provisions.heading: Use BCP 47 Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Which locale identifiers break BCP 47, with no other identifier form named in the documentation? Look at the locale identifiers in the catalogs and routes.
provisions.statement: Use BCP 47 locale identifiers.
provisions.rationale: BCP 47 is the identifier form routes, catalogs, browsers, and libraries recognize: one tag such as `nl` travels unchanged from the address bar to the catalog lookup. A home-grown form needs translation at every boundary and puzzles every new developer.

provisions.heading: Use One Catalog Root
provisions.evidence: Which catalogs sit outside the application-owned root, with no other root named in the documentation? Look at the catalog folders.
provisions.statement: Keep catalogs under one application-owned locale root.
provisions.rationale: One application-owned root tells every developer and tool where catalogs live, so a new locale lands beside the old ones instead of in a folder nobody checks. Scattered catalogs split the set, and one of them misses the fallback check.

provisions.heading: Confirm Every Writing Tool
provisions.evidence: Which writing tools perform a write without the person's confirmation? Look at each writing tool's handler and its tests.
provisions.statement: Every tool that writes MUST refuse until the person confirms the write.
provisions.rationale: A model misreads intent the way any agent does: it can pause the wrong subscription or delete the record the user asked about. Refusing each write until the person confirms keeps the person behind every change while leaving reads fast. Without confirmation, one misunderstood sentence becomes a changed record nobody confirmed.

provisions.heading: Exclude Secrets and Personal Data
provisions.evidence: Which tool descriptions or log lines carry a secret or personal value? Look at the tool descriptions and the server's log calls.
provisions.statement: Tool descriptions and logs MUST exclude secrets, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, and personal data from every field they carry.
provisions.rationale: Tool descriptions travel to the model on every call, and logs persist for operators long after the call ends. A secret copied into either grants access to whoever reads it next, and personal data in either spreads beyond the consent that collected it. Descriptions and logs name the fields without carrying the values.

provisions.heading: Pass Server Instructions at Initialize
provisions.evidence: Which initialize responses carry no `instructions` value, or one that omits transport, audience, write surface, or refusal behavior? Look at the server's initialize handler and its test.
provisions.statement: An MCP server MUST pass an `instructions` value at initialize stating its transport, its audience, its write surface, and its refusal behavior.
provisions.rationale: The MCP initialize response carries server instructions that the client loads once per session, while each tool description loads per call. Scope and policy therefore belong at the server level, where they hold for every call: the transport, the audience, the write surface, and the refusal behavior. Tool mechanics stay in the tool descriptions, which the model reads when it chooses a tool. Without server-level instructions, each tool repeats the policy differently or omits it, and the model plans calls the server refuses.
provisions.example: "Runs over stdio, one account per process, against the hosted API. Reads cover the account's own data, and three tools create or change records. A policy refusal returns the refusal code, and a write needing a person's confirmation refuses until they give it."

provisions.heading: Record the Server as an Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Which shipped MCP servers have no `mcp` entry point titled for them? Look at the entry point list.
provisions.statement: A project shipping an MCP server MUST record it as an entry point of kind `mcp` whose title names the MCP server.
provisions.rationale: The entry point record names how callers arrive: `litespec/core/edges#give-each-entry-point-a-kind` keeps one closed set of kinds, and an MCP server is a channel a local model client calls, so it takes the kind `mcp` and its title says which protocol it speaks. Without the record, the server's reach stays invisible to reviewers of the access records.

provisions.heading: Scope Each Tool to Named Use Cases
provisions.evidence: Which tool descriptions name no use case or permission they reach? Look at each tool description beside its use case grant.
provisions.statement: Each tool MUST name the use cases and permissions it reaches.
provisions.rationale: Each tool opens product behavior to a model acting for the user, so the team names exactly which use cases and permissions each tool reaches. Without the named scope, a reviewer cannot tell whether a tool reads one account or writes across many, and a broad tool ships without the scrutiny its reach needs.

provisions.heading: State the Distribution and Update Path
provisions.evidence: Which server documentation pages omit install or update steps? Look at the server's documentation.
provisions.statement: The server documentation MUST state how a user installs and updates the server.
provisions.rationale: The server runs on the user's machine, not on the product's servers, so no deployment pipeline updates it. Without documented install and update steps, users run stale servers with stale tool descriptions, and a security fix waits on users who never learn it exists.

provisions.heading: State the Refusing Side on Each Refusal
provisions.evidence: Which refusals carry no `Needs:`, `Needs confirmation:`, or `Refused:` prefix, with no other vocabulary named in the documentation? Look at the tools' refusal messages.
provisions.statement: Prefix an input-shape refusal with `Needs:`, a human-confirmation refusal with `Needs confirmation:`, and a server-side refusal with `Refused:`.
provisions.rationale: A refusal without a source sends the model guessing: it rephrases input the server rejected on policy, or it waits for a person when its own input was malformed. The prefix names the failing side, so the model repairs its own input after `Needs:`, asks the person after `Needs confirmation:`, and reports the server after `Refused:`, instead of retrying a refusal no retry satisfies.

provisions.heading: Write One Tool Description for One Decision
provisions.evidence: Which tools break the title, behavior, parameter polarity, or side-effect rules? Look at each entry in the declared tools directory.
provisions.statement: An MCP tool MUST title its action imperatively, describe its behavior declaratively, use positive parameter polarity, and state its side effects.
provisions.rationale: The [MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18) carries the title and description to the model, and the model plans its calls from those words. An imperative title names the action, while a declarative description states what happens instead of commanding the caller, so the server's guidance and the model's own plan do not compete. A positive boolean such as `paused` avoids the inverse polarity that a model answers wrongly, and a stated side effect answers the reviewer who asks what the call changed.

provisions.heading: Accept Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Which event handlers keep wrong state when the same message arrives twice? Look at the handler tests that deliver a message twice.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST handle the same message more than once.
provisions.rationale: The target can accept a message while the Worker crashes before recording completion, and the requeued claim then dispatches it again. Delivery promises at-least-once, so every event handler handles the same message more than once without corrupting its state.

provisions.heading: Audit Outbox Replay
provisions.evidence: Which replays omit the actor, reason, time, or failure, or edit the payload? Look at the replay code and its audit records.
provisions.statement: An outbox replay MUST record actor, reason, time, and failure without editing the payload: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A replay dispatches a message the system already handled or dead-lettered, so the team records who replayed it, why, when, and which failure it answers. Without that record, a duplicate delivery looks like a dispatcher bug instead of an operator's decision, and nobody can reconstruct the choice.

provisions.heading: Avoid Automatic Durable-Bus Adoption
provisions.evidence: Which dispatchers run on a durable bus package with no pinned manifest entry or documented choice? Look at the manifest and the dispatch transport.
provisions.statement: Use project-owned Marten records and Worker dispatch unless a manifest-pinned durable package passes a shared-transaction integration test.
provisions.rationale: A durable bus package earns its place only when an integration test proves it commits the message in the same transaction as the business work. Until that evidence exists, project-owned Marten records with Worker dispatch carry delivery without depending on behavior nobody verified.

provisions.heading: Await Target Acceptance
provisions.evidence: Which outbox records mark completion before the target accepts the message? Look at the Worker's completion code and the target's acceptance response.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT mark an outbox record complete before the target boundary accepts it.
provisions.rationale: Marking a record complete before the target accepts it declares a delivery that never happened, and no retry follows because the record looks done. The Worker waits for the target boundary's acceptance before recording completion.

provisions.heading: Back off Unavailable-Store Polling
provisions.evidence: Which Worker loops poll an unavailable store without backoff or rate-limited logging? Look at the Worker's poll loop and its outage tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST apply bounded backoff and rate-limited logging when its outbox store is unavailable.
provisions.rationale: A Worker that polls a dead store on a tight loop writes an exception per iteration and fills disks and log quotas before anyone reads the first one. Bounded backoff with rate-limited logging keeps the Worker alive and quiet until the store returns.

provisions.heading: Bound Delivery Retries
provisions.evidence: Which retry schedules lack a bound, backoff, or jitter? Look at the dispatcher's retry code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST use bounded exponential backoff with jitter.
provisions.rationale: A failing target with ten thousand pending messages meets a retry storm when every message retries at once on a fixed interval. Bounded exponential backoff with jitter spreads the retries over time and caps the total, so the target recovers instead of drowning.

provisions.heading: Classify Message Kinds
provisions.evidence: Which outbox records name no message kind, or an integration event that does not cite its integration-event record? Look at the outbox record type and the messages staged.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST name its message kind as integration event, journey-step command, or provider side effect, with an integration event citing its integration-event record.
provisions.rationale: An integration event, a journey-step command, and a provider side effect dispatch through different owners and transports, so the record names which one it holds. The integration event cites its integration-event record, so the staged message traces to the published fact it carries.

provisions.heading: Classify Permanent Delivery Failure
provisions.evidence: Which permanent failures retry past their bound, or lose their investigation and replay data? Look at the dispatcher's failure classification and its tests.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST classify permanent failures, stop automatic retry at its retry bound, and retain safe investigation and replay data.
provisions.rationale: Some failures never clear on retry: a deleted destination, a rejected payload, a revoked credential. Retrying those forever burns resources and buries the real backlog, so the dispatcher classifies them, stops at its retry bound, and keeps the evidence an operator needs to investigate and replay safely.

provisions.heading: Declare Published Facts as Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Which `emits` effects name no integration-event record, or one without direction, payload, and trust? Look at each `emits` effect and the integration-event record it names.
provisions.statement: Each `emits` effect MUST name an integration-event record carrying direction, payload, and trust.
provisions.rationale: A published fact without a record is a promise nobody versioned: readers depend on fields no page states, and a field change breaks them without a diff. The integration-event record states the direction, the payload with its classifications, and the trust readers place in it. The [edges page](../core/edges.md) states the declaration and the record.

provisions.heading: Define Claim Ownership
provisions.evidence: Which claims take no owner, expiry, or fencing value, or hold them outside a short transaction? Look at the claim code in the outbox store.
provisions.statement: An outbox claim MUST use a short transaction with the lease owner, lease expiry, and fencing value that `litespec/ext/jobs#store-execution-leases` defines.
provisions.rationale: Several Workers poll the same store, so each dispatch attempt needs one owner: the lease owner, the lease expiry, and the fencing value name it. The short transaction takes the claim without holding locks into the delivery itself.

provisions.heading: Deliver Each Event to Each Handler Separately
provisions.evidence: Which events reach several handlers as one delivery? Look at the outbox delivery records for each handler.
provisions.statement: The outbox MUST deliver an event to each of its handlers as a separate delivery with its own retries and dead letter.
provisions.rationale: One delivery for all handlers retries every handler when one fails. Each handler therefore gets its own delivery with its own retries and dead letter, and each delivery still ends in repeat-safe handling under `litespec/ext/outbox#accept-repeated-delivery`.
provisions.example: A loan-borrowed event feeds a due-notice handler and a statistics handler. The notice delivery retries on its own schedule while the statistics delivery stays complete.

provisions.heading: Deploy Readers Before Writers
provisions.evidence: Which release plans deploy an additive writer before its readers? Look at the deployment order in the release runbook.
provisions.statement: A release MUST deploy compatible readers before writers for additive event versions.
provisions.rationale: In a mixed-version rollout, old and new records sit in one store. Deploying compatible readers before the writers that emit new shapes keeps every record dispatchable at every step; the reverse order strands new records until the readers catch up.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Claimed Records in Worker
provisions.evidence: Which Worker loops dispatch unbounded batches or skip recording an outcome? Look at the dispatcher's claim and batch code.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST claim pending outbox records, dispatch a bounded batch, and record success or retry information.
provisions.rationale: Dispatch needs time, retries, and network calls that no request transaction can hold. The Worker claims pending records, dispatches a bounded batch, and records each outcome, so the request commits fast while delivery proceeds on its own schedule.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Journey-Step Commands in a New Scope
provisions.evidence: Which journey-step commands run inline in the dispatcher scope with no documented choice? Look at the dispatcher's journey-step code.
provisions.statement: Dispatch a journey-step command through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope.
provisions.rationale: A journey-step command is a full command with validation, authorization, and its own transaction, not a subroutine of the dispatcher. Sending it through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope runs the whole application pipeline for it.

provisions.heading: Distinguish Dependency Outage
provisions.evidence: Which outbox metrics use the wrong instrument type for store availability or claimed-message outcomes? Look at the metrics the outbox publishes.
provisions.statement: A dispatcher MUST distinguish an unavailable outbox store from a failed claimed message.
provisions.rationale: A dead outbox store and a failed delivery ask for different recoveries: the first needs a database restored, the second needs one destination investigated. Each carries its own signal. The store's availability is a gauge the readiness endpoint reads, while a claimed message's outcome is a counter carrying the result, following [the OpenTelemetry metrics specification](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/). A single error counter cannot tell an operator whether to restore a database or investigate one destination.

provisions.heading: Emit Excluded Reactions and Jobs After Commit
provisions.evidence: Which excluded reactions or jobs emit before their commit succeeds, or stage an outbox record? Look at each excluded reaction's and job's emit call.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job the outbox excludes MUST emit after its commit succeeds without staging an outbox record.
provisions.rationale: Without an outbox record, nothing survives a crash between the commit and the emit, so the reaction or job emits immediately after its commit succeeds and accepts the loss. Emitting before the commit risks worse: it fires for a change the database then rolls back.

provisions.heading: Exclude Manually Repeatable Reactions and Jobs
provisions.evidence: Which reactions or jobs whose loss the operators accept still carry outbox records? Look at the outbox records and the reactions and jobs they name.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT activate outbox for a reaction or job whose loss the operators accept and which they can repeat manually.
provisions.rationale: Outbox storage, dispatch, retries, and replay exist to prevent loss; a reaction or job whose loss the operators accept and can repeat by hand needs none of that machinery. The reaction's or job's `onFailure` states its handling, and the use case page records the accepted loss.

provisions.heading: Exclude Request-Transaction Dispatch
provisions.evidence: Which request paths dispatch a durable message inside the request transaction? Look at the endpoint and command handler paths.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST NOT dispatch a durable message inside the request transaction.
provisions.rationale: A network call inside the request transaction holds database locks while the outside world answers, and a slow target slows every request behind it. The request commits only to make the message eligible; the Worker performs the delivery later.

provisions.heading: Gate Dispatch on Readiness
provisions.evidence: Which unready hosts keep dispatching or polling a store that cannot serve requests? Look at the readiness check and the Worker's dispatch loop.
provisions.statement: A Worker host exposing readiness MUST gate dispatch and stop polling stores that cannot serve requests.
provisions.rationale: A host that reports unready still serves traffic it cannot finish when its Workers keep polling dead stores. Gating dispatch on readiness stops the polling, so the host fails fast and recovers instead of churning against storage that cannot answer.

provisions.heading: Group Outbox Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Which outbox infrastructure sits outside `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/` with no other home named in the documentation? Look at the outbox code folders and the project's documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep outbox record, storage, claim, and dispatch infrastructure under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/`.
provisions.rationale: The outbox record, storage, claim, and dispatch code form one mechanism with one owner. Keeping it under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/` puts every persistent dispatch question in one folder instead of scattered across the project.

provisions.heading: Identify Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Which event handlers process a repeated message as new work? Look at each handler's Command or side-effect boundary.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST use message ID or a business idempotency key at its Command or side-effect boundary.
provisions.rationale: Handling a repeat means recognizing it: the message ID or a business idempotency key gives the event handler a stable identity to check at its command or side-effect boundary. Without that key, the handler processes the repeat as new work and pays, notifies, or ships twice.

provisions.heading: Isolate the Worker Host
provisions.evidence: Which outbox Worker hosts share a project with the request host, with no documented choice? Look at the solution's projects.
provisions.statement: Keep the outbox Worker host in its own project.
provisions.rationale: The Worker runs as its own process with its own lifetime, scaling, and configuration, apart from the request host. Its own project keeps that independence visible and stops request concerns leaking into dispatch configuration.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Mapping with Integration
provisions.evidence: Which provider mappings sit in the shared dispatch path with no documented choice? Look at the dispatch code and the integration projects.
provisions.statement: Keep Integration Event-to-provider mapping in the integration that owns the side effect.
provisions.rationale: Each provider speaks its own transport with its own mapping, retries, and quirks. The integration that owns the side effect owns that mapping, so a provider change touches one integration instead of the shared dispatch path.

provisions.heading: Model Outbox Lifecycle States
provisions.evidence: Which outbox states lack a sealed record under the abstract base, or a documented transition? Look at the outbox state types and their transitions.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST model its lifecycle as an abstract state base with one sealed record for each of pending, processing, dispatched, and dead-letter.
provisions.rationale: `pending` becomes `processing`, and `processing` becomes `dispatched`, `pending`, or `dead-letter`, while audited replay moves `dead-letter` back to `pending`. Three of the four states carry data the others do not: `processing` holds a lease expiry, `dispatched` holds a dispatch time, and `dead-letter` holds a failure reason and an attempt count. A four-value label forces those onto nullable columns that mean something in one state each, which is the shape `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-closed-set-of-domain-values-as-a-closed-type-hierarchy` removes everywhere else.
provisions.example: `OutboxState.Processing` carries one unexpired lease before a dispatcher records `OutboxState.Dispatched` or a retry state.

provisions.heading: Plan Undispatched Rollback Records
provisions.evidence: Which rollback runbooks omit records the new writer staged but nobody dispatched? Look at each rollback runbook record.
provisions.statement: A rollback Runbook MUST include records created by the new writer but not yet dispatched.
provisions.rationale: Rolling back the deployment does not roll back the store: records the new writer staged but nobody dispatched stay behind. The rollback Runbook names how the previous version handles them, or they sit undispatched with no owner and no reader.

provisions.heading: Preserve Message Identity During Retry
provisions.evidence: Which retry or replay paths mint a new message ID? Look at the dispatcher's retry and replay code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST preserve message ID across retry and replay.
provisions.rationale: The target suppresses a repeat by recognizing its identity, which works only when every retry and replay carries the same message ID. A dispatcher that mints a new ID per attempt turns each retry into a new message the target processes again.

provisions.heading: Protect Active Worker Compatibility
provisions.evidence: Which new messages carry a type or schema version that an active Worker cannot read? Look at the Worker's readers and the messages the WebApi emits.
provisions.statement: New WebApi code MUST emit a message only after every active Worker can read its type and schema version.
provisions.rationale: WebApi writers and Worker dispatchers deploy independently, so a writer can run ahead of the oldest active Worker. When the writer emits a shape that Worker cannot read, those messages dead-letter on arrival through no fault of their own.

provisions.heading: Publish Backlog Indicators
provisions.evidence: Which of the six backlog indicators does the deployment leave unpublished? Look at the metrics the Worker exports.
provisions.statement: An outbox deployment MUST publish pending count, failed count, oldest pending age, attempts, dispatch duration, and success rate.
provisions.rationale: Pending count, failed count, oldest pending age, attempts, dispatch duration, and success rate together show whether delivery keeps up: growth in the backlog or age reveals a stall, while duration and success rate reveal a struggling target. Without these indicators, the first sign of failure is a customer asking where their message went.

provisions.heading: Record Durable Delivery Behavior
provisions.evidence: Which delivery specifications leave out the guarantee, downstream boundary, duplicate behavior, retry horizon, or recovery runbook? Look at each durable-delivery specification.
provisions.statement: A durable-delivery specification MUST document delivery guarantee, downstream boundary, duplicate behavior, retry horizon, and recovery runbook.
provisions.rationale: Delivery crosses a system boundary, so the team agrees up front on the guarantee, the boundary, the duplicate behavior, the retry horizon, and the runbook that recovers when delivery fails. Without that agreement, the writer assumes once-only delivery while the target assumes retries, and both discover the mismatch in production. The agreement lands before the first message does.

provisions.heading: Reject Independent Outbox Commits
provisions.evidence: Which outbox writers use a separate connection or commit? Look at each writer source and its path into the business session.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST NOT use another connection or independent commit for required durable delivery.
provisions.rationale: Two commits on two connections can split around a crash: the business change persists while the message rolls back, or the message persists for a change that never happened. Sharing one PostgreSQL database does not make separate transactions atomic, so the message joins the business transaction instead.

provisions.heading: Release Claim Transactions Before Calls
provisions.evidence: Which claim transactions stay open across a network call? Look at the Worker's dispatch path.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT hold an outbox claim transaction open during a network call.
provisions.rationale: A network call to a slow target can last seconds or minutes. Holding the claim transaction open across that call pins database locks and connection slots, starving the Workers behind it; releasing the claim first lets the database serve other work while the call runs.

provisions.heading: Requeue Expired Claims
provisions.evidence: Which expired claims stay out of eligible work? Look at the requeue query in the outbox store and its tests.
provisions.statement: An outbox store MUST return expired claims to eligible work.
provisions.rationale: A Worker can die between claiming a record and dispatching it. Returning expired claims to eligible work lets a live Worker pick them up, so one crash delays a message instead of losing it.

provisions.heading: Restrict Completion to Current Lease Owners
provisions.evidence: Which record updates run without checking the current lease and fencing value? Look at each update statement in the outbox store.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST update an outbox record only while it owns the matching lease and fencing value.
provisions.rationale: A Worker that lost its lease, through a crash, a pause, or an expiry, can wake up after another Worker claimed the same record. Checking the lease and fencing value before each update stops the stale Worker from overwriting the current owner's result.

provisions.heading: Restrict Message Retry to Claimed Records
provisions.evidence: Which retry or poison-handling paths act on records that hold no claim? Look at the dispatcher's retry and poison code.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST apply message retry and poison handling only to claimed outbox records.
provisions.rationale: Retry and poison handling act on a claimed message; when the store itself is down, no claim exists and no message waits for delivery. Running retry logic against the outage double-counts attempts and can dead-letter messages whose only fault was an unreachable store.

provisions.heading: Serialize Durable Messages
provisions.evidence: Which pending durable messages reach no serialized outbox record? Look at the outbox writer and its record type.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST serialize each pending durable message into an outbox record.
provisions.rationale: The command scope ends when the request ends, while dispatch happens later in a Worker that never saw the request. Serializing the message into an outbox record gives that Worker everything it needs after the scope is gone.

provisions.heading: Set Delivery Alerts
provisions.evidence: Which alert thresholds sit outside a setting record derived from a use-case delivery target? Look at the setting records beside each use case.
provisions.statement: An outbox deployment MUST set alert thresholds as setting records from its use-case delivery target.
provisions.rationale: A shipment notice delayed an hour and a receipt delayed a week carry different business consequences, so each use case sets alert thresholds from its own delivery target. Setting records hold those thresholds, so the alert fires when delay passes what the business accepted.

provisions.heading: Stage After-Commit Effects in the Outbox
provisions.evidence: Which after-commit `emits` or `runs` effects, or domain events, stage outside the transaction of their aggregate changes? Look at each command handler's effects and the outbox writes beside them.
provisions.statement: A use case declaring `after-commit` `emits` or `runs` effects MUST stage each effect in the outbox in the same transaction as its changes.
provisions.rationale: After-commit timing promises the message follows the commit: staged in the same transaction, the change and its message share one fate. An `emits` effect is a domain event the aggregate raises, and persistence stages that event in the outbox in the same commit as the aggregate, as `litespec/backend/application#emit-declared-integration-events-after-commit` requires. An effect sent from memory instead would vanish on a crash between the commit and the send. `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-every-effect-with-one-verb-and-its-timing` states the effect verbs and their timing, and `async` effects dispatch without the transaction.

provisions.heading: Stage Messages with Business Work
provisions.evidence: Which pending durable messages stage outside the scoped session of their aggregate changes? Look at each command post-handler and its session.
provisions.statement: A command post-handler MUST stage pending durable messages in the same scoped business session as its aggregate changes.
provisions.rationale: The business change and its message share one fate: both persist or neither does. Staging the message in the same scoped business session as the aggregate changes puts both under one commit, so a crash can never leave an accepted change without its message or a message without its change.

provisions.heading: Store Failure and Completion Evidence
provisions.evidence: Which outbox records drop their last error summary or completion time? Look at the outbox record type and its update code.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST retain its last error summary and completion time.
provisions.rationale: When delivery stalls, the operator opens the record first: the last error summary says why the previous attempt failed, and the completion time says which records finished. Without that evidence on the record, each investigation starts from scattered logs instead.

provisions.heading: Store Required Message Fields
provisions.evidence: Which outbox records lack identity, kind, type, schema version, time, payload, tenant, state, attempt, or next-attempt data? Look at the outbox record type.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST contain message identity, kind, stable type, schema version, time, payload, tenant, state, attempt, and next-attempt data.
provisions.rationale: The dispatcher, the retry logic, and the operator each read the record: identity and type route it, the schema version selects its reader, time and tenant scope it, and state, attempt, and next-attempt data drive the retry. A field stored nowhere forces one of those readers to guess.

provisions.heading: Support Coexisting Message Producers
provisions.evidence: Which application versions that can coexist have no reader in the dispatcher? Look at the dispatcher's version selection and its tests.
provisions.statement: A deployed dispatcher MUST process records from every application version that can coexist during rollout or rollback.
provisions.rationale: During rollout and rollback, several application versions share one store and write different valid shapes into it. The dispatcher reads from every version that can coexist, or the deployment itself causes delivery failures. Each message record therefore carries its own shape version, and the dispatcher selects a reader from that value. Adding an optional member with a defined absent-value behavior needs no new version. Removing a member, renaming one, narrowing a type, or changing a discriminator needs a new version, and the reader for each version stays until no record carries that version.

provisions.heading: Version Message Types
provisions.evidence: Which outbox messages lack a stable type name or an explicit schema version? Look at each outbox message type.
provisions.statement: An outbox message MUST use a stable type name and explicit schema version.
provisions.rationale: An outbox record outlives the deployment that wrote it, so the dispatcher meets records written by several versions at once. A stable type name with an explicit schema version tells the dispatcher which reader parses each record; without the pair, one shape change breaks every record written before it.

provisions.heading: Bound Plan Amounts in Settings
provisions.evidence: Which plan allowances live outside a setting the gated use case cites? Look at the gated use cases beside their settings.
provisions.statement: Each amount a plan allows MUST live as a setting the gated use case cites.
provisions.rationale: An allowance buried in code changes only with a release, and each plan's number hides in a different branch. A setting states the range, the setter, and the bound behavior, and the gated use case cites it, so raising a tier edits the setting instead of the code. `litespec/core/access#cite-the-setting-or-plan-behind-every-entitlement` requires the citation, and `litespec/core/use-cases#hold-every-setting-default-to-a-requirement` holds a commercial default to its requirement.
provisions.example: The export-row cap lives as `setting/spending.max-export-rows` with an operator-set value, and the export command cites it.

provisions.heading: Gate Behavior Through Permissions
provisions.evidence: Which gated use cases declare no permission in their grant, or one that a plan without the entitlement grants? Look at each gated use case's grant.
provisions.statement: A gated use case MUST declare a permission that only an entitled plan grants.
provisions.rationale: The permission chain already joins actors to use cases: the actor holds a role, the role allows a permission, and the use case declares it in its grant, as the [access page](../core/access.md) states. A plan grants its permissions through that chain, so entitlement is a grant like any other instead of a second access system beside the first.

provisions.heading: Hide Unentitled Actions on Screens
provisions.evidence: Which screens show an action the acting plan does not entitle? Look at each screen's actions.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST NOT offer an action the acting plan does not entitle.
provisions.rationale: The server refuses what the plan does not entitle, and the screen reflects that refusal before the call: a button for an unentitled action invites a failure the product already decided. Hiding or disabling the action shows each plan only what it may run.

provisions.heading: Record Each Plan Once
provisions.evidence: Which plans lack a record with their entitlements, or share a record with another plan? Look at the requirement pages under `.litespec/intent/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting `plans` MUST record each plan once with its name and entitlements.
provisions.rationale: A plan named in two places disagrees the day one updates without the other: one record promises what the gate refuses. One record per plan holds the name and the entitlements, so a plan change is one edit in one place.
provisions.example: The team tier names the export use case and the row cap it unlocks.

provisions.heading: Refuse Runs Beyond Entitlement
provisions.evidence: Which runs past their plan end outside the named refusal result? Look at the use case tests for plan limits.
provisions.statement: A use case run past its plan MUST end in the refusal result the use case names for that run.
provisions.rationale: A run past its plan is a refusal like any other: it ends in the named refusal result with its stable code, as the [behavior page](../core/behavior.md) states, so callers branch on one code instead of guessing from an error page. The code stays stable while prices and allowances move.

provisions.heading: Resolve the Acting Plan from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Which acting plans resolve from caller input instead of verified subscription state? Look at the plan resolution code.
provisions.statement: The product MUST resolve the acting plan from verified subscription state, never from caller input.
provisions.rationale: The plan decides what runs, so only verified subscription state resolves it: a plan the caller supplies itself is a choice, not a fact. The [multitenancy extension](tenancy.md) treats tenant identity the same way.

provisions.heading: Resolve the Acting Plan in the Authorization Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Which use cases find the acting plan outside the authorization pipeline, with no plan-resolution convention naming where? Look at the authorization pipeline and that convention.
provisions.statement: Resolve the acting plan where the pipeline authorizes the use case.
provisions.rationale: Authorization already runs in the pipeline with the actor and the target in hand. Resolving the plan there gives every use case the same answer from the same verified state, instead of each handler querying subscriptions its own way.

provisions.heading: Authenticate and Authorize Subscriptions
provisions.evidence: Which connection tests accept an unauthenticated connection, or a scoped subscription with no authorization check? Look at the connection and subscription tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST authenticate each connection and authorize every user-, tenant-, or resource-scoped subscription.
provisions.rationale: Connecting proves who the caller is; it says nothing about which user's, tenant's, or resource's updates the caller may hear. Each user-, tenant-, or resource-scoped subscription checks its own authorization, so one valid connection cannot listen in on another tenant's data.

provisions.heading: Bound Realtime Resources
provisions.evidence: Which of the four deployment bounds lack a setting record beside the deployment? Look at the setting records and the deployment configuration.
provisions.statement: A realtime deployment MUST set four setting-record bounds: concurrent connections per host, receive message size, parallel invocations per connection, and client timeout.
provisions.rationale: Each open connection holds memory, each message costs CPU, and a flood of either starves the host. The deployment sets four bounds as setting records - concurrent connections per host, receive message size, parallel invocations per connection, and client timeout - with each value drawn from the deployment's own connection count and message size and the observation that produced it. [The platform's realtime security guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/signalr/security) names the same settings.

provisions.heading: Declare Realtime Freshness
provisions.evidence: Which realtime-served queries lack an immediate or advisory freshness object on their output? Look at the served query beside the realtime use case.
provisions.statement: A query served over realtime MUST declare a `freshness` object with `mode` of `immediate` or `advisory` on its output.
provisions.rationale: A realtime channel delivers an update seconds after the change, so the served query promises `{"mode": "immediate"}`; where the pushed value still awaits a later decision, it promises `{"mode": "advisory", "authority": "<record id>"}` naming the record that holds the authoritative value. Without the declared freshness, a client cannot tell whether the live value is final or provisional.

provisions.heading: Place Realtime Code at Outer Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Which realtime transport code sits outside the documented boundaries, with no realtime-placement convention? Look at the WebApi, Infrastructure, and `lib/realtime/` folders.
provisions.statement: Keep hubs or endpoints in WebApi, publication adapters in Infrastructure, and browser connections under `lib/realtime/`.
provisions.rationale: Hubs, endpoints, publication adapters, and browser connections deal in transport and provider detail, not business rules. Keeping them at the outer boundaries leaves business features owning only the narrow functions they call.

provisions.heading: Reconnect and Refresh Authoritative State
provisions.evidence: Which clients reconnect without bounded backoff, or skip the authoritative refresh after a gap? Look at the recovery tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime client MUST reconnect with bounded backoff and refresh authoritative state after a connection gap.
provisions.rationale: Connections drop, and a notification sent during the gap never arrives. Bounded backoff reconnects without hammering the server, and refreshing authoritative state after the gap replaces whatever the missed notifications would have changed.

provisions.heading: Record Realtime Need
provisions.evidence: Which realtime use case pages lack the polling record, measured cost, update target, expected connections, or recovery behavior? Look at each realtime use case page.
provisions.statement: A realtime use case MUST document polling behavior, measured cost, update latency, expected connections, and recovery behavior.
provisions.rationale: Open connections cost memory, CPU, and operating attention on every host, so the team writes down what polling costs, what the update target requires, and how many connections to expect before choosing transport. The use case page carries that record, so a later reviewer sees which measurements justified the choice.

provisions.heading: Record Transport Support
provisions.evidence: Which realtime use case pages name no transport choice or expected hosted-platform support? Look at each use case page.
provisions.statement: A realtime use case MUST record its transport choice and expected hosted-platform support.
provisions.rationale: Hosted platforms limit connection duration, idle timeouts, and transport upgrades in ways that differ per host. Recording the transport choice with its expected platform support surfaces the mismatch before deployment instead of during the first long-lived connection.

provisions.heading: Reject Cosmetic Realtime Adoption
provisions.evidence: Which realtime decisions cite no measured update requirement? Look at the use case page beside each realtime transport.
provisions.statement: A product MUST NOT activate realtime only to make an interface feel immediate.
provisions.rationale: Realtime transport that serves only a feeling of immediacy spends connection capacity and operating attention without moving any target. The extension asks for a measured update requirement first, so polling stays where polling suffices.

provisions.heading: Reject Unbounded Slow-Client Buffering
provisions.evidence: Which server code paths buffer a slow client's stream without a bound or backpressure? Look at the connection and send code.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST NOT buffer an unbounded stream for a slow client.
provisions.rationale: A client that reads slower than the server writes grows its buffer without end, consuming host memory meant for every subscriber. Bounded buffering with backpressure disconnects or slows the laggard instead of letting one slow reader starve the rest.

provisions.heading: Revalidate Long-Lived Access
provisions.evidence: Which connections keep streaming after their token or session expires? Look at the revalidation tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST revalidate long-lived access according to token and session lifetime.
provisions.rationale: A connection can outlive the grant that opened it: tokens expire, roles change, sessions end. Revalidating access on token and session lifetime closes the connection whose grant died instead of streaming updates to a caller who no longer qualifies.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Through Narrow Functions
provisions.evidence: Which features subscribe to the raw connection instead of a use-case-specific function? Look at each feature module's realtime calls.
provisions.statement: Let feature modules subscribe through narrow use-case-specific functions.
provisions.rationale: A feature that touches the raw connection spreads subscription strings and payload shapes through business code. Narrow use-case-specific functions show each subscription's inputs and effects beside the feature that owns them.

provisions.heading: Tolerate Notification Ordering Differences
provisions.evidence: Which duplicate or reordered notifications leave client state wrong? Look at the client state tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime client MUST safely handle duplicate and out-of-order notifications.
provisions.rationale: The transport can deliver a notification twice or deliver two of them out of order. A client that applies each notification as an absolute update corrupts its state on the first duplicate; a client built for repeats and reordering converges on the truth either way.

provisions.heading: Use Server-Sent Events for Notifications
provisions.evidence: Which one-way notifications travel over a boundary other than server-sent events? Look at the notification endpoints in code.
provisions.statement: A one-way server notification use case MUST use server-sent events.
provisions.rationale: A notification that flows one way, from server to browser, needs no bidirectional channel with groups and fallback. Server-sent events carry it over plain HTTP, which passes through proxies and firewalls without extra negotiation.

provisions.heading: Use SignalR for Interactive Messaging
provisions.evidence: Which bidirectional use cases run without SignalR groups, messages, or fallback? Look at each use case's hub code.
provisions.statement: A use case requiring bidirectional messages, server groups, or transport fallback MUST use SignalR.
provisions.rationale: Two-way messages, server-managed groups, and transport fallback need a channel built for interaction, which one-way events cannot provide. SignalR supplies all three, so the use case that needs them takes SignalR instead of stretching events past their shape.

provisions.heading: Declare the Release Stage
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a `stage` selection with a missing or unknown `releaseStage`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST declare `pre-production` or `production` as its release stage in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The release stage is a project fact, not a departure from any rule, so it lives as data in the `stage` selection: `releaseStage` holds `pre-production` or `production`, while each deferral lives in its own departure record. Without the declared stage, tools and reviewers cannot tell which provisions the project owes today.
provisions.example:
A consumer with no customer data in any deployment declares the early stage.

```yaml
selectedExtensions:
  - id: stage
    criterion: no deployment holds customer data
    releaseStage: pre-production
```

provisions.heading: Defer Named Provisions Until Promotion
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` refuses a deferral departure naming an unknown provision, and any deferral in `production`; `litespec model check` reports `departure-expired` for a departure past its `expiresOn`.
provisions.statement: A `pre-production` consumer MUST record each deferred provision as a departure expiring at promotion, with a `production` consumer carrying no deferred provision.
provisions.rationale: An early-stage deferral without a named end becomes permanent by neglect. Each departure names the deferred provision in `covers` with the date its deferral ends in `expiresOn`, and the promotion decision names the same provisions, so promotion closes every deferral at once.
provisions.example:
Each deferral is a departure covering its provision until promotion.

```yaml
type: departure
id: departure/compat-classification-until-promotion
title: Compat Classification Until Promotion
covers:
  - litespec/ext/compat#classify-breaking-contract-changes
paths:
  - apps/api/**
reason: No consumer reads the contract before the first deployment.
exit: Promotion to production ends the deferral and the classification applies.
expiresOn: 2026-12-01
```

provisions.heading: Promote Through a Recorded Decision
provisions.evidence: Which promotion decisions under `.litespec/intent/decisions/` come after the first deployment holds customer data, or leave a deferred provision open? Look at the decision records beside the deferrals they end.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record its promotion to `production` as a decision before its first deployment holds customer data, ending every deferred provision.
provisions.rationale: Promotion is the moment relaxed provisions end, and an unrecorded moment never arrives: the relaxed provisions last until somebody notices they never ended. The decision stands in git before the first deployment holds customer data, so the data sits under full rules from day one. The decision also covers the migration and cutover work that moves customer data into production.

provisions.heading: Apply Cross-Tenant Disclosure Policy
provisions.evidence: Which cross-tenant responses break the documented not-found or forbidden policy? Look at the API tests.
provisions.statement: A cross-tenant resource response MUST use the documented not-found or forbidden policy.
provisions.rationale: A caller that names another tenant's resource forces an answer: pretend it does not exist, or admit it exists and refuse. The product documents one policy and applies it to every cross-tenant response, so callers cannot probe for resources through inconsistent answers.

provisions.heading: Audit Actions Taken Under Delegation
provisions.evidence: Which actions under delegation record no delegation grant? Look at the audit records of delegated actions.
provisions.statement: An action that an actor takes under delegation MUST record the delegation grant used.
provisions.rationale: An acted-for action without a marker reads exactly like the delegator's own action, so a reviewer cannot tell who actually acted. Recording the delegation grant used puts the acting party on the record beside the delegator. `litespec/ext/audit#record-delegated-administrative-access` states the same marker for administrative grants.

provisions.heading: Avoid Unplanned Isolation Models
provisions.evidence: Which mixed isolation models trace to no decision, or to a decision with no data evolution plan? Look at each mixed model beside its decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant system MUST NOT mix isolation models without a decision and data evolution plan.
provisions.rationale: One part of the product on shared tables and another on separate databases answers which rows each tenant sees two ways. Each mixed model needs its own decision with a data evolution plan, or backup, restore, and incident response each guess which guarantee covers which data.

provisions.heading: Bound Every Delegation in Time
provisions.evidence: Which delegations carry neither an expiry nor a revocation path? Look at each delegation record.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST carry an expiry or a revocation path.
provisions.rationale: A grant with no end outlives its reason: the assistant keeps acting after the engagement ends, and nobody reopens the pairing because no date asks for it. An expiry ends the pairing on its date, and a revocation path ends it on demand. Either way, the end is stated beside the grant instead of left for an incident to discover.

provisions.heading: Declare Delegation Grants on Both Sides
provisions.evidence: Which delegations lack a delegator grant or an acting grant? Look at each delegation's grants.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST declare the delegator grant naming who may be acted for and the acting grant naming who may act.
provisions.rationale: Delegation lets one actor act for another, so a grant on one side alone leaves the other side unreviewed. The delegator grant names the role at its scope that may be acted for and the permissions open to delegation; the acting grant names the role permitted to act and the pairing it acts under. `litespec/core/access#grant-across-tenants-only-through-declared-delegation` requires both declarations.
