provisions.example: An assistant acts for a manager only where the manager delegation grant and the assistant acting grant both name the pairing.

provisions.heading: Define Tenant Isolation
provisions.evidence: Which adoption decisions name an isolation model without its guarantee or operating trade-off? Look at the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant decision MUST define shared-table, schema, or database isolation and state its guarantee and operating trade-off.
provisions.rationale: Shared tables, separate schemas, and separate databases isolate differently and operate differently: each choice moves work between queries, migrations, backups, and scaling. Naming the model with its guarantee and its operating trade-off tells every later choice which isolation it can rely on.

provisions.heading: Isolate Administrative Cross-Tenant Access
provisions.evidence: Which administrative cross-tenant use cases name no platform-scope permission, or have a run with no audit record? Look at the use case permissions beside the audit trail.
provisions.statement: An administrative cross-tenant operation MUST require a permission the actor holds through a role at platform scope, writing an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Support and operations sometimes reach across tenants, and that exceptional reach needs exceptional control: a permission held through a role at platform scope, with an audit record for every use. Without both, one support login becomes an unscoped key to every customer's data. Grants that let one tenant act for another follow [Declare Delegation Grants on Both Sides](#declare-delegation-grants-on-both-sides) instead.

provisions.heading: Pass Tenant Scope Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Which Domain code reads ambient tenant state, with no tenant-scope convention naming how the Domain receives scope? Look at the Domain code.
provisions.statement: Pass tenant scope through Application messages or trusted ports rather than ambient Domain request state.
provisions.rationale: Domain logic that reads the tenant from ambient request state depends on the host to run at all, which complicates tests and reuse. Passing the scope through Application messages or trusted ports keeps the tenant visible in the call and the Domain free of host state.

provisions.heading: Protect Tenant Diagnostics
provisions.evidence: Which error, log, metric, or trace outputs hold another tenant's identifiers or data? Look at the output samples in the tests.
provisions.statement: Errors, logs, metrics, and traces MUST NOT reveal another tenant's business identifiers or data.
provisions.rationale: Errors, logs, metrics, and traces travel to people the API never authorized: support screens, dashboards, and log stores shared across tenants. Scrubbing other tenants' identifiers and data from diagnostics keeps the disclosure policy whole past the API boundary.

provisions.heading: Prove Delegated Calls with Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Which delegations prove no allowed call, or no refused call, with scenarios? Look at the delegation scenarios.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST prove an allowed call and a refused call with scenarios.
provisions.rationale: A pairing described only in prose hides where its grant stops: the allowed assistant and the uninvited one read alike. A scenario walking an allowed call and a scenario ending a call without delegation in the derived forbidden result pin the boundary as checked facts. `litespec/core/access#prove-hierarchies-derived-trust-and-delegation-with-scenarios` requires both scenarios.

provisions.heading: Record an All-Tenant Operation
provisions.evidence: Which all-tenant run records omit the actor, operation, reason, tenant count, or reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption bound? Look at the run records.
provisions.statement: An all-tenant operation MUST record actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption decision bound.
provisions.rationale: A documented scope states what an operation may touch, not what one run touched, and the run is what a tenant asks about after an incident. An all-tenant run is also the one case where no single tenant's audit trail holds the whole event. [The OWASP logging guidance](https://owasp.org/www-project-cheat-sheets/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet) treats an administrative action over many subjects as one event to record: actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption decision bound. When the audit extension is selected, the record is an audit record; otherwise it stays a standalone record.
provisions.example: A support export covering every tenant records the operator, the export, the tenant count, and the incident it was run for.

provisions.heading: Record Delegation Grants with Roles
provisions.evidence: Which delegation grants sit off their role page, with no delegation-records convention naming where grants live? Look at the role pages beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Record each delegation grant on the role page that holds it.
provisions.rationale: The grant qualifies the role: the delegator role names who may be acted for, and the acting role names who may act. Recording each grant on its role page keeps the pairing beside the permission it extends, so a review reads both at once.

provisions.heading: Record the Tenant Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Which tenant adoption decisions omit the source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, evolution path, or enumeration bound? Look at the decision under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting `tenancy` MUST record a decision naming tenant source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, evolution path, and enumeration bound.
provisions.rationale: Tenant source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, and evolution path interact across every boundary, so one decision records them together before code assumes any of them. The enumeration bound caps how many tenant identifiers an all-tenant record lists.

provisions.heading: Reject Unrestricted Tenant Input
provisions.evidence: Which tenant resolver paths accept a tenant identifier from request data? Look at the tenant resolver code.
provisions.statement: A tenant resolver MUST NOT accept an unrestricted tenant ID from request data.
provisions.rationale: A tenant ID taken straight from request data lets any caller name any tenant. Rejecting unrestricted input keeps the request from choosing a data boundary outside its authenticated context.

provisions.heading: Resolve Tenant Identity from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Which trusted host boundaries resolve the tenant from a source that is not authenticated? Look at each boundary's tenant resolution.
provisions.statement: A trusted host boundary MUST resolve tenant identity from verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source.
provisions.rationale: The tenant decides which data the request may touch, so only a trusted host boundary resolves it: verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source. An identity the caller supplies itself is a choice, not a fact.

provisions.heading: Scope Delegated Grants to Named Permissions
provisions.evidence: Which delegations name no delegated permission, or open all permissions? Look at each delegation's permission list.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST name the permissions it delegates, never all permissions.
provisions.rationale: A delegation open to every permission hands the whole tenant to the acting party: one pairing meant for reading reports also moves money. Naming each delegated permission bounds the pairing to what the delegator intended, and each new permission needs its own review in the pull request before the acting party holds it.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Use Case to Its Tenant Reach
provisions.evidence: Which use cases declare none of own, cross, public, or none in their access tenant scope? Look at each use case's access declaration.
provisions.statement: Every use case in a multi-tenant product MUST declare its tenant scope as own, cross, public, or none in `access`.
provisions.rationale: The tenant scope bounds which tenant data the call may touch: own stays inside the caller tenant, cross reaches across tenants, public works beyond tenant boundaries, and none touches no tenant data. Without the scope, a read inside one tenant and a read across all tenants look the same. `litespec/core/access#scope-every-grant-to-its-tenant-reach` states the values.
provisions.example: An expense report declares `own`, a finance search across companies declares `cross`, a public catalog declares `public`, and a health check declares `none`.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant Operations
provisions.evidence: Which backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support, or investigation procedures state no one-tenant or all-tenant scope? Look at each procedure.
provisions.statement: Backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support access, and incident investigation MUST document one-tenant or all-tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support access, and incident investigation each touch more data than one normal request. Documenting each as one-tenant or all-tenant tells the operator how much data the run touches before it starts.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant-Owned Records
provisions.evidence: Which documents, queries, constraints, cache keys, outbox records, reactions, jobs, exports, or storage paths in code carry no tenant scope? Look at the code for each kind.
provisions.statement: Every tenant-owned document, query, unique constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and object-storage path MUST include tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Documents, queries, unique constraints, cache keys, outbox records, reactions, jobs, exports, and object-storage paths each form a boundary where tenants meet. Leaving tenant scope out of any one of them discloses or mixes customer data through exactly that gap.

provisions.heading: Use One Tenant Accessor
provisions.evidence: Which trusted host boundaries read the current tenant through more than one accessor, with no tenant-access convention naming where readers find the tenant? Look at the tenant accessors in code.
provisions.statement: Use one current-tenant accessor at the trusted host boundary.
provisions.rationale: Every boundary reads the current tenant, and two accessors can disagree about which tenant is current. One accessor at the trusted host boundary gives every reader the same answer from the same trusted source.

provisions.heading: Use Selected Tenant Storage Support
provisions.evidence: Which session-creation code resolves the tenant outside that provider's tenancy support? Look at each provider's session creation.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant persistence implementation MUST resolve its tenant at session creation through the selected provider's own tenancy support.
provisions.rationale: Session creation is the point that matters: a session opened without a tenant serves an unscoped next query. Resolving the tenant then, through the selected provider's own tenancy support, scopes every query the session runs, so no query carries the concern alone. Adding the filter per query instead leaves every new query one omission away from reading across tenants. The baseline provider resolves the tenant from the registered tenancy at session creation; an Entity Framework Core implementation resolves it when the context is created and applies it through a query filter convention.

provisions.heading: Use Typed Tenant Identities
provisions.evidence: Which tenant references carry no `TenantId` type, with no other type named by the tenant-identity convention? Look at the tenant references in code.
provisions.statement: Represent tenant identity with a strongly typed `TenantId`.
provisions.rationale: A bare string tenant ID passes anywhere a string passes: into an actor field, an aggregate key, or a log line. A strongly typed `TenantId` fails compilation at each of those mistakes instead of failing in production.

provisions.heading: Verify Actor and Target Tenancy
provisions.evidence: Which protected operations pass when the actor and target tenants mismatch? Look at the authorization tests.
provisions.statement: A protected multi-tenant operation MUST confirm actor and target tenancy, with the needed permission held at the resolved scope and the target belonging to it.
provisions.rationale: Checking the caller alone leaves the target unchecked: an authorized caller can still name a resource from another tenant. The operation confirms both sides through one chain: the actor holds a role at the resolved scope, the role allows the permission, the use case declares that permission in its grant, and the target belongs to the same scope.

provisions.heading: Bind Blazor Routes to Their Address
provisions.evidence: Which route entries declare more than one `@page` directive, or read query values from the URL by hand? Look in the route files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST declare its address in one `@page` directive and take its query values as `[SupplyParameterFromQuery]` properties.
provisions.rationale: The `@page` directive is the one place the router reads an address, and a query property the framework fills keeps the input typed.
provisions.example: The expense list route declares `@page "/expenses"` and takes its page number as a `[SupplyParameterFromQuery]` property.

provisions.heading: Build Blazor Forms on the Shared Form Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Which Blazor forms bypass the shared form entry point? Look in the form components under `Routes/` and `Modules/`.
provisions.statement: A Blazor form MUST build on the form entry point of the shared package, which wraps `EditForm`.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field wiring and the same display for a refusal on its field.
provisions.example: The expense claim form in `Modules/expenses/` uses the shared form entry point and no `EditForm` of its own.

provisions.heading: Declare Blazor Outside the Controlled UI Contract
provisions.evidence: Which Blazor frontends declare no entry point record naming Blazor and its replacement boundaries? Look in the entry point records.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST declare an entry point record naming Blazor and the boundaries that replace the controlled UI contract.
provisions.rationale: The controlled contract covers React and Svelte, so a Blazor frontend declares what replaces its checks instead of reporting as one with nothing to check.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Blazor entry point record names Blazor and the shared package boundaries that replace the controlled contract.

provisions.heading: Keep Blazor Test Mocks to the Owned Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Which tests replace the component model, `NavigationManager`, or the typed store? Look in the test doubles.
provisions.statement: A Blazor test MUST NOT replace the Razor component model, the `NavigationManager` service, or the typed store.
provisions.rationale: Those three are the stack's own behavior, and a stand-in for any of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: An expense list test renders the real component and seeds the typed store with claims.

provisions.heading: Keep Class and Style Bindings Out of Blazor Page Code
provisions.evidence: Which Blazor components under `Routes/` or `Modules/` set a `class` or `style` attribute? Look in the `.razor` files there.
provisions.statement: A Blazor component under `Routes/` or `Modules/` MUST NOT set a `class` or `style` attribute on any element.
provisions.rationale: The shared package's composites own spacing, size, and placement, so a class or style attribute in route code is a second layout that no composite answers to.
provisions.example: The expense total in `Routes/ExpenseList.razor` draws through a shared composite and sets no class attribute.

provisions.heading: Keep Layouts and Error Components Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Which layout or error components carry a screen mark? Look in `Frame/` and the route files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor layout component or error component MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout or error component draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it links an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: `Frame/MainLayout.razor.cs` carries no `<implements>` mark.

provisions.heading: Keep the Blazor Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Which Blazor files sit outside `Frame/`, `Routes/`, and `Modules/`? Look in the project tree.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST hold the frame in `Frame/`, one `.razor` file per address in `Routes/`, and the use-case code in `Modules/`.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed roots let a reader and a tool find the frame, the addresses, and the use-case code in the same place in every Blazor frontend.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense console keeps its frame in `Frame/`, the expense list route in `Routes/ExpenseList.razor`, and the expense use-case code in `Modules/expenses/`.

provisions.heading: Load Blazor Route Data Before Its View Renders
provisions.evidence: Which route views draw a read before its `OnInitializedAsync` finishes? Look in each route file.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST read each value it shows from the typed store in `OnInitializedAsync` before its view renders.
provisions.rationale: The typed store is the one shared cache on this stack, so a load there before the first render gives the view one answer for each read.
provisions.example: The expense list route loads its claims from the typed store and shows its loading state until the load finishes.

provisions.heading: Localize Blazor Copy Through a Pinned Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Which Blazor copy bypasses the pinned dictionary library, or misses fill, plural, typed keys, or a declared fallback? Look in the copy call sites.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST resolve its copy through a dictionary library pinned in `packages.nuget` that meets the locale-dictionary contract.
provisions.rationale: A pinned library keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language, with the fill, plural, and fallback behavior the contract states.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console resolves the "Receipt required" sentence through its pinned dictionary library in every language it ships.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Blazor Route Entry with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Which route entries lack a screen mark on their partial class? Look in each `.razor.cs` file under `Routes/`.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST carry the `<implements>` mark of the screen it renders on its partial class in its `.razor.cs` file.
provisions.rationale: The mark links the address to the screen record the way a .NET handler carries its use-case mark, so the builder and the check read one link.
provisions.example: `ExpenseList.razor.cs` carries `/// <implements>screen/claimwick-app.expense-list</implements>` on its partial class.

provisions.heading: Name Blazor Drawings with the Visual Suffix
provisions.evidence: Which custom drawings sit in `.razor` files whose names lack the `.visual.razor` suffix? Look in the project tree.
provisions.statement: A Blazor file holding a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.razor`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix marks the one place outside the composites, so a reader and a tool find every custom drawing in one search.
provisions.example: A receipt-scan preview is `ReceiptPreview.visual.razor`.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Only Through MarkupString
provisions.evidence: Which Blazor components write raw HTML through another type? Look for `MarkupString` and raw markup in the `.razor` files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only as a `MarkupString` value.
provisions.rationale: `MarkupString` is the one type Blazor renders without encoding, so every raw HTML sink is a type a search finds.
provisions.example: The expense note renders its sanitized HTML through `(MarkupString)` after its recorded sanitization decision.

provisions.heading: Run Blazor Logic Tests on xunit.v3
provisions.evidence: Which logic tests run on another runner, or outside a plain .NET test project? Look in the test projects.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST run its logic tests as plain .NET test projects on `xunit.v3`, the version `packages.nuget` pins.
provisions.rationale: Logic tests need no browser, so a plain .NET runner keeps them fast, and one pinned runner keeps every test project on the same version.
provisions.example: The expense total rule has its test beside its module, in an xunit.v3 test project.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure in the Frame's Route Error Component
provisions.evidence: Which route failures render outside `Frame/RouteError.razor`? Look in the route files and the frame.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route MUST show its failure through `Frame/RouteError.razor`, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One route error component gives every route failure the same recovery and the same problem state.
provisions.example: An expense list that fails to load shows the problem state from `Frame/RouteError.razor` with its trace identifier.

provisions.heading: Use a Layout for the Blazor Shell
provisions.evidence: Which routes repeat frame markup instead of rendering inside the shell layout? Look in the route files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor shell MUST be a layout component that inherits `LayoutComponentBase` and holds the frame every child route shares.
provisions.rationale: A layout draws the shared frame once, so each route draws only its own page.
provisions.example: `Frame/MainLayout.razor` holds the navigation bar and the cross-route values every expense route shows.

provisions.heading: Validate Blazor Route Parameters Before Loading
provisions.evidence: Which route loads read an address parameter before validating it? Look in each route's load.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST validate each address parameter before its load reads it.
provisions.rationale: An address comes from outside the component, so a load that reads an unchecked value fails inside the page instead of at its boundary.
provisions.example: The expense list route rejects a page number below one before it reads the typed store.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Composite to the Shared Package
provisions.evidence: Which layout, control, or surface drawn by two pages is missing from the shared package exports? Look in the shared package exports and the drawing pages.
provisions.statement: A layout, a control, or a surface a second page needs MUST be added to the shared UI package, not written inside an application.
provisions.rationale: The second page that needs a layout, control, or surface proves the piece is shared, not page-specific. Written inside one application, it is reviewed against one use, styled for one context, and invisible to the floorplans that would carry it, so the third page writes it a third time or copies the first copy. Adding it to the shared package puts it where every page finds it and where its design is judged against every use.

provisions.heading: Compose Composites in Page Code
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-import-invalid` with the file and the refused import, tagged `[litespec/frontend/components#compose-composites-in-page-code]`. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A component under a route or module folder MUST import only the shared package's documented entry points.
provisions.rationale: A composite fixes its layout and exposes only the inputs its job needs, so every page that uses it draws the same shape. If page code could reach past the composite to the primitives, one page would tune spacing or order for itself, and the next page would copy that tuning instead of the composite. The product would then hold as many layouts as pages.
provisions.example:
An expense section in the expenses app draws its facts, its state, and its commands through shared composites, and declares no element, class, or style binding.

```text
EntitySection "title"
  StatusBadge "state"
  DetailActions "commands"
```

The section imports only the shared package entry point, so the layout it draws is the one the shared package owns for every other entity page.

provisions.heading: Expose Card and Section Titles as Headings
provisions.evidence: Which visible card, panel, or section titles render as non-heading elements? Look in the route suite output, which resolves each as a heading.
provisions.statement: Render a visible card, panel, or section title as a heading at its correct level.
provisions.rationale: Some primitive sources render a title prop as a plain text element. That removes the title from the page outline, so screen-reader users lose it as a navigation point and the route suite's heading check misses it. Rendering the title as a heading at its correct level keeps the outline and the test in agreement.

provisions.heading: Keep Component Inputs Narrow
provisions.evidence: Which composite inputs name a client, a store, or an aggregate instead of values and callbacks? Look in the shared package component signatures.
provisions.statement: A composite MUST receive the values and callbacks it needs, not a client, a store, or an aggregate.
provisions.rationale: The shared package serves applications it was not written against. A composite that takes a client, a store, or an aggregate takes one application's data model as its input, so it fits no application with a different model, and a change to that model breaks the shared package. Values and callbacks keep the composite free of any application's shape: the page translates its model into plain inputs, and the composite renders what it is given.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Values Typed Until Display
provisions.evidence: Which display strings are produced before the presentation boundary, or without an explicit locale and zone? Look in the presentation boundary and the components feeding it.
provisions.statement: Keep branded and generated identifier types until the presentation boundary converts them.
provisions.rationale: Dates, money, and status values carry meaning a display string loses: the instant, the amount, the code. Converting early spreads formatting choices across every component that touches the value, and each one picks its own locale and zone. Keeping the typed value until the presentation boundary converts it in one place, with explicit locale and zone behavior.

provisions.heading: Keep Error Boundaries Scoped
provisions.evidence: Which route failures render outside the route error surface, and which component boundaries leave their surroundings unusable? Look in the route error surfaces and the boundary components.
provisions.statement: Use the route error surface for route failure, and a component boundary only where recovery keeps the page usable.
provisions.rationale: An error boundary that catches a failure with no recovery of its own hides the error and leaves the surrounding page broken but silent. The route error surface owns route failure, with a designed recovery; a component boundary earns its place only where the rest of the page stays usable without the failed part. Each stack page names the error surface for its stack.

provisions.heading: Keep Shared UI in One Package
provisions.evidence: Which shared primitives or composites live outside the shared package? Look in the workspace packages and the application sources.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST hold its shared primitives and its composites in one shared UI package, with no copy in an application.
provisions.rationale: When two applications each hold a copy of one primitive, the first upstream update changes one copy and misses the other. Both copies still compile, so nothing reports the split, and the two applications drift into two visual languages. One package gives every application the same component, so one update reaches every screen.
provisions.example: The primitives sit in one folder beside the composites, and the composites import them.

provisions.heading: Make Touch Targets Fit a Finger
provisions.evidence: Which pointer target on a touch layout measures below 44 by 44 pixels? Look in the route suite output at the phone breakpoint.
provisions.statement: Size every pointer target at least 44 by 44 pixels where the primary pointer is coarse, and keep the 24 by 24 pixel minimum everywhere else.
provisions.rationale: The 24 pixel minimum of WCAG 2.5.8 stops a mouse user from missing a control, but a finger covers more than that, and a staff member approving expenses on a phone taps Reject when they meant Approve. A larger target on coarse pointers keeps dense desktop tables while giving touch layouts room. The mobile stacks already size targets for a finger.

provisions.heading: Name Components for Their Role
provisions.evidence: Which component names hide the role they play? Look in the shared package and module sources.
provisions.statement: Name a component for the role it plays, such as `ExpenseLinesSection` or `ReplayDeliveryDialog`.
provisions.rationale: A name such as `ExpenseComponent` or `GenericModal` describes the file type, so it fits any component and tells a searcher nothing. A name that states the role, such as `ExpenseLinesSection` or `ReplayDeliveryDialog`, tells the next author what the component does before they open it, and keeps two components for two jobs from sharing one vague name.

provisions.heading: Place a Drawing No Composite Makes in an Exception File
provisions.evidence: Which custom styling sits outside the files whose names mark drawings outside the composites, or uses values other than semantic theme tokens? Look in the exception files each stack page names.
provisions.statement: An exception file MUST declare custom styling only with semantic theme tokens.
provisions.rationale: Some drawings have no composite: a budget treemap, a receipt-scan preview, or a public marketing frame. Refusing them entirely would push the drawing into arbitrary values that no token governs, which is harder to find and restyle than a declared exception. The exception file keeps the drawing visible: its name says this page draws outside the composites, and semantic tokens keep it inside the product palette. Each stack page names the file pattern that marks an exception for its stack.

provisions.heading: Prefer a Composite over a Primitive
provisions.evidence: Which page sources import a primitive where the shared package provides a composite? Look in route and module imports.
provisions.statement: Page code MUST import a composite wherever the shared package provides one.
provisions.rationale: The composite holds the product's decision for one job: which layout, which behavior, which tone. The bare primitive holds none of those, so a page that imports it makes each decision again for itself, and two pages answer the same question two ways. Refusing the replaced primitive in page code sends every page to the decision already made.
provisions.example: `Card` is `Section`, `Table` is `DataTable`, `Badge` is `StatusBadge`, and `Input` and `Field` are the form fields.

provisions.heading: Render Control States
provisions.evidence: Which controls miss a disabled or pending state, allow a second submission while one is in flight, or leave recovery unusable? Look in the shared package components.
provisions.statement: A control MUST render disabled and pending so that a second submission stays impossible while one is in flight and recovery stays usable.
provisions.rationale: A control with no disabled state invites a second submission while the first is still in flight, and a control with no pending state shows no sign that anything is happening. Blocking the duplicate submission and keeping recovery usable give the user one safe path: wait, or recover. State names are glossary terms, as under `litespec/frontend/components#render-data-states`.

provisions.heading: Render Data States
provisions.evidence: Which data components miss a loading, empty, error, forbidden, or ready state, or name a state outside the glossary? Look in the shared package components and the glossary.
provisions.statement: A data component MUST render loading, empty, error, forbidden, and ready.
provisions.rationale: A component that renders only its ready state leaves the user with a blank region while data loads, after it fails, or when there is nothing to show. Each missing state is a screen with no design and no test visiting it. Naming every arrival state up front gives each one a designed drawing. A route adds `not-found` under `litespec/frontend/rendering#represent-route-states`, because a missing target resolves at the route rather than inside a component. Each state name is a term in the project glossary.

provisions.heading: Sanitize Untrusted Rich Content
provisions.evidence: Which untrusted rich content renders without a recorded decision naming the sanitizer, the allowed elements and attributes, the link policy, and the test cases? Look in the decision records and the rendering components.
provisions.statement: A component MUST NOT render untrusted rich content without its recorded sanitization decision.
provisions.rationale: Rich content written by one user renders in another user's browser, so unsanitized markup is a script injection path: whoever writes the content runs code as every user. The recorded decision names the sanitizer, the allowed elements and attributes, the link policy, and the test cases, so the boundary is explicit and reviewable instead of a different ad-hoc escape on every page.

provisions.heading: Show a Focus Indicator That Stands Out
provisions.evidence: Which control shows no focus indicator, or one below 3:1 against its surroundings, on keyboard focus? Look in the route suite output and the shared package's focus styles.
provisions.statement: A control MUST show, on keyboard focus, an indicator that reaches 3:1 contrast against the colors next to it, drawn in place of any platform indicator it removes.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: a keyboard user finds their place on the page by the indicator alone, and a faint ring on a gray row is no place at all. The indicator shows on keyboard focus rather than on every click, so pointer users see no ring they did not ask for, and keyboard users always see one. For example, the Approve button on an expense row shows a ring that stays visible on the selected row's tinted background.

provisions.heading: Support Keyboard, Focus, Labels, and Announcements
provisions.evidence: Which interactive UI lacks keyboard operation, visible focus, semantic elements, programmatic labels, or status announcements? Look in the route suite output.
provisions.statement: Interactive UI MUST support keyboard operation, visible focus, semantic elements, programmatic labels, and asynchronous status announcements.
provisions.rationale: Keyboard operation, visible focus, semantic elements, programmatic labels, and status announcements come free with platform controls and all break at once in a custom control. A mouse-only control locks out keyboard users, a missing label leaves screen-reader users guessing, and a silent update leaves anyone who does not see the screen change unaware of it. Starting from a platform control keeps all five properties, and the composite keeps them for every page that uses it. The five properties above are the ones a component can satisfy on its own. [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) adds criteria that only a flow or a page can satisfy, so each route answers them where the criterion applies: | Criterion | Level | What it means for the UI | |:---|:---|:---| | 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose | AA | A field collecting information about the user names its purpose, so the browser can fill it. | | 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast | AA | A control's boundary, state, and focus indicator reach 3:1 against what surrounds them. | | 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide | A | Content that moves or updates on its own for more than five seconds can be paused. | | 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) | AA | A focused control stays at least partly visible under a sticky header, bar, or panel. | | 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) | AAA | A focused control stays fully visible. | | 2.4.13 Focus Appearance | AAA | The focus indicator meets the stated minimum area and contrast. | | 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures | A | Every swipe, pinch, or multi-point action has a visible single-pointer alternative. | | 2.5.7 Dragging Movements | AA | Every drag action has a single-pointer alternative. | | 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) | AA | A pointer target measures at least 24 by 24 pixels, or meets the stated spacing. | | 3.2.6 Consistent Help | A | A help mechanism sits in the same relative order on every page that has one. | | 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) | AA | A command that moves money or changes recorded data can be reviewed, confirmed, or reversed. | | 3.3.7 Redundant Entry | A | Information already given in the same process is not asked for again. | | 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | AA | Sign-in offers a path with no cognitive function test. | | 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) | AAA | That path asks for no object recognition or personal content test either. | | 4.1.3 Status Messages | AA | A status that appears without a focus move reaches assistive technology through a live region. | The level column marks which target each criterion belongs to: AA for every project, AAA for a project that targets AAA.

provisions.heading: Use a Composite for a Content Image
provisions.evidence: Which content images render outside the shared image component or against the text policy for their kind? Look in page sources for unwrapped images.
provisions.statement: An informative or decorative image MUST render through the shared image component, which owns its shape, its sizing, and its fallback.
provisions.rationale: An informative image needs meaningful alternative text, and a decorative image needs empty alternative text so assistive tools skip it. A source and label written directly in a page bypass both rules: the author tracks which kind each image is and writes the matching text, on every page. The shared image component owns the shape, the sizing, the fallback, and the text policy, so each image gets the handling its kind needs. The raw-element rule refuses unwrapped images in page code under `litespec/frontend/components#use-composites-for-layout-and-interaction-in-page-code`.

provisions.heading: Use Composites for Layout and Interaction in Page Code
provisions.evidence: Which layout or interactive elements appear in route and module sources? Look in route and module sources; each stack page names the refused elements and the composite each refusal names.
provisions.statement: A component under a route or module folder MUST NOT declare a layout or interactive element.
provisions.rationale: A raw element is only markup: it carries no focus handling, no state behavior, and no accessibility wiring, so each page that declares one rebuilds behavior the composite already carries, usually worse. The lint refusal names the composite to use instead, so the author gets the replacement in the same message as the refusal and does not have to search the shared package.

provisions.heading: Use Declared Visual Variants
provisions.evidence: Which repeated variants bypass the shared variant helper or carry literal values in composites? Look in the shared package components.
provisions.statement: A repeated component variant MUST use theme tokens through the shared package's variant helper rather than repeated literal values.
provisions.rationale: When each composite writes its own pixel values, colors, or conditional branches for one variant, the copies start equal and drift with every later edit, because nothing points the author at the other copies. The variant helper holds each variant once, in theme tokens, so a change to the variant reaches every composite that uses it and every value stays inside the theme.

provisions.heading: Write No Class Name in Page Code
provisions.evidence: Which class or style bindings appear in route and module sources? Look in route and module sources; each stack page names the bindings its lint refuses.
provisions.statement: A component under a route or module folder MUST NOT declare a class or style binding.
provisions.rationale: The floorplan and the display composites own every spacing, size, and placement choice on a page. A class or style binding in route code is a second layout that answers to no composite, and the next route copies it because it looks like the local way to draw. Two sources of layout then disagree on the first redesign, so keeping classes out of page code leaves the floorplan as the one place a visual change lands. Each stack page names the class and style bindings this rule covers for its stack.

provisions.heading: Announce the Outcome of an Optimistic Update
provisions.evidence: Which reconciled outcomes differing from the shown value announce through no live region? Look in the route tests asserting the announcement.
provisions.statement: An optimistic update MUST announce its reconciled outcome through a live region when the server result differs from the value shown.
provisions.rationale: A rollback is a silent visual change: the shown value changes back with no event a screen reader announces. The user heard the optimistic value confirmed and hears nothing when it is withdrawn, so they act on a value the server refused. Announcing the reconciled outcome through a live region tells them what actually holds. [The ARIA live-region technique](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/aria/ARIA19) is the mechanism, and a test of the route asserts the announcement.

provisions.heading: Assign State to the Narrowest Owner
provisions.evidence: Which values live above their narrowest owner instead of the query cache, the address, form state, or component state? Look in the state declarations.
provisions.statement: A value MUST live with the narrowest owner that can hold it: server data, then the address, then form state, then the component's own state.
provisions.rationale: This provision gives each value the smallest audience that can use it. The [Where State Lives](#where-state-lives) concept names the order and why keeping a value above that owner costs unrelated components work and hides changes.

provisions.heading: Build a Form on the Shared Form Library
provisions.evidence: Which forms bypass the shared package form entry point or its registered field components? Look in the form sources and the shared package form entry point.
provisions.statement: Build a form on the shared package's form entry point and its registered field components.
provisions.rationale: A form library used directly in every use-case folder gives each folder its own fields, its own validation wiring, and its own error display, and none of them knows how to show a refusal on its field. The shared package's form entry point and registered field components hold those decisions once, so every form validates, renders, and refuses the same way.

provisions.heading: Classify State
provisions.evidence: Which aggregates introducing state name no durable, device-local, or derived classification on their page? Look on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: An aggregate introducing state MUST classify it as durable, device-local, or derived.
provisions.rationale: The classification decides what happens to the state: durable state is persisted, versioned, and exported, device-local state is persisted but excluded from export, and derived state is never persisted. Without a declared classification each reader guesses, and a value the user made can end up unpersisted while a computed value ends up stored and stale.
provisions.example: The expense draft for the Rotterdam client visit is durable state, the device copy of the receipt photo is device-local state, and the expense total for EXP-1042 is derived state computed from its lines.

provisions.heading: Generate the Client from the Published Contract
provisions.evidence: Which client, type, schema, or operation option is handwritten instead of generated from the published OpenAPI document? Look in the generated client directory and the contract it names.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST generate its client, types, schemas, and operation options from the API's published OpenAPI document.
provisions.rationale: A handwritten copy of a request, a response, or a schema drifts from the contract silently: the API changes, the copy still compiles, and the page sends a request the API no longer accepts. A generated client turns the same contract change into a compile error in every application at once, at every call site the change affects.

provisions.heading: Keep a Calendar Date Free of a Time Zone
provisions.evidence: Which dates with no time of day travel or display as instants converted through a time zone? Look in the date sends and renders beside the trip, payout, and billing reads.
provisions.statement: A date with no time of day, such as a trip day, a payout day or a billing month, MUST travel and display as a calendar date, never as an instant converted through a time zone.
provisions.rationale: A trip starting 8 October shows as 7 October to a reader west of the server once a date passes through a zone. The calendar date means the same day to every reader, wherever they sit. The frontend sends and renders the date itself, with no zone attached.

provisions.heading: Keep Schemas Use-Case Specific
provisions.evidence: Which form schemas or view models sit in a shared location with only one use case reading them? Look in the use-case folders and the shared schema locations.
provisions.statement: Keep a form schema or a view model in its owning use-case folder until a second use case needs it.
provisions.rationale: A schema shared before its second use case exists is a contract written for one reader. The second use case then either contorts itself to fit or breaks the first reader by changing the shared shape. Keeping a form schema or view model in its owning use-case folder until a second use case needs it lets the shared shape emerge from two real readers.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Out of Browser Storage
provisions.evidence: Which refresh tokens, provider secrets, or privileged credentials sit in browser storage or browser-visible variables? Look in the storage writes and the public variables.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT store a refresh token, a provider secret, or a privileged credential in browser storage or a browser-visible variable.
provisions.rationale: Local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, and a build-time public variable are all readable by any script on the page, so a secret kept there is available to the same injected script the secret is meant to resist. Refresh tokens, provider secrets, and privileged credentials therefore stay out of the browser entirely. A preference the user chooses, such as a theme or a locale, is not a secret and can be stored under a named key in the frame.

provisions.heading: Keep the Client Boundary in the Frame
provisions.evidence: Which client configuration, problem mapping, or download helpers sit in a use-case folder instead of the frame root? Look in the frame root and the use-case folders.
provisions.statement: Place the client configuration, problem mapping, and download helpers in the frame root, keeping them out of every use-case folder.
provisions.rationale: The client configuration, the problem mapping, and the download helpers serve every use case, so a copy in each use-case folder turns one change to the base address or the headers into an edit per folder, with the missed folder failing at runtime. The frame root holds them once, where every use case reaches them and no use case duplicates them.

provisions.heading: Keep the Session in an API Owned Cookie
provisions.evidence: Which tokens sit in frontend sources instead of the API-owned HTTP-only cookie? Look in the API session handling and the frontend sources.
provisions.statement: The API MUST hold the browser session in an HTTP-only cookie, with frontend code holding no token.
provisions.rationale: Every value a script can read is a value any script on the page can read, including a script an attacker injected. Tokens kept in frontend code or browser storage are therefore readable by the same attack the session is meant to resist. The API runs the authorization code flow and keeps the tokens encrypted in an HTTP-only cookie the browser sends on its own, so frontend code holds no token. A refused sign-in lands on a signed-out page rather than on an error, because the user is not signed in.

provisions.heading: Localize Copy Through Locale Dictionaries
provisions.evidence: Which copy bypasses the locale dictionaries, or misses fill, plural, chunking, typed keys, or a declared fallback? Look in the locale dictionaries and the copy call sites.
provisions.statement: Copy MUST resolve through locale dictionaries with fill and plural support, one chunk per language, and typed keys with a declared fallback.
provisions.rationale: One sentence written in two components drifts at the first rewording, because the author finds one copy and misses the other. A dictionary per language keeps each sentence in one place, keyed by a typed key the compiler checks, with fill and plural support so variable content and counts render correctly in every language. One chunk per language keeps a user's download to the language they read, and a key the catalog lacks fails where the declared fallback says it fails instead of rendering a raw key.
provisions.example: A workspace that carries its own dictionary machinery still meets the same contract.

provisions.heading: Make Optimistic Behavior Recoverable
provisions.evidence: Which optimistic updates lack a declared client identity, conflict behavior, rollback, or reconciliation path, and which money, irreversible, or uncertainly authorized actions run optimistically instead of waiting for the server? Look in the optimistic update definitions.
provisions.statement: An optimistic update MUST declare its stable client identity, its conflict behavior, its failure rollback, and its reconciliation path.
provisions.rationale: An optimistic update shows a value the server has not confirmed. Without a stable client identity the retry after a failure creates a duplicate; without declared conflict behavior two writers overwrite each other silently; without a rollback path a failed update leaves the shown value wrong. Declaring identity, conflict behavior, rollback, and reconciliation up front makes each of those cases designed instead of improvised. Money, irreversible actions, and uncertain authorization skip optimism entirely and wait for the server result.

provisions.heading: Map Every Failure to One Problem Type
provisions.evidence: Which failures render outside the one problem type? Look in the frame problem mapping and the error surfaces.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST convert every failure into one problem type, deciding from its code.
provisions.rationale: A raw response body carries whatever the API included: field names, internals, sometimes data kept from the user. Rendering it leaks that content and gives the user no consistent recovery path, because each failure looks different. One problem type gives every failure the same shape: the page branches on the published code, so its decision survives a reworded message, and the problem carries the trace identifier support needs to find the request.

provisions.heading: Name the Zone for Every Timestamp
provisions.evidence: Which timestamp formatters run without an explicit IANA zone resolved from the shown record? Look in the formatter call sites.
provisions.statement: A formatter rendering a timestamp MUST receive an explicit IANA time zone, resolved by the caller from the record the screen shows.
provisions.rationale: An instant from the API carries no zone, so a formatter left to pick one shows the user's own zone: a payout cut-off reads as midnight in the user's city instead of the office's. The caller resolves the zone from the record the screen shows: a record with its own zone states it, otherwise the account's zone applies, and an account that chooses none falls back to UTC. Passing the zone explicitly makes each timestamp name whose day it belongs to.

provisions.heading: Place a Field Refusal on Its Field
provisions.evidence: Which field problems miss their fields, bypass the frame helper, or close the form? Look in the forms and the frame helper.
provisions.statement: A field problem MUST reach the field it names through the frame's one helper, with the form staying open until resolved or abandoned.
provisions.rationale: The frame's one helper puts each problem on the field it names, so the user sees what to fix where they fix it. Above a long form, a summary links to each field in error, so a problem below the fold is still one tap away. The summary is a navigation aid added to the messages on each field, never replacing them. The form stays open until each problem is resolved or the user abandons the form, so no input is lost to a closed dialog.

provisions.heading: Place a Refusal Beside What Was Refused
provisions.evidence: Which refusals render away from the refused record or control, or without the application's sentence and code in the markup? Look in the screen's page files beside the refusing controls.
provisions.statement: A refusal MUST render beside the record or control that was refused, in the sentence the application holds for that code.
provisions.rationale: A refusal at the top of a page says that something failed but not what, so the user scans the page to find the control that caused it. Rendered beside the refused record or control, the refusal answers both questions at once. The sentence comes from the application's own dictionary for that code rather than from the response body, so the words stay consistent and translatable; the code in the markup lets a test provoke the refusal by name.
provisions.example: Submitting an expense above the receipt threshold with no receipt refuses with `spending.receipt-missing` under `result/submit-expense.receipt-missing`. The page renders the application's sentence for that code beside the Submit control, carries the code in the markup so a test provokes it by name, and keeps the trace identifier in the detail in copyable form.

provisions.heading: Read a Permission from the Session
provisions.evidence: Which offered commands exceed the permissions the session actor holds at the record scope? Look in the page command guards and the session shape.
provisions.statement: A page MUST offer a command only when the session actor holds its permissions at the record's scope, with the API deciding every command.
provisions.rationale: Permissions are the project's permission records: an actor holds a role at a scope, a role allows permissions, and a use case needs permissions. The page reads the permissions the signed-in actor holds from the session the API returns, and offers only the commands those permissions allow at the record's scope, so the user meets no offer that ends in a refusal. The API still decides every command, so an action offered in error is refused rather than executed.

provisions.heading: Regenerate the Client Rather Than Editing It
provisions.evidence: Which hand edits sit below the generated directory, making the committed client differ from fresh generation output? Look in the generated directory and the generator command.
provisions.statement: Regenerate the client from the document, and edit nothing under the generated directory.
provisions.rationale: A hand edit under the generated directory works until the next generation overwrites it, so the change appears sound and then silently disappears. Regenerating from the document keeps the committed output provably equal to the contract: a reviewer regenerates and compares, and any difference is either a contract change or an edit belonging outside the generated directory.

provisions.heading: Route a Personal Value in a Header
provisions.evidence: Which person-naming values travel in the query string instead of contract-declared headers? Look in the contract headers and the call sites.
provisions.statement: A value naming a person MUST travel in a request header rather than the query string, with the contract declaring the header each operation reads.
provisions.rationale: A query string leaks: proxies log it, the browser keeps it in history, and the next page the user opens receives it as the referrer. A value naming a person therefore travels in a request header the contract declares per operation, where it reaches the API without landing in those three places. The address keeps its own copy for filters and paging, so a filtered list stays a link somebody can share.

provisions.heading: Route Use Cases Through Application
provisions.evidence: Which screens or components compose Domain calls or write storage instead of invoking an Application handler carrying a `Command` or `Query` role suffix? Look in the screen and component sources.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST invoke an Application handler carrying a `Command` or `Query` role suffix for each use case rather than compose Domain calls or write storage.
provisions.rationale: The handler is the one place a use case exists: its validation, its rules, and its result. A screen or component that composes its own sequence of Domain calls and storage writes creates a second definition that no record names and no test pins down. Routing every use case through a handler keeps the screen or component a caller and the handler the definition.
provisions.example: The expense screen invokes the submit-expense Application handler for EXP-1042 rather than composing the Domain expense calls and writing the expense store itself.

provisions.heading: Set the Write Marker on Every Request
provisions.evidence: Which writes lack the configured marker header of the form `X-<Project>-Request`? Look in the client configuration and the API write acceptance.
provisions.statement: A client MUST send its marker header on every write, with the API accepting a cookie-authenticated write only when it carries that header.
provisions.rationale: A browser attaches its cookies to a cross-site request on its own, so the cookie alone fails to distinguish the page's own write from a forged post submitted from another site. The marker header separates the two: the page's client adds it to every write, and a page on another site adds no custom header without a preflight, which the API grants to no foreign origin. The API therefore accepts a cookie-authenticated write only when the header is present. The header name varies by project, so configuration owns it rather than code; it has the form `X-<Project>-Request` with the value `1`.

provisions.heading: Update the Cache a Command Changed
provisions.evidence: Which successful commands leave a changed query cached, or invalidate a query their answers left unchanged? Look in the command call sites and the cache keys.
provisions.statement: A successful command MUST invalidate every query whose answer it changed, and no other query.
provisions.rationale: The query cache owns freshness: a page renders the cached answer, not a new request. A command that leaves a changed query cached shows the old record until something else happens to refetch, so the user's own write appears to have no effect. Invalidating exactly the queries the command changed refreshes what changed; invalidating more costs a needless request per affected page.
provisions.example: The generated client holds both sides of one write: the expenses route calls the submit operation with the expense values, and the list reads through the list operation. After the submit succeeds, the page invalidates the list query and no other query, so the list shows the new expense without refetching unrelated pages.

provisions.heading: Use One Configured Client per Application
provisions.evidence: Which reads or writes bypass the one configured client? Look in the frame client configuration and the call sites.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST configure the generated client once, and route every read and write through it.
provisions.rationale: The configured client owns the base address, the credentials, the headers, and the mapping from a failure to a problem. A call that builds its own request opts out of all four at once: it can point at the wrong host, miss the session cookie, skip the write marker, and surface a raw failure outside the page's problem shape. Routing every read and write through the one client keeps those four decisions in one place.

provisions.heading: Validate a Form with the Generated Schema
provisions.evidence: Which forms validate against a handwritten restatement instead of the generated request schema extended with application rules? Look in the form sources and the generated schemas.
provisions.statement: A form MUST validate against the generated schema for its request body, extended with the application's own rules rather than replaced by them.
provisions.rationale: The generated schema is the contract's statement of what the API accepts, so it holds even where the browser accepts more. Validating the form against it refuses bad input before the request leaves the page. The application extends the schema with the message shown for each rule and any rule beyond the contract's reach, rather than replacing it, so the form refuses everything the API refuses.

provisions.heading: Accept App Links in the Host Activity
provisions.evidence: Which app links the host Activity misses on a cold start or while running? Look at the intent filter and both overrides.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST receive app links in `OnCreate` and `OnNewIntent`, through an `IntentFilter` with `AutoVerify` set.
provisions.rationale: Handling both entry points lets a cold start and a link that arrives while the app runs open the same screen, and `AutoVerify` lets the platform open the app instead of a browser.
provisions.example: A link to `https://claimwick.example/claims/` opens the claim screen named by its path, whether the app was closed or open.

provisions.heading: Apply System Insets to Each Screen
provisions.evidence: Which screens place a control or text under a system bar or a cutout? Look in the screen layouts and the inset handling.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST apply the system bar and display cutout insets it reads from `WindowInsets` to its controls and text.
provisions.rationale: The window supplies these insets, so reading them from `WindowInsets` keeps controls and text clear of the bars and cutouts on every device.
provisions.example: The expense claim screen pads its submit button by the system bar inset while its background draws full bleed.

provisions.heading: Declare Android Outside the Controlled UI Contract
provisions.evidence: Which Android frontends declare no entry point record naming Android and its replacement boundaries? Look in the entry point records.
provisions.statement: An Android frontend MUST declare an entry point record naming Android and the boundaries that replace the controlled UI contract.
provisions.rationale: The controlled contract covers React and Svelte, so an Android frontend declares what replaces its checks instead of reporting as one with nothing to check.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Android entry point record names Android and the native view review that replaces the controlled contract.

provisions.heading: Hold One Navigation Controller in the Platform Project
provisions.evidence: Which screens navigate without the controller, or which second controller holds navigation state? Look in the screen classes and the host Activity.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST hold its navigation controller in one class in the platform project, owned by the host Activity.
provisions.rationale: One controller holds the current screen, the open overlay, and the history, so no screen navigates on its own.
provisions.example: The Claimwick controller is one class that the host Activity creates and that every expense screen raises events to.

provisions.heading: Keep Android Core Test Mocks to the Owned Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Which core tests replace a Domain type or an Application handler? Look in the test doubles.
provisions.statement: A core test MUST NOT replace the Domain types or the Application handlers it proves.
provisions.rationale: A stand-in for the code under test proves the stand-in, so the test reaches the rule only through the real types and handlers.
provisions.example: The expense claim test builds a real Domain claim and calls the real submit handler, and replaces only the platform storage adapter.

provisions.heading: Keep Hosts and Failure Views Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Which host Activities or failure views carry a screen mark? Look in the platform project.
provisions.statement: A host Activity or a failure view MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A host or failure view draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it links an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The host Activity class carries no `<implements>` mark.

provisions.heading: Keep Screen Styles in Resources
provisions.evidence: Which screen classes set a color, font, or margin in code? Look in the screen classes.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST take its colors and text styles from `Resources/values/styles.xml` and set no style value in code.
provisions.rationale: Resources hold every color and text style in one place, and a screen that sets a value in code is a second style that no resource answers to.
provisions.example: The expense total uses the `TotalText` style from `Resources/values/styles.xml` and sets no color in its screen class.

provisions.heading: Keep the Android Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Which screen classes sit outside `Screens/`, or hold use-case logic instead of calling Application handlers? Look in the platform project and the core projects.
provisions.statement: An Android frontend MUST hold its frame in the host code of the platform project, its routes as screen classes under `Screens/`, and its use-case code as Application handlers.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed homes let a reader and a tool find the frame, the screens, and the use-case code in the same place in every Android app.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Android app keeps its navigation host in `Claimwick.Android`, the expense list screen in `Screens/Expenses/`, and the expense handlers in the Application project.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Android Screen with Its Screen Record
provisions.evidence: Which screen classes under `Screens/` lack a screen mark? Look in each screen file.
provisions.statement: A screen class under `Screens/` MUST carry the `<implements>` mark of the screen it renders, in the form the .NET stack states.
provisions.rationale: The mark links the screen to its record the way a .NET handler carries its use-case mark, so the builder and the check read one link.
provisions.example: `ExpenseListScreen` carries `/// <implements>screen/claimwick-app.expense-list</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Read Android Copy Through the Generated Resource Class
provisions.evidence: Which copy strings a screen reads by a literal name instead of the generated class? Look in the screen classes and the layouts.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST read every copy string through the generated `Resource` class, with its fallback in `Resources/values/strings.xml`.
provisions.rationale: The generated class gives every copy key a typed name, and the default values folder gives every key a fallback when a language lacks it.
provisions.example: The expense list reads its empty-state sentence as `Resource.String.ExpenseListEmpty`, and the Spanish file supplies the translation.

provisions.heading: Request Audio Focus Before Playing Sound
provisions.evidence: Which sound playback runs without an `AudioFocusRequest`, or keeps playing after focus is lost? Look in the playback call sites.
provisions.statement: A screen that plays sound MUST request audio focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` before it plays, and pause when focus is lost.
provisions.rationale: One speaker serves every app, so the platform arbitrates only the apps that ask for focus, and pausing on loss yields to navigation prompts and calls.
provisions.example: A confirmation chime plays only after the app holds audio focus, and a phone call pauses it.

provisions.heading: Request Permissions at the Point of Use
provisions.evidence: Which runtime permissions are requested in `OnCreate` or before the action that needs them? Look in the host Activity and the action handlers.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST request each runtime permission through `RequestPermissions` when the action that needs it starts, never in `OnCreate`.
provisions.rationale: A request at the point of use arrives when the visitor knows what it is for, and the same permission answers a question the visitor just asked.
provisions.example: The camera permission is requested when the visitor taps Scan receipt, not at launch.

provisions.heading: Route the Back Gesture Through the Activity Dispatcher
provisions.evidence: Which back gestures bypass the Activity's dispatcher, or leave the app from a screen other than the first? Look in the host Activity and the controller.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST deliver the system back gesture to the navigation controller through its `OnBackInvokedDispatcher`.
provisions.rationale: The dispatcher is the platform's own path for the back signal, so predictive back reaches the controller as the same overlay-then-screen-then-leave order on every screen.
provisions.example: A back gesture on the expense detail screen closes an open overlay first, then steps back to the expense list.

provisions.heading: Run Android Core Tests on xunit.v3
provisions.evidence: Which core tests run on another runner, or need an emulator or device? Look in the core test projects.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST run its core tests as plain .NET test projects on `xunit.v3`, the version `packages.nuget` pins.
provisions.rationale: Core tests need no emulator, so a plain .NET runner keeps them fast, and one pinned runner keeps every core project on the same version.
provisions.example: The expense claim rule has its test in an xunit.v3 project beside the Domain project it proves.

provisions.heading: Store Navigation State in the Activity Bundle
provisions.evidence: Which navigation state the controller holds outside the saved bundle? Look in the host Activity and the controller.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST save the navigation controller's state in its `Bundle` from `OnSaveInstanceState` and restore it in `OnCreate`.
provisions.rationale: The platform ends the process in the background when memory runs short, and the saved bundle returns the visitor to the same screen with the same overlay and history.
provisions.example: After the platform ends the Claimwick process, the app reopens on the expense detail screen with its overlay still open.

provisions.heading: Store Persisted State in App-Private Storage
provisions.evidence: Which persisted state or user media sits outside `Context.FilesDir`, or is written in place? Look in the storage adapters.
provisions.statement: Persisted state and user media MUST live under `Context.FilesDir`, written atomically.
provisions.rationale: The app's own sandbox keeps the data away from other apps and the shared media library, and an atomic write keeps the previous complete file if a write stops midway.
provisions.example: The expense receipts the visitor adds are copied into the app's files directory and replace their previous copy only after the new one is whole.

provisions.heading: Use the System Pickers for Media
provisions.evidence: Which screens pick photos or files through another intent, or request a storage permission to do so? Look in the picking call sites and the manifest.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST pick photos through the Photo Picker action `android.provider.action.PICK_IMAGES` and files through `android.intent.action.OPEN_DOCUMENT`.
provisions.rationale: Both pickers grant access to the chosen items only, so the app needs no storage permission to read one receipt.
provisions.example: Adding a receipt photo opens the Photo Picker, and the visitor's choice is the only image the app receives.

provisions.heading: Call the Server Only Through the Generated Client
provisions.evidence: Which backend calls in a `server` app bypass the generated client in `{ProjectName}.Client`? Look in the backend call sites.
provisions.statement: A `server` consumer's app MUST call the backend only through the generated client in `{ProjectName}.Client`.
provisions.rationale: The generated client owns the base address, the credentials, the headers, and the mapping from a failure to a result. A call that builds its own request opts out of all four at once: it can point at the wrong host, miss the session, and surface a raw failure outside the handler's result shape. Routing every backend call through the one client keeps those decisions in one place. This realizes litespec/frontend/data#use-one-configured-client-per-application.

provisions.heading: Copy Picked Media into the App
provisions.evidence: Which imported media keeps a stored picker URI instead of a copy in app-private storage? Look in the media imports.
provisions.statement: Media picked from the device MUST be copied into app-private storage on import rather than kept as a reference to the picker's URI.
provisions.rationale: A picker's URI is a loan, not a gift: the platform can revoke it when the picker closes, and the source file can move or vanish. A screen holding only the URI shows a broken image after either happens. Copying the media into app-private storage on import keeps the app's copy under the app's own control.

provisions.heading: Keep Persisted State in App-Private Storage
provisions.evidence: Which persisted state or user-added media lives outside app-private storage, or writes without a temporary file? Look in the storage writes.
provisions.statement: Persisted state and media the user adds MUST live in the app's private storage, written atomically.
provisions.rationale: App-private storage keeps the user's data inside the app's own sandbox, away from other apps and from the shared media library. A crash mid-write leaves a half-written file, so each write lands in a temporary file that then replaces the target, keeping the previous complete file until the new one is whole. Media the user adds travels with the state that references it, so an export or a reinstall keeps both together.
provisions.example: The filed expense report persists as versioned durable state in app-private storage, with the photographed receipts beside it in the same private files.

provisions.heading: Load Persisted State Once
provisions.evidence: Which persisted state loads outside startup, or renders a screen before the typed store is ready? Look in the startup sequence and the screen loading states.
provisions.statement: Persisted state MUST load once at startup into a typed store that screens read from, with screens showing a loading state until it is ready.
provisions.rationale: Storage reads are slow and fallible, so the product reads once at startup into a typed store that screens read from. A screen that reads storage on render pays an input-output call per frame and can render half-loaded state. A screen renders its loading state until the store finishes loading, so it never shows an unloaded store as ready.

provisions.heading: Make Refusals Explicit
provisions.evidence: Which handler unions miss success or a named refusal, and which screens leave a refusal unmapped to a message? Look in the handler result types and the screens.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST return a typed result union covering success and each named refusal, with each screen mapping every refusal to a message.
provisions.rationale: Signaling a refusal through `null`, an empty collection, or a bare boolean tells the caller that something was refused but not what. Every caller then guesses, and two callers guess differently. A typed result union names success and each refusal, so each screen maps every refusal to the message the application holds for it. This realizes litespec/frontend/data#map-every-failure-to-one-problem-type.

provisions.heading: Refuse Commands While Offline
provisions.evidence: Which screens queue a command while offline without a recorded local convention naming the queued commands and their replay order, and which offline screens show no failure state? Look in the command call sites and the offline screens.
provisions.statement: While the network is unavailable, a screen shows its failure state and queues no command; the user retries the command in the foreground when the network returns.
provisions.rationale: A queued command runs later against state the user cannot see, so an expense submitted on a train can land after its trip closed or its approval policy changed. Showing the failure state keeps the refusal where the user caused it, and queuing nothing keeps every command tied to the screen that sent it. A project that needs offline capture states its local convention and its replay rules instead of letting each screen improvise a queue.
provisions.example: Filing expense EXP-1042 for the Rotterdam client visit with no network shows the failure state on the expense screen and sends nothing; the user submits the expense again when the network returns.

provisions.heading: Declare Only Used Permissions
provisions.evidence: Which app manifest permissions do no current features use? Look in the app manifest beside the features.
provisions.statement: The app manifest MUST declare only the permissions the app's current features use.
provisions.rationale: Each declared permission is a promise the app's features must keep: a declaration without a feature asks for the trust nothing uses. Stale declarations accumulate as features are removed, and each one costs the app a question the user should never have been asked. Declaring only what current features use keeps the manifest an honest list of the app's needs.

provisions.heading: Hold Audio Focus While Playing Sound
provisions.evidence: Which audible playback skips audio focus or keeps playing on focus loss? Look in the playback code.
provisions.statement: An app playing audible sound MUST request audio focus and pause when it loses focus.
provisions.rationale: One speaker serves every app, so playback without focus talks over navigation prompts, calls, and other players. Requesting focus before playing lets the platform arbitrate, and pausing on focus loss yields to whatever took it. Resuming waits for focus to return rather than grabbing it back.

provisions.heading: Keep Device Work in the Foreground
