provisions.heading: Date and Time Field
provisions.evidence: Which built calendar input breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built date, duration, and range fields beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-text-field-with-a-calendar-that-opens-beside-it`
provisions.rationale: One typed field with a calendar beside it stays the pick. There is always a way to type, and the calendar serves a reader who would rather click. The three text inputs are the runner-up where accessibility review demands them; they cost the slowest entry in the form. A date and a time on one row are the other alternative where a form always takes both. Never ship the native date input: it draws the browser chrome instead of the application control.

provisions.heading: Email Body Editor
provisions.evidence: Which built message composer breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built subject-plus-body forms and variable chips beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `subject-plus-body-with-variable-chips`
provisions.rationale: The subject plus body with variable chips is the pick: the sentence is written and the facts are placed where they belong. The side-by-side spender preview is the runner-up, because a template is proven once it is seen filled. Plain text with a variable list is the other alternative where a mail client must read text. Never ship a template with no preview: variables are spelled in one place and filled in another, and only a filled copy shows that they meet.

provisions.heading: Expose a Field Error to Assistive Technology
provisions.evidence: Which built field misses its invalid state or its error reference while its error shows, or carries either before it is touched? Open the built forms and read each field's attributes with its error shown and hidden.
provisions.statement: A field MUST set `aria-invalid="true"` and point `aria-describedby` at its error only while the error shows.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification asks that an error be described in text, and WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value asks that the field expose its state. The two attributes together tell a screen reader which field failed and what it says. An empty required field carries neither until the reader has touched it, so it is not read as invalid first.

provisions.heading: Keep Submit Enabled to Reveal Errors
provisions.evidence: Which built submit control disables itself while the form holds errors? Open the built forms with errors and press each submit.
provisions.statement: A submit control MUST stay enabled while the form holds errors, so pressing it moves focus to the summary or the first field in error.
provisions.rationale: A disabled submit gives no reason and no way forward. The reader presses a live submit and lands on the summary or the first field in error, which names what to fix. The form refuses the submit and keeps every entered value.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Required Field
provisions.evidence: Which built required field lacks a visible marker or the `required` attribute, and which form explains the marker nowhere above its first field? Open the built forms and read each required field and the line above the first one.
provisions.statement: Every required field MUST carry the `required` attribute and a visible marker that the form explains once, above its first field.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions asks that a required field say so before it is submitted. The marker shows it to a sighted reader and the attribute announces it to a screen reader. One explanation above the first field teaches the marker once for the whole form.

provisions.heading: Match the Keyboard to the Value
provisions.evidence: Which built numeric, code, or identifier field keeps the default text keyboard with no recorded reason? Open the built fields and the project's recorded departures.
provisions.statement: Set `inputmode` on a numeric or code field for its value, and turn off autocorrect and autocapitalize on an identifier field such as an IBAN or a reference.
provisions.rationale: The phone keyboard matches the value, and autocorrect does not rewrite an IBAN. A reader entering a booking reference meets keys for the value instead of the full alphabet.

provisions.heading: Money Field
provisions.evidence: Which built amount input breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built amount, currency, and total fields beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `text-input-currency-in-the-label-symbol-inside`
provisions.rationale: The text input with the currency in its label stays the pick. The label names the currency for a screen reader, and the field accepts any amount a reader types, including a comma or a point as the decimal separator. The restated payout total is the runner-up: it belongs on every amount an approver sees, because it stops the fee from surprising either side at payout. The preset amount chips are the other alternative for a round amount that repeats. Never ship the stepper: a continuous amount cannot be reached by stepping.

provisions.heading: Name Every Field with a Visible Label
provisions.evidence: Which built field lacks a visible label naming its value? Open every form on built screens and read each field's label.
provisions.statement: Every field MUST carry a visible label that names its value.
provisions.rationale: A placeholder disappears on the first keystroke, so a filled field with no label no longer says what it holds. Screen readers announce the label, and sighted staff returning to a filled form read it to check each value before saving. Without a visible label, both groups guess what each value means.

provisions.heading: Picking a Period
provisions.evidence: Which built range picker breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built presets, month pickers, and painted calendars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `two-date-inputs-with-presets`
provisions.rationale: Keep two typed dates with presets. One tap covers the common windows, typing covers the rare ones, and both edges stay visible. The painted calendar is the runner-up for reporting screens where the window itself is the question. The month picker is the other alternative for a report that runs by calendar month. Never ship presets alone with no typed fallback: no preset reaches the filing-to-payout window the payout check wants.

provisions.heading: Refuse Enter While Text Is Being Composed
provisions.evidence: Which built field acting on Enter submits half-composed text from an input method? Open the built tag inputs and fields acting on Enter, and confirm a candidate with Enter.
provisions.statement: A field that acts on the Enter key MUST ignore it while an input method is composing text.
provisions.rationale: A reader typing a vendor name in Japanese or Chinese confirms a candidate with Enter. The tag input or inline rename that submits on that keystroke sends half-composed text. Waiting for composition to end keeps the submitted value whole.

provisions.heading: Repeatable Group
provisions.evidence: Which built code group breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built stacked cards and inline tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `stacked-cards-one-per-type`
provisions.rationale: The stacked cards are the pick: one card per code with its ceiling and allocation readable at once, and one command to add another. The table with inline editing is the runner-up for reviewing many codes, where changing three ceilings should cost three fields and no navigation. One section per repetition is the other alternative for creation, where each code is new. Never ship a group whose repetitions cannot be removed: a code added by mistake must leave without taking its claimed amounts with it.

provisions.heading: Reporting a Refused Submit
provisions.evidence: Which built submit-error report breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built summaries and per-field messages beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-summary-above-the-form-plus-a-message-on-each-field`
provisions.rationale: Keep the summary with focus, plus per-field messages. It meets WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3, and the links carry the reader to each field. Validation on leaving each field is the runner-up as a complement, never a replacement: it confirms good values early but cannot orient a reader facing three errors. Messages on the fields only are the other alternative for a short form. Never ship the dialog summary: it hides the form the reader must fix. Whatever the form reports, it keeps every entered value, as [keep the reader's input through a failure](feedback-and-states.md#keep-the-readers-input-through-a-failure) states.

provisions.heading: Show a Field Error After the Field Is Left
provisions.evidence: Which built field shows an error while it is still being typed, or keeps one after the value turns valid? Open the built forms, type in each field, leave it, fix it, and read when the message appears and clears.
provisions.statement: A field error MUST appear only once the user leaves the field with a changed value or submits the form, and disappear as soon as the value becomes valid.
provisions.rationale: An error shown while the reader is still typing scolds an unfinished value, and one that lingers after the fix makes the reader doubt the fix. The message appears once the field is left or the form is submitted, and it clears as soon as the value turns valid.

provisions.heading: Slug or URL Field with a Preview
provisions.evidence: Which built address input breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built slugs, transliterations, and availability checks beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `slug-with-the-live-address-under-it`
provisions.rationale: Keep the slug with its live address under it. The reader types the short part and reads the full address before saving. Transliteration from the name is the runner-up for creation, where typing the same words twice is pure overhead. The address as a fact is the other alternative once it is shared. Never ship an address that cannot be read before it is saved.

provisions.heading: State Each Field's Purpose
provisions.evidence: Which built field collecting information about the user lacks the `autocomplete` token for its purpose? Open the built forms and read each such field's token.
provisions.statement: A field collecting information about the user MUST carry the `autocomplete` token for its purpose.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose asks that the purpose of each such field be programmatically determinable. The token lets the browser fill a bank account holder or an email once instead of the reader typing it on every claim. The reader checks the filled value instead of typing it again.

provisions.heading: Switch or a Checkbox
provisions.evidence: Which built toggle breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built switches, checkboxes, and instant applies beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-switch-with-the-label-and-its-consequence`
provisions.rationale: The switch with its consequence stated stays the pick. The label says what is on, and the line under it says what turning it off does. Instant apply with an undo toast is the runner-up for low-risk settings a reader flips often. A checkbox is the other alternative where the off state is the default. Never ship a switch whose label names the control instead of the outcome.

provisions.heading: Tag Input
provisions.evidence: Which built tag chip breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built chips, popover lists, and inherited tags beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chips-with-type-to-add-and-suggestions`
provisions.rationale: The chips with type-to-add and suggestions are the pick: new words are allowed and old ones are offered, so `travel` is spelled once. A checkbox list in a popover is the runner-up where the tag set is closed and counted. Free text split on commas is the other alternative where a list is pasted in. Never ship free text with no suggestions: it grows `travel`, `Travel`, and `travel-meals` side by side.

provisions.heading: Take a Name in One Field of Any Script
provisions.evidence: Which built name entry splits the name or refuses letters outside Latin? Open the built staff and spender forms and enter a name in a non-Latin script.
provisions.statement: A person's name MUST be one field that accepts letters of any script.
provisions.rationale: Given and family names are not universal, and splitting them forces staff into parts their name lacks. A Latin-only rule refuses real staff. One field taking letters of any script holds every name the back office meets.

provisions.heading: Text Field and Its States
provisions.evidence: Which built text input breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built labels, counts, and growing areas beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `label-above-help-under-six-states-on-one-page`
provisions.rationale: The six-state reference page stays the pick, because it is the only option that pins every state one field must draw. Inline confirmation of a good value is the runner-up for create forms, where it saves a refused submit. Floating labels are the other alternative for a compact form. Never ship the placeholder as the label: it vanishes on the first keystroke, and its color misses contrast.

provisions.heading: Upload Field
provisions.evidence: Which built file input breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built drop zones, CSV reads, and progress rows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-drop-zone-that-states-what-it-accepts`
provisions.rationale: The drop zone that states its types and size limit stays the pick. Nobody learns the limit by being refused. The per-file progress tray is the runner-up for imports of several files, where one bar per file beats one bar for all. A CSV upload that states its columns first is the other alternative where the file must match a fixed shape. Never ship a CSV upload with no stated columns: a file refused for a format nobody stated is a refusal the application caused.

provisions.heading: Work That Is Not Saved
provisions.evidence: Which built unsaved marker breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built dirty flags, drafts, and save bars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-visible-unsaved-marker-beside-the-save`
provisions.rationale: Keep the visible unsaved marker beside Save. A reader never has to remember whether anything was typed. The save bar pinned to the top is the runner-up for long settings pages where the form actions scroll out of view. Autosave with a saved marker is the other alternative for a note written over several sittings. Never ship silent autosave on money or access: each save would be an audited command, and an audit entry per keystroke batch is not a trail a reader can follow.

provisions.heading: Align Money to the Right with Its Currency
provisions.evidence: Which built money column centers its figures or hides a currency? Open the money columns on built tables.
provisions.statement: A table MUST right-align a money column and show the currency of every amount in it.
provisions.rationale: Right alignment lines up place value down the column, so a reader compares hundreds against thousands without reading each figure digit by digit. A currency on every amount keeps EUR 125.00 distinct from a bare 125.00, so an export or a screenshot never leaves finance guessing which money it shows.

provisions.heading: Announce a List's Result Count
provisions.evidence: Which built list stays silent after a filter, search, or selection change? Open built lists, change the view and the selection, and listen for one announcement per change.
provisions.statement: A list MUST announce its result count after a filter or search and its selection total after a selection changes, once per change through the page's polite status region.
provisions.rationale: A filter that narrows 268 expenses to 58 without a word leaves a screen-reader user on a list that changed under them. A bulk selection of "3 selected, EUR 412.00" is otherwise silent, so the reader acts without knowing the scope. The count goes through the page's polite status region in `litespec/frontend/patterns/feedback-and-states#announce-each-status-by-its-urgency`, once per change. This is WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages.

provisions.heading: Bulk Action Bar
provisions.evidence: Which built selection bar breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built count bars, pills, and dialogs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-bar-above-the-table-naming-the-count`
provisions.rationale: Keep a bar above the table naming the count and the money. On a reversals page the total is the thing a reader checks before acting. The runner-up is a floating pill, for reversible bulk work such as resending receipts or tagging, where the bar leaves the table in place. Never ship the bar at the foot. On a long table the action sits off screen while the checkboxes that enabled it do not.

provisions.heading: Choosing the Columns
provisions.evidence: Which built column set breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built choosers and saved views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `five-columns-nothing-removable`
provisions.rationale: Keep the default five columns. They answer which expense, who, when, what state, and how much. The runner-up is the Columns popover. Add it once more than one team asks for a sixth fact such as method or cost centre. Saved views are the later answer, when finance and the auditors want different tables. Never ship the question-shaped headers. They cost width and read as a form.

provisions.heading: Exporting the List
provisions.evidence: Which built download flow breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built CSV buttons, dialogs, and background exports beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-export-button-that-downloads-csv`
provisions.rationale: Keep one Export button that downloads the filtered rows as CSV. The accountant job costs one click and no decisions. Prefer a background export past a few thousand rows where a download would time out. Never ship copy as the only export. Copying the visible page silently drops every row past the pager.

provisions.heading: Filters
provisions.evidence: Which built filter control breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built controls, panels, and facet buttons beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-filter-per-category-visible`
provisions.rationale: Show one visible control per category. A reader sees what can narrow the table without opening anything, and each category keeps its own control. The runner-up is faceted buttons with counts. Prefer it once a category holds more than a few values and the reader needs the split before choosing. Never ship every category inside one dropdown. It hides the applied state and contradicts the stated rule.

provisions.heading: Grouped Rows
provisions.evidence: Which built group header breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built day, trip, and flat groupings beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `grouped-by-day-with-subtotals`
provisions.rationale: Keep grouped by day with subtotals. It answers what today paid without a chart and without leaving the list. The runner-up is grouped by trip with collapse toggles. Prefer it once trips grow so one day of rows stops fitting. Collapsed rows stay findable: the browser's find opens the group that holds a match. Never ship two group levels: month-then-day nesting turns the list into a tree that paging cannot cross.

provisions.heading: Inline Row Expansion
provisions.evidence: Which built expandable row breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built expense lines and decision states beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `expand-to-the-order-lines`
provisions.rationale: Keep expansion to the expense lines. It answers what the spender claimed, which is the question asked from the list. The runner-up is expansion to lines with decision state. Prefer it on the decision list where handover is the work. Never ship expand-all: twenty expanded rows is a page nobody can scan, and one click fires a read per row.

provisions.heading: Keep a List's View in Its Address
provisions.evidence: Which built list loses its filters, sort, or page on refresh? Open built lists, change the view, and reload the address.
provisions.statement: A list MUST keep its filters, sort order, and page in the URL, and its expanded groups where it groups rows.
provisions.rationale: A view kept in the address survives the back button, a refresh, and a pasted link, so all three return to the same rows. Without it, opening one record loses the filters the reader set, and a link sent to a colleague opens the unfiltered first page instead of the rows under discussion.

provisions.heading: Keep the Header Row in View
provisions.evidence: Which built tall table loses its header on scroll or hides a focused row under it? Open built long lists and scroll with the keyboard.
provisions.statement: Keep the header row of a table taller than the viewport visible while it scrolls, with no focused row hidden under it.
provisions.rationale: A header that scrolls away leaves a long expense list without column names, so the reader scrolls up to relearn which column is which. A focused row hidden under a fixed header looks lost even though focus sits on it. Keeping the header in view with focus clear of it answers both. This is WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured.

provisions.heading: Make a Scrolling Table a Named Region
provisions.evidence: Which built sideways-scrolling table misses its focus stop, name, or edge cue? Open built wide tables at 390 px and tab to each table edge.
provisions.statement: A table that scrolls sideways MUST sit in a named region that takes keyboard focus and shows a cue at each edge it can still scroll.
provisions.rationale: A keyboard user on a 390 px screen has no other way to reach the columns past the edge, because a sideways scroll without a focus stop is pointer-only. A sighted user has no sign that more columns exist without a cue at the scrolling edge. The named region gives the table a stop in the tab order and a name for assistive technology. This is WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard.

provisions.heading: Mark the Sorted Column
provisions.evidence: Which built sortable header is no button, or which sorted column lacks its direction mark? Open built tables and read each sortable header and the sorted column mark.
provisions.statement: A sortable column header MUST be a button inside its header cell, with `aria-sort` and its direction on the sorted column only.
provisions.rationale: A screen-reader user hears which column orders the expense list and changes it like any button. Without the button shape, the header reads as plain text and sorting stays hidden. Without the mark on the sorted column, the order stays silent even though the rows follow it. This is WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships.

provisions.heading: Money Column
provisions.evidence: Which built amount column breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built aligned figures and reversal columns beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `number-only-right-aligned`
provisions.rationale: Keep the number only. The header names the currency and repeating EUR on every row is noise. Prefer the reversed part under the charged amount where reversals are the work rather than the exception. Never ship money as a share of the total. A derived percentage column answers a question no expenses list is asked.

provisions.heading: Pagination
provisions.evidence: Which built page control breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built chevrons, load-more buttons, and compact pagers beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `count-left-numbered-pages-right`
provisions.rationale: Keep the count with numbered pages. The reader can jump, and the range still says where they are. The runner-up is the compact pager, where width is tight and nobody jumps further than one page at a time. Never ship the jump field. Typing a page number then Enter is slower than clicking for almost every reader.

provisions.heading: Pinned and Resizing Columns
provisions.evidence: Which built fixed column breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built frozen first columns beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-order-column-pinned-while-the-rest-scroll`
provisions.rationale: Keep the expense column pinned while the rest scroll. The row stays named at any scroll position, and it costs no control. The runner-up pins the actions too. Prefer it once rows carry inline commands that must stay reachable. Never ship draggable widths in a first release: per-user widths are stored state that support cannot see and screenshots cannot hold.

provisions.heading: Row Actions
provisions.evidence: Which built row command breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built inline actions, row menus, and side previews beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-inline-action-the-rest-in-a-row-menu`
provisions.rationale: Keep one inline command with the rest in the row menu. The common job stays one click away and the row stays narrow. Prefer the side preview where acting needs the record context, such as the lines before a resend. Never ship hover-revealed actions. Hover fails on touch, and a second focusable render doubles the table for no gain.

provisions.heading: Row Density
provisions.evidence: Which built row height breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built 24, 32, and 40 pixel rows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `40-pixels-the-default`
provisions.rationale: Keep 40 pixels. Two lines fit, the row scans, and it matches the default size. The runner-up is 32 pixels, for a working queue where every row is read once and acted on. Never ship a density control the reader sets. Most readers set it once, and a screenshot suite then holds three versions of every page. The phone answer is a record list.

provisions.heading: Searching with Highlighted Matches
provisions.evidence: Which built list search breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built highlighted cells and scoped searches beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `matches-highlighted-in-the-cells`
provisions.rationale: Highlight the matches in the cells. The reader sees why each row matched without opening it. Prefer a scope control once readers search across trips and must say which one. Never ship a match column on its own. It spends a column stating what the highlight already shows.

provisions.heading: Shape a List by Its Container
provisions.evidence: Which built list switches shape by screen width instead of its container? Open built lists in narrow panels on a wide screen.
provisions.statement: Switch a list between its table and its cards by the width of the region that holds it, not the width of the screen.
provisions.rationale: The expense table in a record's side panel has a phone's width on a desktop screen, so a screen-wide breakpoint keeps it a table where cards read better. Measuring the holding region switches each list at the width it actually has. One list on a page stays a table while its neighbor turns to cards.

provisions.heading: Sorting
provisions.evidence: Which built sort control breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built arrows and phone sort controls beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `every-sortable-header-carries-an-arrow`
provisions.rationale: Give every sortable header its own arrow. The arrow states that headers sort on touch screens too. The runner-up is headers on a desktop with a Sort control on the phone list. It becomes necessary the moment the table turns into rows below 640 pixels. Never ship multi-column sort. No finance question needs two keys.

provisions.heading: Status in a Column
provisions.evidence: Which built state badge breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built tones, badges, and reason lines beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `tone-only-on-the-states-that-block`
provisions.rationale: Give a tone only to the states that block. Disputed and Awaiting payment take a badge because somebody must act. Paid and Completed stay plain words. Prefer the reason on a second line for a disputes queue where the word alone never answers why. Never ship progress marks. Four blocks per row on a 268-row list cannot serve a lifecycle that branches.

provisions.heading: Table's Own States
provisions.evidence: Which built table state breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built no-data, failed-read, and slow-read states beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `no-data-yet-table-replaced`
provisions.rationale: Keep each state as its own sentence for its own fact. No data yet replaces the table. A failed refresh keeps the chrome and names how old the rows are. A slow read names what is loading. Never ship a bare spinner over the table body. Rows that shift when the data lands move the row the reader already chose.

provisions.heading: The Layout of a Short List
provisions.evidence: Which built short-list layout breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built cards, table rows, and date-led lists beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `trip-cards-with-a-budget-bar`
provisions.rationale: Keep cards with a progress bar. A handful of trips reads better as cards than as rows. The bar answers the only question the list exists for. The runner-up is a date-led list. Prefer it once the year holds dozens of trips and cards stop fitting. Never ship a month calendar for this question: it answers when, which the list is never asked.

provisions.heading: Align Figures in a Column
provisions.evidence: Which built figure column wanders instead of lining up by place? Open built amount, count, and quantity columns and read down each one.
provisions.statement: An amount, count, or quantity shown in a column MUST use tabular figures, so digits of equal place sit under each other.
provisions.rationale: Proportional figures give each digit its own width, so a column of them wanders and equal places stop lining up. A reversal column whose digits wander is misread at a glance, and the wrong row pays for it. Tabular figures give every digit one width, so hundreds sit under hundreds down the whole column.

provisions.heading: Choosing a Period
provisions.evidence: Which built period control differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built chevrons, tabs, and painted calendars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chevrons-either-side-of-the-period-as-the-heading`
provisions.rationale: Ship chevrons beside the heading with a month dropdown. Walking is one click and jumping avoids twelve clicks. The runner-up uses presets with typeable bounds. It fits charts and exports where the period is not a month. Never ship the period as a filter chip. The period is the subject, not a refinement.

provisions.heading: Counting Things
provisions.evidence: Which built tally differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built sidebar counts, tiles, and dated claims beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `counts-in-the-sidebar-on-the-rows-that-hold-work`
provisions.rationale: Keep counts where the reader would otherwise fetch them. The sidebar rows that hold work carry them, and the tabs above a list carry them. The runner-up is the stat tiles with their measure stated. It is the better choice for the home page where the question is how large the month is. Never ship counts with the report that produces them, since the report name is system language on a number page.

provisions.heading: Figure Against an Earlier Period
provisions.evidence: Which built comparison tile differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built deltas, sparklines, and KPI tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `tiles-with-a-delta-pill-and-the-previous-figure`
provisions.rationale: Ship the tiles with a delta pill and the previous figure in words. The comparison is visible and the basis is stated. The runner-up is the tiles with sparklines. It is the better choice on the home page where the shape of the month matters more than one earlier figure. Never ship a bare percentage with no basis, since up 12 percent without the basis is a claim and not a comparison.

provisions.heading: How Much Fits Before It Breaks
provisions.evidence: Which built dense table differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built 390-pixel lists and pinned first columns beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-full-width-with-nothing-truncated`
provisions.rationale: Keep the table at desktop width. Use two-line cells with no truncation. Switch to the record list under 640 pixels. That pair answers honestly at both widths. The runner-up wraps rather than truncates. It fits where one column holds names of any length. Never ship shortened figures near a statement. A rounded money figure is not a money figure.

provisions.heading: Mark a Moment with Its Machine Value
provisions.evidence: Which built date or moment lacks its machine value? Open built dates and read each time element for its ISO value.
provisions.statement: Render a date or moment in a time element that carries its ISO 8601 value.
provisions.rationale: A reader's wording of a moment varies: 8 Oct, October 8, next Tuesday. Assistive technology and the browser read the exact value from the machine form, not the reader's wording of it. The ISO value keeps the cited moment exact even where the words stay short.

provisions.heading: Numbers at Phone Width
provisions.evidence: Which built narrow figure differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built pairs, per-row figures, and halved charts at 390 pixels beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `kpis-in-pairs-with-the-orders-under-them`
provisions.rationale: Ship the two-column KPI pair with the record list under it. The figures of the day stay visible and every expense keeps its amount right-aligned. The runner-up is the aligned statement. It is the better choice for finance pages where the adding up is the point. Never ship the desktop table unchanged at 390: a table that scrolls sideways for its money column hides the answer.

provisions.heading: Show the Currency of Every Amount
provisions.evidence: Which built figure hides its currency? Open the amounts on built tables, statements, and charts.
provisions.statement: Every amount MUST show its currency.
provisions.rationale: A currency on every amount keeps EUR 125.00 distinct from GBP 125.00 on every screen and export. Without it, a second currency turns each bare figure into a guess, and a pasted number carries no way to settle the guess.

provisions.heading: Showing an Identifier
provisions.evidence: Which built code display differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built monospaced, labeled, and copyable codes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-code-monospaced-labeled-and-copyable`
provisions.rationale: Ship the labeled, monospaced, copyable code on the record. It is the shape of the rule and the one thing a support case needs quoted. The runner-up is the identifier as the record name. It is the better choice for records with no human name, such as a payout reference. Never ship the page with no identifier: a record nobody can quote is a record support cannot help with.

provisions.heading: Spend Against the Budget
provisions.evidence: Which built fill-rate view differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built bars, countdowns, and capacity tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-bar-with-sold-held-and-left-in-words`
provisions.rationale: Ship the progress bar with claimed, held, and left in words. One glance says how far the budget has burned and what is still movable. The runner-up is the per-kind spend table. It is the better choice when one kind is gone and the others are not. Never ship the countdown alone, since EUR 468 left without the budget size hides whether the budget is nearly gone or barely touched.

provisions.heading: Spending by Expense Kind
provisions.evidence: Which built mix chart differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built bars, tiles, and donuts beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `horizontal-bars-with-the-figure-on-each-row`
provisions.rationale: Ship the horizontal bars with the figure on each row. Every kind reads with its count and its money in one glance. The runner-up is the table with a bar in each row. It is the better choice once kinds gain states such as disputed or reversed. Never ship the donut alone, since an angle nobody can read exactly is decoration and not a figure.

provisions.heading: Spending over Time
provisions.evidence: Which built trend chart differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built columns, areas, and sparklines beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `daily-columns-with-the-total-above`
provisions.rationale: Ship the daily columns with the total above and the peak labeled. They answer how much and when in one glance. The runner-up is the cumulative line against the previous quarter. It is the better choice once the budget has a quarter to beat. Never ship the chart without its table, since a figure nobody can read exactly is a figure nobody can cite.

provisions.heading: State the Time Zone of a Shared Moment
provisions.evidence: Which built shared moment omits its zone? Open the dates and times on built screens read across zones.
provisions.statement: A moment shown to readers in different time zones MUST state its time zone.
provisions.rationale: A stated zone keeps 09:32 in Amsterdam from reading as 09:32 in London. Without it, two readers plan the same payout window an hour apart, and finance meets only one of them.

provisions.heading: Statement That Adds Up
provisions.evidence: Which built totals page differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built groups, subtotals, and payout endings beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `groups-subtotals-and-a-grand-total`
provisions.rationale: Keep groups, subtotals, and a grand total. Keep a count under each line. The count is the only completeness check. The runner-up ends in the payouts it became. It fits finance work against bank lines. Add links on every line later as a behavior of the pick. Never ship the one figure option as the statement. It hides how the figure was reached.

provisions.heading: Two VAT Rates on One Page
provisions.evidence: Which built mixed-rate view differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built splits, badges, and per-rate summaries beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-vat-split-under-the-order-total`
provisions.rationale: Ship the VAT split under the expense total. The spender total stays one figure and the books get both rates. The runner-up is the per-rate report with taxable bases, which is the better choice at quarter end when finance files the return. Never ship amounts with no VAT note at all: a lawful amount states what the tax is.

provisions.heading: Vendor's Invoice to the Company
provisions.evidence: Which built supplier bill differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built documents, states, and usage lines beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-invoice-as-a-document-with-the-usage-behind-each-line`
provisions.rationale: Ship the document-style invoice with the usage behind each line: finance sees what the fee paid for without opening another page. The runner-up is the paid invoice with its mandate reference, which is the better state of the same document once the money has moved. Never ship the invoice without its VAT lines: a business invoice without VAT is not an invoice.

provisions.heading: When the Money Arrives
provisions.evidence: Which built payout view differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built upcoming, weekly, and journey views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `upcoming-payouts-with-the-sales-each-one-holds`
provisions.rationale: Ship the list of upcoming payouts with the expenses each one holds: the company sees what goes out and when in one place. The runner-up is the past payouts table with bank references, which is the better choice for finance reconciling against the bank. Never ship the single next-payout tile as the page: one arrival without the ones after it cannot plan a month.

provisions.heading: Writing a Moment
provisions.evidence: Which built date text differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built absolute, relative, and weekday forms beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-form-per-table-with-the-zone-stated-once`
provisions.rationale: Keep one form per table. State the zone once in the header. A column then reads as a column. The runner-up puts absolute over relative. It fits dispute and payout surfaces where recency leads. Never ship relative only on a reconciled page. Nothing there can be cited.

provisions.heading: Writing an Amount
provisions.evidence: Which built money text differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built codes, symbols, and red negatives beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `code-and-two-decimals-in-the-reader-s-language-with-a-true-m`
provisions.rationale: Ship the code format in the reader's language with a true minus. It keeps one convention and answers decimals, negatives and separators: each currency shows the decimals it defines. The runner-up is the plain code table. It shows the same choice without reversal rows. Choose the symbol with code in the header only when the finance screens and the spender screens show the same form. Never ship the no currency option. It loses the currency in exports. Never ship mixed decimals. It breaks the alignment tables exist for.

provisions.heading: Account Menu
provisions.evidence: Which built sign-in menu differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built account controls, in the sidebar foot or header, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `an-avatar-menu-in-the-header`
provisions.rationale: The avatar menu in the header holds the account page, the access statement, and sign-out in one control. The sidebar foot is the runner-up, but it is far from the top of a long page. The account as a page reached from the menu fits a console where account, email, sign-in, and close are separate pages. Never ship the bare sign-out link. An account with no page turns language, sessions, and closing into support messages.

provisions.heading: Breadcrumb
provisions.evidence: Which built parent chain differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open a built four-level trail, with its truncation and parent links, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-trail-as-the-parent-chain`
provisions.rationale: The parent chain with the last item marked current states where a record sits in the tree. The left-truncating trail with an overflow menu is the runner-up for four-level chains, because it keeps the current page visible. The current title as a sibling menu fits records whose siblings are opened together. Never ship no trail at all: on a phone the sidebar is closed, so the trail is the only statement of where a record sits.

provisions.heading: Command Palette
provisions.evidence: Which built jump-to dialog breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built palette, with its grouped results and recent items, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `cmd-k-dialog-with-grouped-results`
provisions.rationale: The grouped Cmd+K dialog puts pages above records, so a typed query answers both where to go and what to open. Recent items first are the runner-up for cost centre and support work that moves between a few records. Search scoped to the current area fits a reader who is already in the right list. Never ship command verbs with a preview as the default palette. Every verb becomes a second path to a use case.

provisions.heading: Draw Sibling Pages as Links, Not Tabs
provisions.evidence: Which built row of sibling pages is a tab list instead of links? Open each built row and check the address changes and the Back button returns.
provisions.statement: A row of sibling pages MUST be a navigation landmark of links with `aria-current="page"` on the current page, leaving the tab list for switching panels within one page.
provisions.rationale: A screen reader announces a tab list as panels on one page, so a reader who opens Receipts from a tab expects the address to stay and the Back button to skip it. A navigation landmark of links tells the truth: each page has its own address, and the Back button returns to the page before it. WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships and criterion 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value require the announced role to match the behavior.

provisions.heading: Give Every Page Its Own Address
provisions.evidence: Which built screen cannot be opened directly from its copied link? Paste three copied addresses into a fresh tab.
provisions.statement: Every page MUST have its own URL that opens it directly.
provisions.rationale: A direct address lets a reader share, bookmark, and reopen a page, and lets a notification or a record link to it. Without it, support cannot send the page under discussion, and a refresh drops the reader back to the start.

provisions.heading: Header Bar
provisions.evidence: Which built top band breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built trip header, with its company name and deployment identity, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-bar-with-the-company-name`
provisions.rationale: The bar with the company name and the acting person states the two facts a support conversation needs before anything else. The bar as the breadcrumb is the runner-up when the trail would otherwise repeat the page title. The deployment identity band fits a sandbox deployment, where naming the deployment avoids confusion with production. Never ship no bar at all: burying the theme and language in the sidebar foot turns a visible control into three taps.

provisions.heading: Help and Support
provisions.evidence: Which built guidance entry differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built help surfaces, from sidebar entry to contextual hints, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `contextual-help-beside-the-page-it-explains`
provisions.rationale: The guide for the current page in a side panel answers the question without leaving the record. A help page from the sidebar is the runner-up index for a reader who knows what to ask. Help search inside the command palette fits a console where navigation queries already go to one input. Never ship no help entry: a finance lead stuck at the office with a queue has nowhere else to turn.

provisions.heading: Icons in the Frame
provisions.evidence: Which built label or action carries an icon outside the recorded set? Open the built frame, with its labeled actions and marked current item, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `an-icon-beside-every-label`
provisions.rationale: An icon beside every label reinforces the label rather than replacing it, which makes seven areas easy to read at a glance. Icons only for the actions, with words for the areas, are the runner-up where icon budget is short. Words only fit a small set of areas with no icon set to keep. Never ship state-carrying icons in the frame: theme and language as bare glyphs force the reader to hover both to tell them apart.

provisions.heading: Language and Theme
provisions.evidence: Which built switch differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built locale and appearance controls, in the header and account menu, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-theme-following-the-system-with-an-override`
provisions.rationale: The theme follows the device because few readers change it during a day and the device already states the preference, with System, Light, and Dark offered in the account menu for the reader who overrides it. The language stays in the header showing its value because a wrong language makes every other word unreadable. Both switches in the header, each showing its value, is the runner-up for a product whose staff switch theme during a shift. Never ship with no language switch. One language is a commercial decision about which companies Claimwick serves. Claimwick already serves companies in two languages.

provisions.heading: Mark the Current Section
provisions.evidence: Which built screen fails to highlight the area holding its open page? Open three built screens reached by link, notification, and search.
provisions.statement: The navigation MUST mark the section that holds the current page.
provisions.rationale: A marked section tells a reader who arrived from a link, a notification, or a search which area holds the open page. Without it, every page looks like the start, and the reader reopens the sidebar to learn where they already are.

provisions.heading: Notification Inbox
provisions.evidence: Which built attention list breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built inbox and bell, with triage and unread states, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-bell-in-the-header-with-a-dropdown-panel`
provisions.rationale: A bell with a dropdown panel keeps the count visible on every page and answers what changed without leaving the list being worked. The inbox page is the runner-up for support days with dozens of items, where triage needs filters. Needs attention on the home page fits a console where the first page is the only queue. Never ship no notifications. Polling seven areas by hand is how a dispute deadline is missed.

provisions.heading: Sidebar
provisions.evidence: Which built area list breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built console frame, with its grouped areas and marked item, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `grouped-areas-with-expandable-sub-items`
provisions.rationale: The grouped areas with expandable sub-items keep seven areas in two levels. The counts beside groups are the runner-up for areas that hold a queue, such as reversals. Recent pages above the areas fit a reader who resumes the same few records. Never ship the flat list of every page. Over a hundred entries is an index, not a map, and it belongs in the command palette.

provisions.heading: Tabs Within a Page
provisions.evidence: Which built tab row differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built in-page tabs, with the active tab in the URL, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-shipped-tab-row-with-the-tab-in-the-url`
provisions.rationale: The tab row with the active tab in the URL carries the facet in a pasted link. The row is drawn as tabs but built as navigation links, one address per page, following Draw Sibling Pages as Links, Not Tabs. The current page is marked by more than color: weight or an underline. On a narrow screen the row scrolls on one line and keeps the current page in view, never wrapping. Tabs as real links are the runner-up and the most defensible alternative, because middle click and the back button behave as expected. Headed sections on one page fit a record with a handful of facets that all fit. Never ship the segmented control for facets: three segments is its ceiling and it cannot carry counts or overflow.

provisions.heading: Workspace Switcher
provisions.evidence: Which built cost centre picker breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built switcher, with recent workspaces first, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-workspace-switcher-at-the-top-of-the-sidebar`
provisions.rationale: A workspace switcher at the top of the sidebar moves the whole console without visiting the list. The trail sibling menu is the runner-up on record pages four levels deep, where the sidebar context is far away. Recent workspaces first in the palette fit a reader who switches by keyboard. Never ship back-to-list as the only path. It costs the most to exactly the companies with the most cost centres.

provisions.heading: Calendar or Schedule Page
provisions.evidence: Which built date view breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built month grids, agendas, and week lanes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `month-grid-with-trips-marked`
provisions.rationale: The month grid stays the pick: ninety-three trips ahead need density, and the grid shows the month the list cannot. The agenda list is the runner-up. Prefer it on a phone, where seven columns become unreadable whichever way they are drawn. The week lanes are the other runner-up for a company with few cost centres and a clash to spot. Never ship the week lanes as the default. Two cost centres fit, and the third cost centre breaks the shape.

provisions.heading: Editor Page
provisions.evidence: Which built preview screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built form-plus-preview splits, drawers, and floating panels beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `form-left-live-preview-right-one-save`
provisions.rationale: Form left with a live preview right stays the pick. Every control writes straight into the preview, and nobody saves to find out what a change looks like. The floating panel is the runner-up. Prefer it when the visual dominates, such as a cover image judged at real size. The preview drawer is the other runner-up when the form needs the full page. Keep the preview beside the form or over it. A preview above the form scrolls away with every edit, which defeats a live preview.

provisions.heading: Error or Not-Found Page
provisions.evidence: Which built dead end breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built not-found, outage, and refused views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `centered-not-found-with-links-back`
provisions.rationale: The centered not-found with links back stays the pick: it says what happened, says where to go, and does both in one glance. The permission refusal is the runner-up. Prefer it whenever the page knows who can resolve it, because Back is not a fix. The full-page outage is the other runner-up when a provider failure blocks the page. A retry button on a page that will never exist is a promise that cannot be kept. Name the state and the next step instead.

provisions.heading: Form Page
provisions.evidence: Which built input screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built sections, labeled blocks, and one-question flows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-section-one-column-of-fields-cancel-beside-save`
provisions.rationale: One section, one column, Cancel beside Save stays the pick. A single command reads as a list of questions with one place to submit and one to leave. The stacked blocks are the runner-up when the form carries several labeled groups. The one-question-per-screen flow is the other runner-up when each answer changes the next question and nothing may be skipped. Three steps for work that fits one page is one step too many.

provisions.heading: Home Page
provisions.evidence: Which built start screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built queues, tiles, and next actions beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `work-first-tiles-second`
provisions.rationale: Work first, tiles second stays the pick. The manager reads the queue and stops, and the figures wait below for the curious reader. The my-work split is the runner-up. Prefer it once assignment is a real command and two people share one queue. The tiles-first layout is the other runner-up for a reader who opens the page to check a number. Never ship the tiles-first layout as the default. Three stat tiles push the queue below the fold and the page reads as a report instead of a task list.

provisions.heading: List Page
provisions.evidence: Which built collection screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built searches, views, and filter bars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `search-and-a-state-filter-only`
provisions.rationale: Search plus one state filter stays the pick. Two controls answer the two questions readers ask, and a bare list needs only the filter added. The row of views is the runner-up for the states a reader returns to. The dense filter bar is the other runner-up past a few hundred rows across many spenders, where the query is restated in words. A list page holds one table, and a second table is a second route wearing a disguise. Views can replace the state filter, but they never replace the search box.

provisions.heading: Live Operations Page
provisions.evidence: Which built wall display breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built counts, cost centres, and exception views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-count-the-cost-centres-the-exceptions`
provisions.rationale: The count with cost centres and exceptions stays the pick. The finance lead reads one number first, then the per-cost-centre split, then only what needs a person. The exceptions-only view is the runner-up. Prefer it on the wall display once the day is steady and the count is already known. The full-screen count is the other runner-up for a display read from across the room. A page that lists every payout is a log, not a live view. Keep the count in the header and the exceptions above the fold.

provisions.heading: Name the Page in One Heading
provisions.evidence: Which built screen splits its title across headings or omits it? Open every built page and read its top-level heading.
provisions.statement: Each page MUST show one top-level heading that names the record, list, or task it holds.
provisions.rationale: One heading names the open record, list, or task, so a reader who arrived from a link or a search knows where they landed. Without it, two headings compete for that job, and the reader guesses which line to trust while assistive tech announces the wrong one.

provisions.heading: Onboarding or Setup Page
provisions.evidence: Which built first-run guide breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built checklists, wizards, and templates beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `checklist-with-a-progress-bar`
provisions.rationale: The checklist with a progress bar stays the pick: it states the three steps, shows which is done, and waits without leading. The stepper wizard is the runner-up. Prefer it when a step cannot be skipped and the next depends on the last. Starting from a template is the other runner-up when the first trip is a known shape. Three saves for a first run is three chances to leave half set up.

provisions.heading: Outcome Page
provisions.evidence: Which built result screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built statements, references, and refusal outcomes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-statement-one-next-step`
provisions.rationale: One statement with one next step stays the pick. A reader who came to learn whether it worked leaves in one glance. The refusal outcome is the runner-up, for the same frame with the fix in the primary place. The confirmation band is the other runner-up when the flow leaves a reference the reader must keep. A moment is not a place. An outcome the reader may need to return to belongs on a page, not in a toast.

provisions.heading: Queue
provisions.evidence: Which built batch-selection screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built select-all banners, play modes, and per-row checkboxes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `select-all-on-the-page-banner-for-the-rest`
provisions.rationale: Select all on the page, then the rest from a banner, stays the pick. It is the clearest answer to the select-all problem, and money deserves the second click. The play mode is the runner-up. Prefer it when each decision needs different information and batch work is rare. A checkbox on every row is the other runner-up for a queue whose bulk job is small and capped. Keep the search box and the filter in place while rows are selected. A bulk bar that replaces the toolbar makes the layout jump mid-decision and hides the controls the reader wants to refine it.

provisions.heading: Record Page
provisions.evidence: Which built single-record screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built summaries, tabs, and asides beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `summary-sections-aside-for-history`
provisions.rationale: Summary with sections and history in the aside stays the pick. What defines the record runs down the main column while history supports it from the side. The properties rail is the runner-up. Prefer it when the aside must carry editable values rather than history. The tabs layout is the other runner-up for a record with more facets than three sections allow. Never put the record's facts in the header. A dense header pushes every command below the fold on a phone and fights the trail for space.

provisions.heading: Report Page
provisions.evidence: Which built figures screen breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built period pickers, range controls, and trend cards beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chevron-pair-with-the-period-as-the-heading`
provisions.rationale: The chevron pair with the period as the heading stays the pick. A reader cannot mistake a chevron for a tab, and the list still allows a jump across months. The cards with sparklines are the runner-up. Prefer them mid-month when the question is trend rather than settlement. The typed range is the other runner-up for a report over an arbitrary span. Label each month control with its direction. A pair of unlabeled buttons leaves the reader guessing which one goes back.

provisions.heading: Settings Home
provisions.evidence: Which built setup index breaks from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built grouped links, settings trees, and search indexes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `grouped-links-one-line-each`
provisions.rationale: Grouped links stay the pick. Each area names what it holds, the page never grows a form, and thirty routes fit in a handful of sections. The left navigation is the runner-up. Prefer it once areas gain enough depth to deserve their own tree. The searchable list is the other runner-up for a reader who knows the name of the setting. Group by the thing, never by how often it changes: readers look for a thing, not for how often they change it.

provisions.heading: Keep Destructive Commands Out of the Primary Place
provisions.evidence: Which built record header hands a destructive command the primary style? Open the headers on built record screens and read each command's tone.
provisions.statement: A destructive command MUST NOT take the primary action's place or style in a record header.
provisions.rationale: The primary place draws the hurried click, so it holds only the safe next step. A destructive command styled or placed as primary turns a routine visit into a retired policy or a voided expense, with no step between intent and loss.

provisions.heading: Previous and Next Record
provisions.evidence: Which built neighbor step differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built jump searches and list drawers beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chevrons-beside-the-breadcrumb`
provisions.rationale: Keep the chevrons beside the breadcrumb. They keep the list order. They cost almost no space. The runner-up is the jump-by-search option. It fits readers who know the next record number rather than its neighbor. Prefer the list drawer on triage queues where the reader skims many records. Never ship movement without a position: chevrons that never say 4 of 268 leave the reader lost in the queue.

provisions.heading: Property List with Copy
provisions.evidence: Which built copyable fact differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built confirmations and identifier cards beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `every-identifier-copies`
provisions.rationale: Keep the always-visible copy button on each identifier. Support reaches for it without hunting. The runner-up is the in-place confirmation option. It fits records where a miscopied reference causes real mistakes. Prefer the grouped card only where identifiers are quoted together, such as a reference pasted into a dispute. Where the same copy control repeats in every row of a table, it shows on hover and on keyboard focus and stays visible on a touch screen, and a repeated click restarts its confirmation instead of being ignored. Hover-only copy fits nowhere: touch screens have no hover and the button would never appear. Never ship a property list whose long values clip without a way to expand them.

provisions.heading: Record Aside
provisions.evidence: Which built side column differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built decision panels and ownership rails beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `history-in-the-aside-sections-in-the-main-column`
provisions.rationale: Give the pick to history in the aside. History supports the expense without describing it, which is exactly what the aside slot is for. The runner-up is the decision panel. It is the better choice on records that wait for someone, such as a dispute with a deadline. Prefer the people and labels aside on records a team hands between shifts. Never ship an empty aside by accident: an expense with nothing pending and no history reads as a rendering fault.

provisions.heading: Record Attachments
provisions.evidence: Which built file section differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built evidence groups and thumbnail grids beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-file-list-with-a-drop-zone`
provisions.rationale: Keep the file list with a drop zone. Each row names the file and its kind. It names who added it and its size. The drop zone invites the next file. The runner-up is the evidence-grouped option. It fits a dispute: Ben asks for kinds there rather than files. Prefer the thumbnail option only where images dominate, such as receipt photos. Never ship a section that is only a drop zone: a record whose files hide behind an upload control reads as empty.

provisions.heading: Record Change History
provisions.evidence: Which built audit trail differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built per-field histories and full-page logs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `history-as-a-tab-on-the-record`
provisions.rationale: Keep the history tab on the record. It keeps one route. The tab state stays in the URL. A reader checking a claim opens History without losing the expense. The runner-up is the per-field history. It fits disputes about one value such as the email that carried the receipt. Prefer the full-page log only for long-lived records whose trail outgrows a tab. Never ship the money-only trail as the audit: the edits that explain the money are missing there.

provisions.heading: Record Header
provisions.evidence: Which built title row differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built facts and overflow menus beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `title-state-breadcrumb-one-primary-action`
provisions.rationale: Keep the title, state, breadcrumb, and one primary action. The state beside the title answers the first question on every record. The runner-up is the overflow menu option. It is the better choice once a record carries four or more commands. Prefer the facts option only where the record's own facts are the reason to open it: a tall header pushes the sections below the fold. Never ship a header with no title. Every page carries exactly one `h1`, which automated checks enforce.

provisions.heading: Record Notes
provisions.evidence: Which built annotation feed differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built scope toggles and mixed feeds beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-notes-section-with-the-composer-on-top`
provisions.rationale: Keep the notes section with the composer on top. The newest note reads first. Internal scope is the default. It cannot leak. The runner-up is the internal-or-spender composer. It fits records where staff write to the spender from the same box. Prefer notes mixed into the timeline only where what the team wrote explains what the system did next. Never ship notes without a scope marker: a reader who cannot tell internal from spender-visible will write the wrong one.

provisions.heading: Record Summary
provisions.evidence: Which built fact block differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built copy buttons and figure tiles beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `facts-about-the-record-itself`
provisions.rationale: Keep the facts about the record itself. A trip summary states when, where, and what it may spend, which is the identity of the record rather than its support. The runner-up is the copyable identifiers option. It is the better choice on records a reader quotes elsewhere, such as an expense read out on the phone. Prefer the tiles option only where the reader checks four figures at a glance rather than reading the facts line by line. Never ship values with no section: a row of values standing on the canvas breaks the rule that a section is the only box.

provisions.heading: Record Tabs
provisions.evidence: Which built facet row differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built side rails and three-tab rows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `four-tabs-with-the-active-one-in-the-url`
provisions.rationale: Keep the four tabs with the active one in the URL. Four stays inside every cited ceiling, and each panel repeats its tab label as a heading. The runner-up is the side rail option. It is the better choice past five facets or where one facet is a long form. Prefer three tabs with the fourth as its own page only where the fourth facet is long enough to stand as a page. Never ship tabs with icons in their labels: icons are forbidden in tab labels, and they add a second channel for one meaning.

provisions.heading: Record the Reader May Not Change
provisions.evidence: Which built locked record differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built access requests and whole-page refusals beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-commands-are-refused-the-record-is-not`
provisions.rationale: Keep the refused commands on a readable record. Auditors can read an expense and cannot reimburse it, and each refusal names the grant that would allow it. The runner-up is the ask for access option. It is the better choice where access is routinely granted, such as an intern joining finance. Prefer the whole-page refusal only where the record itself is out of the reader's reach: it names the grant, and it costs the reader every fact on the page. Never ship a role switcher on production: acting as somebody is a development capability, and the button would be a security hole with a label on it.

provisions.heading: Record Timeline
provisions.evidence: Which built event feed differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built filters and history tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `newest-first-with-actor-and-timestamp`
provisions.rationale: Keep the newest-first timeline with actor and timestamp. It answers who and when on every line. The runner-up is the filtered timeline. It is the better choice once a record carries dozens of entries across kinds. Prefer the table option only where the history is the record rather than context. Never group the main history by actor: it destroys the chronological order a timeline exists to give.

provisions.heading: Related Records
provisions.evidence: Which built relation link differs from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built previews and editable tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `each-relation-is-a-link-with-its-state`
provisions.rationale: Ship the link with state list. Each relation is a link carrying its own state, so a reader can jump and knows what they will find. The runner-up is the preview card option. It is the better choice where the parent facts decide the next step, such as a receipt read against its trip. Prefer the editable table only where the relation itself is the work, such as the exceptions to a policy. Never ship a cross-reference line in the description: it cannot carry the parent state and it hides where a reader does not look.

provisions.heading: Show One Primary Action in a Record Header
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `PATTERN_INVALID` for a wireframe header holding two primary actions.
provisions.statement: A record header wireframe MUST show at most one primary action.
provisions.rationale: One primary action names the step readers take most often next on the record, such as Message spender on expense EXP-1042. Without that single answer, two equal buttons force the reader to compare labels on every visit, and the hurried click lands on the wrong command.

provisions.heading: Whole Record Screen
provisions.evidence: Which built record page orders its parts differently from the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built summary, money-first, and tabbed screens beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `summary-three-sections-history-in-the-aside`
provisions.rationale: Keep the record-page shape with a summary, three sections, and history in the aside. Spender, lines, and money each keep their own section. The runner-up is the money-first layout. It fits finance readers who reconcile payments against reversals. Prefer the tabbed layout only once a record outgrows three sections. Never ship the phone layout as the desktop page: stacked sections waste most of the width there.

provisions.heading: Build the Server Data Cache per Request
provisions.evidence: Which server rendering reuses a data cache across requests instead of constructing it inside each request? Look in the server request setup.
provisions.statement: A server-rendered frontend MUST construct its data cache inside each request.
provisions.rationale: A server renders for many users at once. A data cache shared across requests serves the next user the previous user's answer, leaking one actor's data to another with no error to report it. Constructing the cache inside each request gives every user a fresh cache that dies with the response.

provisions.heading: Keep Address Parameters Validated by a Schema
provisions.evidence: Which routes leave address parameters, filters, or page outside a validated schema? Look in the route parameter schemas.
provisions.statement: A route MUST declare its address parameters in a validated schema, including its filters and its page.
provisions.rationale: A validated schema makes the address the whole input: a shareable address restores the same filters and page, and validation refuses a malformed address at the boundary instead of rendering a page from nonsense values.
provisions.example: The list schema declares its own text field and spreads the shared paging fields.

provisions.heading: Keep Authenticated Caching Explicit
provisions.evidence: Which cached actor-specific reads lack a declared cache key, partition, invalidation owner, or security review beside the read definition? Look in the read definitions setting cache keys.
