provisions.statement: Actor-specific data MUST declare its cache key, partition, invalidation owner, and security review before caching, beside the read definition setting the key.
provisions.rationale: A cache entry that ignores whose data it holds serves one actor's answer to another user: the classic leak behind a shared cache. Declaring the cache key, the partition, the invalidation owner, and the security review beside the read definition forces each cached actor-specific read to name its boundary before it caches. An uncached read is the safe default, and a cache partitioned per request is the safe server shape.

provisions.heading: Keep Layouts Stable
provisions.evidence: Which layouts carry a provider that some child route never needs? Look in the layout definitions.
provisions.statement: Keep a layout to the frame and the providers every child route needs.
provisions.rationale: A layout wraps every route beneath it. A feature-specific provider placed in a shared layout forces unrelated routes to carry its download, its state, and its failure modes. Keeping a layout to the frame and the providers every child route needs keeps each route's cost to what it uses.

provisions.heading: Keep Proxy Behavior at the Edge
provisions.evidence: Which proxy rules decide identity or authorization instead of routing only? Look in the proxy rules.
provisions.statement: A development or edge proxy rule MUST route only, and never decide who the actor is or what the actor may read.
provisions.rationale: A development or edge proxy runs before the request reaches the API, with no view of the record or the permissions an authorization decision depends on. A proxy rule that decided who the actor is or what the actor may read would enforce a different boundary than the API, and the two would disagree on the first edge case. The proxy routes and nothing else; the API owns identity and authorization.
provisions.example: A development proxy forwards `/api` and `/auth` to the API and changes nothing else.

provisions.heading: Keep Server-Only Code Identifiable
provisions.evidence: Which modules reading request headers, cookies, or server secrets sit in files unnamed or unplaced for the server? Look in the server file names and places.
provisions.statement: Keep a module reading a request header, a cookie, or a server secret in a file whose name and place show the server ownership.
provisions.rationale: A module that reads a request header, a cookie, or a server secret breaks when it runs in the browser, and worse, it can drag the secret into the client download. A file whose name and place show server ownership turns an accidental browser import into a build error, and carries the same fact to a reader browsing the tree.

provisions.heading: Load Each Route and Each Language Separately
provisions.evidence: Which routes or languages ship in a shared download, or load an icon set or language whole? Look in the route bundles and the dictionary loader.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST load each route and each language as its own download, with no icon set or language loaded whole.
provisions.rationale: A user opens one address and reads one language, so downloading every route and every language up front wastes time on code and copy outside that path. Each route and each language ships as its own download: a user in Dutch who stays on the dashboard downloads neither English nor the routes outside that path. No icon set or language loads whole for the same reason.
provisions.example: A dictionary loader returns one language. Each route file or folder ships as its own download.

provisions.heading: Load Route Data Before Rendering
provisions.evidence: Which routes render before their reads load through the one shared cache? Look in the route loaders and the cache definitions.
provisions.statement: A route MUST load each read it needs through one shared cache before its view renders.
provisions.rationale: A view that renders before its reads complete shows a spinner after it appears, then swaps the spinner for content: two drawings for one navigation, with layout shifting between them. Loading each read through one shared cache before the view renders gives the page its data in place. The cache owns freshness, so the router keeps no second copy that could disagree.
provisions.example: An entity route loads its record and every read the record's own sections need.

provisions.heading: Move Focus on a Route Change
provisions.evidence: Which route leaves focus on the old link or the page body after a navigation inside the application? Look in the route suite output.
provisions.statement: A route change inside the application MUST move keyboard focus to the new route's top-level heading.
provisions.rationale: A full page load starts focus and the screen reader at the top of the new page, but a client-side navigation replaces the content under a focus that stays on the link just used, or falls back to the page body. A keyboard user then tabs through the old position and a screen-reader user hears nothing change. Moving focus to the heading reads the new page's title and starts the next Tab from there, as WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order expects. For example, opening EXP-1042 from the expense list lands focus on the heading "EXP-1042, Ava, EUR 125.00".

provisions.heading: Prefetch a Route on Intent
provisions.evidence: Which route prefetches land outside the shared cache, or feed a second router cache? Look in the router prefetch wiring.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST prefetch the route the user signals intent toward, without treating that prefetch as a cache beyond the shared cache.
provisions.rationale: When the user signals intent toward a route, by hovering a link or focusing a menu item, prefetching loads that route's data into the shared cache before the navigation starts, so most navigations render from data already in place. The prefetch fills the shared cache only: a router that kept its own second cache would serve a stale answer beside the fresh one.

provisions.heading: Read Route Data from the Route Cache
provisions.evidence: Which views read under another key than the cache entry their route filled, or handle a failed read outside the route error boundary? Look in the view data reads and the route loaders.
provisions.statement: A view MUST read route data through the same cache entry its route filled.
provisions.rationale: A view that reads under another key issues a second request for data the route already loaded, and the two answers can disagree when the data changes between them. Reading through the same cache entry the route filled renders the data the route approved. A failed read reaches the route's error boundary, which draws the shared problem state instead of a half-rendered view.

provisions.heading: Represent Route States
provisions.evidence: Which data-driven routes miss a loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, or ready behavior, or leave an absent address outside the shared outcome page? Look in the route state definitions.
provisions.statement: A data-driven route MUST define its loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, and ready behavior.
provisions.rationale: A blank region while a request is pending or failed gives the user no signal: the page reads no different when loading than when broken. Defining loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, and ready behavior gives each state a designed drawing, and the root not-found handling draws the shared outcome page for an absent address. These six are the states a route has. A control adds `disabled` and `pending` under `litespec/frontend/components#render-control-states`, because both describe a control rather than a route. A route adds `not-found`, which a control does not, because a missing target resolves at the route.

provisions.heading: Split Long Client Work
provisions.evidence: Which client task runs longer than 50 milliseconds without yielding? Look in the browser performance traces of the heaviest routes.
provisions.statement: Split client work that runs longer than 50 milliseconds, such as an import preview or a report total, into chunks that give the browser a turn between them.
provisions.rationale: While script runs, the page answers no click and no key, so a staff member previewing 1,204 imported payouts sees a frozen screen and clicks again. Giving the browser a turn between chunks keeps every input answered within one frame, and the total blocking time the measured checks record stays low.

provisions.heading: Use a Shared Layout for a Shell
provisions.evidence: Which shells sit outside a shared layout, or add an address segment? Look in the layout definitions.
provisions.statement: Give a shell a layout holding the frame every child route shares.
provisions.rationale: A shell is the frame every child route shares: navigation, header, and providers. A shared layout holds it without adding an address segment, so the shell stays out of links and every child route renders inside the same frame.

provisions.heading: Keep a Route Entry Thin
provisions.evidence: Which route entries hold reusable logic or reference another route entry? Look in the route entries.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST hold its input, its load, and its component, with no reusable logic and no reference to another route entry.
provisions.rationale: A route entry serves one address: its input, its load, and its component. A column definition or validation rule written there is unreachable from the second route that needs it, so the second route writes its own copy. A reference from one route entry to another makes one address depend on another, so changing the first breaks the second. Reusable logic belongs in modules, where both routes import it.
provisions.example: An expense list route validates its search, prefetches its read, and composes one screen from module components.

provisions.heading: Keep a Use Case Folder Flat
provisions.evidence: Which use-case folders hold a subfolder? Look in the module tree.
provisions.statement: A folder named for one use case MUST hold files and no subfolder.
provisions.rationale: A subfolder inside a use case folder names a grouping the backend does not have, so the one-to-one mirror between the two trees stops at that point. Past the subfolder, the reader can no longer translate names by rule, and nothing reports where the translation broke. Files directly in the use case folder keep the mirror checkable to the bottom.

provisions.heading: Keep Applications Independent
provisions.evidence: Which frontends import source from another frontend? Look in the import statements.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT import source from another frontend.
provisions.rationale: Each application owns its routes, its environment, its session handling, its words, its tests, and its deployment, so it can change, test, and ship on its own. An import from another application's source ties the two together: a change to one breaks or redeploys the other. Code two applications genuinely share moves down into a shared package, which names neither application.

provisions.heading: Keep Shared Packages Non Application Specific
provisions.evidence: Which shared packages hold page composition, feature state, authentication policy, or application components? Look in the shared package sources.
provisions.statement: A shared package MUST NOT contain page composition, feature state, authentication policy, or application components.
provisions.rationale: Shared packages hold what serves every frontend and names none of them: the generated client, the shared UI package, the locale dictionaries, and the frontend tooling. Page composition, feature state, authentication policy, or application components kept there would bind every application to one application's choices. Application-specific code stays in the application, where it can change without touching the rest.

provisions.heading: Locate Cross-Route Values in the Frame
provisions.evidence: Which client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, shell data, or browser uses sit outside the frame? Look in the frame.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST place cross-route values in its frame: client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data.
provisions.rationale: Client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data cross every route. A route holding one of them holds a copy beside every other route's copy, with nothing keeping the copies equal. The frame holds each once, where every route reaches it. A browser API a use-case module needs belongs in the frame for the same reason: a module renders and reads data rather than touching the device.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Route with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a route entry with no mark, `mark-count-invalid` (level S) for one with more than one, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming no screen of the route's entry point.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST carry one mark naming the screen it renders, in the form its stack page states.
provisions.rationale: The route is where a screen record becomes code, and its folder or file name only resembles the screen. One mark makes the link written and checkable: a web route exports the same typed `litespec` constant a use-case module exports, so a wrong identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran, and a Blazor component or an Android destination carries the .NET mark the .NET reader already reads. Each stack page states its route entry, the file or class that carries the mark, and that layouts, error pages, and route groups are not route entries: the [Svelte Stack](web/svelte/stack.md), [React Stack](web/react/stack.md), [Blazor Stack](blazor/stack.md), and [Android Stack](mobile/android/stack.md) pages state theirs. The use cases a screen offers are not marked on the route; the builder computes them from its calls.
provisions.example: The `<script module>` of the Claimwick expense list page exports `export const litespec = { implements: "screen/claimwick-app.expense-list" } as const satisfies LiteSpecMark;`.

provisions.heading: Mirror the Backend Use Case Path in Kebab Case
provisions.evidence: Which use-case folders sit outside `{module}/{aggregate}/{use-case}/` in kebab case, or resolve to no backend folder of the same names? Look in the module tree and the structure test proving the mirror.
provisions.statement: A use-case folder MUST sit under the modules root at `{module}/{aggregate}/{use-case}/` in kebab case, or at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` for a query describing no one aggregate, resolving to the one backend use case folder of the same names inside its `UseCases/` folder.
provisions.rationale: A reader holding a specification page finds the frontend code by translating three names to lowercase folders. No second map, index, or naming register stands between the specification and the code, so an agent given a use case id resolves its frontend folder by rule. The backend holds one folder per use case, so the mirror names one folder. The frontend structure test holds the mirror on every build under `litespec/frontend/testing#prove-the-module-mirror-in-a-structure-test`.
provisions.example:
One backend folder and its frontend counterpart are the same path in two spellings.

```text
<backend>/Orders/Orders/UseCases/SearchMerchantOrders/
<frontend>/modules/orders/orders/search-merchant-orders/
```

For example, the Claimwick product lists expenses through `use-case/spending.list-expenses`, implemented in the backend under `Spending/Expenses/UseCases/ListExpenses`. The web frontend serves it from the same path in kebab case: `lib/modules/spending/expenses/list-expenses` in the Claimwick example, beside the screen record `screen/claimwick-app.expense-list`.

```text
<backend>/Spending/Expenses/UseCases/ListExpenses/
<frontend>/modules/spending/expenses/list-expenses/
```

The three backend names become three lowercase folder names, so a reader holding the use case finds the frontend code by translating Spending, Expenses, and ListExpenses. The `UseCases/` segment carries no frontend spelling.

A query that describes no one aggregate has its record home under `use-cases/` beside its module, so its folder mirrors that home with two names instead of three: a query named `use-case/spending.read-spending-summary` would live at `<frontend>/modules/spending/use-cases/read-spending-summary/` and `<backend>/Spending/UseCases/ReadSpendingSummary/`. The running Claimwick example holds no such module-level query.

The diagram shows the backend path beside its frontend mirror, with one arrow per translated segment.

![The backend folder Spending, Expenses, ListExpenses beside the frontend folders spending, expenses, list-expenses, with one arrow mapping each backend segment to its kebab-case spelling.](../assets/diagrams/frontend-use-case-path.svg)

provisions.heading: Order Imports from Routes to Shared Packages
provisions.evidence: Which imports point against the route to module to frame to shared package direction? Look in the import statements.
provisions.statement: An import MUST point from a route to a module to the frame to a shared package, and never in the reverse direction.
provisions.rationale: Imports pointing from routes to modules to the frame to shared packages keep addresses, use-case code, cross-route values, and shared code in separate layers. A reverse import collapses two layers: a module importing a route ties use-case code to one address, and a shared package importing an application ties every application to one application's choices. One direction keeps each layer usable without the layers above it.
provisions.example:
This direction shows the allowed dependency path.

```text
Routes -> modules -> frame -> shared packages
```

The direction refuses three imports: a module reaching a route, a shared package reaching an application, and a frame module reaching into one module's use-case folder for a second module's data.

provisions.heading: Organize a Frontend into Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Which frontend files sit outside the frame, routes, and use-case modules split? Look in the frontend folder roots.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST organize its code into a frame, routes, and use-case modules.
provisions.rationale: Three parts give every file one home by answering one question: is it cross-cutting, is it an address, or does it serve one use case. Without the split, shared values hide inside routes, use-case code hides inside shared folders, and no author can tell where a new file belongs. The three parts make the answer mechanical.
provisions.example:
Each stack names these three parts for its own toolchain.

```text
{frontend}/
  frame/     client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
  routes/    one entry per address
  modules/   one folder per backend module, aggregate, and use case
```

provisions.heading: Place a Shared File in the Folder That Owns It
provisions.evidence: Which files read by several use cases sit outside the narrowest folder holding every consumer? Look in the aggregate and module folders.
provisions.statement: A file read by several use cases of one aggregate MUST sit flat in that aggregate's folder.
provisions.rationale: A file read by several use cases of one aggregate belongs flat in that aggregate's folder: the lowest folder holding every consumer. There it sits beside its consumers, found by browsing rather than through an index, and moving it changes nothing outside the aggregate. A file read by several aggregates rises one more level, to the module folder, by the same rule.
provisions.example: Three expense queries share one tab strip, so the tab strip sits flat in the aggregate folder. A file read by several aggregates sits flat in the module folder.

provisions.heading: Place Tests at Their Ownership Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which logic tests sit outside their module, and which browser suites sit outside the one tests root per frontend? Look in the module folders and the tests roots.
provisions.statement: Place a logic test beside its module, and keep browser suites under one tests root per frontend.
provisions.rationale: A logic test beside its module is found from the code it covers and runs with it. Browser suites instead share one fixture set and one deployment per frontend, so scattering them beside modules would split the fixtures and the runs. One tests root per frontend keeps the browser suites together.

provisions.heading: Reject a Folder Name That Owns Nothing
provisions.evidence: Which folders under an application's `src` carry a refused name? Look in the application folder tree.
provisions.statement: A folder under an application's `src` MUST NOT be named `shared`, `common`, `utils`, `util`, `helpers`, `misc`, `components`, `hooks`, `types`, or `services`.
provisions.rationale: A folder named `shared`, `utils`, or `components` can refuse nothing: every author with a file of unclear ownership drops it there. The folder collects unrelated code that escapes review against the use cases it serves, and finding a file means searching a pile instead of translating a use case path. The refused names force each file into the folder that owns it. The rule covers an application's `src`, not a shared package's internals, which the package owns.
provisions.example: A shared query three use cases read sits flat in the aggregate folder, not in a `shared/` folder beside them.

provisions.heading: Use Explicit Public Entry Points for Shared Packages
provisions.evidence: Which application imports reach past the documented public entry points of shared packages? Look in the application imports and the package manifests.
provisions.statement: Expose a shared package only through its documented public entry points.
provisions.rationale: A shared package is free to rearrange its internals between releases. An application importing an internal path couples itself to that layout, so the next rearrangement breaks the application. Documented public entry points are the stable surface the package keeps.

provisions.heading: Assert Each Declared Refusal by Its Code
provisions.evidence: Which declared refusals do no evidence specifications reach and assert by result code? Look in the evidence specifications.
provisions.statement: An evidence specification for a use case declaring a refusal MUST reach that refusal and assert it by its result's code.
provisions.rationale: A refusal the test leaves unreached renders where no reader looks: it appears in a log, or nowhere at all. Reaching it and asserting it by its result's code proves two things at once: the page renders the refusal, and the code the page shows is the code the result declares. The scenario records the situation that reaches it, so the test documents how the refusal is provoked.
provisions.example: The refusal alert carries the code, so the assertion names it.

provisions.heading: Assert the Result a Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `proves-unreached` (level S) for a browser test reaching the screen whose assertions in the same test hold neither the refusal code nor the success result's declared text or code.
provisions.statement: A browser test that proves a scenario MUST assert the result the scenario ends in by its refusal code or by the success result's declared text or code.
provisions.rationale: Reaching the screen shows the page opened; the assertion shows the ending the result promises. Holding the refusal code or the success text in the same test ties the proof to the named result, and a money-moving use case that a test only reads leaves completion unshown, so the test submits it.
provisions.example: The browser specification for `scenario/list-expenses.listing-own-expenses-succeeds` opens the expense list on `screen/claimwick-app.expense-list` and asserts the expenses table, the listed ending the success result `result/list-expenses.listed` promises.

provisions.heading: Isolate Browser Tests
provisions.evidence: Which browser tests depend on another test's data, authentication context, or expected state? Look in the browser specifications.
provisions.statement: A browser test MUST create or identify its own data, its own authentication context, and its own expected state.
provisions.rationale: A test that depends on execution order or on leftover data fails for reasons unrelated to the change under review, and passes only when the suite runs in one order. Creating its own data, its own authentication context, and its own expected state makes each test runnable alone and in any order. A test spends no seeded record; it creates the record it needs.

provisions.heading: Keep Test Support Narrow
provisions.evidence: Which test support files hold more than render helpers, one shared API helper, and locator helpers? Look in the test support files.
provisions.statement: Limit test support to render helpers for required providers, to one API helper that every specification shares, and to the locator helpers.
provisions.rationale: Test support that grows into render frameworks, data builders, and custom runners becomes a second application with its own untested surface. Limiting it to render helpers for required providers, one shared API helper, and locator helpers keeps it small: a change to the actor header or the idempotency key reaches the fixtures rather than every specification.

provisions.heading: Mark the Scenario a Browser Test Proves
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-unknown` (level S) for a `proves` annotation naming no record a test may prove, or naming a journey.
provisions.statement: A browser test that proves a scenario MUST carry a `proves` annotation naming that scenario.
provisions.rationale: The annotation, built by the `proves` helper the generated records file exports, names the lowest record the test verifies exactly as a backend test mark does, and a wrong identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran. A title tag claims proof without anything reading it, so the written annotation is the link the builder counts.
provisions.example: The browser specification at `apps/web/tests/expenses/list-expenses.spec.ts` in the Claimwick example carries `proves("scenario/list-expenses.listing-own-expenses-succeeds")`.

provisions.heading: Match Test Level to Risk
provisions.evidence: Which pure logic lacks a logic test, which navigation or integration lacks a browser specification, and which address lacks the route contract? Look in the test files beside the modules and under the tests roots.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST use a logic test for pure logic, a browser specification for navigation and integration, and the route contract for every address.
provisions.rationale: A browser run costs seconds and a deployment; a unit test costs milliseconds and nothing else. Proving pure logic through the browser makes the suite slow without making it stronger, while proving navigation with unit tests proves nothing about the running page. Logic tests take pure logic, browser specifications take navigation and integration, and the route contract covers every address, so each risk is proved at the cheapest boundary that represents it.

provisions.heading: Name the Journey a Journey Test Walks
provisions.evidence: Which browser tests that walk several screens carry a `journey` annotation naming the journey and a `proves` mark for each scenario they drive and assert? Look in the browser tests and their annotations.
provisions.statement: A browser test that walks several screens MUST carry a `journey` annotation naming the journey and a `proves` mark for each scenario it drives and asserts.
provisions.rationale: A journey is not a proof target: it is achieved through use cases, so a journey test proves the scenarios it drives, and journey coverage is computed from them. The `journey` annotation tells a reader which walk the test rehearses without claiming that the walk itself is proven.
provisions.example: The submit-and-reimburse walk carries `journey: journey/submit-and-reimburse` and proves the scenarios it drives and asserts on each screen it reaches.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario at One Boundary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `proves-duplicate` (level A) for a scenario with `proves` marks on more than one test.
provisions.statement: A scenario MUST carry one `proves` mark, on the test at the cheapest boundary that represents its risk.
provisions.rationale: An API test proves a business outcome faster and more steadily than a browser test, and a browser test is the only proof that a page offers the use case and renders its result. When both assert one scenario, marking both makes the slower test a second witness nobody needs and doubles the work when the scenario changes. The scenario whose risk is the outcome is proved at the API, and the one whose risk is what a person sees is proved in the browser.
provisions.example: `scenario/list-expenses.listing-own-expenses-succeeds` is proved by the browser specification at `apps/web/tests/expenses/list-expenses.spec.ts`, the cheapest boundary that shows what a person sees on the expense list. A scenario whose risk is a business outcome alone is proved at the API boundary instead.

provisions.heading: Prove the Module Mirror in a Structure Test
provisions.evidence: Which module folders does the structure test fail to resolve to backend use-case folders, and which refused folders does it name? Look in the structure test.
provisions.statement: A frontend calling the API MUST hold a test asserting that its module tree resolves to the backend use-case folders and names no refused folder.
provisions.rationale: The module mirror is the claim that makes a specification findable from a folder path: translate three names, land on the code. Without a check, the backend adds or renames a use case and the frontend tree silently stops matching, so the translation lands nowhere. A test asserting the mirror on every build, and naming no refused folder, keeps the translation true. The same test can also assert no import between use case folders or between modules, which no lint rule checks.
provisions.example: The structure check resolves each folder name against the backend's module tree.

provisions.heading: Reach a Screen That Offers the Scenario's Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `proves-unreached` (level S) for a browser test whose `page.goto` targets match no screen offering the claimed scenario's use case.
provisions.statement: A browser test that proves a scenario MUST reach a screen that offers the scenario's use case by a `page.goto` literal or template matching that screen's `address`.
provisions.rationale: A test proves a scenario when it drives the use case through the page a person uses, so proof follows exercised behavior rather than a claim. Matching the `page.goto` target against the screen `address` templates is the deterministic reach the reader computes; a test that only clicks through navigation names no screen it proved on.
provisions.example: The evidence specification opens `/expenses`, the address of `screen/claimwick-app.expense-list`, which offers `use-case/spending.list-expenses`.

provisions.heading: Read the Deployment for Its Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Which browser tests hard-code a record identifier instead of reading it from the running deployment? Look in the browser specifications.
provisions.statement: Read a record identifier a browser test needs from the running deployment, and fall back to an absent identifier when the deployment holds none.
provisions.rationale: A hard-coded record identifier passes against the deployment it was copied from and fails against the next, where that record does not exist. Reading the identifier from the running deployment keeps the test true wherever it runs. Falling back to an absent identifier still visits the route as a not-found page, which is a state a reader can reach anyway.

provisions.heading: Run Browser Checks Through the Command Line
provisions.evidence: Which browser suites run outside the command line, or without per-route and per-file addressing? Look in the suite runner and the CI invocation.
provisions.statement: A browser suite MUST run through the command line, addressable per route and per file.
provisions.rationale: The command line is the interface every runner shares: the developer, the drill, and the integration job all invoke the same command. A check that runs only inside an editor plugin or a proxy runner leaves the next investigator with no way to repeat it. Addressable per route and per file, the suite also runs just the check under review instead of the whole suite.

provisions.heading: Test Observable States
provisions.evidence: Which tests assert internal state instead of observable behavior in the states their situation reaches? Look in the test assertions.
provisions.statement: A frontend test SHOULD assert observable behavior in each state applicable to what the test covers: loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, pending, validation, and success.
provisions.rationale: An assertion on internal state passes while the rendered page stays broken, because nothing ties the variable to what the reader sees. Asserting observable behavior in each state the test's situation reaches, from loading and empty through error, forbidden, not-found, pending, validation, and success, ties the test to the reader's view. The scenario states which states its situation reaches, so a logic test asserts only states its level reaches. The project records each state as a term with labels per language.

provisions.heading: Use Network Mocks for Component Tests
provisions.evidence: Which component or logic tests needing HTTP answer without contract-generated network mocks, or with the generated client out of the path? Look in the component tests and the mock generation.
provisions.statement: A component or logic test that needs HTTP MUST serve its answers through network mocks generated from the published contract.
provisions.rationale: A mocked client replaces the generated code with a guess of what it returns, so the test proves the mock rather than the component. A network mock generated from the published contract answers the same HTTP request the browser would send, so the generated client stays in the path it takes in production and the component is tested through the client the page actually uses.
provisions.example: The workspace keeps one mock-generation command that regenerates them.

provisions.heading: Check Every Route
provisions.evidence: Which discovered routes fail a route suite check? Look in the suite output and the CI job logs.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST pass each route suite check.
provisions.rationale: The route suite visits every route and asserts each check the Concepts section names: the floorplan, the reference, accessibility, the heading, the landmark, reflow, text spacing, target size, keyboard use, the focus move on a route change, each color scheme, reduced motion, and status announcements. The suite discovers its routes from the application route definition, so a new route is checked with no new specification. Every route passing every check keeps each address inside the contract by default.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Route from One Floorplan
provisions.evidence: Which routes render zero or several floorplans without recording a freestyle decision? Look in the route sources and the suite output reading the floorplan name from each frame.
provisions.statement: A route MUST render exactly one floorplan from the declared set, unless it is a recorded freestyle route.
provisions.rationale: The floorplan fixes the layout, the heading position, and the slots, so a reviewer reads which floorplan a route composes and knows what the page looks like before opening it. The slots take domain values only: the aggregate state, the use cases that state permits, and the refusal results of the called use case. Exactly one floorplan per route keeps each page to one known shape, unless it is a recorded freestyle route.
provisions.example: An expense route composes the entity floorplan and fills each slot from the expense.

provisions.heading: Declare a Closed Floorplan Set
provisions.evidence: Which floorplans miss the design contract Patterns section or their when-to-use rule? Look in the design contract.
provisions.statement: The `Patterns` section of the design contract MUST list every floorplan the package provides, each with a when-to-use rule.
provisions.rationale: A floorplan with no when-to-use rule leaves the choice to resemblance: two authors pick different floorplans for one kind of page, and the kind ships in two layouts. Listing every floorplan with its rule in the design contract's Patterns section makes the choice mechanical. A floorplan outside the list is a design decision for the package, not a route-level choice.
provisions.example:
The section states each floorplan and the question that selects it.

```markdown
## Patterns

| Floorplan | Component | Use it when the user |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `list-page` | `ListPage` | Finds one record among many. The page shows the result count. |
| `entity-page` | `EntityPage` | Acts on one record: its facts, its state, and the actions that state permits. |
| `form-page` | `FormPage` | Supplies the input of one command, with one primary action. |
```

provisions.heading: Derive Each Page Type from a Named Reference
provisions.evidence: Which routes name neither their page type reference nor, for a freestyle route, their decision record? Look in the route sources.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST name its page type's reference, with a freestyle route naming its decision record instead.
provisions.rationale: An author with no named reference invents a page from primitives, and the next author invents another page for the same type. Naming the page type's reference keeps every page of one type on the one drawing it derives from, so the type stays one design. A freestyle route names its decision record instead, since it derives from no reference.

provisions.heading: Give Every Input a Visible Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which input boundary token falls below 3:1 against its surface in a declared color scheme? Look in the token definitions and the rendered form fields.
provisions.statement: The boundary of a text field, select, checkbox, radio, or switch MUST reach 3:1 contrast against the surface it sits on.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: a reader with low vision finds a field by its edge, and a field drawn at the faint separator step disappears into the page. Giving inputs their own boundary token keeps separators quiet and controls findable. For example, the amount field on the Claimwick expense form keeps a visible edge on the card behind it in both color schemes.

provisions.heading: Govern Behavior Packages
provisions.evidence: Which behavior packages name no decision record justifying them, or render outside baseline components and tokens? Look in the package declarations and the decision records.
provisions.statement: A behavior package MUST name the decision record justifying it for the capability it supplies, and render through baseline components and tokens.
provisions.rationale: A behavior package adds a capability the design baseline lacks, such as a chart or a rich editor, and naming the decision record that justifies it for that capability keeps the decision tied to the need. The decision follows the capability rather than the visual catalog, so no package duplicates a component the design baseline already provides. Rendering through baseline components and tokens keeps the new capability inside the product's look.

provisions.heading: Hold the Declared Base Color
provisions.evidence: Which token values sit outside the declared baseline without a recorded departure? Look in the token definitions and the departure records.
provisions.statement: A token definition MUST carry only the values the declared baseline publishes, except under a recorded departure.
provisions.rationale: A token value outside the published ramp is a second palette beside the declared one, and the next author copies the value because it looks intentional. Carrying only the values the declared baseline publishes keeps the palette to what the design baseline designed. A recorded departure keeps the deliberate choice visible in the design contract instead of hidden in the tokens.

provisions.heading: Keep a Blocked Command Visible with Its Reason
provisions.evidence: Which commands blocked only by state or role vanish instead of staying visible and disabled with the reason beside them? Look in the command surfaces.
provisions.statement: Leave a command blocked only by the current state or role visible and disabled, with the reason beside it.
provisions.rationale: A command blocked only by the current state or role stays visible and disabled, with the reason beside it. The user looking for the action learns it exists and why it is unavailable, such as a missing permission or an unmet precondition. A control that vanishes instead looks like a product that does not offer the action at all.

provisions.heading: Keep Layout Inside Floorplans
provisions.evidence: Which route files declare layout outside floorplan and display composites? Look in the route sources.
provisions.statement: Route code MUST NOT declare layout outside its floorplan and display composites.
provisions.rationale: A layout declaration in a route file is a second layout beside the floorplan: the route draws its own spacing while claiming the floorplan's shape. The next route copies the declaration because it looks like the local way to draw, and the floorplan stops describing what routes render. Floorplan and display composites own layout, so one change there reaches every route composing them.

provisions.heading: Keep Separators at the Subtle Step
provisions.evidence: Which structural separators run darker than the published border step? Look in the token definitions and the rendered separators.
provisions.statement: A structural separator MUST NOT be darker than the border step the declared base color publishes.
provisions.rationale: A separator darker than its neighbors reads as emphasis, so authors stop trusting the token and start picking weights by eye. The border step the declared base color publishes keeps every structural separator at one weight, so weight carries no accidental meaning. An input's boundary is not a separator: it shows where a control is, and `litespec/frontend/ui#give-every-input-a-visible-boundary` sets its contrast.

provisions.heading: Keep Tokens in One Definition
provisions.evidence: Which applications declare their own token value, and which shipped definitions carry a literal color? Look in the application and shared token definitions.
provisions.statement: An application MUST use the shared token definition and declare no value, with no literal color in any shipped definition.
provisions.rationale: One token definition is what makes two applications look like one product. An application uses the shared definition and declares no value of its own, so no second definition introduces a value the first has no opinion about. A definition the shared package ships declares no literal color, so every value traces to the declared baseline.

provisions.heading: Pin the Baseline in the Shared Package
provisions.evidence: Which pinned manifest baselines install outside the shared UI package, or install more than once? Look in the shared package manifest and lock, and the application manifests.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST install the pinned baseline from `litespec.manifest.yaml` once, into its shared UI package.
provisions.rationale: The design baseline installed once in the shared UI package gives every application the same primitives at the same pinned version. Installing per application makes a copy per application, and each copy drifts on its own update schedule with nothing reporting the split. An additional design-baseline source is permitted only under a departure recorded against this provision.

provisions.heading: Prove UI Behavior and Appearance
provisions.evidence: Which changes name no evidence the matrix assigns to their class? Look in the change descriptions and the named evidence.
provisions.statement: A primitive, composite, token, source, floorplan, or route change MUST name the evidence in the matrix in this section.
provisions.rationale: Each change class carries different risk: a token change reaches every route in every profile, while a primitive change reaches one component. The matrix maps each class to the narrowest evidence that represents its risk, so a change runs the evidence its reach requires and no more. | Change class | Narrowest evidence | |:---|:---| | Primitive or variant | The component test for that primitive | | Floorplan or display composite | The route suite on one route that composes it | | Token or global style | The route suite on one route in each profile | | Route | The route suite on that route, and every test proving a result it calls | | Pattern decision | The catalog entry changes with its implementation | | Fork | The fork record and the component test | | Behavior package | The accessibility check for the capability it supplies |

provisions.heading: Publish a Design Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-design-contract-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/ui#publish-a-design-contract]` for a missing contract, a missing metadata block, a package mismatch, or a missing required section. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST publish one design contract with its shared UI package, carrying the required sections: Brand, Tokens, Patterns, Do, Do Not, Motion, Browser Support, Voice.
provisions.rationale: An author that has read no contract picks their own tokens, motion, browser features, and voice for each page. The picks differ on the next page, and the user sees the difference as clutter: same product, different looks. One design contract published with the shared UI package keeps every answer in one file. Motion states the durations and what each becomes under the reduced-motion setting, and Browser Support states the target every platform feature is judged against. A Vocabulary section naming the composites a page reaches for is optional.
provisions.example:
The metadata block names the package and the floorplans it provides.

```yaml
schemaVersion: 2
package: "@claimwick/ui"
profile: application-balanced
patterns:
  - work-page
  - list-page
  - entity-page
```

provisions.heading: Record a Freestyle Route
provisions.evidence: Which freestyle routes name no decision record justifying their layout? Look in the freestyle routes and the decision records.
provisions.statement: A route that composes no declared floorplan MUST name the decision record that justifies its layout.
provisions.rationale: A route that composes no declared floorplan is either the first consumer of a floorplan that does not exist yet or a genuine one-off. Naming the decision record that justifies its layout makes either case reviewable and keeps the declared set closed. A second route of the same shape is the signal to add the floorplan instead of recording another freestyle route.

provisions.heading: Record a Frontend Outside the Controlled Contract
provisions.evidence: Which frontends outside the controlled platforms declare no entry point record naming their platform and replacement boundaries? Look in the entry point records.
provisions.statement: A frontend outside the controlled platforms MUST declare an entry point record naming that platform and the boundaries replacing this contract.
provisions.rationale: A device client with no shared component and no router sits outside the floorplan set and the component rules: the contract's checks do not apply to it. Declaring an entry point record that names its platform and the boundaries replacing this contract keeps the decision visible, instead of letting the frontend report as one with nothing to check.

provisions.heading: Restrict Styling to Semantic Tokens
provisions.evidence: Which styles use raw values instead of semantic tokens? Look in the stylesheets and the shared package definition.
provisions.statement: A style MUST use a semantic token rather than a raw value.
provisions.rationale: A raw value in a style answers to no token: the theme leaves it unchanged through every restyle, and the next author copies the value instead of the token. The shared package definition is the authoritative style surface, holding the tokens, the fonts, and the documented resets. A style built from semantic tokens stays inside the product's visual language by construction.

provisions.heading: Select a Command Surface by Size
provisions.evidence: Which commands use a surface other than the one the Concepts table assigns to their input? Look in the command surfaces.
provisions.statement: A command MUST use the surface the Concepts table assigns to its input.
provisions.rationale: The surface fits the input: a button for a reversible action, a confirmation dialog for an irreversible one, a form dialog for one to four inputs, and a form page beyond that. A form dialog with more inputs than the table allows scrolls, loses its title, and hides the refusal beside the field that caused it. An oversized surface for a small command costs the user attention the command has no use for.

provisions.heading: Select a Tone from the Closed Set
provisions.evidence: Which applications lack a state-to-tone mapping, or map a state outside the exhaustive table of glossary terms? Look in the application state mapping.
provisions.statement: A state indicator MUST take one tone from the closed set, each application declaring its state-to-tone mapping once as an exhaustive table of glossary terms.
provisions.rationale: A page that picks its own color picks a meaning nobody agreed to: the same red celebrates on one screen and warns on another. One state-to-tone mapping per application, declared once as an exhaustive table of glossary terms, makes the same state read the same way on every screen. A new state fails to compile until its tone and its word exist, so no state ships uncolored or mislabeled.

provisions.heading: Select One Visual Authority
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-package-invalid` for controlled frontends with no `ui.package` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, and `ui-dependency-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/ui#select-one-visual-authority]` for a second general-purpose visual dependency. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST record one shared UI package in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: Two general-purpose visual systems in one workspace make every component choice ambiguous: each screen picks its source, and the product ships two looks. Recording one shared UI package in `.litespec/project.yaml` settles the source for every controlled frontend. A frontend outside the contract declares another platform and says what replaces the contract.

provisions.heading: Show the Trace ID in Error Detail
provisions.evidence: Which visible errors hide the trace identifier from copyable detail? Look in the error surfaces.
provisions.statement: Every visible error MUST show its trace identifier in copyable form in the error detail, from the problem body or the `X-Trace-Id` header.
provisions.rationale: Support reads the trace identifier to find the failed request, and the user copies it from the detail without retyping. Shown in copyable form from the problem body or the `X-Trace-Id` header, it connects the user's report to the server's logs. The headline carries what happened in words; the identifier belongs in the detail.

provisions.heading: Use the Product Profiles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-frontend-invalid` for a controlled frontend with no `ui` block declaring its density profile or a profile outside `public-light`, `application-balanced`, `admin-dense`. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Select one density profile from `public-light`, `application-balanced`, or `admin-dense` for each controlled frontend.
provisions.rationale: Density is a property of the audience: `public-light` suits a surface a user meets once, `application-balanced` suits a surface a signed-in staff member works in, and `admin-dense` suits a surface an operator reads all day. All three profiles share one design baseline, so choosing per frontend changes density without changing the visual language.

provisions.heading: Enforce Trusted Types on Raw Markup
provisions.evidence: Which raw markup sink runs outside the named policy, or which frontend sends no Trusted Types directive? Look in the Content Security Policy header and the violation reports.
provisions.statement: A web frontend SHOULD send `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` in its Content Security Policy and pass every raw markup string through one named policy that calls the sanitizer `litespec/frontend/components#sanitize-untrusted-rich-content` records.
provisions.rationale: A recorded sanitizer protects only the calls that remember to use it. Trusted Types makes the browser refuse any raw string written into `innerHTML` or a similar sink, so a component that forgets the sanitizer fails in testing instead of in a staff member's browser. Framework runtimes and libraries also write markup through those sinks, so a team first sends the policy as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, reads the reports, and enforces it once every reported sink passes through the named policy.

provisions.heading: Keep Component Boundaries Typed
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on an untyped Svelte prop, event, or snippet, and the consumer-supplied type-check command fails on an untyped React prop or event. The consumer's configuration provides the type-check command.
provisions.statement: A component MUST type its props, its events, and its snippets under strict mode.
provisions.rationale: An untyped prop fails at the call site the next author writes, which is the most expensive place to learn a shape: after writing the code that uses it. Strict mode turns that failure into a build error at the author's own call. Typed events and snippets do the same for what the component reports and what it lets callers fill in. React components carry props and events; Svelte components add snippets.

provisions.heading: Refuse Page Code Violations with ESLint
provisions.evidence: Which refused element, binding, or layout utility does the consumer's lint command report outside visual files in route and module code? Look at the lint output the consumer's configuration produces in CI.
provisions.statement: Route and module code MUST pass the ESLint rules that refuse raw layout and interactive elements, class and style bindings, and layout utilities outside visual files, with each refusal naming the composite to use.
provisions.rationale: A lint gate that only refuses leaves the author searching the shared package for the replacement; a refusal that names the composite answers with the error. The refusal-to-composite map is approved once per stack, and each stack page names the mechanism that enforces it. Visual files stay allowlisted, because a drawing no composite makes has no composite to name. This gates litespec/frontend/components#use-composites-for-layout-and-interaction-in-page-code, litespec/frontend/components#write-no-class-name-in-page-code, and litespec/frontend/ui#keep-layout-inside-floorplans.

provisions.heading: Add the TanStack Query Plugin to the Client Generator
provisions.evidence: Which client generator configurations omit the `@tanstack/react-query` plugin? Look in the generator configuration of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: The client generator MUST add the `@tanstack/react-query` plugin.
provisions.rationale: The plugin gives every generated read a query key, so the cache entries of every route share one shape.
provisions.example: The library product's client generator adds the `@tanstack/react-query` plugin, so each generated loan read has a query key.

provisions.heading: Apply the Page-Code Lint to Route and Module Code
provisions.evidence: Which route or module files use a refused import or JSX element without a lint finding? Run the page-code lint, then compare its findings with the files under `src/routes` and `src/modules`.
provisions.statement: The page-code lint MUST apply import restrictions and JSX element restrictions in route and module folders, with visual files allowlisted.
provisions.rationale: A lint refusal that names the composite to use lets the author replace a raw element when writing it, not in review.
provisions.example: The lint refuses a raw `div` in `src/routes/loans.tsx` and names the `Stack` composite to use instead.

provisions.heading: Declare Route Search Parameters in validateSearch
provisions.evidence: Which routes read a search parameter without declaring it in `validateSearch`? Look at each route file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST declare its search parameters in `validateSearch`.
provisions.rationale: A declared check runs before the route reads a parameter, so the route receives a typed value or a refusal.
provisions.example: The library loan list route declares its page number in `validateSearch`.

provisions.heading: Hold a Route's Parts in Its Route File
provisions.evidence: Which route files keep their search parameters, loader, or component in another file? Look at each file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route file MUST hold its search parameters, its loader, and its component.
provisions.rationale: One file for the three parts lets a reader see an address, its inputs, its data, and its screen together.
provisions.example: The library loan list route file holds its page number, its loader, and its component.

provisions.heading: Keep Layouts, Error Components, and Route Groups Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Which layout routes, error components, or route groups export a screen mark? Look at the non-entry files under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A pathless layout route, an error component, or a route group MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout, an error component, or a group draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it ties an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The underscore layout route in the library product exports no screen mark.

provisions.heading: Keep React Test Mocks to the Owned Libraries
provisions.evidence: Which tests replace the rendering library, the router, or the query library? Look at the mocks in each test file.
provisions.statement: A test MUST NOT replace the rendering library, the router, or the query library.
provisions.rationale: Those three are the stack's own behavior, and a stand-in for any of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: The library loan list route test renders with the real router and query library and replaces only the network call.

provisions.heading: Keep the React Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Which files under `src` sit outside `src/app`, `src/routes`, and `src/modules`, or which address has two files under `src/routes`? Look at the `src` tree of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: A React frontend MUST hold the frame in `src/app`, one file per address in `src/routes`, and the use-case code in `src/modules`.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed homes let a reader and a tool find the frame, the routes, and the use-case code in the same place in every React frontend.
provisions.example: In the library product, the frame sits in `src/app`, the loan list route is `src/routes/loans.tsx`, and the loan use-case code sits in `src/modules/loans`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Tone Table in One States File
provisions.evidence: Which state-to-tone mappings live outside `src/app/states.tsx`? Look for tone maps in the `src` tree.
provisions.statement: The state-to-tone table MUST live in `src/app/states.tsx`.
provisions.rationale: One file holds every state's tone, so a state reads the same tone on every route.
provisions.example: The library product maps the overdue state to its warning tone in `src/app/states.tsx`.

provisions.heading: Load Intent Targets Before Navigation
provisions.evidence: Which links preload a route without filling the query cache? Look at the router link setup in the `src` tree.
provisions.statement: Intent preloading MUST fill the query cache before navigation.
provisions.rationale: A preload on hover or focus fills the cache before the click, so the target route draws from data it already holds.
provisions.example: Hovering the loan link fills the loan page key, so the click draws the loan list from the cache.

provisions.heading: Mark Each React Route Entry with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Which route entries export no screen mark from their route file? Look at each route file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST export its screen mark from its route file as the same typed constant a use-case module exports.
provisions.rationale: A mark in the route file ties the address to its use case where the address is declared, so the builder and the check read one link.
provisions.example: The library loan list route file exports the typed screen mark for the loan list screen.

provisions.heading: Meet the Locale-Dictionary Contract with the Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Which copy bypasses the dictionary library, or misses fill, plural, typed keys, or a declared fallback? Look at the copy call sites under `src`.
provisions.statement: The dictionary library MUST meet the locale-dictionary contract that the web data page states.
provisions.rationale: One contract keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language, with the same fill, plural, and fallback behavior.
provisions.example: The library product resolves its overdue-loan sentence through its dictionary library in every language it ships.

provisions.heading: Name Drawings with the Visual Suffix
provisions.evidence: Which custom drawings sit in `.tsx` files whose names lack the `.visual.tsx` suffix? Look in the component folders.
provisions.statement: A file that holds a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.tsx`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix marks the one place outside the composites, so a search finds every custom drawing in one pass.
provisions.example: The library loan due-date sparkline is `LoanSparkline.visual.tsx`.

provisions.heading: Prefetch Route Reads in the Loader
provisions.evidence: Which routes read data in their component without a loader prefetch? Look at each loader under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST prefetch its reads in its loader.
provisions.rationale: A loader fills the query cache before the component draws, so the first render has its data.
provisions.example: The library loan list loader fetches the loan page for the page number that `validateSearch` checked.

provisions.heading: Read Route Data with useSuspenseQuery
provisions.evidence: Which route data reads use another query hook or a key the loader does not fill? Look at each route file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route file MUST read its route data with `useSuspenseQuery` over the key its loader filled.
provisions.rationale: Reading the filled key keeps the component on the data the loader fetched.
provisions.example: The library loan list component reads its page with `useSuspenseQuery` over the same key the loader filled.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Only Through dangerouslySetInnerHTML
provisions.evidence: Which React components write raw HTML through another prop or API? Look for `innerHTML` and raw markup in the component files.
provisions.statement: A React component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
provisions.rationale: One named prop makes every raw HTML sink a name a search finds, and a review can check each use.
provisions.example: The library loan note renders its sanitized HTML through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` after its recorded sanitization decision.

provisions.heading: Run the Registry Build Command
provisions.evidence: Which registry build scripts run a command other than `shadcn build`? Look at the scripts in each frontend's `package.json`.
provisions.statement: The registry build command MUST be `shadcn build`.
provisions.rationale: One registry command builds UI artifacts the same way in every React frontend.
provisions.example: The library product builds its registry with `shadcn build`.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure in the Route Error Component
provisions.evidence: Which route failures render outside the route error component? Look at the error handling of each route under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route failure MUST render in the route error component, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One error component gives every route failure the same problem state and the same recovery.
provisions.example: A library loan list that fails to load shows the shared problem state with its trace identifier.

provisions.heading: Use Named Props for Class and Style Bindings
provisions.evidence: Which React components bind a class or style through another prop? Look at the JSX in the component files.
provisions.statement: A class or style binding in a React component MUST use `className` or `style`.
provisions.rationale: Two fixed prop names keep styling in one vocabulary that the lint and a reviewer can read.
provisions.example: The loan row in `src/app/components/LoanRow.tsx` sets its tone through `className` and sets no `style` prop.

provisions.heading: Use the Shared Package Form Hook
provisions.evidence: Which React forms bypass the shared package form hook? Look at the form files under `src`.
provisions.statement: A React form MUST build on the form hook of the shared package.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field wiring and the same display for a refusal on its field.
provisions.example: The library loan request form uses the shared form hook and no form library of its own.

provisions.heading: Use the TSX Extension on Shared Files
provisions.evidence: Which shared React files use an extension other than `.tsx`? Look at the `src` tree of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: A shared React file MUST use the `.tsx` extension.
provisions.rationale: One extension lets the compiler, the lint, and a search treat every shared React file the same way.
provisions.example: In the library product, the shared loan status helper is `src/app/loan-status.tsx`.

provisions.heading: Define Route Metadata Deliberately
provisions.evidence: Which public routes miss a title, description, canonical address, or indexing policy, and which private routes miss a `noindex` marker? Look in the route metadata.
provisions.statement: A public route MUST define its title, its description, its canonical address, and its indexing policy, while a private route refuses indexing.
provisions.rationale: A public route's title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy are what a search result and a shared link show; without them the page arrives as a bare address. A private route refuses indexing, because an indexed console address exposes to search what a signed-in user believes is private.
provisions.example: A channel route states `og:*` tags and one alternate per language. A console route ships a `noindex` meta tag in its document.

provisions.heading: Generate the Records File into the Frame
provisions.evidence: `litespec model render` writes each frontend's file into its frame from its own entry points, and `litespec model check` reports `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming a use case or screen outside its frontend's entry points.
provisions.statement: A frontend's generated `litespec-records.ts` MUST sit in its frame folder and hold only the use cases and screens of that frontend's own entry points.
provisions.rationale: The records file is a cross-route value every module and route imports, which is what the frame holds on both stacks: `src/app/` on React and `src/lib/app/` on Svelte, so no stack-specific folder is needed. A union holding every browser use case of the project would let one frontend mark a use case only another frontend reaches, and the type check would pass; a union per frontend makes that mistake a type error. The file exports the `UseCaseId` and `ScreenId` unions, the `LiteSpecMark` type, and the `proves` helper browser tests annotate with.
provisions.example: `litespec model render` writes `apps/web/src/lib/app/litespec-records.ts` for the Claimwick web frontend, whose `UseCaseId` holds the use cases its entry point reaches and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Locate the Frame in the App Folder
provisions.evidence: Which cross-route values or browser uses sit outside the frame folder their stack page names? Look in the frame folder and the route and module sources.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST place cross-route values in the frame folder its stack page states: client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data.
provisions.rationale: Client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data cross every route. Filed in the frame folder, each has one home; filed in a route, each exists once per route with copies to keep equal. A browser API reached from a use-case module belongs here too, because a module renders and reads data rather than touching the device. This realizes litespec/frontend/structure#locate-cross-route-values-in-the-frame.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Use-Case Module with Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a use-case folder exporting no `litespec` constant, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for one naming a use case its path does not mirror; for a folder at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` the mirrored use case is the one its module and use-case segments name, with no aggregate segment.
provisions.statement: A frontend use-case folder MUST export one `litespec` constant whose `implements` names its use case, typed against the generated union of use-case identifiers.
provisions.rationale: The folder path mirrors the backend use case, which tells a reader where to look but tells a tool only a resemblance. A typed constant is the frontend mark in both mark styles: a mistyped identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran, and the route files import the module instead of restating the identifier. The calls a screen makes through the generated client remain the computed `calls` link; the mark adds the written link from the screen to the use case it serves. A query folder at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` mirrors a use case with no one aggregate, so its expected mark still names `use-case/<module>.<use-case>`, from the module and use-case segments alone.

provisions.heading: Refuse Stack-Specific Folder Names
provisions.evidence: Which React folders take the name `lib`, and which Svelte folders under `src/lib` take the name `stores`? Look in the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A React folder MUST NOT be named `lib`, nor a Svelte folder under `src/lib` be named `stores`.
provisions.rationale: A `lib` folder on React would sit beside `src/app` as a second frame, and `src/app` already holds the frame. A `stores` folder on Svelte would gather shared state in one place, while the rules put shared state in the frame or beside its readers. Refusing both names stops the second home before anything moves into it.

provisions.heading: Use the Frontend Application Tree
provisions.evidence: Which frontend trees break from the frame, routes, and modules layout their stack page states? Look in the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST use the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states.
provisions.rationale: The frame, routes, and modules layout gives every file one predictable home: cross-route values in the frame, one address per route file or folder, and use-case code under the module that owns it. A reader moves from a use case to its code by path alone, on either stack. This realizes litespec/frontend/structure#organize-a-frontend-into-frame-routes-and-modules.
provisions.example:
React:

```text
apps/{frontend}/
  src/
    app/       the frame: client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
    routes/    one file per address, compiled into a typed route tree
    modules/   one folder per backend module, aggregate, and use case
  tests/
    unit/      logic tests
    routes/    the route contract suite
    e2e/       evidence specifications
  package.json
  vite.config.ts
```

Svelte:

```text
apps/{frontend}/
  src/
    routes/    one folder per address, with a page per folder
    lib/
      app/       the frame: client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
      modules/   one folder per backend module, aggregate, and use case
  tests/
    unit/      logic tests
    routes/    the route contract suite
    e2e/       evidence specifications
  svelte.config.js
  vite.config.ts
  package.json
```

The generated route artifacts, build output, and dependency folders stay untracked.

provisions.heading: Use the Generated Route Tree
provisions.evidence: Which build or type-check scripts skip the router's generate command, and which generated artifacts stay tracked? Look in the package scripts and the version control status.
provisions.statement: Generate the typed route artifacts from the files under `src/routes` with the router's own command, and keep them untracked.
provisions.rationale: The typed route artifacts derive from the files under `src/routes`, so generating them with the router's own command and leaving them untracked keeps one source of truth. Committed artifacts add a second copy that a renamed route file leaves behind.

provisions.heading: Add the TanStack Query Plugin to the Client Generator
provisions.evidence: Which client generator configurations omit the `@tanstack/svelte-query` plugin? Look in the generator configuration of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: The client generator MUST add the `@tanstack/svelte-query` plugin.
provisions.rationale: The plugin gives every generated read a query key, so the cache entries of every route share one shape.
provisions.example: The Claimwick client generator adds the `@tanstack/svelte-query` plugin, so each generated expense read has a query key.

provisions.heading: Apply the Page-Code Lint to Route and Module Code
provisions.evidence: Which route or module files use a refused import or element without a lint finding? Run the page-code lint, then compare its findings with `src/routes` and `src/lib/modules`.
provisions.statement: The page-code lint MUST apply the import and element restrictions through the Svelte ESLint processor, with visual files allowlisted.
provisions.rationale: A lint refusal that names the composite to use lets the author replace a raw element when writing it, not in review.
provisions.example: The lint refuses a raw `div` in `src/routes/expenses/+page.svelte` and names the `Stack` composite to use instead.

provisions.heading: Declare Route Parameters in a Schema
provisions.evidence: Which routes read a parameter without declaring it in a schema? Look at each route folder under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST declare its parameters in a schema.
provisions.rationale: A declared schema checks each parameter before the route reads it, so the page receives a typed value or a refusal.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list page declares its page number in a schema.

provisions.heading: Hold a Route's Parts in Its Folder
provisions.evidence: Which route folders keep a parameter schema, a load, or a component outside the folder? Look at each folder under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route folder MUST hold its parameters, its load, and its component.
provisions.rationale: One folder for the three parts lets a reader see an address, its inputs, its data, and its screen together.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list folder holds its page number schema, its load, and its page component.

provisions.heading: Keep Layout Files, Error Pages, and Route Groups Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Which layout files, error pages, or route groups export a screen mark? Look at the files under `src/routes` other than `+page.svelte`.
provisions.statement: A layout file, an error page, or a route group MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout, an error page, or a group draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it ties an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `+layout.svelte` exports no screen mark.

provisions.heading: Keep Route Group Names in Router Syntax
provisions.evidence: Which folders under `src/routes` hold a shared layout without parentheses? Look at the folder names under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route group MUST keep its parenthesized folder name.
provisions.rationale: The parentheses are router syntax: a group folder without them becomes an address the router serves.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console keeps its `(console)` group, so its expense pages share one layout without adding an address.

provisions.heading: Keep Svelte Test Mocks to the Owned Libraries
provisions.evidence: Which tests replace Svelte, SvelteKit, the query library, or the form library? Look at the mocks in each test file.
provisions.statement: A test MUST NOT replace Svelte, SvelteKit, the query library, or the form library.
provisions.rationale: Those four are the stack's own behavior, and a stand-in for any of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense page test renders with the real query library and replaces only the network call.

provisions.heading: Keep the Svelte Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Which files under `src` sit outside `src/lib/app`, `src/routes`, and `src/lib/modules`, or which address has two folders under `src/routes`? Look at the `src` tree of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: A Svelte frontend MUST hold the frame in `src/lib/app`, one folder per address in `src/routes`, and the use-case code in `src/lib/modules`.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed homes let a reader and a tool find the frame, the routes, and the use-case code in the same place in every Svelte frontend.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense console keeps the frame in `src/lib/app`, the expense list page in `src/routes/expenses/+page.svelte`, and the expense use-case code in `src/lib/modules/spending/expenses`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Tone Table in One States File
provisions.evidence: Which state-to-tone mappings live outside `src/lib/app/states.ts`? Look for tone maps in the `src` tree.
