provisions.statement: The state-to-tone table MUST live in `src/lib/app/states.ts`.
provisions.rationale: One file holds every state's tone, so a state reads the same tone on every route.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console maps the overdue state to its warning tone in `src/lib/app/states.ts`.

provisions.heading: Load Intent Targets Before Navigation
provisions.evidence: Which links preload a route without filling the query cache? Look at the link setup in the `src` tree.
provisions.statement: Intent preloading MUST fill the query cache before navigation.
provisions.rationale: A preload on hover or focus fills the cache before the click, so the target page draws from data it already holds.
provisions.example: Hovering the Claimwick expense link fills the expense page key, so the click draws the list from the cache.

provisions.heading: Mark Svelte Route Entries
provisions.evidence: Which route entries export no screen mark from the `<script module>` of `+page.svelte`? Look at each `+page.svelte` under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST export its screen mark from the `<script module>` of its `+page.svelte` as the same typed constant a use-case module exports.
provisions.rationale: A mark in the page ties the address to its use case where the address is declared. SvelteKit refuses any export from a `+page.ts` other than its own options and underscore-prefixed names, so the mark belongs in the page.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list `+page.svelte` exports the typed screen mark in its `<script module>`.

provisions.heading: Meet the Locale-Dictionary Contract with the Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Which copy bypasses the dictionary library, or misses fill, plural, typed keys, or a declared fallback? Look at the copy call sites under `src`.
provisions.statement: The dictionary library MUST be `svelte-i18n` or machinery that meets the locale-dictionary contract that the web data page states.
provisions.rationale: One contract keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language, with the same fill, plural, and fallback behavior.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console resolves its receipt-required sentence through `svelte-i18n` in every language it ships.

provisions.heading: Name Drawings with the Visual Suffix
provisions.evidence: Which custom drawings sit in `.svelte` files whose names lack the `.visual.svelte` suffix? Look in the component folders.
provisions.statement: A file that holds a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix marks the one place outside the composites, so a search finds every custom drawing in one pass.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense receipt sparkline is `ExpenseSparkline.visual.svelte`.

provisions.heading: Name the Module Extension on Each Import
provisions.evidence: Which imports omit the module file extension? Look at the import lines in the `src` tree of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: Each import MUST name its module file extension.
provisions.rationale: SvelteKit 3 requires the extension, because it resolves each import to its exact file.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console's import of the words module ends in `.ts`, as in `#lib/app/words.ts`.

provisions.heading: Prefetch Route Reads in the Load
provisions.evidence: Which routes read data in their page without a load prefetch? Look at each load under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST prefetch its reads in its load.
provisions.rationale: A load fills the query cache before the page draws, so the first render has its data.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list load fetches the expense page for the page number its schema checked.

provisions.heading: Read Route Data with a Query Creator
provisions.evidence: Which route data reads use a key the load does not fill? Look at each page under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST read its route data with a query creator over the key its load filled.
provisions.rationale: Reading the filled key keeps the page on the data the load fetched.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list page reads its page with a query creator over the same key its load filled.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Only Through One Template Tag
provisions.evidence: Which Svelte components write raw HTML through another API? Look for `{@html}` and raw markup in the component files.
provisions.statement: A Svelte component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only through `{@html}`.
provisions.rationale: One template tag makes every raw HTML sink a name a search finds, and a review can check each use.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense note renders its sanitized HTML through `{@html}` after its recorded sanitization decision.

provisions.heading: Resolve Imports Through the Lib Alias
provisions.evidence: Which imports reach `src/lib` through a relative path instead of `#lib`? Look at the import lines of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: Imports MUST resolve through the `#lib` alias that `package.json` declares in its `imports` field as `"#lib/*": "./src/lib/*"`.
provisions.rationale: One declared alias lets a reader and a tool see every import of frame and module code without counting relative steps.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console imports frame code through `#lib/app/words.ts`.

provisions.heading: Run the Registry Build Command
provisions.evidence: Which registry build scripts run a command other than `shadcn-svelte build`? Look at the scripts in each frontend's `package.json`.
provisions.statement: The registry build command MUST be `shadcn-svelte build`.
provisions.rationale: One registry command builds UI artifacts the same way in every Svelte frontend.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console builds its registry with `shadcn-svelte build`.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure in the Route Error Page
provisions.evidence: Which route failures render outside `+error.svelte`? Look at the error handling of each route folder under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route failure MUST render in the route error page, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One error page gives every route failure the same problem state and the same recovery.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense list that fails to load shows the shared problem state from `+error.svelte` with its trace identifier.

provisions.heading: Use Named Attributes for Class and Style Bindings
provisions.evidence: Which Svelte components bind a class or style through another attribute? Look at the markup in the component files.
provisions.statement: A class or style binding in a Svelte component MUST use `class`, `class:`, `style`, or `style:`.
provisions.rationale: Four fixed attribute forms keep styling in one vocabulary that the lint and a reviewer can read.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense status chip toggles its overdue tone with `class:overdue` and sets no raw `style` attribute.

provisions.heading: Use the Shared Package Form Creator
provisions.evidence: Which Svelte forms bypass the shared package form creator? Look at the form files under `src`.
provisions.statement: A Svelte form MUST build on the form creator of the shared package.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field wiring and the same display for a refusal on its field.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense form uses the shared form creator and no form library of its own.

provisions.heading: Use the Svelte Extension on Shared Files
provisions.evidence: Which shared Svelte files use an extension other than `.svelte`? Look at the `src` tree and the shared package of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: A shared Svelte file MUST use the `.svelte` extension.
provisions.rationale: One extension lets the compiler, the lint, and a search treat every shared Svelte file the same way.
provisions.example: The shared expense total is `ExpenseTotal.svelte` in the shared package.

provisions.heading: Write Components in Runes Mode
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on a legacy reactive statement or an untyped `$props` call.
provisions.statement: A component MUST hold its local state in runes, with props from `$props` and derived values from `$derived`.
provisions.rationale: Runes are the reactivity model the compiler understands: `$state` for local state, `$props` for inputs, and `$derived` for computed values. Legacy reactive statements and untyped prop access bypass that model and behave differently under the compiler. An effect covers what derivation cannot express, so nothing needs the legacy forms.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Test Without an Assertion
provisions.evidence: `pnpm eslint` reports `vitest/expect-expect` for each test that contains no assertion.
provisions.statement: Lint MUST fail a Vitest or Playwright test that contains no `expect` assertion, through the `expect-expect` rule.
provisions.rationale: A test that calls code and asserts nothing passes unless something throws, so it raises coverage while proving nothing. The `expect-expect` rule of the Vitest ESLint plugin reports each such test before it runs, at no measurable cost. The rule is free and maintained under MIT.

provisions.heading: Build Within the Browser Support Target
provisions.evidence: Which platform feature in the shared package or a route falls outside the declared tier with no fallback beside it? Look in the stylesheets and components against the design contract's Browser Support section.
provisions.statement: The shared package and the routes MUST use only web platform features in the tier the design contract's Browser Support section names, or carry a fallback beside each other feature.
provisions.rationale: A feature outside the declared tier breaks silently for the staff member whose browser lacks it: a dialog that never opens, a layout that collapses, a control that does nothing. Naming one tier in the design contract lets every author and agent judge a feature against the same line, and the decision order in the Concepts section says what to write when a feature falls outside it.
provisions.example: A design contract that declares Baseline widely available lets the expense record header switch its layout with a size container query, which belongs to that tier, with no fallback. A tooltip placed with CSS anchor positioning, which belongs to neither tier yet, keeps the script positioning of the baseline popover component instead.

provisions.heading: Give Moving Content a Pause Control
provisions.evidence: Which moving or self-updating content runs longer than five seconds with no pause, stop, or hide control? Look in the routes that show live feeds, carousels, or animated status.
provisions.statement: Content that moves, scrolls, or updates on its own for more than five seconds MUST offer a control that pauses, stops, or hides it.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide: a ticker of incoming expenses or a rotating banner pulls the eye away from the form a staff member is filling in, and a screen-reader user hears it interrupt. A pause control gives the reader the page back.

provisions.heading: Honor Reduced Motion
provisions.evidence: Which route still slides, scales, or loops an animation with reduced motion emulated? Look in the route suite output.
provisions.statement: A route MUST run no spatial, scaling, or looping animation while the reader's system asks for reduced motion.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions: a drawer that slides or a card that zooms can bring on nausea or dizziness for a reader with a vestibular condition. Under reduced motion, a transition becomes a short fade or nothing, and every animation still ends in its final state, so the screen shows the same result without the movement. The design contract's Motion section names what each duration becomes. The mobile stacks hold the same rule in `litespec/frontend/mobile/screens#honor-reduced-motion`.

provisions.heading: Mark the Route Suite and Goldens with What They Prove
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a test in a frontend's `routeSuite` or `visualGoldens` with no `proves` annotation, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for one naming a scenario.
provisions.statement: The route suite and every visual golden MUST carry a `proves` annotation for each UI provision, pattern provision, or quality requirement they enforce.
provisions.rationale: The route suite is the one place accessibility is enforced for every page, and a visual golden is the one place a pattern's look is held, yet neither proves anything a tool can read while it names nothing. Marking them turns the suite into the evidence for the UI provisions it checks, and each golden into the evidence for the pattern it protects, so a passing run marks those records tested. Neither proves a scenario: a route suite asserts every page, not one use case. Each frontend names its route suite in `routeSuite` and its goldens in `visualGoldens` in its `frontends[]` entry, so the check has a named subject instead of a convention.
provisions.example: Claimwick's route suite, named in its web frontend's `routeSuite`, carries `proves("litespec/frontend/ui#check-every-route")`.

provisions.heading: Publish One Registry Item per Floorplan
provisions.evidence: `shadcn build` on React or `shadcn-svelte build` on Svelte exits zero, and `registry.json` lists one item per declared floorplan.
provisions.statement: The shared package MUST publish a registry whose build exits zero and which lists one item per floorplan the design contract declares.
provisions.rationale: Without an installable page for each floorplan, an author invents a page from primitives and the next author invents another. One registry item per floorplan the design contract declares gives every page type a reference the author installs before writing. A registry build that exits zero proves every item still builds.

provisions.heading: Render Each Declared Color Scheme
provisions.evidence: Which route fails the route suite in a declared color scheme, or which root omits `color-scheme`? Look in the route suite output and the shared stylesheet.
provisions.statement: A web frontend MUST declare on its root element the color schemes its tokens define and pass the route suite in each of them.
provisions.rationale: A token set with a dark scheme that no check renders ships unreadable text to every staff member whose device is set to dark. Declaring `color-scheme` also lets the browser draw scrollbars, form controls, and the page before styles load in the matching scheme, so nothing flashes white. A product that defines only a light scheme declares `color-scheme: light` and is checked in that scheme only.

provisions.heading: Restrict CSS Decisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-class-invalid` for each arbitrary value, raw palette value, and important modifier, and `ui-stylesheet-invalid` for each inline style, with its file.
provisions.statement: A Tailwind class MUST use a semantic token rather than an arbitrary value, a raw palette value, or an important modifier.
provisions.rationale: Semantic tokens keep every class inside the governed palette, spacing, and type scales. An arbitrary value, a raw palette value, or an important modifier steps outside them: the value answers to no token and survives every restyle. The approved CSS surface is the shared package's stylesheet, holding the Tailwind import, the tokens, the fonts, and the documented resets. The source scan skips build output and reports authored feature CSS. This realizes litespec/frontend/ui#restrict-styling-to-semantic-tokens.

provisions.heading: Set Text Sizes in Relative Units
provisions.evidence: Which font-size token is written in `px`? Look in the shared package's token stylesheet.
provisions.statement: A font-size token MUST use `rem` rather than `px`.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text: a reader who sets a larger default text size in the browser or the system expects every page to follow it, and a size fixed in pixels ignores that setting. A `rem` token scales with the reader's setting, and the reflow and text-spacing checks then prove that the layout still holds.

provisions.heading: Track Source Changes
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` recomputes each digest and reports `ui-sourcelock-invalid` for changed primitive source.
provisions.statement: The shared package's source lock MUST record the pinned CLI, the registry address, the paths, the normalized digest, and the dependencies for each primitive.
provisions.rationale: The source lock records the pinned CLI, the registry address, the paths, the normalized digest, and the dependencies for each primitive. Normalizing source before hashing lets two workspaces compute the same digest for identical source. One lock beside one copy is what makes a changed primitive report a fork instead of passing unreported. `litespec model render` writes the digests, the preset and the CLI pin, so a person reviews a changed digest in the pull request diff and never computes one. Settled by [decision/0024-keep-the-ui-source-lock](decision/0024-keep-the-ui-source-lock).

provisions.heading: Use the Source Update Procedure
provisions.evidence: Which update branches miss the pinned CLI, the dry-run output, or the separate review of regenerated files and local composites? Look in the update branches.
provisions.statement: Update the primitive source on a branch that pins the CLI, starts clean, and reviews the regenerated files and the local composites separately.
provisions.rationale: Running `view`, `--dry-run`, and `--diff` first shows what the update changes before anything is written. The regenerated files and the local composites change for different reasons, upstream source versus product adaptation, so one review cannot cover both. The branch pins the CLI and starts clean, so the run is repeatable and the diff shows only the update.

provisions.heading: Assert Loading, Stability, and Blocking Time per Route
provisions.evidence: Which route in the Lighthouse CI run has no assertion for largest contentful paint, cumulative layout shift, or total blocking time? Look in the Lighthouse CI configuration.
provisions.statement: Assert, for each route the Lighthouse CI run visits, a largest contentful paint of at most 2.5 seconds, a cumulative layout shift of at most 0.1, and a total blocking time of at most 200 milliseconds, as the median of three runs.
provisions.rationale: A Lighthouse CI assert that names no metric passes every build. Largest contentful paint says when the page's main content shows, cumulative layout shift says whether it jumps while the staff member reads, and total blocking time stands in for interaction to next paint, which a lab run cannot measure because no one clicks. The defaults are the values the web community treats as good, and the median of three runs keeps one slow run from failing a build. Field interaction to next paint is measured in production, where the [operations page](operations.md) places its signals.

provisions.heading: Check Documentation on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `page-section-missing`, `page-heading-invalid`, or `project-invalid` (level G) for a page or configuration that breaks its contract, and `prose-missing` (level A) for a record that lacks its prose field.
provisions.statement: The docs job MUST run on every pull request and fail on a page that breaks the page contract, configuration, or prose rules.
provisions.rationale: Documentation breaks take many small forms: a record with a missing field, a rejected term, a misconfigured path, a page outside its [page contract](../core/authoring.md). Each one is trivial to fix at the pull request that introduced it and hard to trace once later pages build on it. Running the docs job on every pull request catches each break where it started.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Contracts Fresh
provisions.evidence: Regenerating OpenAPI and API types from source on the pull request produces no diff.
provisions.statement: CI MUST regenerate committed OpenAPI and API types from source deterministically and fail on any difference.
provisions.rationale: A committed contract that no longer matches its source sends consumers a stale API: a frontend builds against operations the backend no longer serves. Regenerating from source on CI and failing on any difference proves the committed files match the code. Generation stays deterministic, with no timestamps, machine paths, or unstable ordering, so an identical source always yields identical files.

provisions.heading: Refuse Backend Calls Outside the Generated Client
provisions.evidence: The contract job report shows a clean regeneration and a lint report with no backend call outside the generated client.
provisions.statement: The contract job MUST fail a pull request whose frontend code calls the backend outside the generated client.
provisions.rationale: Regenerating the contract proves the committed client matches the API, but a hand-written fetch beside it still compiles and drifts on the next contract change. Failing the pull request keeps every backend call inside the generated client that `litespec/frontend/data#use-one-configured-client-per-application` names, so a contract change breaks the build at the call sites that must move.

provisions.heading: Run Applicable Gates on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: The pull request checks list shows each selected job passing, with skipped jobs recorded with their reason.
provisions.statement: Every pull request MUST run the jobs the jobs table selects for its changed areas.
provisions.rationale: Each job guards one surface, so a pull request that skips the job for its changed area merges unchecked work. A job skipped because its surface did not change is recorded with that reason on the pull request, which keeps the skipped surface visible to the reviewer. A project that selects the Delivery extension adds its supply-chain gate as one of these jobs under `litespec/ext/delivery#enforce-the-supply-chain-gate`.

provisions.heading: Run Measured Checks on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a measured requirement with no check or no passing run.
provisions.statement: The measure job MUST run the check each measured requirement names for its kind.
provisions.rationale: Each kind has one tool, as the measured-checks table on this page maps: k6 thresholds for API latency and errors, Lighthouse CI assert for frontend performance and weight, axe in the route suite for accessibility, OpenTelemetry signals for availability and latency objectives, and an ASVS 5.0 level with the ZAP baseline, free static analysis, OSV-Scanner, and Gitleaks for security. The tools write their result files under `TestResults/`, the builder reads them the way it reads test runs, and `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a measured requirement with no check or no passing run. Every tool the table names is free and maintained; CodeQL is used only on public repositories, as `litespec/quality/security#scan-every-pull-request-with-a-free-static-analyzer` states.

provisions.heading: Bound External Calls
provisions.evidence: Does each network call declare a timeout, a cancellation path, and bounded retries for idempotent operations only? Look at each HTTP client registration and its resilience policy.
provisions.statement: Every network call MUST declare an explicit timeout and cancellation path, with retries only for idempotent operations named by a bounded retry policy.
provisions.rationale: Every network call waits on a system the product does not control. Without an explicit timeout and cancellation path, one slow provider holds a request thread until that unrelated system recovers, and each held thread is one less thread for healthy requests. Retries stay bounded and idempotent-only, because retrying a call that already acted repeats the act.

provisions.heading: Emit Correlated Diagnostics
provisions.evidence: Do logs and traces carry correlation identifiers, and do metrics carry service labels? Look at one request's logs, traces, and metrics in the telemetry backend.
provisions.statement: A host MUST emit structured logs, traces, and metrics, with correlation identifiers on logs and traces and service labels on metrics.
provisions.rationale: Each running service is a host, and one request often crosses several. Logs and traces carry timestamp, level, service, environment, trace identifier, and span identifier, and metrics carry service and environment labels. The correlation identifiers let one request be followed across every host it touched, which is the only trail a cross-host failure leaves. Stable event names keep dashboards working across releases instead of breaking each time a message is reworded.

provisions.heading: Keep Production Secrets Out of the Repository
provisions.evidence: Do production values live on the host, with only placeholders in the repository example file? Search the tree for production values and read the example file.
provisions.statement: Production environment values MUST live on the host, never in the repository, under `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data`.
provisions.rationale: A secret committed once lives in history after deletion, readable to everyone the repository ever reaches, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states. Keeping production values on the host and only placeholders in a repository example file keeps the values with the deployment that needs them and out of every clone.

provisions.heading: Keep Runbooks Near Project Documentation
provisions.evidence: Does each runbook sit under `.litespec/implementation/runbooks/` or its module's runbooks folder, with its fields, or does the convention name another arrangement? Look at the runbook folders and their headings.
provisions.statement: Place a runbook under `.litespec/implementation/runbooks/` when it answers product-wide failures, or under `.litespec/implementation/modules/<module>/runbooks/` when every record naming it sits in one module, stating trigger, impact, prerequisites, procedure, verification, recovery, and escalation, covering restore, rollback, schema failure, leaked secrets, dependency outages, and extension recovery.
provisions.rationale: An alert names its runbook, and the reader follows the pointer under pressure. A runbook sits at product level when it answers product-wide failures and under its module when every caller sits in one module, so each pointer resolves to a procedure with the same fields: trigger, impact, prerequisites, procedure, verification, recovery, and escalation. A runbook kept anywhere else breaks the pointer the alert gave.

provisions.heading: List Every Sub-Processor
provisions.evidence: Does each provider the release calls appear on the generated sub-processor list? Compare the release's provider clients with `.litespec/implementation/operations/sub-processors.md`.
provisions.statement: A release MUST call only providers the generated sub-processor list names from the project's provider actors.
provisions.rationale: Customers ask which providers touch their data, and the sub-processor list is the answer. The model builder renders it from the provider actor records, so a provider added in code but missing from the list answers that question wrong. Generating the list from records keeps the answer and the code in step.

provisions.heading: Operate Background Work Independently
provisions.evidence: Does the Worker publish its own health, processing rate, failure count, retry count, oldest pending age, and shutdown behavior? Look at the Worker's health endpoints and metrics.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST publish its own liveness, readiness, processing rate, failure count, retry count, oldest pending age, and shutdown behavior.
provisions.rationale: A Worker fails on its own schedule: its queue grows, its retries climb, its oldest item ages, while WebApi keeps answering health checks. Without its own liveness, readiness, processing rate, failure count, retry count, oldest pending age, and shutdown behavior, the failure stays invisible until the backlog is the incident. WebApi readiness otherwise hides a failed Worker while the queue grows unobserved.

provisions.heading: Pass Trace Context in the W3C Format
provisions.evidence: Does one configured propagator read and write W3C trace context on every host? Look at the telemetry setup of each host.
provisions.statement: A host MUST read and write trace context as the [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers, using one configured propagator.
provisions.rationale: An identifier that each host formats its own way correlates nothing across the boundary between them. `traceparent` is the format OpenTelemetry implements and every managed backend accepts, so a trace crosses a frontend, an API, a background host, and a provider without translation. One propagator, the component that reads and writes the headers, is the part that matters: two configured propagators produce two identifiers for one request, and the trace splits at whichever hop reads the other one.
provisions.example: The trace identifier in a Problem Details response is the `trace-id` field of the current `traceparent`, which is what `litespec/backend/api#return-stable-problem-details` returns.

provisions.heading: Point Every Runtime Record at Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does a pipeline stage stamp `litespec.use_case` on the span, log scope, and error report of each mediated message? Look at the mediator pipeline and one error report per host.
provisions.statement: A host MUST carry the use-case identity of every mediated message, resolved from the generated registry, as `litespec.use_case` on its span, its log scope, and its error report.
provisions.rationale: A trace identifier joins the runtime records of one request to each other, but not to the specification: a person holding a slow span, a log line, or an error report still has to guess which use case it was. The identity is already a generated value, so a pipeline stage reads it from the registry once per message and stamps it on every surface under one name, and reactions, jobs, and outbox consumers carry it as well as requests. A metric carries it only as a label on an instrument whose series stay bounded: a duration histogram labeled by every use case multiplies its series by hundreds, so request instruments label by module instead.
provisions.example: A Claimwick request to submit an expense opens a span and a log scope carrying `litespec.use_case = use-case/spending.submit-expense`, and an unhandled failure inside it reaches the error tracker with the same tag.

provisions.heading: Separate Liveness and Readiness
provisions.evidence: Does `/health/live` answer without dependency checks, while `/health/ready` includes the critical dependencies? Look at the health check registrations of each host.
provisions.statement: A host MUST expose `/health/live` without dependency checks and `/health/ready` including its critical dependencies.
provisions.rationale: Liveness answers whether the process is alive; readiness answers whether it can safely serve traffic. When a dependency fails, readiness fails so the orchestrator stops sending traffic, while liveness stays true so the orchestrator does not restart a healthy process. One endpoint for both forces a choice between serving traffic the application cannot handle and restarting a process that only needs its dependency back.

provisions.heading: Start the Stack with One Local Command
provisions.evidence: Does one command named in the consumer `AGENTS.md` start WebApi, PostgreSQL, the frontends, and the Worker? Look at `AGENTS.md` and the AppHost project.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST start WebApi, PostgreSQL, configured frontends, and its Worker where one exists, with one local command named in the consumer `AGENTS.md`.
provisions.rationale: A stack that needs several terminals and a wiki page starts differently for every developer, and the differences become bug reports nobody can reproduce. One named command brings WebApi, PostgreSQL, the frontends, and the background Worker up together, so every developer and every agent starts from the same running system. The baseline command is Aspire's `AppHost`, with `ServiceDefaults` supplying the shared discovery, health, resilience, and telemetry defaults its resources rely on. A workspace that orchestrates the same set another way satisfies this rule with its own command: the obligation is that one command brings the stack up, not that one tool does.

provisions.heading: Apply Erasure and Export to Every Store
provisions.evidence: Do erasure and export reach every store on the inventory, with backups expiring inside their retention bound? Look at the erasure and export jobs and the backup retention setting.
provisions.statement: Erasure and export MUST reach every store holding personal data, with backups expiring inside the retention bound the retention schedule states.
provisions.rationale: Personal data lives in logs, search indexes, and outboxes beside the database. A request honored in the database but left in a log export answers half the duty and breaks the promise to the person. A backup cannot answer field by field, so it carries a retention bound instead, and the data ages out with the backup.

provisions.heading: Authorize Each Target Resource
provisions.evidence: Does each protected operation pass the application guard from its use case's declared permissions? Look at the guard decision for each protected operation in the authorization tests and the pipeline.
provisions.statement: The application guard MUST authorize every protected operation from its use case's declared permissions, as `litespec/backend/application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline` states, with endpoints adding only coarse policies.
provisions.rationale: One decision from one declaration stops two operations about the same record from asking different questions. The use case declares the permissions it needs, the guard resolves the actor's roles at the target's scope, and the decision follows. A message whose target must be the caller carries no target (`litespec/core/access#remove-a-target-that-must-be-the-caller`). A handler never compares the caller with a target and never throws the forbidden refusal itself; the guard decides. Endpoints add only coarse policies, because a policy that cannot see business data cannot decide about an aggregate.

provisions.heading: Bound Abuse at Exposed Endpoints
provisions.evidence: Does each public, authentication, webhook, search, and upload endpoint declare its setting with key and rejection response? Look at the setting records beside each endpoint.
provisions.statement: A public, authentication, webhook, search, or upload endpoint MUST declare its limit as a setting record with key and rejection response.
provisions.rationale: Public, authentication, webhook, search, and upload endpoints invite abuse: credential stuffing, scraping, flooding. Declaring the bound as a setting record names the key that isolates one caller and the rejection response the caller sees. The rejection is `429` with a stable code, so legitimate callers can back off and retry.

provisions.heading: Derive the Actor from Claims
provisions.evidence: Does WebApi map verified claims through the one current-actor accessor, with no request data supplying the actor? Look at the actor resolution in WebApi.
provisions.statement: Actor resolution MUST follow `litespec/quality/security#use-one-current-actor-abstraction`.
provisions.rationale: Actor resolution has one home: the WebApi boundary, which maps verified claims to identity, roles, and scopes through the one current-actor accessor. Request data never supplies the current actor, because anything the caller sends can name anyone. One resolution path keeps every operation answering "who acts" from the same verified source.

provisions.heading: Keep a Personal-Data Inventory per Store
provisions.evidence: Does the inventory name the fields, purposes, and retention of each store that holds personal data? Look at the inventory document beside the stores it lists.
provisions.statement: A platform holding personal data MUST keep a personal-data inventory per store naming the fields, purposes, and retention of each store.
provisions.rationale: Export, erasure, and breach answers each ask the same opening question: which stores hold this person's data, which fields, for which purposes, and for how long. An inventory the team can read answers it in one place. Without it, each request starts with a search across logs, indexes, and outboxes, and the store nobody remembers stays out of the answer.

provisions.heading: Keep Backend Authentication Provider-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Does the backend authentication setup validate issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and required claims, with no identity header accepted? Look at the authentication configuration in WebApi.
provisions.statement: A backend MUST validate issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and required claims through OIDC and JWT Bearer.
provisions.rationale: The backend accepts one thing: a token whose issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and required claims validate through OIDC and JWT Bearer. Provider-specific login and session behavior belongs to a frontend or an extension, because the API cannot recheck a login flow it cannot see. An unsigned token, an unvalidated decode, or a client-supplied identity header is never accepted: each one lets a caller mint its own identity.

provisions.heading: Keep One Limit Store Across Replicas
provisions.evidence: Do all replicas read their rate and concurrency counters from one store? Look at the counter configuration of each deployment that runs more than one replica.
provisions.statement: A deployment running more than one replica MUST hold its rate and concurrency counters in one store that every replica reads.
provisions.rationale: A per-process counter multiplies the declared limit by the replica count, so the limit the specification states is not the limit the system applies. The multiplier also changes whenever the deployment scales, which makes the effective limit unstated and unreviewable. One store every replica reads keeps the applied limit equal to the declared one.

provisions.heading: Keep Personal Data Out of Logs
provisions.evidence: Do logs, traces, and diagnostic records carry personal data in clear? Search the log sinks and a sample of recent log output for personal fields.
provisions.statement: A log, trace, or diagnostic record MUST NOT carry personal data in clear.
provisions.rationale: Logs flow to stores the product does not control: collectors, dashboards, long-term archives. Redaction at the sink fails once, in one pipeline, and the cleartext is already downstream. A field never emitted fails nowhere.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Out of Tracked and Observable Data
provisions.evidence: Does any source, log, trace, exception message, generated file, URL, snapshot, container layer, or browser storage hold a secret? Search the tree and a sample of log and trace output for key and token values.
provisions.statement: A secret MUST NOT appear in source, logs, traces, exception messages, generated files, URLs, snapshots, container layers, or browser storage.
provisions.rationale: Every place a secret lands is a place it leaks from: source reaches every clone, logs and traces reach every dashboard reader, URLs reach every proxy log, snapshots and container layers outlive the process, and browser storage reaches the user. Platform secret stores hold the values instead, and diagnostics redact sensitive configuration before it is emitted, so the value never enters the observable stream.

provisions.heading: Keep Secure Headers in Host Configuration
provisions.evidence: Do the secure headers sit in one host location, or does the convention name another arrangement? Look at the host configuration.
provisions.statement: Define Content Security Policy, frame restrictions, content-type protection, referrer policy, and transport security in one host location.
provisions.rationale: Content Security Policy, frame restrictions, content-type protection, referrer policy, and transport security form one set: the browser reads them together. Spread across middleware registrations, one of them is always the header nobody remembers. One host location keeps the set reviewable as a whole.

provisions.heading: Limit Public Error Detail
provisions.evidence: Does each public error carry the HTTP API error contract shape, with no stack trace, SQL, or provider body? Look at the error responses the endpoint tests assert.
provisions.statement: A public error MUST use the error contract `litespec/backend/api#return-stable-problem-details` defines.
provisions.rationale: The error contract has one home: the HTTP API rules. Every public error then carries the same stable shape with nothing extra. A stack trace, SQL, connection detail, provider body, uncontracted internal identifier, or authorization reason that reveals resource existence gives an attacker the system's structure with every error.

provisions.heading: Minimize Sensitive Data
provisions.evidence: Does each use case collect, return, log, export, and retain only the fields its input and results declare? Look at each use case's input and result types and its log calls.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST collect, return, log, export, and retain only the fields its input and results declare.
provisions.rationale: Data the use case never collects cannot leak from it. Collecting, returning, logging, exporting, and retaining only the declared fields keeps each use case's exposure exactly what its page promises. A use case handling sensitive data states its classification, access, retention, deletion, and audit behavior on its page, so the promise is written where the fields are.

provisions.heading: Parameterize Database Input
provisions.evidence: Does each external value reach the database through a query API call or a SQL parameter? Look at the repository code and each raw SQL file.
provisions.statement: An external value reaching the database MUST travel through a provider query API or a parameterized SQL parameter.
provisions.rationale: String concatenation or interpolation into raw command text makes the value part of the statement, so a crafted value rewrites the query. A provider query API or a parameterized SQL parameter keeps the value as data. The provider query API is Marten's under the baseline, and it parameterizes. The reporting extension owns the reviewed raw SQL patterns.

provisions.heading: Protect Browser Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does each frontend ship framework escaping, a Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and rich-content sanitization? Look at the frontend host configuration and the response headers it sends.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST apply framework escaping, a documented Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and sanitization of allowed rich content.
provisions.rationale: The browser is hostile ground: injected scripts, forged requests, malicious redirects, and hostile markup all arrive as ordinary page content. Framework escaping, a documented Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and sanitization of allowed rich content each blocks one of those attacks. A route guard or hidden control is presentation, so it never replaces API authorization.

provisions.heading: Protect Live Data at Rest
provisions.evidence: Does each live store carry encryption, or does a departure cover this provision? Look at each store's encryption setting and the departure records.
provisions.statement: Live data at rest MUST carry encryption or a departure covering this provision.
provisions.rationale: Live data at rest outlives the process: disks, snapshots, and replicas each hold a copy outside the application's control. Encryption keeps each copy unreadable without its key. Where encryption does not apply yet, the departure covering this provision keeps the gap visible with its reason, exit, and expiry date instead of silent.

provisions.heading: Record Security Audit Events
provisions.evidence: Does each security audit event record actor, action, target, outcome, timestamp, trace identifier, and reason? Look at the audit writes and a sample of audit records.
provisions.statement: A security audit event MUST record actor, action, target, outcome, timestamp, trace identifier, and available reason.
provisions.rationale: An incident review reconstructs who did what to which target, with what outcome and why. Without actor, action, target, outcome, timestamp, trace identifier, and reason on each security event, the reconstruction is guesswork. Audit records follow a documented retention and access policy, exclude secrets, and stay available for incident review. A consumer that activates the audit extension records the event through that extension instead, which states a wider field set, a classification rule, and a tamper-evidence rule.

provisions.heading: Report a Breach Within Its Deadline
provisions.evidence: Does the breach procedure name the person who acts, a backup person, and the deadline the constraint record states? Look at the breach runbook and the constraint record it cites.
provisions.statement: A breach-notification procedure MUST name the person who acts and a backup person and meet the deadline the applicable constraint record states.
provisions.rationale: A breach deadline starts running at discovery. The applicable constraint record states the deadline the outside rule sets. A deadline with nobody named to meet it slips past the team, and one named person fails on the first absence. Naming both before anything happens keeps the procedure starting on time.

provisions.heading: Restrict a Protected Collection in the Database
provisions.evidence: Does each protected collection query apply its authorization scope as a database predicate before paging? Look at each query handler that returns a collection.
provisions.statement: A protected collection query MUST apply its authorization scope as a database predicate, before paging, rather than filter a materialized result.
provisions.rationale: A collection has no single target, so the check that `litespec/quality/security#authorize-each-target-resource` states has nothing to resolve against: the scope must become part of the database query itself. Reading the unrestricted set already exposes the rows to the process, and a page assembled from them leaks the total count even when every row is dropped. Filtering after the load is the shape [OWASP lists as broken object level authorization](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/2021/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/).
provisions.example: A query for an organization's orders adds the organization predicate to the database query. It does not load every order and drop the ones the caller may not read.

provisions.heading: Restrict Cross-Origin Access
provisions.evidence: Does the cross-origin policy list its origins, methods, headers, and credential mode, with no wildcard origin? Look at the cross-origin configuration in each host.
provisions.statement: A cross-origin policy MUST list its allowed origins, methods, headers, and credential mode without using a wildcard origin.
provisions.rationale: A wildcard origin lets any site call the API with the user's credentials, which turns every malicious page into an API client. Listing allowed origins, methods, headers, and credential mode keeps each cross-origin caller explicit. Validated configuration owns the allowlist, so an unlisted origin cannot arrive by mistake. Deployment-owned origins are allowed when the allowlist shape is validated at startup.

provisions.heading: Rotate Production Secrets
provisions.evidence: Does each production secret carry an inventory entry with its location and next rotation date, beside its revocation runbook? Look at `.litespec/implementation/operations/secrets.json` and the runbooks.
provisions.statement: A production secret MUST have a secret-inventory entry naming its storage location and next rotation date, with revocation and recovery in a runbook.
provisions.rationale: Every secret leaks eventually: through a departing teammate, a copied file, an old backup. A secret-inventory entry with storage location and next rotation date keeps each secret's lifetime bounded, and rotation allows overlap while clients switch. Procedures, logs, artifacts, and audit records carry no secret value, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, and revocation and recovery live in a runbook.

provisions.heading: Scan Every Pull Request with a Free Static Analyzer
provisions.evidence: Does the static analysis report for the pull request show a departure for each accepted finding? Look at the analyzer report and the departure records.
provisions.statement: CI MUST scan every pull request for security findings with a free static analyzer.
provisions.rationale: CodeQL is free only on public repositories, where no paid plan is required; on a private repository the project uses a free alternative and records the choice in its CI documentation. An accepted finding lives as a departure covering the finding, with its reason, exit, and expiry date, so each acceptance stays visible and dated.

provisions.heading: Scan Every Release with the ZAP Baseline
provisions.evidence: Does the ZAP result file under `TestResults/` show no medium or high alert for the pull request? Look at the ZAP report.
provisions.statement: CI MUST scan the running API with the ZAP baseline on every pull request.
provisions.rationale: The ZAP baseline runs the spider with passive scanning and no active attacks, so it is safe on every pull request, with a WARN, FAIL, and IGNORE config file. Its JSON report feeds the model with the other measured results, and the scan passes with no medium or high alert. ZAP is free and maintained under Apache-2.0.

provisions.heading: Set an ASVS Level as the Security Target
provisions.evidence: Does the security quality requirement name its ASVS 5.0 level, with a passing measure? Look at the requirement record and its measure.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST set an ASVS 5.0 level as its security target.
provisions.rationale: ASVS 5.0 defines three levels, L1, L2, and L3, with each requirement verifiable to pass or fail, and the organization picks one by risk. The level lives on a quality requirement with its measure, as `litespec/core/intent#state-the-measure-on-a-counted-requirement` states, so the target is checked rather than declared. The level choice and any accepted finding are each decided once by a person.

provisions.heading: Test the Resource Authorization Matrix
provisions.evidence: Does each protected operation pass every caller in the matrix, or does the convention name another set? Look at the authorization tests beside each protected operation.
provisions.statement: Cover anonymous, invalid-token, unrelated-actor, owner, and each privileged grant for every protected operation.
provisions.rationale: Authorization fails one caller at a time: the anonymous caller who gets in, the unrelated actor who reads another tenant's row. Covering anonymous, invalid-token, unrelated-actor, owner, and each privileged grant for every protected operation proves each caller separately. The matrix also covers disclosure behavior and the collection query predicate. A UI redirect or hidden control is not evidence.

provisions.heading: Treat an Unsalted Digest as Personal Data
provisions.evidence: Does each unsalted digest of personal data receive the handling its source data receives? Look at each hashing call on a personal field and the storage class of its result.
provisions.statement: An unsalted digest of personal data MUST receive the same handling as the data itself.
provisions.rationale: A digest without a salt reverses by table lookup: anyone holding a table of common values recovers the original. It hides nothing, so it gets none of the relaxed handling a truly one-way value earns. The same handling as the data itself keeps the digest from leaking what the data would.

provisions.heading: Use Deny-by-Default Policies
provisions.evidence: Does each new endpoint require authentication unless it carries `AllowAnonymous` on purpose? Look at the fallback policy and each endpoint marked `AllowAnonymous`.
provisions.statement: Set a fallback policy requiring an authenticated user, and mark each public endpoint with `AllowAnonymous` intentionally.
provisions.rationale: A new endpoint nobody secured is a public endpoint by accident. A fallback policy requiring an authenticated user keeps each new endpoint protected until somebody marks it public on purpose with `AllowAnonymous`. Named role or scope policies add coarse checks while the guard retains resource authorization.

provisions.heading: Use One Current Actor Abstraction
provisions.evidence: Does WebApi expose one current-actor accessor, or does the convention name another arrangement? Look at WebApi's identity code and the convention.
provisions.statement: Expose one narrow current-actor accessor in WebApi that maps verified claims to typed identity, roles, and scopes.
provisions.rationale: One narrow accessor in WebApi keeps claims mapping in one place: typed identity, roles, and scopes, mapped once. Application receives the actor through input that WebApi creates, or through a narrow trusted port when behavior must stay host-independent. A second accessor invites a second interpretation of the same claims.

provisions.heading: Validate at Trust Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does each trust boundary validate transport shape and file metadata before use? Look at the endpoints, the upload handlers, and the provider response readers.
provisions.statement: A trust boundary MUST validate transport shape and file metadata before use, leaving message checks to application validators as `litespec/backend/application#separate-input-validation-from-invariants` states.
provisions.rationale: Message shape, required values, length, range, format, and pagination bounds stay with the application validators that `litespec/backend/application#separate-input-validation-from-invariants` names, and business invariants stay with Domain. Each layer then answers only the questions it can see. Database content, provider responses, file contents, and generated text stay untrusted when they cross into a new output context, because validation for one context proves nothing about the next.

provisions.heading: Derive Expected Values from the Scenario
provisions.evidence: Which test assertions repeat values outside the Then of their scenarios? Look at each assertion beside its scenario text.
provisions.statement: A test MUST take its expected values only from the Then of the scenario it proves.
provisions.rationale: Expected values read from the code under test restate what the code does, so the test passes with the code whatever the specification says. The scenario's Then holds the expected ending, and the test asserts exactly that ending. The agent obligation behind this rule lives in `litespec/core/agent#take-expected-values-from-the-scenario`, with held-back example rows checked after implementation under `litespec/core/agent#verify-refusals-and-calculations-against-held-back-examples`.
provisions.example: A scenario whose Then says the expense is submitted asserts the submitted state and the returned identifier from the scenario text. The test author reads no handler code to learn the expected values.

provisions.heading: Keep the Test Projects the Size Requires
provisions.evidence: Which required test project is missing for the declared size, or which test project no page names? Look at the test folders beside `size` in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A project MUST hold each test project its declared size requires, as the testing page of each selected stack names them.
provisions.rationale: The size decides which test projects prove the records. A project short of one has records that no boundary proves, and a project with an unnamed extra project collects tests that no page placed. Each stack names its projects on its testing page, so the required set reads in one place per stack.
provisions.example: A large backend holds the architecture, integration, and acceptance projects that its backend testing page names. A small backend holds the first two.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Rule Through Its Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Which rule claims stand without a proved scenario claim on the same test? Look at each rule claim.
provisions.statement: A rule claim MUST confirm only through a scenario the same test proves.
provisions.rationale: Each rule holds where its kind says: an invariant inside the aggregate, a precondition at the guard, a calculation in its pure evaluation, a cross-aggregate rule at the store or the reacting use case. A scenario that walks through that point exercises the rule, so the rule claim rides on the scenario proof instead of carrying its own enforcement-point mark. A calculation rule earns its proof from a scenario carrying the examples table that `litespec/core/domain-model#tabulate-every-calculation-with-examples` requires.
provisions.example: A test proving the scenario for an expense above the threshold with no receipt claims the receipt rule alongside the scenario. The scenario sends the command and asserts the `spending.receipt-missing` refusal, and the rule claim confirms because the same test proves the scenario. No separate mark names the validator or the store.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: Which scenarios lack a proving test with its mark, boundary call, and passing run? Look at the book beside the test bodies.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST be proved by a test carrying its proves mark, calling its use case through the public boundary, and asserting the result the scenario names.
provisions.rationale: A scenario states one behavior the product shows, and the proves mark is the test's claim that it shows it. A test that drives the use case through its steps, its message, or its endpoint exercises the public boundary; a test that constructs a handler, an aggregate, or a repository reaches past it and proves nothing. The assertion names the result: the success fields for a success, the refusal code inside an assertion for a refusal. A reaction or job scenario is proved the same way: its test fires the trigger and asserts the result of the use case the reaction or job runs. A scenario no test proves is recorded as a departure with its reason and expiry date. The latest test run marks each confirmed claim passing or failing.
provisions.example: An acceptance scenario for submitting an expense carries the mark for `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`, drives the submit-expense steps, and asserts the submitted expense. An integration test for the same scenario constructs the submit-expense message, sends it through the host, and asserts the same result. The mark names the scenario, the call crosses the public boundary, and the model builder confirms the claim from the test body.

provisions.heading: Refuse Surviving Mutants on Changed Lines
provisions.evidence: Which changes landed with survivors above the recorded threshold and no covering departure? Look at the mutation report beside the departure records.
provisions.statement: Gate each change on the project's recorded mutation threshold over its changed lines, starting at zero surviving mutants; each equivalent mutant is recorded as a departure covering the mutation finding.
provisions.rationale: Mutation testing seeds small faults into changed lines and runs the suite: each killed mutant is a fault the tests catch, and each survivor is a fault they miss. The gate counts survivors on changed lines only, so every change arrives proven. A project-wide percentage confounds suite size with strength, and a full nightly run serves as a trend rather than a gate. An equivalent mutant preserves behavior by construction, so no test kills it; the departure records that judgement with its reason and expiry instead of blocking the change forever.
provisions.example: A change touching the receipt check runs mutation over those lines with the scenario suite. Survivors at or below the recorded threshold let the change land; the rest send the change back for a stronger assertion, or into a departure when the mutant is equivalent.

provisions.heading: Use Evidence Rather Than One Coverage Target
provisions.evidence: Which build gates name a coverage percentage as sufficient? Look at the build gates beside the coverage numbers.
provisions.statement: A repository MUST NOT treat one coverage percentage as the definition of sufficient testing.
provisions.rationale: A single coverage percentage rewards tests that execute lines without asserting behavior: a suite reaches the target while proving no scenario. Coverage stays useful as review input, so the project collects line and branch numbers without treating any value as sufficient. The evidence is scenario proof, domain edge cases, integration boundaries, security behavior, and architecture rules, with mutation results on changed lines under `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines`.

provisions.heading: Use One Mock Rule for Every Stack
provisions.evidence: Which test doubles replace the project's own repositories, handlers, modules, or generated contract types, rather than an outside provider or a non-deterministic value? Look at each test double and the mocks each test file imports.
provisions.statement: A test MUST substitute only what the code under test does not own and what is not deterministic, and never the code's own repositories, handlers, or modules.
provisions.rationale: A substitute stands in for code the test does not run, so each one replaces the project's own behavior with the author's guess of it. A test that stubs its own repositories, handlers, or modules proves the guess instead of the code. A substitute earns its place only where the code under test cannot reach the real thing: an outside provider it does not control, another deployable it calls over the network, such as the API a frontend calls, or a value that changes between runs, such as the clock or randomness. Settled by [decision/0032-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack](decision/0032-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack).
provisions.example: A payment test substitutes the card provider and a fixed clock, and runs the expense handler against the real expense repository; a Claimwick web component test answers its API calls with network mocks generated from the published API document.

provisions.heading: Keep Documentation Directories Out of Build-Artifact Ignore Rules
provisions.evidence: Each documentation directory stays tracked; `git check-ignore` reports no match for the record paths under `docs/`.
provisions.statement: Exclude a documentation directory from a build-artifact ignore rule that matches it by accident.
provisions.rationale: Platform `.gitignore` templates match broad names, and a documentation directory with such a name silently stops being tracked. Excluding the documentation directory from the rule keeps records tracked, and `git check-ignore` confirms each record is visible.
provisions.example:
```gitignore
[Oo]utput/
!docs/<directory>/
!docs/<directory>/*.yaml
!docs/<directory>/*.md
```

Confirm with `git check-ignore docs/<directory>/<file>.yaml` that no record is ignored.

provisions.heading: Keep Environment Examples Beside Applications
provisions.evidence: Each frontend and deployable host directory holds a `.env.example` with required names and safe values; where replaced, the project documentation names the central example location.
provisions.statement: Keep a `.env.example` beside each frontend and deployable host listing required names and safe values.
provisions.rationale: A new developer copies the example to start, and a reviewer reads it to learn which names the application needs. Beside the frontend or host it documents, next to the options module that reads those names, the example changes in the same edit as the names. Anywhere else, it goes stale without anyone noticing.

provisions.heading: Keep Local Overrides Untracked
provisions.evidence: Developer overrides live in ignored local files or a platform secret store, with no second tracked environment-specific source.
provisions.statement: Keep developer overrides in ignored local files or a platform secret store.
provisions.rationale: Developer overrides differ per machine by nature: ports, paths, local endpoints. Committing them turns one developer's setup into everyone's default. Ignored local files or a platform secret store keep overrides personal, and no second committed source competes with the deployment platform for the same value.

provisions.heading: Keep Logging Configuration Provider-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Application source logs through standard abstractions, with exporter configuration in hosts; where replaced, the host configuration names the project's own logging setup.
provisions.statement: Emit structured logs through standard logging abstractions and keep exporter configuration in hosts.
provisions.rationale: Application code writes through standard logging abstractions, and each host configures its exporter. Application code then carries no provider choice, so switching a log backend stays inside deployment settings instead of touching every call site.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Outside Source Control
provisions.evidence: Each tracked configuration file carries only safe defaults and placeholders; real values live in user secrets or the deployment platform.
provisions.statement: A tracked configuration file MUST keep secrets out of tracked and observable data, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, and contain only safe defaults and placeholders.
provisions.rationale: A tracked file reaches every clone and stays in history after deletion. Local development uses user secrets and hosted environments use the deployment platform, so no real value needs to be tracked. Safe defaults and placeholders keep the tracked file runnable as documentation.

provisions.heading: Pin the JavaScript Toolchain
provisions.evidence: Root `package.json` declares `packageManager` and a Node.js engine matching the manifest releases; CI provisions the same releases.
provisions.statement: Root `package.json` MUST declare the manifest pnpm stack release in `packageManager` and a Node.js engine matching the manifest node stack release.
provisions.rationale: Different Node.js or pnpm releases resolve, build, and lint differently. Declaring the manifest pnpm release in `packageManager` and a matching Node.js engine keeps every developer and CI on the same toolchain. CI provisions that Node.js release and invokes the declared pnpm release, so local and CI resolve identically.

provisions.heading: Pin the React Version in the ESLint Flat Config
provisions.evidence: Each React ESLint flat config sets a concrete `settings.react.version`.
provisions.statement: When the workspace holds a React frontend, its ESLint flat config MUST set a concrete `settings.react.version` rather than leave it at `detect`.
provisions.rationale: Version detection calls context APIs that the pinned ESLint release removed, so `detect` fails under the pinned toolchain. A concrete `settings.react.version` skips detection entirely and lints against the version the workspace ships.

provisions.heading: Use One Frontend Dependency Graph
provisions.evidence: The workspace holds one root `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and `pnpm-lock.yaml`, with no nested lockfile tracked.
provisions.statement: A TypeScript workspace MUST use one root `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and `pnpm-lock.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: One root manifest and one lockfile resolve one version of each package for the whole workspace. A nested lockfile lets one application resolve a different version than the workspace CI installs, so local builds and CI builds disagree about the same code. One graph keeps every install identical.

provisions.heading: Validate Backend Configuration at Startup
provisions.evidence: Each backend section binds a settings type that fails startup on a missing field, a bad range, or a bad format; read the settings types beside the backend host.
provisions.statement: A backend configuration section MUST bind to a named settings type validated for required fields, ranges, and formats at startup.
provisions.rationale: A missing or malformed setting fails somewhere: at startup with a named field, or at the first request that needs it with a downstream error. Binding each section to a validated settings type fails at startup, while the deployment can still stop. Reading a required setting through a raw configuration lookup defers the failure to the first request that needs it.

provisions.heading: Validate Frontend Environment Access
provisions.evidence: Each frontend reads environment values only through `src/lib/env.ts`, with server-only values apart from browser-visible ones.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST read environment variables through one validated module separating server-only from browser-visible values, at `src/lib/env.ts` through the framework alias.
provisions.rationale: A frontend bundle ships to the browser, so every value it reads is public. One validated module at `src/lib/env.ts` separates server-only values from browser-visible ones in a single place a reviewer can read. Browser-visible names use the framework prefix, so an unprefixed value stays out of the bundle.

provisions.heading: Approve New Packages Explicitly
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-undeclared` (level S) for a direct package in the bill of materials that the manifest does not pin and no decision admits, and `admission-invalid` (level G) for an `admits` entry missing any of its six facts.
provisions.statement: A package absent from the manifest MUST be admitted by a technical decision whose `admits` entry names the package with its owning layer, license, processing location, account owner, failure behavior, and operating cost.
provisions.rationale: A package arrives with a cost nobody revisits: updates, advisories, license review, and migration work, and a hosted one adds a place personal data may travel and an account someone must own. The decision answers those while the alternatives are still fresh: its options and choice give the use case and the alternatives, its `reopenedWhen` gives the removal condition, and its `admits` entry gives the facts a dependency gate asks per package. A baseline package lands in the manifest in the same change as its decision. A consumer-owned package lands in the consumer's central file instead, because the manifest belongs to the LiteSpec release rather than to the consumer.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` chooses a PDF library over an HTML-to-PDF browser and admits `nuget:PdfSharp` with layer `Infrastructure`, license `MIT`, location `in-process`, account owner `none`, failure behavior "the receipt download fails and the expense stays readable", and operating cost `none`.

provisions.heading: Assign Each Baseline Package to Its Owning Layer
provisions.evidence: Each baseline package sits in the owning layer the table in this section assigns; where replaced, the admitting decision names the project's own owning layer.
provisions.statement: Assign each baseline package to the owning layer named in the table in this section.
provisions.example:
| Layer | Direct package groups |
|:---|:---|
| Domain | None |
| Application | Required abstractions only, plus the declared read boundary |
| Infrastructure | Providers and adapters required by implemented ports |
| WebApi | Host, authentication, and documentation packages |
| Test code | Test-only packages |

A new package joins the narrowest layer that needs it. A central version entry does not authorize every layer to reference that package: the table decides who takes what. A consumer references conditional packages only after their extension activates.

provisions.heading: Follow the Declared Dependency Graph
provisions.evidence: Each layer and module dependency follows the declared graph; read the references between layer folders under `apps/api/src` and the imports in `apps/`.
provisions.statement: A dependency between layers or modules MUST follow the declared graph and add no other edge.
provisions.rationale: The declared graph is the list of crossings review checks. An undeclared edge lets a layer reach past its boundary, and review finds no graph that forbids it. Each new edge then needs an explicit decision instead of arriving silently with an import.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Free of Provider Packages
provisions.evidence: The Application layer folders reference only messaging abstractions, read abstractions, and the declared read boundary; read those folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: Application MUST depend only on messaging abstractions, required read abstractions, and the one declared read boundary.
provisions.rationale: Application coordinates use cases through abstractions; Infrastructure hides the technology behind them. A provider package in Application makes the coordination layer depend on the technology Infrastructure was meant to hide, so a provider change reaches two layers. Only messaging abstractions, required read abstractions, and the one declared read boundary stay.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Dependency-Free
provisions.evidence: No Domain layer folder needs an external package or framework; read the Domain layer folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: The Domain layer MUST depend on no external package or framework.
provisions.rationale: Domain holds business rules, and business rules outlive frameworks. Depending on no external package or framework keeps the rules testable and portable on their own. Persistence, messaging, web, injection, serialization, and logging libraries all stay outside.

provisions.heading: Keep Frontend Applications Isolated
provisions.evidence: No import in one frontend names another application's source or another module's internal feature files.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT import another application's source or another module's internal feature files.
provisions.rationale: When one frontend imports another's source, neither can change its internals without checking the other, so the two release as one. A frontend also stays out of another module's internal feature files for the same reason. Sharing goes through a shared package with a documented public entry point that depends on no application.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Packages Dependency-Light
provisions.evidence: The generated API types package carries no dependencies, and the shared client carries only the generator runtime, its query plugin, and those types; where replaced, the client package manifest names the project's own client dependency set.
provisions.statement: Keep generated API types free of dependencies and limit the shared client to the pinned generator's runtime, its query plugin, and those types.
provisions.rationale: Generated types mirror the API contract, and the shared client only carries them to queries. Keeping the types free of dependencies and the client limited to the generator's runtime, its query plugin, and those types keeps regeneration a pure function of the contract. A generated package that owns state, UI behavior, or authentication policy stops being regenerable.

provisions.heading: Keep Providers in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Database providers, external SDKs, and resilience, discovery, and serialization adapters appear only in the Infrastructure layer folders; read those folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: A database provider, external SDK, resilience, discovery, or serialization adapter MUST live in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: A database provider, an external SDK, and resilience, discovery, and serialization adapters all change with their technology. Keeping them in Infrastructure keeps each provider change inside one layer, apart from the read boundary the ownership table assigns to Application.

provisions.heading: Keep Test Dependencies in Test Projects
provisions.evidence: No production project manifest references an assertion, substitution, host, container, or architecture-test package; where replaced, the project documentation names the shipped helper and its reason.
provisions.statement: Keep assertion, substitution, host, container, and architecture-test packages inside test projects.
provisions.rationale: Assertion, substitution, host, container, and architecture-test packages exist to verify code, not to run it. Referenced by a production project, a test package ships to production with its own dependencies and advisories. Keeping them inside test projects keeps the shipped graph free of verification weight.

provisions.heading: Keep the Approved Web UI Dependency Boundary
provisions.evidence: Each React frontend manifest takes UI packages only from `uiBaseline`, and each Svelte one only from `uiBaselineSvelte`, in `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A React web frontend MUST take its UI packages from the `uiBaseline` in `litespec.manifest.yaml`, and a Svelte web frontend from `uiBaselineSvelte`.
provisions.rationale: A fixed UI baseline keeps every screen drawing from the same design system, styling, base components, icons, and utilities. Taking UI packages only from `uiBaseline` for React and `uiBaselineSvelte` for Svelte keeps that set reviewed and versioned in one place. Each baseline pins the design system, styling, base components, icons, and the utility packages the installed source imports directly.

provisions.heading: Pin Every Dependency Version Centrally
provisions.evidence: Every version resolves through central management or the committed lockfile within the manifest major where one exists; no version sits inline in a module file.
provisions.statement: Every dependency version MUST resolve through central management or the committed lockfile, within the major `litespec.manifest.yaml` pins where it pins one.
provisions.rationale: An inline version in one module file is invisible to the file that is supposed to own it, so two modules drift to two versions of the same package. Central management or the committed lockfile resolves every version in one owned place. The manifest pins the major of each baseline package, so a consumer takes a patch without waiting for a LiteSpec release; it pins an exact version only where a check depends on exact output. The manifest belongs to the LiteSpec release rather than to the consumer, so a consumer's exact versions live beside its code, admitted by `litespec/workspace/dependencies#approve-new-packages-explicitly`.
