Settled by [decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major](decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major).
provisions.example: Claimwick's central version file holds Marten at 9.50.2 while the manifest pins `9.x`, so a patch lands without a LiteSpec release. Its receipt PDF library sits exact in the same file with a decision record, because the manifest names only the baseline stack.

provisions.heading: Align Business Names Across Layers
provisions.evidence: One business name for each module spans Domain, Application, endpoints, features, and documentation; where replaced, the project documentation names the project's own per-layer names.
provisions.statement: Use one business name for a module across Domain, Application, endpoints, features, and documentation.
provisions.rationale: One business name per module keeps every layer pointing at the same word. The Posts module maps to `Shop/Posts`, `features/posts`, and `.litespec/behavior/modules/posts` without translation. A second name in any layer reads as a second concept that does not exist.

provisions.heading: Anchor Aggregate-Owned Types on the Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Each aggregate-owned type name in `apps/api/src` begins with its aggregate root name, through nesting or prefix.
provisions.statement: An aggregate-owned type's qualified name MUST start with its aggregate root's full name.
provisions.rationale: Leading with the root name reveals the owner without folder context. The rule covers events, states, child entities, values, and discriminated unions. A type nested inside a declaring type inherits that type's prefix through its qualified name, so `PostState.Published` satisfies the rule while a flat `PostStatePublishedState` repeats the anchor twice.
provisions.example: `PostPublishedEvent` and `PostState.Published` both lead with `Post`. `PublishedState` declared at namespace level does not.

provisions.heading: Avoid Generic Type Names
provisions.evidence: Each type name in `apps/api/src` avoids the listed generic names where a narrower name exists; where replaced, the project documentation names the kept name and its reason.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: Avoid `Manager`, `Helper`, `Processor`, `Common`, `Utility`, `BaseService`, `DataService`, `MessageBus`, `Engine`, `Facade`, `Wrapper`, and `Factory` when a narrower name exists.
provisions.rationale: A generic name invites unrelated responsibility, because nothing in it excludes the next addition. A narrower name states what the type does and, by exclusion, what it does not. `Factory` is generic on a class and exact on a named static aggregate factory method, so the default names the class and not the method.

provisions.heading: Derive Boundary Names from the Ubiquitous Term
provisions.evidence: Each route segment and JSON field name derives from its current aggregate or ubiquitous term; where replaced, the project documentation names the project's own boundary naming.
provisions.statement: Derive route segments and JSON field names from the current aggregate or ubiquitous term.
provisions.rationale: Route segments and JSON field names are the contract clients read. Deriving them from the current aggregate or ubiquitous term, the Domain's shared word for the concept, keeps the contract speaking the Domain language. Renaming a Domain concept then renames its boundary names, so the contract and the language stay aligned.

provisions.heading: Group Event Handlers by the Fact They Handle
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` (level S) for an event handler declared outside the `On{Fact}` folder its event names.
provisions.statement: Each event handler MUST live in a folder named `On{Fact}`, the event name without its `Event` suffix, inside the `UseCases/` folder of the subscriber module, and be named `{Action}On{Fact}Handler`.
provisions.rationale: The folder answers "what happens when this fact is recorded?" with one listing: one folder holds every handler of that fact in that module. The subscriber is the module whose records the handler changes, or for a handler that changes nothing, the module that owns the fact. A folder named for the handler instead scatters one fact across as many folders as handlers.
provisions.example: `Lending/UseCases/OnLoanBorrowed/SendDueNoticeOnLoanBorrowedHandler` sends the due notice when a loan is borrowed.

provisions.heading: Keep Namespaces Aligned with Folders
provisions.evidence: Each namespace starts with its product name and follows the folders beneath the project root; where replaced, the project documentation names the project's own namespace root.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: Start a namespace with the product name and follow the folders beneath the project root.
provisions.rationale: Starting the namespace with the product name and following the folders beneath it puts each type exactly where its namespace says. Including `src` or `apps` couples the type name to a workspace layout decision. The project root is the directory holding the project file, so every folder above it stays outside the namespace.

provisions.heading: Name Asynchronous Operations Completely
provisions.evidence: Each asynchronous operation name reveals asynchrony, and each cancelable operation signature takes cancellation explicitly; read the public signatures in `apps/api/src`.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: An asynchronous operation MUST reveal its asynchrony in its name and accept cancellation explicitly when the operation is cancelable.
provisions.rationale: A caller decides from the signature whether to await and what to cancel. Naming the asynchrony and accepting cancellation explicitly put both answers in the signature. An operation is cancelable when it performs I/O or awaits; anything else has nothing to cancel.

provisions.heading: Name Exceptions by Failed Rule
provisions.evidence: Each exception name states its failed rule, with Domain rejections in `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception` form leading with the aggregate root.
provisions.statement: An exception name MUST state the rule that failed, using `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception` for a Domain rejection.
provisions.rationale: An exception name is the first diagnosis: it states which rule failed on which type. `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception` puts both in the name. `DomainType` is the aggregate root or an anchored owned type, so the name always starts with the aggregate root.

provisions.heading: Name Repository Variables After Their Interface
provisions.evidence: Each repository parameter, field, or local carries the name of its interface without the `I` prefix.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, job
provisions.statement: Each repository parameter, field or local MUST be named after its interface without the `I` prefix, ending in `Repository`.
provisions.rationale: A short plural name hides which aggregate the variable guards: `orders` could be a list, a query, or the repository, and each reader guesses. Naming the variable after its interface keeps one name per repository at every use site, so a reviewer reads the dependency from the name alone.
provisions.example: A parameter of type `IExpenseRepository` is named `expenseRepository`, and a field of type `ILoanRepository` is named `loanRepository`.

provisions.heading: Name Result Parts After Their Result
provisions.evidence: Each type nested in a use-case result carries the full result name as its prefix.
provisions.statement: Each type nested in a use-case result MUST be named after the result it belongs to, as `{UseCase}QueryResult{Part}` or `{UseCase}CommandResult{Part}`.
provisions.rationale: A result part named for its own shape instead of its result collides with every other use case shaping the same thing: two summaries named `PostSummary` answer different queries with different fields. Leading with the full result name keeps each part beside the result it belongs to in every listing, and keeps command coordination apart from query projection without opening the file.
provisions.example: `ListPostsQueryResultItem` belongs to `ListPostsQueryResult`, and `ReadLoanQueryResultHold` belongs to `ReadLoanQueryResult`.

provisions.heading: Use Architectural Suffixes
provisions.evidence: Each type name and each frontend file name carries the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table.
provisions.artifact: state-record, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, endpoint, job
provisions.statement: An architectural type MUST carry the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table.
provisions.example:
An event handler folder starts with `On` and names the business fact without the `Event` suffix: `OnPostPublished` holds `NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler` for `PostPublishedEvent` (`litespec/workspace/naming#group-event-handlers-by-the-fact-they-handle`). The `On` prefix already marks the handler, and folder names carry no technical suffix, so `OnPostPublishedEvent` is wrong. The event type keeps its `Event` suffix (`litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root`).

Application types keep their full suffix: `{UseCase}Result`, `{UseCase}Handler`, and `{UseCase}Validator` shorten away the command-or-query distinction the full name carries. A result part carries the full name of its result, as `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result` states, not a bare summary name like `PostSummary`. The full role suffix distinguishes command coordination from query projection without opening the file.

HTTP transport types keep their full suffix too: `{UseCase}Request` and `{UseCase}Response` shorten away the boundary marking. `Model` marks the type as passive boundary data rather than an operation or rich business object. Other project-owned, passive HTTP DTOs also name their concrete role and end in `Model`, such as `ListPostsResponseItemModel` or `PaginationModel`.

A polymorphic transport model mirrors a Domain discriminated union (`litespec/backend/api#mirror-a-domain-closed-set-as-a-transport-model-of-the-same-shape`). Its abstract base names the concept and each sealed case names its case, with both ending in `Model`: `FulfillmentOutcomeModel` and `ShippedFulfillmentOutcomeModel`.

The transport name drops the Domain union's aggregate prefix, such as `OrderFulfillmentOutcome`, while its discriminator string keeps the Domain union's stable case code unchanged.

provisions.heading: Use Current Language Features
provisions.evidence: Production code targets the pinned language version and uses its current constructs; read the toolchain pins and the language idioms in `apps/api/src`.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: Production code SHOULD target the pinned language version and use its current construct over an older equivalent.
provisions.rationale: A pinned language version gives every writer the same constructs. Using the current construct over its older equivalent keeps one idiom across the codebase instead of one per author. In the dotnet stack, collection expressions, pattern matching, and primary constructors express the same intent with less incidental code.

provisions.heading: Use Intent-Revealing Boolean Names
provisions.evidence: Each boolean property and method name in `apps/api/src` starts with `Is`, `Has`, `Can`, or a precise verb.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A boolean property or method SHOULD use `Is`, `Has`, `Can`, or a precise verb.
provisions.rationale: A boolean answers a yes-or-no question, so its name asks one. `Is`, `Has`, `Can`, or a precise verb make the question explicit: `HasLines` and `CanPublish` state a condition. `LinesPresent` and `CheckPublish` state neither a question nor an answer, so the caller reads the body to learn the polarity.

provisions.heading: Use Predictable Frontend Names
provisions.evidence: Each frontend folder uses kebab-case, each component file and export uses PascalCase, and each React hook file uses `use-{name}`.
provisions.statement: A frontend folder MUST use kebab-case, a component file and its export PascalCase, and a React hook file `use-{name}`.
provisions.rationale: Kebab-case folders, PascalCase components with matching exports, and `use-{name}` hooks give every file one predictable name. One mapping lets a reader move between the documentation tree and the source tree without translation, and lets an agent derive the file from the feature name.

provisions.heading: Declare Size and Application Stacks in Project Config
provisions.evidence: `.litespec/project.yaml` at the workspace root declares `size` and one stack for the backend and for each frontend.
provisions.statement: `.litespec/project.yaml` MUST declare `size` as `small` or `large` and one stack for the backend and for each frontend.
provisions.rationale: Size decides which record types and test projects apply: small or large selects the project's required-record set. Each stack decides which technology pages and checks apply to its application. Declaring both in `.litespec/project.yaml` lets tools and reviewers read the selection from one file. The [scope page](../core/scope.md) states the full selection.

provisions.heading: Keep Consumer Documentation at the Root
provisions.evidence: Every record path sits under the root `.litespec/` directory.
provisions.statement: Project records MUST live under the root `.litespec/` directory.
provisions.rationale: Project records describe the product, not the standard and not the code. Placing them inside the application tree makes them disappear when it is rewritten. The root `.litespec/` directory keeps records in a place that survives replacing the standard or rewriting the application.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated API Contracts in Packages
provisions.evidence: Generated OpenAPI types sit in `packages/api-types/` and the thin client in `packages/api-client/` once two frontends consume the API; with one frontend, that frontend keeps both outputs.
provisions.statement: Place generated OpenAPI types in `packages/api-types/` and a thin client in `packages/api-client/` when more than one frontend consumes the API.
provisions.rationale: Generated OpenAPI types and their thin client belong to every frontend that reads the API. With more than one consumer, `packages/api-types/` and `packages/api-client/` keep one copy each. A single frontend may own both locally until a second consumer appears.

provisions.heading: Keep Orientation Documents Separate from Canonical Records
provisions.evidence: Each `README.md` under `.litespec/` links to its record and restates no record content.
provisions.statement: A README under `.litespec/` MUST link to the record rather than restate its content.
provisions.rationale: A README orients; a record decides. A README that restates a decision becomes a second authored source that drifts from the record it summarizes, until the two disagree and neither is trusted. Linking to the record keeps one source with many pointers.

provisions.heading: Keep Production and Test Code Separate
provisions.evidence: Production files sit under `apps/api/src/` and test files under `apps/api/tests/`, with no test helper shipped beside production code.
provisions.statement: Production code MUST live under `apps/api/src/` and test code under `apps/api/tests/`.
provisions.rationale: Production code under `apps/api/src/` and test code under `apps/api/tests/` keep the two graphs apart by path. The split makes a test dependency reaching production code visible in the path itself, and keeps test helpers from shipping with the product.
provisions.example:
The backend tree is:

```text
apps/api/
  <backend project manifest>
  src/
  tests/
```

provisions.heading: Keep Runnable Applications Under Apps
provisions.evidence: Each directory under `apps/` runs on its own, and each directory under `packages/` is imported by an application.
provisions.statement: An independently runnable frontend, API, or deployed host MUST live under `apps/{name}/`.
provisions.rationale: Each root makes one promise: `apps/` runs, `packages/` is reused. A reusable package under `apps/` or deployable code under `packages/` inverts that promise, so neither location tells the reader what it holds. One home per kind keeps the promise readable.

provisions.heading: Keep the Generated Model Out of Source Control
provisions.evidence: No path under `.litespec/model/` is tracked in git; `git ls-files .model` prints nothing.
provisions.statement: The generated `.litespec/model/` folder MUST stay out of source control.
provisions.rationale: The model builder writes generated working files there, such as frontend facts, while it builds the model from records, code, routes, tests, and test runs. Tracking them would commit derived files beside their sources, and every commit would carry stale working files until somebody rebuilds. The folder is rebuilt rather than reviewed.

provisions.heading: Limit Shared TypeScript Packages
provisions.evidence: Each package under `packages/` is imported by at least two consumers, or carries generated output shared by design; read the imports in `apps/`.
provisions.statement: A shared TypeScript package MUST have at least two consumers or carry generated output shared by design.
provisions.rationale: A shared package with one consumer pays versioning, publishing, and cross-package edits for an audience of one. Requiring two consumers or generated output shared by design keeps sharing deliberate. The baseline permits shared configuration, generated API types, a thin client, and CSS theme tokens.

provisions.heading: Name Frontends by Audience
provisions.evidence: Each directory under `apps/` carries an audience name; where replaced, `frontends` in `.litespec/project.yaml` names the project's own frontend names.
provisions.statement: Name a frontend for its audience, such as `web`, `admin`, `portal`, or `docs`.
provisions.rationale: `apps/web` tells the reader who it serves; `apps/frontend` tells them only what it is built with. Naming each frontend for its audience keeps the folder meaningful when the technology changes. `frontend`, `client`, or `app` names the technology rather than the audience it serves.

provisions.heading: Use the Canonical Root Tree
provisions.evidence: The workspace tree matches the canonical tree in this section, with each record at its type's home under `.litespec/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer workspace MUST use the canonical root tree declared in this section.
provisions.example:
Consumer workspaces use this shape:

```text
{repo}/
  .config/
    dotnet-tools.json
  .litespec/
    project.yaml
    glossary.yaml
    intent/
      product.yaml
      goals/ problems/ constraints/ decisions/ research/ actors/ roles/ journeys/
      modules/
        {module}/
          module.yaml
          goals/ problems/ constraints/ decisions/ research/
          features/
            {feature}.yaml              requirements as entries
    behavior/
      rules/                            cross-module invariants only
      external-systems/                 create with the first product-level external system
      entry-points/
        {entry-point}/
          entry-point.yaml
          screens/
            {screen}.yaml
      modules/
        {module}/
          permissions.yaml
          use-cases/ rules/ reactions/ jobs/ notifications/ settings/ integration-events/ external-systems/
          {aggregate}/
            aggregate.yaml
            {use-case}.yaml             results and scenarios as entries
            events/ rules/
    implementation/
      decisions/ api/ guides/ operations/ patterns/ writing/ runbooks/
      operations/
        limits.yaml                     create with the first limit record
        secrets.json                    create with the first secret
        log/                            create with the first operations entry
      entry-points/
        {entry-point}/                  UI catalog, captures and patterns
      modules/
        {module}/
          decisions/ runbooks/
    governance/
      departures/                       create with the first departure record
      modules/
        {module}/
          departures/
    proof/                              generated registers, gate files and run outputs; no authored records
    model/                              generated; ignored
  apps/
    api/
      <backend project manifest>
      src/
      tests/
    {frontend}/
    apphost/                            when one host runs more than one application
  packages/
  AGENTS.md
  <toolchain pin file>
  package.json                          when a frontend or TypeScript package exists
  pnpm-lock.yaml                        when a frontend or TypeScript package exists
  pnpm-workspace.yaml                   when a frontend or TypeScript package exists
```

A backend stack binding names the files that realize the entries in angle brackets.

The example places neither the backend application nor a frontend application at the workspace root. Under `behavior/modules/`, each module folder holds one folder per aggregate in plural kebab-case form. A module with one aggregate of the module's own name may stay flat.

A record file lives at the home the [model page](../core/model.md) names for its type. An entry lives in its home file: requirements in their feature file, permissions in their module's permissions file, results and scenarios in their use case file, and rules and events in their aggregate file or type folder. Each entry point is one record in its own folder, with its screens beside it.
